In SE 10 a wall between the two peoples was proposed, and the council threw it out as needless, since the peoples were keeping apart well enough without one. The minute that rejects it runs to four lines. The fourth reads They do not come south. Five of the twelve initialled it, and the other seven did not sign against it. The library keeps that minute under glass. It is a small leaf, and a good deal of the age is written on it.

The law came north in the same fashion. In SE 8, at Seann Bhral, Eilidh nic Leòid, first of the circuit justices, ruled that land held by the Tuathaich under human title passed to the Crown, while the right to work it stayed with the holders and their heirs. The Leòid ruling is cited in nearly every land case of the age.

Seven summers later she carried it north herself.

The court at Ceann mhòr sat in the heat of an t-Iuchar, late in the month, in SE 15, with the windows open on the square and the flies drifting in. Eilidh nic Leòid had nineteen cases before her. Seventeen were Tuathaich suits over land, and in each the same kind of paper came up to the bench: a human title, brown at the folds, under the seal of a magistrate who had sailed west. She read every one to the end, and would not be hurried, while the suitors stood in their best coats and sweated. Then she took up her own ruling and read that too, aloud, so that the room should hear what the law was, and gave judgment.

In fifteen of the seventeen she found for the Crown. She was exact. The law she was exact about had been made for one people, and she had made it. Her rulings became the kingdom's first law-book.

Some years before, in SE 7, Walter Hale had asked leave to open schools in the north that taught in the humans' tongue. The council answered that the kingdom's schools taught in Ròdais and it had no others. The Moot's minute calls the answer "clear, at least." In the middle of the winter of SE 15 Agnes Pike opened such a school at Doire ghlas anyway, with Moot money and without leave, and within ten years there were nine. The council never licensed them and never shut them. For most of the age that was the kingdom's way with the north: it forbade little there, and helped with less.

V. Of the Mountain, the Guilds and the Fair

By SE 11 the mine was yielding as much as it had under the humans, and then more. The work was the same work. Only the owners had changed.

The Crown granted the Sloc Mòr, the great shaft at Achadh dhomhain, to Uisdean mac Ùisdein of Cathair mhòr, whose house had held an overseer's post under the humans. The Crown took a fifth. Those were the humans' terms with the names changed. The council would not end the day-and-night working the humans had ordered, and so the mountain was still given no season of rest. The custodians entered a protest, and then went down and blessed the shafts. The hewers had a saying for it:

Cha d' fhuair a' bheinn fois a-riamh, is cha d' fhuair sinne. The mountain never got its rest, and neither did we.

Families from the hungry east came to the vein-towns for wages, and Muileann dhearg doubled in three years. The humans' railway was mended to the pithead, and in an Dàmhair of SE 12 the first ore train ran from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg, under the kingdom's name, on the humans' rails. At Muileann chrom the families who worked the little shunting engines were counted apart and lived apart, in rows beside the lines. For forty years the public buildings of the south went up in the Sloc Mòr's grey spoil-stone, sold under the Mac Ùisdein quarry-mark.

In SE 13 the apprentice-binding of the Holy Age was taken up again, and this time the charters said in so many words that it was for Ròdaich applicants. The Guild of Hewers came first, its oath sworn with a hand laid on a lump of ore, and the shipwrights, chandlers, lamp-makers and weavers came after. The Tuathaich boys already bound to Ròdaich masters were released from their indentures. Some went north. Most stayed on as day-labour, outside the guilds and beneath their wages. The rule kept them where the pay was worst.

Off Cathair gheal, ships that flew no flag began to raid the north-western coast, and some of their crews were men who had served the human administration. The Tuathaich towns suffered first, undefended. In SE 20, having asked twice and been sent nothing, the fishermen of Cathair gheal armed their own boats and drove the raiders out of the bay. The council then fined the town for bearing arms without a licence. The town paid.

On 16 an Dàmhair, SE 21, in the reddening of the year, the fair at Muileann òg was established, and it grew to be the greatest recurring gathering on the island. Its first toll-mistress, Oighrig nic Mhathain, set down its rules, and one of them was this: that Tuathaich goods be sold only through Ròdaich factors. They are still read aloud when each fair opens. Two years after, the Còmhrag began at Ceann leathan, a yearly melee that the south called an old custom of arms, and where, more and more, men who had nowhere else to spend their anger spent it. Two men died in the first one that anyone remembers.

On 7 an t-Ògmhios, SE 24, in the green of early summer, there was a cluster of births among the shunting families, the generation called Splatter and Dodge's. Seachran and Brean were among them. They would grow up to be the closest allies of a man not yet born.

VI. Of the Library at Muileann chaol

On 1 an Cèitean, SE 16, which was Bealltainn, the fires were lit on the hills round Muileann chaol to bring the summer in, and their smoke hung over the town all day. Ailean mac Iain spent that day in a cellar.

He had been named first keeper of the new library, and had brought the council's minute-books with him, and the remains of the humans' tithe ledgers in their boxes. Now the townsmen led him down a stair to the custodians' rolls, which had lain there since the Severance war, stacked on planks above a wet floor, the lowest gone as soft as bread. He untied one and read three lines by the light from the stair. Then he sent for lamps, and a table, and a boy to fetch and carry.

He spent years having them read, and as they were read he had every date in them turned into the civil calendar, the day and month the humans had brought, and set in the years of its age as the copyists' table of the ages divided them. He had come to dislike the count of the Diosal, which ran backwards into the thousands for everything older than the sunwise turn, and he said that a people should not have to name every year of its life after the day its kin went away. Before the year was out, a chur san Leabharlann, to put it in the Library, meant to make a thing settled and beyond dispute. A clerk once used it in his hearing.

"The library settles nothing," said Ailean Leabhar, for so they called him by then. "It only keeps."

The phrase outlived him all the same. The library now keeps the fullest surviving record of everything told in this book, and the reader should bear that in mind.

In SE 18, as the nights drew in, an office was made to keep the kingdom's record, and from its books this book is drawn. The first royal chronicler, Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, a council clerk, kept her record at Muileann chaol and would not keep it at the capital. She wrote in her first entry that a record kept beside the throne is kept for the throne. The same order that made her office bade the kingdom's records count their years as Ailean Leabhar counted them, each age from its own first event, and Gormshuil headed her first year the eighteenth of the Severance Era. It was the first year so written in the kingdom's own record, and the years of the Diosal went into the old books. She sent clerks to every shire to copy parish books, grave-lists and harbour rolls. The south filled forty chests. The northern shires filled one, for few of the Tuathaich would talk to the clerks.

The five lighthouses of the humans were given Ròdaich keepers. At Baile chrom, on the Tuathaich coast, the keeper's warrant bade him report what he saw by land as well as by sea. In time he reported that the Grey Night sect kept its vigil in the lighthouse's own shadow. The council took no action.

The library also dug. At Làrach an Dùin its trenches turned up walls older than any Ròdaich building and no writing at all, and the finds were catalogued as belonging to the Old Ones, purpose unknown. At Làrach an Teampaill the houses of the Seann Spioradan asked it not to dig, and the keeper entered the ruin as measured and let be. The obelisk near Cnoc bheag bore signs that matched no script known on the island. In this age as in every age, the Seann-Dhaoine appear only in what they left, and in what the living will not do near it.

When Ailean Leabhar died in SE 40, Mòrag nic Coinnich became keeper. She began the practice, kept ever since, of writing beside each item where it came from. In SE 42 Gormshuil laid down the chronicle. Her last entry is a list of what the record did not hold: the northern towns' own accounts, the humans' treaties in their own tongue, and the Board's surveys. Her successor, Tormod mac Sheumais, called Tormod Pinn for the speed of his hand, copied that list into the front of his first book and added nothing to it. He struck nothing out, either.

VII. Of Brìghde and Eòghan, and the First Word of the Depletion

Niall died, and his daughter Brìghde was crowned on 31 an Lùnastal, SE 22, at summer's end, and no one contested it. It was a mortal succession in an aristocracy that stood very near the undying. It seemed nothing strange then. Gormshuil wrote that the succession came mar a thàinig Niall, and that is the only idiom she let into the chronicle in all her years.

On 12 am Màrt, SE 26, in the raw end of winter, the survey reports first began to say, very quietly, that the vein's yield was falling.

Iain mac Ruairidh of the Mine Board, whom the hewers called Iain Mapa, had spent long months crawling the faces of the Sloc Mòr with a lamp and a chain, and he knew what he had found before he had finished finding it. The vein was thinning to the east and to the south, and it was thinning in a way that did not argue.

He carried his survey to the Board himself, rolled and tied, and laid it on the table in front of three men who did not unroll it while he was in the room.

"It will be considered," said the one in the middle.

"I should like a receipt," said Iain Mapa.

The clerk looked at him as though he had asked for a kiss. But he wrote one, and signed it, and Iain Mapa folded it into his pocket-book and went home. The survey was filed and never circulated. Soon after, he was sent to the silver works at Muileann chiar.

The next year the Board moved its clerks to Cathair mhòr and made a rule that its surveys were to be kept there and not sent to the library. The state did nothing for years. The library could not know what it was never sent. It knows now, and it counts those years as part of the Depletion.

Brìghde's reign ended young, and no cause was ever made public. Her cousin Eòghan was crowned on 11 an Gearran, SE 28, amid the first true strife over a succession that the restored kingdom had known. The chronicler's entry gives the fact and nothing more, and no chronicler since has added to it. In an Dùbhlachd of that year the council's minutes recorded votes against a succession for the first time. They name the councillors and not their reasons. Two of them did not sit again.

On 9 an Cèitean, SE 29, in the green of an Cèitean, Dubhan was born, mortal, into the confinement the Severance had made, decades after the war that had shut the island to the people his line came from. No chronicle of that year mentions him, and none could have.

The kingdom went on round the Depletion it had not announced. In SE 33 the second census measured, for the first time, the gap between Ròdaich and Tuathaich living. The report was never made public. A census clerk, Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire, left a note among her papers saying that she had asked to see it and had been refused, and that note is the only mention of the report outside the council.

That year Walter Hale died, and the Moot chose Mary Coyle, a fisherman's widow, the first woman in its chair. The Còmhrag grew bloodier. In SE 36 six fighters died, and the custodians asked for it to end. The fair-wardens of Ceann leathan, whose town lived off the crowds, refused.

On the first day of an t-Iuchar in SE 39 a gallery gave way under Muileann dhearg, in the reopened Cill ghlas district, along a line the surveyors had marked as sound. Thirty-one hewers died. It was small beside the Rending. It was the same fault. New rules for digging followed. They were written for Ròdaich workers, and near the Tuathaich country they were kept loosely, and by intent. At the pits round Àth leathan, where Ròdaich overseers worked Tuathaich hands, the timbering rules were posted on the pit-head door and never paid for. The overseers' books show the timber ordered and never delivered. Àth leathan will come into this book again.

VIII. Of the Search for a Second Vein

After Muileann dhearg the Guild of Hewers bound sixty apprentices to fill its rolls, and not one of them was Tuathaich. On Samhain eve of SE 40 fire ran through the fair at Muileann òg. Its court sat in a field the next morning, and the fair went on, and Oighrig nic Mhathain died of her burns. That winter the Rail Board refused to carry the Moot's goods, and the north's wool went south by cart, a week on the road. The north calls that way the Carters' Road. The south has no name for it.

In the dark of the year's end in SE 41 the Moot began a register of Tuathaich hewers killed or maimed in the western pits, since no Ròdaich book counted them. It has been kept ever since, and never sent south. In those years Dubhan was a child in the north, watching a caste that did not age hold every true advantage on an island to whose edge his own forebears had been pushed. The obsidian was never his to inherit.

The age had its good keepers too. When the dry years came back to Achadh shean in SE 43, the council sent grain up the ore line out of the Sloc Mòr's share, and nobody in the shire died of hunger. The maor had twelve wells dug to the rock, and four of them are still drawn from.

Of Ciorstaidh nic Artair it is told at Tobar dhearg that her father, the keeper of the light there, drowned going out to a boat on the reef, and that she went out after him and brought the boat's crew in. She took his warrant, and set a belled post on the reef. While she kept the light, no boat went aground there.

On 12 an t-Samhain, SE 46, when the leaves were down, the druid schools, Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, whom many still call Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, woke out of their long sleep. Their founding question, why the vein answers some hands and not others, mattered again now that the vein was running short. Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain lectured in Flidais's sacred wood near Muileann chiar, and at Caol shean her students copied the census line on the obsidian-touched and argued over it in the open, which the Rite did not do. They set the old pillars and the obelisk side by side and found signs in common, and no meaning. Seonaid wrote that the Old Ones had been here and had said so, and that nobody living could hear them.

In SE 50 Alasdair mac Ùisdein, grandson of the first holder of the Sloc Mòr, borrowed against his house's share to go looking for a second vein. The Board lent its surveyors and the Crown lent its name. Seonaid wrote to the Board that the search asked the wrong question. Her school had always asked why the vein answered some hands; nobody had asked why there was only one vein. The Board filed the letter.

The search failed. Forty-one shafts went down between the hills above Dùn dhearg and the moors south of Baile ruadh, and none of them struck the vein. Afterwards Mòrag nic Coinnich found in the library a list from the Holy Age that named those same hills as searched and barren. The kingdom had repeated a failure that its own library could have warned it of, had anyone thought to ask. The house of Mac Ùisdein paid part of Dùn dhearg's damages and sold half its share back to the Crown. The dry shafts at Baile ruadh were left open to the sky, and sheep fell into them, and one child, before the shire fenced them at its own cost.

In SE 55 Mary Coyle laid down the chair, and Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan came after her, the first speaker born after the Severance. He had taught young Tuathaich to bind books when the southern guilds would not take them. That winter the fair gave one day to northern goods. They were still sold through factors, but under the makers' own marks, and it was the first time a Tuathaich name had been written on anything sold there. The first such mark was the Doire ghlas weavers' grey twill, with a white thread at the selvedge. Within the year the weavers of Baile chiar were weaving a white thread into theirs.

On 11 am Màrt, SE 56, the Depletion could no longer be denied.

Catrìona nic Neacail, the surveyor-general, had drawn the last untouched sections of the vein, and they were smaller than anyone wished to admit. When the drawing was finished it fitted on one sheet. Because a sheet so small wanted explaining, she went down into the Board's files at Cathair mhòr to learn how long the thinning had been going on.

It took her the best part of a week, by a smoking lamp. Near the bottom of a press she found a survey of the faces of the Sloc Mòr, rolled and tied, in a hand she did not know. It showed the vein thinning to the east and the south, and it was thirty years old.

She published her map. She sent the library a copy of Iain Mapa's survey, with a note of the day the Board had received it, and within the year she resigned. Iain Mapa died at Muileann chiar the next spring. His own copy of the survey was found among his papers with the Board's receipt pinned to it. He had kept the proof that he told them.

Muileann dhearg lost a third of its households. Its Fèidh hall was shut, and its bell was sold to Caol shean, where it still rings the students in to their lectures.

IX. Of Mairead and the Failing of the Ore

Mairead was crowned on 29 an Dàmhair, SE 58, in the fall of the leaf. Eòghan's reign had ended in the decade the Depletion came into the open, and she was heir to a kingdom whose founding wealth was plainly failing. That year the Guild of Hewers bound no apprentices, for the first time since its charter.

The north began building things that did not hang on the mountain. In SE 59 wool mills went up at Doire ghlas with Moot money. The Rail Board refused to carry their cloth, until the circuit justice at Seann Bhral, Ruairidh mac Phàdraig, ruled that the Board was a carrier of the Crown and must carry for anyone who paid. It was the first ruling the Moot ever won in a Ròdaich court. The Board appealed, and the council let the appeal lapse without a reason given.

In SE 60 the Crown bought the last of the house of Mac Ùisdein's working shafts, and from then on the Board worked the vein in the Crown's name alone.

On 1 an t-Iuchar, SE 61, Dubhan began his experiments, trying to make a fuel to stand in for the ore out of what the mines threw away. They all failed, and the record of those years scarcely troubles to name them. In that same month the lowest galleries of the Sloc Mòr were let flood, because the pumps cost more to run than the ore beneath them was worth. The Board's minute calls it a pause.

The chronicle of those years is full of small alarms. Panthers came across the south-west, beasts named in the Holy Age lists and not seen in living memory, and the old list named the year after them as a hungry one. At Muileann chrom the yard families stopped the ore trains for three days over cut wages; the Board settled on the fourth day and dismissed eleven men on the fifth. Then the harvest after the panthers came in good, and Tormod Pinn drew a line through his own note of the year before. This book has always liked him for it.

In the autumn of SE 64 the third census published its figures openly, the first census in the kingdom's history to do so. It was a small reform, and nothing in the frame of the kingdom moved because of it.

A month later the figures were read at Caol mhòr. Daniel Frayne sat in the Moot's chair with his hands flat on the table, the way he sat when he meant to keep them still. The clerk read the columns in a flat voice. In every column the census clerks had chosen to take, the northern towns stood at about half the Ròdaich measure. Nobody in the room was surprised. They had simply never heard it read aloud from the kingdom's own paper.

When the clerk had done, there was a long quiet. Then Daniel Frayne drew the minute-book towards him and wrote two words, and the words are the whole of the minute: Now written.

The census carried a line for the obsidian-touched, as the first one had, giving a number and nothing else. Tormod Pinn copied it into the chronicle without comment, as Gormshuil had done before him.

Tormod Pinn died at his desk in SE 65 and Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh became royal chronicler. She was the first to add, at the foot of each year, a note of what the record could not learn. Her first concerned the northern shires. The census clerks there had been told the figures and had not counted them, and the figures they were told were the Moot's. So the kingdom's first honest census was honest in the north because the Moot had supplied the numbers.

Mòrag nic Coinnich now called the shires' record-chests in to Muileann chaol. At Seann Tarr the shire keeper burned his chest in the yard sooner than send it, saying that the shire's record belonged in the shire, and that chest is lost. In SE 67 the library doubled its holdings, and from then on the history of Rodos was kept in one place instead of many.

No Tuathaich record was called in. The Moot's minute-books, the schools' registers and the vigil-books of Baile chrom stayed in the north in private keeping. The new wing was built of Sloc Mòr stone. The shires' chests filled three floors, and the fourth was left empty for what had not been sent. It is empty still, or near enough.

In the west the Board was drawing back. In SE 68 it closed the branch line to Àth leathan, citing the falling yield of the western pits. The Tuathaich hewers there kept working under their own pit captains and paid the Crown's fifth by the Leòid ruling, and the Board took the payments and entered them as arrears. At Cnoc thais the pits passed to their hewers in the same way. The south did not notice; it wanted nothing in the western hills any longer.

In SE 70 Raghnall mac Mhuirich became keeper of the library. The price of ore-fuel at the fair doubled, and at Cnoc fhiadhaich households were found picking ore off the spoil-heaps to burn. The Board posted watchmen from the town, who saw nothing.

X. Of the Eve of Dubhan

The summer of SE 71 came in dry and dear. The poorer streets of the capital were darker than they had been since the humans first lit them, the Guild of Hewers bound no apprentices, and the fair's court could not hold its price. So far as the kingdom's own record knew, its seventy-first year held nothing larger than a watch set on the spoil-heaps, whose watchmen saw nothing.

In the north Dubhan was at his work still, as he had been for ten years, boiling and burning what the pits threw away. Nobody in the capital was watching him, and nobody in the Library knew his name. One night near midsummer, the tellers of the north say, he banked his fire and slept beside it, as he had on a hundred nights before, and did not know that the morning would open a new count of the island's years, which no one would begin to keep for fourteen years yet.

Here the Fifth Book ends, on the eve of dubhan. The Library closes the Age of the Kingdom on that night and not an hour after it, and the Severance Era with it. The Sixth Book begins in the morning.

The Sixth Book: An Aois Dhubhain, the Age of Dubhan

DE 1 – 27

Bho latha a' chiad dubhain cunntar na bliadhnaichean às ùr. From the day of the first dubhan the years shall be counted anew.

— the council's proclamation of the Dubhan Era, 5 an Cèitean, DE 15

I. Of Dubhan's Fire

On 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1, about midsummer, the first working dubhan was made, and from that morning the island counts the years of its sixth age, the Dubhan Era, though nobody counted them so for fourteen years. It was crude, and it burned. Nobody yet traded in it; for the while it was one man's answer to a crisis that the caste in power had still not faced. At the foot of that year Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh wrote that a fuel made without the vein was reported from the north, and that she had not seen it. That is the first mention of dubhan in the royal record, and she spelled the word three ways in two lines.

In the capital the poorer streets were left dark to save ore. By DE 3 ore was sold at the fair only by the sack, and at last only by the lump, for altars.

Cathal was crowned on 1 an Lùnastal, DE 3, the feast of Lùnastal, by Macha's rite. Mairead's reign had ended while Dubhan's experiments still failed more often than they worked, and Cathal did not yet know how near his kingdom's answer lay. The new dies at the mint still pressed the obsidian ink into the seal.

The fuel came south within three years. In DE 4 a company of shipmasters set up a dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast, the first outside the north, and how they came by the making of it they never told. The high custodian wrote to the houses of the Rite that the new fuel was not forbidden, since it was not ore, and not blessed, since it was not ore. It sold its first year's making to the south-coast boats and the capital's lamp-houses, and the dark streets were the first to be lit again.

In DE 6 the five coastal beacons, which had burned obsidian-lit flame for more than a century, were the first works of the kingdom to be turned over to dubhan by decree.

Ciorstaidh nic Artair was grey by then, but nobody else was let carry the lantern. Inside its thick glass the flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg burned with the dark, coloured edge that only obsidian gives. She carried it into the Rite's house at Seann Skell in the late spring, down the hall between the custodians of four shires, who stood in their rows and did not speak. Her boots were loud on the flags.

At Brìde's altar she set the lantern down and opened its little door. The flame leaned towards the air, and steadied. Nobody told her to go, so she stayed, and so did they, while the last of the ore burned down. It took longer than anyone had thought. When the flame shrank to a blue bead and then to nothing, a thread of smoke went up and hung under the roof, and one of the custodians let out a breath as if he had been holding it the whole while.

The south coast has a song of that day in more than one form. This is the shortest:

Dh'fhalbh an lasair às an tùr, tha solas ann, ach chan ann leinn. The flame has gone out of the tower; there is a light there, but it is not ours.

At Baile chrom, on the Tuathaich coast, the change was made by Tuathaich fitters from Caol mhòr, because the Lighthouse Board had none of its own to send so far. The keeper's report names none of them.

After that the change came to everything, and it came fast. On 1 an Cèitean, DE 8, Bealltainn, the Rail Board ran its first dubhan engine on the ore line. It carried no ore. The drovers sold their oxen for lorries. On 25 an t-Ògmhios, DE 9, the fitters at Seann Skell set a lorry's engine under a closed carriage for the high custodian of the Rite, the first carriage on the island that needed no horse, and on 5 an t-Iuchar, DE 13, buses began to run out of the capital to Inis mhòr and Cathair mhòr. The roadside inns put in dubhan lamps, and centuries of oil and wick were gone within a decade. At An Leòmhann Buidhe the landlord kept one wick lamp burning over the door beside the new ones, and a wick lamp over an inn door is still called a Leòmhann.

In DE 8 Daniel Frayne died, and the Moot chose Martha Greaves of Doire ghlas, a mill manager. His old pupils rebound the Moot's minute-books from the first meeting onward. The Moot's minute says that a second set was made and hidden elsewhere. The library notes this and has not gone looking.

In DE 10 the last working face under Muileann dhearg was closed. Its families were moved to the Hewers' Row at Seann Toll, and most of them went to work on the dubhan tanks at the river landing. Muileann dhearg was left with its chapel, its graves and a caretaker.

By DE 11 dubhan meant the fuel and no longer the man, years before the trade built on it was whole. A letter of the Fèidh school at Caol shean coined dubhan-tùsail for a first attempt that looks like a dead end until it turns out to be the road. On 30 an Cèitean, DE 12, the Guild of Hewers dissolved itself. Its rolls, its oath-stone of ore and its sick-roll went to the library. Its last master, Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, wrote that the guild had outlived the mountain's patience.

By DE 13 the markets, the army's supply lines and the shipping were all going over to the new fuel. The obsidian caste watched its own source of power fail and did not object. The house of Mac Ùisdein sold the last of its share in the spoil and put its money into dubhan shipping at Ros dhomhain, the only family of the vein that moved before the vein failed it.

In DE 14 the fitters of dubhan engines were chartered as a guild at Seann Skell. Like every guild before it, its rolls were open to Ròdaich only, and the Tuathaich fitters were let go. They went home and fitted engines without a guild. That winter the Moot voted to take up the new fuel, and the delegates of the western pit towns got up and walked out. When the northern depots opened, Martha Greaves wrote in the minute that the north now bought its fire from the south, and she did not say whether that was good.

On 5 an Cèitean, DE 15, the coinage was pegged to the making of dubhan in place of the obsidian reserves, which was a quiet way of owning which of the two now ran the kingdom. At the same sitting the council proclaimed that the Age of the Kingdom had ended with the first working dubhan, and that the kingdom's years were counted anew from that day. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh re-headed fourteen years of her chronicle, and wrote at the foot of the page that she had never before had to move a year she was living in. The obsidian ink was left out of the seal, and the seal was plain. Fearchar Bonn's first dies went to the library, where they lie beside the Hewers' oath-stone. The high custodian protested that a plain seal showed the vein was no longer held sacred. The council answered that the kingdom had never said it did. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh copied both letters into the chronicle. It is one of the few places in the whole record where the kingdom said plainly what it was.

The north has a rhyme from those years, heard there in both tongues. This is its Ròdais form:

Dubh an gual, 's dubh an dubhan, ach cò leis an teine? Black the coal, and black the dubhan; but whose is the fire?

II. Of the Holdouts of the Western Hills

In the spring of DE 16 the western pit towns met at Muileann àrsaidh, apart from the Moot, and agreed to go on working their seams and to sell their coal to any household in the north that would buy it. Àth naomh, with only a few old shafts to its name, joined them, saying it would rather be cold with its neighbours than warm alone. So a knot of northern towns refused to fold themselves into the new trade. They kept to the last workable coal seams sooner than hang their fires on one man's fuel. They were Àth leathan, Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg, and their spokeswoman was Ruth Calder, a pit captain's daughter from Àth leathan. The Moot neither joined nor condemned them. At Cnoc thais Tom Varley opened again two shafts that had lain abandoned since the humans' time. The coal was poor. It was theirs, and it kept the town warm.

In DE 17 Ellen Marsh, a schoolteacher of Doire ghlas, finished eleven books of Tuathaich accounts of the Severance and the settling, taken down from the old people of the north. She asked Leabharlann Muileann chaol, formally, to keep the Tuathaich tellings beside the Ròdaich record. The request was tabled, and it lies on the table yet. Raghnall mac Mhuirich replied that it awaited the council's view on the standing of spoken witness. The council has never given one. Ellen Marsh wrote back that spoken witness had been good enough for the census clerks when they took the Moot's figures. Her letter is filed with the request. It is short, and nobody has answered it.

The holdout pits undersold dubhan across the north, and the Moot's own mills bought their coal. In DE 18 the Board's northern revenue fell by a quarter, the first fall since the Severance, and its report named the western pits as the cause and the Leòid ruling as the cure. Eighty years after Eilidh nic Leòid gave it, her ruling was put to the use the north had always feared. The Board declared the western seams Crown property, holding that the right to work them had lapsed when the holders stopped paying the fifth. The holders answered that they had stopped paying when the Board stopped carrying the coal. Both were true. The pits were ordered shut.

A company of enforcers was posted to Seann Skell in the west, which is another town from the Rite's Seann Skell in the south. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh noted that it was the first armed company the kingdom had sent toward the north since the Severance. Martha Greaves wrote that the western towns would not shut their pits because of a letter, and asked for a year while the Moot talked with them. Her letter was received and filed.

In the autumn of DE 19 the first skirmishes began. Each was too small to name and none was written down, and together they ran straight into open war. At the foot of that year Beathag wrote that clashes were reported in the west, and that she had asked for the Board's reports of them. They were not given. At Muileann àrsaidh the pit-heads were walled and the road from the south was dug across. On 25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 19, which was Christmas Day, Ruth Calder wrote to the council for the western towns and offered the Crown's fifth in coal, if the Board would carry it and let the pits work until the seams were spent. The letter reached the library. No answer to it did.

In DE 20, in the depth of winter, the Moot resolved by nine votes that it was no party to the quarrel and would feed anyone who came to its towns hungry. That summer it filled its granaries at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas beyond the usual. The minute gives no reason. It needed none.

In an Lùnastal Beathag laid down the office, and her clerk Sìleas nic Rath became royal chronicler. It is her record of the war that the library would later seal. In an Dàmhair came the order to mobilise. Regiments that had not been called out since the Severance were formed again and armed again, openly, months before anyone in power would admit that a war was coming. Command went to Somhairle mac Lachlainn, who had risen among the Board's enforcers. The rolls of the Severance companies were brought out of the council's chests to name the new regiments, and the old names were read aloud before new men. The list had been kept for nearly ninety years. Now it was used.

On 25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 20, Christmas Day again, Martha Greaves came to Cathair dhearg with the Moot's petition.

She had kept the feast on the road, in a cold carriage, and she came into the capital in the grey forenoon with the frost still white on the bridge. The Ròdaich keep no feast that day, and the council was sitting. She waited on a bench in a passage for most of an hour, the petition on her knee. Then a clerk said her name, in the Ròdais way, so that for a moment she did not know it for hers.

She was the first speaker of the Moot ever to walk into the council chamber. It was smaller than she had thought, and warm with a dubhan stove. Twelve faces turned to her. She read the petition standing. It asked that the western pits be let alone to work out their seams, which would be spent within a few years in any case. She read it to the end without hurrying, and laid it on the table.

"Received," said the clerk, and wrote.

It was filed. That winter the Rail Board carried arms and dubhan west to Seann Bhral, and the yard at Muileann chrom worked on the trains day and night.

III. Of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War

What is told here of the war comes from the open record, the towns' reports and the Tuathaich tellings; the rest is sealed.

Late in am Faoilleach of DE 21 the hewers of the five towns came together at Àth leathan, where the road from the south goes up into the hills. In the north they tell it like this. It was bitter weather, with a thin snow blowing that would not lie, and the men and women came in by the hill paths with their pit-lamps lit at noon, the sky was so dark. They slept in the pit-sheds, and in the byres with the cattle for the warmth. Ruth Calder went from fire to fire with a list, asking who was here, and who was coming. The Board's lists name her among them, and Tom Varley too.

From Cathair dhearg the regiments marched west, and their carts and lorries ran on dubhan.

The Battle of Àth leathan was fought on 11 an Giblean, DE 21, in the spring, the first great battle of An Cogadh Fada. The state, already leaning on Dubhan's fuel to prop its fading power, moved against the holdouts with its own hand. The open record counts the kingdom's dead and not the holdouts'. The Tuathaich tellings put theirs in the hundreds. Ruth Calder's name does not appear in the open record after that day. Whether she fell there, no teller in the north will say for certain. Her name simply stops.

The holdouts gave up the southern pits and fell back into the hills round Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais. The pits of Àth leathan were flooded on the Board's order, and the field was left unploughed. The seventh regiment was raised on the west coast to hold the road behind the army. Before the month was out a wartime tithe was laid on every sale of dubhan in the kingdom, for the war's sake. It was never lifted. Fleets were raised and sent round the western cape to close the Tuathaich ports of the north-west to every boat but the fishing boats, and to search those.

In an t-Ògmhios the regiments invested Muileann àrsaidh. The town held out for weeks on stored coal and potatoes, and its pit-heads were taken one at a time. Sìleas nic Rath's open record gives the day it fell and nothing more. The army's dubhan was served before any other use, and the capital's poorer streets went dark again, as they had been before the fuel came.

The families of the western pits came into Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas with what they could carry. The Moot fed them from its own stores, as it had resolved to. The council sent nothing and forbade nothing. The Moot's minute records the families' names, and it is among the few Tuathaich records of the war that the library does not hold. Agnes Pike's old school at Doire ghlas was given over to them, and Ellen Marsh, who taught there, took down their accounts. This book would give a good deal to read them.

In an Lùnastal Cnoc thais was taken, after the regiments cut the road to its pits, and Tom Varley's two shafts were fired and sealed. The open record gives the number of holdouts taken and not the number who went on into the hills. Some went on past the hills and out onto the windy coast, beyond the shire lines, and the regiments did not follow them there. With the fleets away in the north-west, raiders out of the east took two salt-boats off Àth bheag and burned a third.

Through the autumn the kingdom went on raising regiments, as if it looked for a longer war. The fourth regiment was quartered at Ceann mhòr in the old human magistrate's house, and the Moot's protest was received.

In an Dùbhlachd the regiments came to Baile chrom on the night of the vigil.

The corporal at the head of the file had come up the coast road expecting shutters and dogs and shouting. There was nothing. Not a lamp showed in any window. No dog barked. The only sound was the sea on the stones and his own men's boots, and even they began to tread softer without being told.

He tried the first door. It was unlatched. Inside, by the grey of the window, a man and a woman and three children sat round a cold hearth with their hands in their laps. None of them spoke. He asked them, in Ròdais and then in the humans' tongue, who else was in the house, and whether there were arms. The man only shook his head, once, slowly, as a man does at a child who has asked a foolish thing in church.

It was the same in the next house, and the next, until the small hours. He wrote in the end that the whole town had been dark and silent, and that it had been searched and nothing found. The regiments' return for that month says as much, and no more.

That month Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg opened their roads without a siege. Their pits were flooded. The open record names no holdouts taken at either.

Late in an Dàmhair of the next year a column of holdouts, several hundred strong, came out of the western hills, and through an t-Samhain it moved south-east through the middle of the island toward the capital. The reason lies in the sealed archive. The Tuathaich tellings give its leader the name Owen Barrow; the open record gives him none. On 6 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, the column passed Muileann òg and made camp on the fields by Muileann ghlas, a day's walk from Cathair dhearg, and the first and third regiments were brought down the fair road to meet it. The booths of the fair-ground were cleared for their camp, and the fair court's books for that year end without a closing entry.

The Battle of Muileann ghlas was fought on 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, four days after, in the short grey days before midwinter. It was the second great battle of the war, and the last. The holdouts were broken in two summers' campaigning. They were the children of humans once pushed to the island's edge, and now they were pushed back again, and the fuel that drove the lorries against them had been made by one of their own. The open record lists the first and third regiments on the field and does not count the column's dead. When word reached the hills, the holdouts still there came down to the seventh regiment's posts on the Àth leathan road. They were disarmed and sent home, and the open record counts their weapons.

So An Cogadh Fada ended on 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, twenty months after it began, and it has been called the Long War all the same. Nine regiments and four fleets were raised in it. All are under arms yet, and each is named for the town where it is stationed.

Before the year was out the Tuathaich had a new saying. Chaidh am fadachadh, they got long-warred, was said first of the defeat in the west, and then of any defeat that comes after holding out too long. It is said as a joke, and the people who say it do not laugh.

IV. Of the Peace, and of the Present Year

The regiments were not stood down. The council kept each at the town where it had been raised and paid them out of the wartime tithe. With the last organised resistance gone, Dubhan's fuel became, in all but law, compulsory across the whole island. The last western seams were flooded and capped with concrete, and after that no coal was dug on Rodos outside the Board's own works. The holdouts taken at Muileann ghlas were marched north as far as the boundary stones, the stones set in SE 1 that nobody had ever been paid to move. The Moot's register gave their names a column of their own. Somhairle mac Lachlainn was given a seat on the council, the first soldier to sit there since the captains of the Severance war.

In DE 23 the kingdom raised a stone at Cathair mhòr, beside the Mac Ùisdein market cross, with the names of the regiments' dead. On the field of Àth leathan the Tuathaich families built a cairn without leave. The seventh regiment's patrols have let it stand, and it grows by a stone or two every time they pass. At Muileann ghlas the field was sown again, and for years its farmer turned up weapons in the furrows and handed them to the first regiment, which keeps a list.

On 14 am Faoilleach, DE 24, the library's whole record of the Long War was sealed from the public for fifty years. It is the only sealed archive in the kingdom's history. What is still open for the war years is Sìleas nic Rath's list of places, the regiments present, and the counts she was allowed to give. Her full record went into the sealed room with everything else. Ailean Leabhar said once that the library settles nothing and only keeps. He never thought it would one day keep a thing it was not let read.

The war left its accounts. The Treasury carried the wartime tithe forward as a standing line under the regiments' pay, and no council minute records a decision to keep it. The fuel-fitters took the contract for the regiments' engines and doubled their rolls, and every new fitter was Ròdaich.

In an t-Ògmhios of DE 25 Anna nic Phàil, councillor for Cathair dhomhain, brought the Moot's petition before the council: that the Tuathaich towns be paid for what they had lost in the war. She spoke for it once. On 10 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25, the proposal was raised in the capital and quietly let die without a vote. The Moot's minute on it is one line long: Allowed to die. Martha Greaves laid down the chair that year, and the Moot chose Peter Hale, great-grandson of its first speaker. The fourth regiment left the magistrate's house at Ceann mhòr. The Moot asked that the house be given to the town. It was given to the maor.

By DE 26 the Tuathaich had one name for the tabled request and the dead motion together: seann-chunntas, an old reckoning that nobody in power will settle and nobody has struck out. Official Ròdaich usage has not taken up the word. This book uses it, since the record should hold the words of both peoples.

That year the mountain was shut, or nearly. The Board closed the upper galleries of the Sloc Mòr and kept one face open, in the Rite's custody, to cut ore for the altars. Twelve hewers were kept on to work it, the last of their trade on the island. On 10 an t-Sultain, DE 26, the last ore train ran to Cathair dhearg. The ore line has kept its name and carries dubhan, wool and soldiers. The second regiment set a guard at the library over the sealed archive, and Raghnall mac Mhuirich wrote to the council that the library had not asked for one. On the northern road, where the boundary stones stand, the sixth regiment keeps posts, and Tuathaich going south show a pass for the first time since the Severance. The council's minute calls the passes temporary. The reader will know by now what the kingdom's temporary measures tend to become.

The last year and this one have been like other years. Tuathaich wool was sold at Muileann òg on its northern day, through Ròdaich factors, as at the first fair. The Còmhrag was fought with staves and fists, and one man died. Ellen Marsh's eleven books have been copied by hand in the northern schools and are kept there; the library's catalogue lists the tabled request and not the books. The Moot met at Caol mhòr under Peter Hale, its minute-books unbroken since Walter Hale's wet afternoon, with no standing in Ròdaich law and no request for any. Every lamp and engine on the island, every ship and every lorry, runs on dubhan; the coinage is pegged to it, and the tithe is taken on every sale. The Treasury's roll for the year stood at 9,568 purses, two parts in three of it from the head-due. In the summer the Rite's twelve hewers cut the year's altar-ore. It filled four baskets, and the high custodian shared it among the houses by lot.

On 7 an t-Sultain, DE 27, as the summer went out, Dubhan himself, an old man now in his sixty-ninth year, won from the council at Cathair dhearg the right to sell dubhan off the island. He had written to the council for a year and sat before it three times. It is the first leave the kingdom has given for any good of Rodos to go beyond its waters since the Severance, and it is narrowly drawn. The Treasury sets each year's measure. The fuel is loaded only at Ros dhomhain, where a clerk of the Treasury takes the tithe on every barrel. The kingdom's depots and the Moot's are served first. The custodians of Òrd Bhrìde seal every hold, since nothing of the vein may be sold, and the Small-Burning Law is not touched by it. Dubhan has told neither the council nor the chronicler who his buyers are. The first tank-hull loaded under the charter went out past the western capes in the autumn, and at Seann Skell the priests of Manannan said the old prayer to keep the sea shut on the day she sailed. Dubhan goes out under that charter and no other.

On 22 an t-Samhain, DE 27, with the lamps lit by mid-afternoon at Muileann chaol, Sìleas nic Rath wrote at the foot of the year that the kingdom's record is whole in every part but two: the war, which is sealed, and the north, which was not asked.

So the account stands on 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27, at the turning of the year's shortest days. The coal is all but gone. The kingdom's trade runs on a name that once belonged to one man, and since the autumn a little of it has gone out past the western capes under his charter. The Ròdaich hold the capital and the sea. The Tuathaich hold the north, and their Church, and a grievance five years old, and a memory of the First Canoe that the people who twice defeated them still call folklore. The restored kingdom promised the island its own again. It kept the humans' tariff, their surveys, their rails and their terms for the mountain, and it kept the humans' children where the humans had put them. It kept faith as well with the drowned towns of the south, and its wells at Achadh shean still draw water.

Here the Sixth Book stops, at the present year, for the chronicle itself goes on. The age that follows has no name yet, because nobody can yet say what began it. It is left to the next chronicler, who will be handed the whole record and, with it, the things still missing from it: the war in its guarded room, which is to be opened fifty years from its sealing if the kingdom keeps its word; the fourth floor at Muileann chaol, built for what was not sent; the eleven books in the north; and the Moot's minutes with their hidden second set. The old reckoning is still owed. Whoever writes the next book should begin by asking for them.

The Annals of Rodos

Every remembered event of the six ages, in order, each on its day. 1590 events.

Age I · An Aois Àrsaidh the Ancient Age · the Vein Era, VE 1 – 9,926

20 am Faoilleach, VE 1
The crack in the stone
A mason splitting rock for a well breaks into a black, glassy vein, and it bleeds colour where it should give dust. Of all the tellings of the beginning on Rodos, this is the eldest.
17 an Giblean, VE 76 Tobar dhìreach
Three wells claim the crack
Tobar dhìreach, Tobar dhubh and Tobar òg each tell that the mason's well was theirs. Tobar dhìreach can show a capped shaft with a dark stain on its lip; the other two have only the telling. Between the three no chronicler has ever judged.
19 am Màrt, VE 151 Tobar dhìreach
The slab over the bleeding rock
The mason's people dig no further. They lay a flat stone over the broken vein, draw no water beside it, and cut their well again a stone's throw off. In this all the tellings agree.
14 an t-Ògmhios, VE 227 Abhainn uaine
The high snowfields shrink
Meltwater off the central mountains cuts the bed that Abhainn uaine follows still. On the gravel terraces of its lower reach lie hearth-stones at three heights, each left as the water rose to it.
16 an Cèitean, VE 303 Achadh dhìreach
The first hearths of the high valleys
Hearths are made at Achadh dhìreach, of pine and heather charcoal, with scrapers of grey flint and the split bones of red deer about them. There is no black glass in them: those who sat there had none of the ore, or would not burn it.
11 an Lùnastal, VE 378 Doire ghlas
The oak comes to the lowlands
The birch and pine of the cold years give way to oak and hazel, as the pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows. The grove that names the place stands on ground that was open heath when the vein was first broken.
22 an Lùnastal, VE 451
The bare north-west
The oak never reaches the north-western horn of the island. The gales off the north-western sea keep it bare, low heather and blanket bog behind the shore without a tree, as it is still. No hearth of that age has been found there.
13 an t-Iuchar, VE 506 Eilean dhubh
Eilean dhubh cut off
The rising sea floods the low neck of land that joined Eilean dhubh to the main island. The hearths of the neck lie drowned under the sand of the sound, and the deer of the island, cut off, grow smaller in the lifetimes after.
1 an t-Iuchar, VE 551 Eilean mhin
Hunters on Eilean mhin
Seal-hunters pitch camps on Eilean mhin, coming there by boat: the first sure sign that anyone on Rodos crossed open water of set purpose. The camps are kept a season at a time and left.
30 an t-Sultain, VE 611 Eilean fhada
Seals on the skerries
Hunters of the north shore go out in skin boats in the autumn gales to the skerries off Eilean fhada, where the grey seals haul out to pup, and take them there. The seal bones in the middens of the north coast bear the same cut-marks as those of Eilean mhin. On Eilean fhada a hard year is counted by the boats the gales kept ashore.
2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 691 Abhainn ìseal
The flood-plain of Abhainn ìseal
Abhainn ìseal, the longest river of the island, settles into the wide bed it keeps now. Fish-weirs of hazel stakes are set across its side channels, and the stakes are renewed in the same holes for generations.
28 an Lùnastal, VE 771 Seann Dunn
The middens of Seann Dunn
The Seann-Dhaoine begin the great mound at Seann Dunn: limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many lifetimes until it stands taller than a man. It is the first sure trace of them. No tool in it is shaped as any later Ròdach shaped tools.
26 an t-Sultain, VE 851 Seann Chwen
The notched net-weights of Seann Chwen
At Seann Chwen the Seann-Dhaoine sink their nets with beach stones, and every stone is notched with the same three strokes. It is the eldest mark on Rodos made again and again of purpose.
1 an t-Iuchar, VE 930 Seann Skell
The mole at Seann Skell
A mole of unmortared boulders is laid out into the Abhainn naomh from the bank at Seann Skell, long enough to shelter a dozen boats from the current. Its foot lies under water still at the lowest tides, and every quay wall built there since stands on it.
30 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,010 Seann Bhral
The steps of Seann Bhral
Two hundred and twelve steps are cut up the cliff at Seann Bhral, from the shingle to the grazing above. Their treads are worn hollow in the middle. How many feet that took, none has reckoned.
4 an Cèitean, VE 1,090 Eilean dhearg
The dead of Seann Vell go to Eilean dhearg
The Seann-Dhaoine of Seann Vell row their dead out to Eilean dhearg and lay them in stone boxes facing the mainland. Forty boxes are counted there. No grave of theirs of this time is found on the mainland.
2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,170 Seann Toll
The fish-channel of Seann Toll
At Seann Toll a channel is cut through a shelf of rock into a pool beside the Abhainn uaine, with a slot for a wattle gate. When the river falls the gate is dropped and the pool emptied by hand. The slot is sharp still.
7 am Màrt, VE 1,249 Seann Warr
The shell causeway of Seann Warr
A road of crushed shell is laid across the reed marsh at Seann Warr, on the western shore of Loch chrom, a little over a mile long and raised a forearm above the reeds. It is the eldest made road on the island that may still be walked.
5 an Giblean, VE 1,329 Seann Tarr
The script appears at Seann Tarr
Rows of signs are cut into the cliff above Seann Tarr, in the script that is found afterwards on the standing stones. It is not Ròdais, and none has read it. No sign of it has a meaning that all accept.
17 an Giblean, VE 1,408 Seann Mhorn
The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn
Stone-lined pits with short flues are built above the beach at Seann Mhorn, to dry the catch over peat smoke. Seven are known. They are the first buildings on Rodos made for a trade, and not for sleep or for the dead.
16 an Cèitean, VE 1,488 Seann Bhrenn
The slipways of Seann Bhrenn
Long ramps of flat stone are laid down into the water at Seann Bhrenn, wide enough for hulls greater than any hide boat. Of the hulls nothing is left, nor any telling of where they went.
7 am Màrt, VE 1,570 Loch chrom
The lake dwellings of Loch chrom
Platforms on oak piles are raised in the shallows of Loch chrom and joined to the shore by plank walks. Whether the Seann-Dhaoine built them, or some other people of those years, is not known.
6 an Gearran, VE 1,647 Seann Dunn
The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn
A whale strands below the southern Seann Dunn, and its ribs are raised for the frames of three round houses roofed with turf. The ribs are set up again in new houses at least twice before they rot.
8 am Faoilleach, VE 1,727 Seann Vell
The round houses of the eastern Seann Vell
At the eastern Seann Vell the Seann-Dhaoine build round houses of dry stone, each with a hearth sunk in the middle of the floor and a drain running out under the wall. Fourteen house-rings are counted there.
10 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,807 Seann Skell
The tower at the north-western Seann Skell
At the least of the Seann Skell places, on the north-west coast, a single round tower of dry stone is raised, hollow-walled, with a stair in the thickness of the wall. It looks out over the water where the Sea-Watcher is afterwards seen.
1 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,886 Seann Toll
The huts of the northern Seann Toll
At Seann Toll on the north coast a cluster of stone huts is built in the lee of a dune. The dune afterwards buries them whole, and the sand keeps them.
2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,970 Seann Bhral
The eastern Seann Bhral
At the Seann Bhral of the south-east coast the Seann-Dhaoine keep a landing and a line of fish-kilns like those of Seann Mhorn. The two places lie within a day's rowing of each other.
4 an Cèitean, VE 2,046 Seann Mhorn
The shell beds of the southern Seann Mhorn
At the second Seann Mhorn, on the southern coast, oyster, whelk and cockle shell is heaped over a whole headland, and there is little else. The oysters of its lowest layers are larger than any taken there since.
5 an Giblean, VE 2,126 Seann Bhrenn
The twin landings of Seann Bhrenn
A second Seann Bhrenn, far to the north-east of the first, has the same long ramps into the water. Whether the two were of one people, or only the name was carried, is not known.
25 an Dàmhair, VE 2,205 Seann Tarr
The cliff-house at Seann Tarr in the east
At the Seann Tarr of the north-eastern headlands a single long house is built into a cleft of the cliff, with the living rock for its back wall. The rock behind the hearth is black with soot to the height of a man.
26 an t-Sultain, VE 2,285 Seann Vell
The north-eastern Seann Vell
The Seann Vell on the Abhainn bheag, a short way above its mouth in the north-east, is a small place of four houses and a boat-shed. No Seann-Dhaoine dwelling on the main island is known further to the north-east.
22 am Màrt, VE 2,370 Seann Skell
The northern Seann Skell
At the Seann Skell below the later Ros gheal, on the north coast, the Seann-Dhaoine lay a second breakwater, shorter than the southern one and curved against the swell of the open sea. The two moles are built the same way, stone by stone.
20 an Giblean, VE 2,444 Seann Vell
The western Seann Vell
At the Seann Vell of the west coast the Seann-Dhaoine dig a line of storage pits into the dune, lined with clay and lidded with slabs. Some held fish bones still when they were opened.
19 an Cèitean, VE 2,524 Làrach an Dùin-fhaire
Làrach an Dùin-fhaire raised
On a spur above the ground where Cathair mhòr now stands, the Seann-Dhaoine build the walled outpost afterwards called Làrach an Dùin-fhaire. Its stones are dressed on the outer face only, and its single gate looks inland, away from the sea.
17 an t-Ògmhios, VE 2,580 Làrach an Dùin
Làrach an Dùin raised
A greater work is raised on the height near Ceann mhin: three rings of wall, a cistern cut into the bedrock, and room within, as it was later reckoned, for four hundred people and their beasts. Whether the builders of the outpost built this also has never been settled.
16 an t-Iuchar, VE 2,636 Àth fhionn
The kerbed way between the forts
A kerbed track, a cart's width and paved with flat slabs, is laid through the ground near Àth fhionn toward both strongholds. It is the only road the Seann-Dhaoine are known to have made away from the shore.
14 an Lùnastal, VE 2,692 Làrach an Teampaill
Làrach an Teampaill raised
A stepped platform of fitted stone is built in the eastern hills, with an altar block on its top step. The altar is set square to the central mountains. Every later temple on Rodos faces some other way.
12 an t-Sultain, VE 2,748 Toll-dubh
The shaft of Toll-dubh in the south-east
A shaft is sunk straight down through the rock at the eastern Toll-dubh, its walls tooled smooth as far as a lamp will show. No spoil lies beside it. Whatever was taken out was carried away, or nothing was.
11 an Dàmhair, VE 2,804 Toll-dubh
The shaft of Toll-dubh in the west
A second shaft of the same making is cut at the western Toll-dubh, far across the island from the first. Stones thrown into either are not heard to land.
9 an t-Samhain, VE 2,851
The First Canoe
Among the coastal Tuathaich families a half-forgotten telling of a voyage is kept, long hushed: a steersman with a name, and a first crossing to an isle of the blessed. Their church tells it as the voyage of Naomh Breandan. The druids of the Old Faith call it idle belief.
8 an Dùbhlachd, VE 2,916 Ceann mhòr
Stakes in the mud below Ceann mhòr
The first sure boats of the north-west coast leave their trace in the tidal mud below Ceann mhòr: a row of mooring stakes and a scrap of stitched hide. Who rowed them, and from where, is not known.
1 an t-Sultain, VE 2,972 Uilebheist na Mara
The Sea-Watcher first sighted
Old sailors tell of a vast creature dwelling in the waters off the north-western coast. No wreck has ever been brought up to prove them wrong.
3 an Lùnastal, VE 3,028 Taigh-solais Baile chrom
The beacon on the Baile chrom headland
A fire is kept on the headland where Taigh-solais Baile chrom now stands, and its ash lies a man's height deep. The tellings say it was lit to warn boats off the water where the Sea-Watcher was seen, and never to bring them in.
29 an Dàmhair, VE 3,084 Ros ruadh
Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh
Seven boats are lost from Ros ruadh in one calm season, with no storm to blame. It is the first loss laid at the door of the Sea-Watcher by name; before this it was feared only in general.
30 an t-Sultain, VE 3,140 Caol mhòr
The seal hunt moves south
The hunters of the north-west leave the open water and work the southern side of the headlands, out of its sight. The seal bones thin in the middens of the north-west and grow at Caol mhòr and Cuan bheag.
8 an Cèitean, VE 3,196 Doire uaine
Signs cut in the Doire uaine hills
Inscriptions are cut on rock faces all across the Doire uaine hills, more than anywhere else on the island, in lines that run for yards. Some lines are cut over and defaced with the same kind of tool that made them.
9 an Giblean, VE 3,251 Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The Hollow Man of Doire uaine
The inscriptions of the Doire uaine hills tell of something that walked without breathing, and fell upon any who lit a fire in its sight.
5 an t-Iuchar, VE 3,308 Doire uaine
The hill fires go under the ground
After the inscriptions the hearths of the Doire uaine hills are dug into pits and roofed with slabs. No open hearth shows in those hills for many lifetimes. The people stay, and hide their light.
6 an t-Ògmhios, VE 3,370 Muileann chiar
The nine at the hill camp
Nine people die inside a hut at the camp where Muileann chiar was afterwards built, and lie where they fell beside a hearth of fresh ash. No wound is found on any bone. The hut is never opened again, and none is buried from it.
21 an Giblean, VE 3,420 Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
Coille Naomh Muileann chiar set aside
A forest is held sacred long before any order of the Old Faith claims it. The trees knew it first, the old telling says, and the people after.
23 am Màrt, VE 3,476 Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
No axe in the grove
The families at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar carry their fuel a half-day's walk sooner than cut a branch within it. The charcoal in their hearths is of every wood but that one.
11 am Màrt, VE 3,532 Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
The white stag of the grove
Three hunters see a white stag at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, and none of them draws. This is the first telling of it. The stag returns in the tellings of every age after, and the druids of later ages name it the white stag of Flidais; in this age it has no god.
9 an Giblean, VE 3,588 Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag left unclaimed
A second forest, that seems older than the first, is never settled, never felled, and never walked from end to end.
12 am Faoilleach, VE 3,644 Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The paths that stop at a line of stones
Tracks are worn toward Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag from three quarters, and all three end at a low line of set stones some way short of the trees. Beyond the stones the ground is not worn.
10 an Gearran, VE 3,700 Doire fhionn
The deer-drives of the eastern forest
Lines of stakes and brush are set to drive the red deer of the eastern woods into a gully near Doire fhionn, where they are killed with spears. The antlers of the greatest stags are stacked apart from the rest.
5 an t-Iuchar, VE 3,751 Cnoc fhionn
The first dog graves
At Cnoc fhionn in the east dogs are buried beside people, each with a shell at its head. No beast was given a grave on Rodos before.
3 an Lùnastal, VE 3,812 Eilean ghorm
The geese of Eilean ghorm
The grey geese that winter on Eilean ghorm come into the tellings for the first time. They come in with the first storm and leave with the last, and none hunts them there.
8 an Cèitean, VE 3,870 Seann Skell
The widest reach of the Seann-Dhaoine
At their height the Seann-Dhaoine hold every coast of the island: the ten places whose names begin with Seann, and the islands off them. Their greatest landing is at Seann Skell, up the Abhainn naomh, where the mole already stands.
6 an t-Ògmhios, VE 3,924 Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The warm springs used
Stone basins are set into the springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh. The people buried near them have old breaks that knitted clean. Here the sick of Rodos are first brought for healing.
29 an Dàmhair, VE 3,980 Làrach an Dùin-fhaire
The gate of the outpost walled up
The single gate of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire is blocked with rubble from within. Those who did it left by another way, or did not leave.
27 an t-Samhain, VE 4,036 Làrach an Dùin-fhaire
Làrach an Dùin-fhaire abandoned
The outpost is deserted. It lay in ruin before the first trusty chronicles, and it is older than any dwelling of the Ròdaich. Who built it none knows.
4 an Giblean, VE 4,092 Làrach an Dùin
The fortress cistern fouled
The cistern of Làrach an Dùin is choked with the bones of cattle, thrown in whole. Its water had served four hundred people. No one draws from it again.
6 am Màrt, VE 4,148 Làrach an Dùin
Làrach an Dùin abandoned
The fortress is deserted in like manner, and is as much a riddle as the outpost. Whether both had the same builders has never been settled.
5 an Gearran, VE 4,204 Làrach an Teampaill
The temple altar stripped
The top stone of the altar at Làrach an Teampaill is prised off and carried away; the sockets that held it are sharp still. It has never been found, and what was cut on it, if anything, is not known.
7 am Faoilleach, VE 4,251 Làrach an Teampaill
Làrach an Teampaill abandoned
The temple is deserted. It is older than any faith that has a name, and its altar looks to the central mountains and the vein beneath them, away from the sea.
9 an Dùbhlachd, VE 4,316 Seann Chwen
The Seann-Dhaoine keep to the shore
The high places are left, and every new work of the Seann-Dhaoine is made within sight of salt water. The middens at the southern Seann Chwen begin to grow as fast as those of Seann Dunn once did.
7 am Faoilleach, VE 4,372 Seann Dunn
The ancient sea-way
The boats of the Seann-Dhaoine keep a lane along the south-east coast, from the river mouth below Seann Dunn round the cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg now stands to the bay of Ceann chaol. Flat landing-stones lie along it a day's rowing apart, some grooved still by hauled keels. The Ròdaich call it Slighe-mhara àrsaidh, the ancient sea-way, and the fishers of that coast keep to it yet.
10 an t-Samhain, VE 4,428 Àth gharbh
The hill-folk of the vein
In the high valleys about the crack dwells a people other than the Seann-Dhaoine. They bury their dead in the ground and not on islands, and they cut no script. Whether they shared the island with the Seann-Dhaoine or came after them, no telling knows; their own word, later, is that they were always there.
12 an Dàmhair, VE 4,484 Àth gharbh
The first small burning
At Àth gharbh a sliver of black glass is burnt to a bead in a peat fire, and the hearthstone round it is stained through with colour. No older burning of the ore is known. It is a small thing: one sliver, one fire.
13 an t-Sultain, VE 4,540 Achadh dhìreach
The stained cloth of Achadh dhìreach
At Achadh dhìreach the hill-folk rub broken ore into the wool of the dead, and it takes streaks of a colour no plant dye makes. It is seldom done: one grave in some thirty.
15 an Lùnastal, VE 4,596 Seann Bhral
A sliver in a Seann Bhral midden
A chip of the black ore, still staining the shell about it, is thrown on a midden at Seann Bhral on the far western coast. By gift, by trade or by theft a piece of the vein came to the Seann-Dhaoine; which, is not known.
17 an t-Iuchar, VE 4,651 Carragh Cnoc bheag
Carragh Cnoc bheag raised
A standing stone is raised, on which four words are afterwards found carved: Bha teine sa chloich, "there was fire in the stone."
11 an Lùnastal, VE 4,708 Carragh Cnoc bheag
The older face of Carragh Cnoc bheag
On the upper face of the stone runs a line of the unread script. The four Ròdais words lie lower, cut with a narrower tool by another hand. When that second hand came is not known.
9 an t-Sultain, VE 4,770 Colbh Cnoc chiar
Colbh Cnoc chiar raised
A second stone is raised, bearing only two words: Cuimhnich an teine, "remember the fire." Who is bidden, and why, none has ever said.
8 an Dàmhair, VE 4,820 Colbh Cnoc chiar
A ring of fire-stones round the pillar
The ground about Colbh Cnoc chiar is trodden hard in a ring and paved with fire-cracked stones. Fires the size of hearths are kept there again and again. Nothing else is left.
6 an t-Samhain, VE 4,876 Calbh Cnoc ghorm
Calbh Cnoc ghorm raised
A third stone is raised, and on it the whole of the saying: Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann. Here, it may be, the belief was first spoken.
17 an Giblean, VE 4,932 Cnoc ghorm
The gatherings at the column
People come to the column at Cnoc ghorm in numbers. The post-holes of shelters for some hundreds lie about it, used and rebuilt many times. Whatever was said there was said to a crowd.
16 an Cèitean, VE 4,988 Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
Tuam Cnoc dhìreach consecrated
A burial-ground grows about a place that none remembers hallowing. Its oldest graves are older than the oldest names that can be read there.
14 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,044 Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
The black chip in the child's grave
A child is buried at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach with a sliver of black glass closed in one hand. The sliver stains still the cloth it is kept in. No other piece of the vein is found with the dead of this age.
13 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,100 Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
The rows at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
The graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach begin to be laid in rows, heads toward the central mountains. The first rows are straight. The later ones bend round older graves that no one will disturb.
22 an Dùbhlachd, VE 5,151
The panther roads
The great cats of the island are first seen to keep their roads, crossing the mountains by fixed ways at fixed seasons. Why they do so no one has learned.
20 am Faoilleach, VE 5,212 Imrich nam Pantar
The crossing season kept
The hill-folk learn the panthers' seasons and keep off the high passes while the cats cross. The camps in the passes stand empty at the same point in every year.
7 an t-Sultain, VE 5,270 Cnoc àrsaidh
Eleven lost on the panther road
A party of eleven from the southern shore goes up into the hills near Cnoc àrsaidh in the crossing season and does not return. Years afterwards their bones are found along the line the cats use still.
9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324 Dùn ìseal
Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings
Ailean Mòr holds the hill where Dùn ìseal now stands and throws up its first ring of bank. With him opens the eldest of the spoken king-lists, afterwards called Rìghrean na Cloiche; it gives no lengths of reign, and it is older than the name Ròdaich.
4 an t-Samhain, VE 5,332 Dùn ìseal
The bank of Dùn ìseal
The first earthwork is raised on the hill at Dùn ìseal: a single bank and ditch, enclosing room for some forty houses. It is the oldest defended place of the hill-folk.
6 an Dàmhair, VE 5,341 Cathair dhearg
Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill
Beathag Ruadh holds the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands. With her opens a second spoken list, kept in the west. The Red Hill list and the list of the Stone Kings make no mention of each other until late in both.
1 am Faoilleach, VE 5,350 Dùn ìseal
Gormshuil nic Ailein
Gormshuil nic Ailein, second of the Stone Kings, is the first woman named in any list on Rodos. One deed is told of her: in a hard winter she moves the herds of Dùn ìseal down to the warm springs and loses none.
3 an Dùbhlachd, VE 5,430 Dùn ìseal
Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones
Dòmhnall Clachach, third of the Stone Kings, sets marker stones along the valley below the hill to part the grazing of Dùn ìseal from its neighbours'. Some stand yet, and are argued over yet.
30 am Faoilleach, VE 5,470
The first named storm
A tempest comes so great that the eldest spoken king-lists give it a name. The name is lost; only the memory of the naming remains.
28 an Gearran, VE 5,470 Seann Warr
The shell road broken
The storm breaks the shell causeway of Seann Warr in three places and floods the marsh behind it with lake water. The Seann-Dhaoine do not mend it, and the broken ends may be seen still.
27 an Giblean, VE 5,550 Dùn ìseal
Fearchar Bacach
Fearchar Bacach, the lame king, rules at Dùn ìseal after the storm and after Dòmhnall Clachach, and is carried to the gatherings in a chair of woven birch. He is the first ruler on Rodos remembered for a hurt.
29 am Màrt, VE 5,590 Cathair dhearg
Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill
Uisdean Mòr, second of the Red Hill list, digs a ditch across the neck of the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands and sets a palisade on it. In his time the palisade burns twice and is twice rebuilt.
31 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,631 Seann Chwen
Strokes on the midden stones
The Seann-Dhaoine begin to cut single strokes on flat stones set at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household. The strokes are not the script. They are simpler: a mark, and then another.
29 an Lùnastal, VE 5,671
The counting of the dead begins
The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin, begin to keep count of their dead. They keep it before ever there were Ròdaich to take up the custom.
3 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,712 Seann Warr
The tally wall of Seann Warr
At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones are built into a wall, each cut with its strokes, some three thousand strokes in all. The wall grows for many lifetimes.
2 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,751 Seann Tarr
The count at Seann Tarr
The counting comes to Seann Tarr in the north-east. There the stones are cut with strokes in fives and set in the floor of a house, and the house is lived in over its own dead.
6 an Giblean, VE 5,793 Seann Warr
The bad years in the counts
The tally stones at Seann Warr, Seann Tarr and Seann Chwen thicken together: more strokes to each stone, more stones to each course. Death comes on three coasts at once. What it was the strokes do not tell.
5 an Cèitean, VE 5,833 Seann Chwen
The half-cut stone of Seann Chwen
At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone is left half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and forsaken. The chisel marks stop in mid-groove.
7 an Gearran, VE 5,874
The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent
After the half-cut stone no work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their script is cut no more. How they ended no telling knows.
8 am Màrt, VE 5,914 Seann Skell
The old names kept
The hill-folk keep the names of the Seann-Dhaoine places and set before them only their own word for 'old': Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen, Seann Skell and the rest. They turn nothing into their own tongue, and the roots of those names are not understood.
11 an Dùbhlachd, VE 5,951 Seann Skell
The old landings taken up
Families of the hill-folk come down the Abhainn naomh and settle in the empty river harbour at Seann Skell, using the old mole and mending none of it. They are not known to have dwelt by the water before.
9 am Faoilleach, VE 5,995 Baile ghorm
Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid
Mòrag Chruaidh, fifth of the Stone Kings, raids the salt-pans on the southern shore at Baile ghorm and carries off the salt. It is the first war in either list. Seven fall on the hill side, and the number is kept.
12 an Gearran, VE 6,006 Baile ghorm
The salt-pans of Baile ghorm
Shallow clay basins are made behind a shingle bar at Baile ghorm, the first salt-works of the island. From this time their salt is found in the hill settlements.
13 am Màrt, VE 6,017 Cathair dhearg
Seonag of the Red Hill
Seonag nic Uisdein holds the Red Hill after her father. It is told that she counted her people by pebbles in a bag, one to a household, and knew by the weight when a household was gone.
11 an Giblean, VE 6,028 Doire shean
The first pots at Doire shean
Pots of coiled clay, fired in open bonfires, are first made at Doire shean on the south-west coast. Within a few lifetimes the whole southern shore uses them.
10 an Cèitean, VE 6,039 Cidhe Beag
The dug-out at Cidhe Beag
A boat hollowed from a single oak trunk, long enough for six, is sunk and left at the landing on Abhainn uaine now called Cidhe Beag. No older boat on Rodos is known in its whole shape.
8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 6,050 Baile ghorm
Iain Dubh killed
Iain Dubh, sixth of the Stone Kings, goes down to raid the salt-pans as Mòrag Chruaidh had done, and is slain on the shingle at Baile ghorm. The list says only that he was brought home.
7 an t-Iuchar, VE 6,100 Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol
The wave at Cnoc chaol
The sea comes far inland over a village on the site of Cnoc chaol and leaves a sheet of sand a hand thick upon its hearths, with the shells of deep-water creatures in it. The village is not rebuilt on the same ground.
5 an Lùnastal, VE 6,150 Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The ground opens at Cill ghlas
A crack a man could fall into opens across the valley at Cill ghlas, and a spring moves a hundred paces downhill. The hill-folk bank the crack with stones and build on neither side of it.
3 an t-Sultain, VE 6,170 Cill ghlas
The fault-line kept clear
