A line of white stones is laid along the old crack at Cill ghlas, and for the rest of the age no house is built within a stone's throw of it. Part of the line remains.
2 an Dàmhair, VE 6,225
The unlit hearth
In a single dwelling a hearth is laid and never lit. Peat keeps it by chance. It is the eldest sign that someone here chose not to burn what could easily have been burned.
31 an Dàmhair, VE 6,279
Peat over the unlit hearth
The house of the unlit hearth lies under three yards of peat, its hearth laid with dry wood and a slip of the ore beside it, none of it burned. Whoever laid it went away and did not come back to light it.
5 an Lùnastal, VE 6,334 Àth gharbh
The measured handful
In all the hill settlements a custom takes hold that no fire shall have more of the ore than one cupped hand can hold. It is nowhere written and everywhere kept. From it the Small-Burning Law of the next age is made.
7 an t-Iuchar, VE 6,389 Achadh dhìreach
The basket burning at Achadh dhìreach
A household at Achadh dhìreach burns a whole basket of the ore at once. The house burns down with three within, and the hearth-stone is found cracked through and running with colour. Ever after the tellings use it to show why the handful is kept.
8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 6,443 Tobar dhìreach
The watchers of the slab
Families near the crack take turns to sit by the slab laid over it, a household at a time, through the dark half of the year. What they watch for, none ever says.
10 an Cèitean, VE 6,498 Fèill Muileann òg
Raghnall Ceannfhionn makes peace
Raghnall Ceannfhionn, seventh of the Stone Kings, meets the holder of the Red Hill at the ford where the fair of Muileann òg is held now, and they agree on salt for wool. Both lists tell of the meeting, and in neither is the other named before it.
29 an t-Samhain, VE 6,531 Fèill Muileann òg
The ford gathering
The meeting at the ford becomes a yearly gathering. Salt, flint, wool, dried fish and pots change hands there, and marriages are made. No meeting-place on the island has been used longer without a break.
31 an Dàmhair, VE 6,570 Cathair dhearg
Murchadh Gearr of the Red Hill
Murchadh Gearr holds the Red Hill after Seonag and keeps the peace of the ford. It is told that he walked the salt road himself every year, to be seen upon it.
2 an Dàmhair, VE 6,597 Ros bheag
Hill-folk on the western shore
Households from the hills settle the bay at Ros bheag, the first of their kind on the west coast. They build in the hill manner, round and turf-roofed, a little back from the beach, and fish from the shore and not from boats.
8 an Gearran, VE 6,629 Seann Skell
Amber from the Hawk bay
Amber is gathered from the wrack on the strands of the Hawk bay and drilled for stringing; lumps of it lie in the middens below Seann Skell. A bead of the same amber lies in the oldest ground of the ford gathering, carried there the length of the island.
3 an t-Sultain, VE 6,670 Cathair dhomhain
The first houses at Cathair dhomhain
Round houses are built by the harbour where Cathair dhomhain now stands, near enough the Red Hill to pay it salt. The Red Hill list counts them among its holder's households.
25 am Màrt, VE 6,702 Cnoc ghorm
Cattle in the north-west
Cattle come to Cnoc ghorm in the north-west, where the settlements had lived on seal, fish and deer. The herds must have been walked up the flint road.
24 an Gearran, VE 6,739 Cathair gheal
The long-house at Cathair gheal
A long-house forty paces long, with byre and hall under one roof, is built on the rise at Cathair gheal. It is the greatest building of the age in the north-west. Twice it burns, and twice it is rebuilt on the same footing.
21 an t-Iuchar, VE 6,775 Toll-dubh
A youth let down into Toll-dubh
A youth is let down on a rope of plaited hide into the eastern Toll-dubh, to the rope's end. He is drawn up alive and never tells what lay at the bottom. No one goes down again in this age.
19 an Lùnastal, VE 6,812 Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
A fire lit in the Doire uaine hills
A herding family, new to the hills, lights an open fire at Doire uaine against the custom. Their hut is found empty, the fire still burning. Thereafter the covered hearth is kept more strictly.
24 an Cèitean, VE 6,848 Loch chrom
The lake dwellings burn
The platforms on Loch chrom burn to the waterline, and the charred piles are left standing in the shallows. No one builds on the lake again in this age.
22 an t-Ògmhios, VE 6,885 Caol leathan
Seal-oil lamps at Caol leathan
Stone lamps with a hollow for seal oil and a wick of moss are used at Caol leathan. They are the first light on Rodos that is not a hearth, and they give little smoke.
27 am Màrt, VE 6,921 Caol fhiadhaich
The fish-traps of Caol fhiadhaich
Wattle fences are staked across the river-mouth at Caol fhiadhaich to trap salmon on the ebb. The same line of stake-holes is used again and again through the rest of the age.
25 an Giblean, VE 6,951 Muileann leathan
The upright looms of Muileann leathan
At Muileann leathan in the north cloth is woven on standing frames, no longer twined by hand. The loom-weights of fired clay lie in rows in the houses, where they fell from the warp.
28 am Faoilleach, VE 6,994
The first tide-count
Someone begins to mark the high-water line against a fixed rock. Why is not told; but the marks are cut at intervals more even than a fisherman's need would ask, as later scholars observe.
26 an Gearran, VE 7,031 Ros dhomhain
A second tide-rock at Ros dhomhain
The high-water marking is copied at Ros dhomhain on a boulder in the harbour mouth, the marks cut at the same intervals as on the first rock. Someone carried the practice there, and the interval with it.
10 am Màrt, VE 7,070 Ros dhomhain
The lake is higher
The marks on the Ros dhomhain rock creep upward from keeper to keeper, and by the end of the age Loch chrom stands a hand higher on the rock than at the first cut. The keepers go on cutting.
8 an Giblean, VE 7,104 Cnoc àrsaidh
The flint of Cnoc àrsaidh
A pit is worked for flint on the hill of Cnoc àrsaidh in the north-west, the only good flint on Rodos. Its grey flakes are carried to hearths from one end of the island to the other.
11 am Faoilleach, VE 7,140 Àth leathan
The flint road
A track is worn by the flint-carriers from Cnoc àrsaidh south and east toward the ford gathering. Near Àth leathan their feet sink it a yard deep.
13 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,176 Àth mhòr
The hawk lintel at Àth mhòr
A hawk is carved on a lintel over a house door at Àth mhòr in the north, wings closed, head turned. It is the oldest carving of a hawk on the island, and of any bird.
10 am Màrt, VE 7,213 Tobar fhiadhaich
Wolves at Tobar fhiadhaich
At Tobar fhiadhaich wolves are buried whole and with care, laid on their sides as people are. No other beast is so buried in this age.
9 an Gearran, VE 7,250 Dùn ìseal
Sìleas Bhàn and the hungry years
Sìleas Bhàn, eighth of the Stone Kings, holds Dùn ìseal through years of failed grazing. No deed is told of her but that she held, and the list goes on after her.
7 an Cèitean, VE 7,289 Gorta Baile chrom
The hunger at Baile chrom
Hunger comes to the settlement on the site of the north-western Baile chrom. Its pots are left full of boiled bark and seaweed, and its grave-rows are doubled. No older hunger on Rodos is tied to a place.
8 an Giblean, VE 7,329 Tiormachd Achadh shean
The drought at Achadh shean
The springs of Achadh shean in the east run dry so long that the field banks are forsaken and grown over. When people return they cut new fields on another line.
4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,370
The naming of the wind directions
The eight winds are named, and every Ròdach sailor after uses the names. Their meaning is dark even to those who speak them, and they have never been changed.
5 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,407 Ceann leathan
The wind-stones of Ceann leathan
Eight tall stones are set in a ring on the point at Ceann leathan, one for each of the named winds. Sailors of every later age touch the stone of the wind they want before they put out.
24 an Cèitean, VE 7,447 Eilean fhada
The wind-names carried to the islands
The eight wind-names are used on Eilean fhada as on the main island. The markers on its high point bear eight cut notches, one facing each way.
25 an Giblean, VE 7,486 Dùn ìseal
Tormod Liath
Tormod Liath, ninth of the Stone Kings, outlives three heirs, and is remembered as old. In his time Dùn ìseal is given its second bank, and its ground is doubled.
4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,524
The Ròdaich name
In this age the hill-folk begin to call themselves Ròdaich and the island Ròdos. The first use is not known; the eldest tellings take both names for granted. With the names goes the belief: they did not come; they were here.
2 an Lùnastal, VE 7,546
The first forbidden marriage
A marriage between two lineages is forbidden, for a reason no surviving telling gives. Already the Ròdaich order themselves by blood, long before the ore gives them cause.
31 an Lùnastal, VE 7,570 Fèill Muileann òg
Lines recited at the ford
At the ford gathering households begin to recite their lines aloud before any marriage is made, seven names back on either side. These are the first genealogies on Rodos. None survives whole.
29 an t-Sultain, VE 7,590 Cnoc dhubh
The first seeking of another vein
Diggers from Dùn ìseal open a trench on a hill near Cnoc dhubh in the east, seeking black rock like the vein's. They leave it unfinished when two of them are crushed by a fall. The trench stays open, and what it would have found is not known.
10 am Màrt, VE 7,612
The stone that would not break
A second opening for a new vein is made elsewhere on the island and fails wholly: common rock, and nothing beneath it. So it is first known that the vein under the mountain is alone of its kind.
8 an Giblean, VE 7,635
The prospecting ends
No one tries a third opening in this age. The Ròdaich hold that the vein chooses where it lies, and that the choice is not theirs to try.
7 an Cèitean, VE 7,651
The first shared meal law
A custom arises, unwritten, that any household with food to spare shall share it before the storm season. Later it is made law, and later ages lean on it more than they own.
5 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,679 Dùn ìseal
Surplus shared at Dùn ìseal
At Dùn ìseal the sharing before the storms is done in the open: every household brings its surplus within the bank, and it is divided by the count of mouths. The custom has no earlier place that is known.
14 an t-Samhain, VE 7,701 Àth shean
A household turned out at Àth shean
A household at Àth shean hides its spare grain in a pit under the floor and brings nothing to the sharing. When the pit is found the household is put out of the settlement with what it can carry. It is the first punishment under the custom that is remembered.
13 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,723 Dùn ìseal
Eilidh Ghlas
Eilidh Ghlas, tenth of the Stone Kings, sends her younger son to the Red Hill to be fostered, the first fostering in either list. The son's name is not kept; only that he went, and that the peace of the ford held while he was there.
25 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,724 Cathair dhearg
Lachlann Ruadh takes the fosterling
Lachlann Ruadh, holder of the Red Hill, takes the son of Eilidh Ghlas into his house. For it he is named Lachlann an Altraim, 'Lachlann of the fostering', and the Red Hill list calls him so more often than by his own name.
26 an t-Samhain, VE 7,726 Tobar dhìreach
Oighrig, first keeper by lot
The families who watch the slab agree to choose one keeper at a time by lot, and no longer to take turns by household. The first lot falls to a woman called Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill, and she keeps the slab for the rest of her life.
28 an Dàmhair, VE 7,727 Tobar dhìreach
The keepers' house
A house is built beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach for the holder of the lot, its door facing the stone. It is rebuilt on the same footing many times. It is the first building on Rodos made only to be near the vein.
29 an t-Sultain, VE 7,728 Tobar dhìreach
The stone cup
Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill has a cup ground out of grey stone to the size of her own cupped hand, that the handful of ore may be the same for every household. The cup is carried round the hill settlements. Whether it outlasts the age is not known.
31 an Lùnastal, VE 7,730 Cnoc chaol
The stone cup copied
Copies of the keeper's cup are ground at Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol, each tried against the first by filling it with water. Thereafter the hill settlements measure the ore with one measure.
28 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,731 Coinneachadh nan Cupan
The meeting of the cups
The keeper's cup and its three copies are carried to a spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach, set side by side on a flat stone and filled from the spring in turn. The place is called Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the meeting of the cups. The hill settlements return to it whenever a cup is broken and a new one must be tried.
2 an Lùnastal, VE 7,732 Eilean chrom
Gilleasbuig Beag takes ore
A keeper by lot, Gilleasbuig Beag, is found with a basket of broken ore in his own house. The households of the hills sit in judgement at the slab, row him out to Eilean chrom, and leave him there without a boat. He is the first known to be exiled for the vein.
4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,734 Tobar dhìreach
The ore returned to the crack
The ore from Gilleasbuig Beag's house is neither burned nor kept. The keeper after him carries it back to the slab and lays it beneath, piece by piece. The tellings make much of it: the ore went home.
4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,735 Dùn ìseal
Calum Ciar asks for the lot
Calum Ciar, eleventh of the Stone Kings, asks that the keeper's lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his sight. The households at the slab refuse him. The list sets down the refusal, which is more than it sets down of most things.
7 an Cèitean, VE 7,739 Dùn ìseal
The kings and the keepers
After the refusal of Calum Ciar the lot is still drawn at the slab. The Stone Kings rule the grazing and the gatherings but not the vein, and the line between the two holds for the rest of the age. It is not yet written anywhere.
1 an Gearran, VE 7,740 Cuan ruadh
A' Ghaoth Dhubh
A storm called A' Ghaoth Dhubh, the Black Wind, strips the thatch from every house on the east coast from Cuan ruadh to Ceann chiar. Of all storms it is the eldest whose name is kept.
8 an Giblean, VE 7,740 Ceann chiar
The sharing holds after the Black Wind
The settlements of the east coast feed the people of Cuan ruadh through a whole winter out of their shared surplus. None on that coast is known to die of hunger that season.
2 am Màrt, VE 7,741 Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
The beacon at Baile ìseal
A fire is built on the eastern cape where Taigh-solais Baile ìseal now stands, kept by the households of the coast in turn. It is lit to bring boats home in a storm, the tellings say, and not to warn them off.
3 am Faoilleach, VE 7,742 Taigh-solais Muileann bheag
The beacon at Muileann bheag
A second shore-fire is kept on the north coast, on the point where Taigh-solais Muileann bheag stands now. Under the tower the ash goes down through three yards of fire-reddened soil.
5 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,742 Taigh-solais Àth dhearg
The beacon at Àth dhearg
Households of the north-east coast keep a fire on the cape where Taigh-solais Àth dhearg now stands, and cut steps up to it from the shore. The steps are narrower than those at Seann Bhral, and less worn.
28 an Cèitean, VE 7,743 Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
The beacon at Tobar dhearg
A fire is kept for the boats of the south coast on the southern cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg stands. With Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag and Àth dhearg the coasts of the island are lit at five points.
31 am Màrt, VE 7,744 Uilebheist na Mara
The Sea-Watcher seen from Seann Skell
Four watchers on the north-western tower at Seann Skell see a back as long as three boats rise and go under off the point. It is the first sighting of the Sea-Watcher tied to a named place and a count of witnesses.
26 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,744 Spùinneadairean-mara
Wreckage in the western water
For a season planks of stitched boats, broken small, wash up along the western shore below the waters where raiders are afterwards seen. No bodies come with them, and no settlement on that coast lacks a boat.
29 an Giblean, VE 7,745 Fèill Muileann òg
Anndra Breac says 'we came'
At the ford gathering Anndra Breac, a teller of the western coast, recites a telling in which the people came to Rodos over the sea. The households of the hills shout him down, and he is put out of the ford for the rest of his life. His telling is not kept; only the memory that he told it.
21 an t-Sultain, VE 7,746 Calbh Cnoc ghorm
The doctrine said at the column
After Anndra Breac, the saying cut on the column at Cnoc ghorm is spoken aloud at the opening of the ford gathering: we did not come; we were here. From this time it is said as a rule, and not only held as a belief.
25 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,747 Ros dhomhain
The keepers of the Ros dhomhain rock
The tide-rock at Ros dhomhain passes to Seònaid Mhòr, who cuts her marks in pairs, one for high water and one for low. Her pairs can be read still. The keepers after her go back to single marks.
20 an Dàmhair, VE 7,747 Inis thais
A third tide-rock at Inis thais
Households at Inis thais cut their own high-water marks on the harbour rock, at the interval of Ros dhomhain. So three rocks are kept side by side. None tells why the interval is what it is.
26 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,748 Ros dhomhain
Ros dhomhain grows
Ros dhomhain becomes the greatest settlement on the shores of Loch chrom, some sixty houses round the tide-rock. Its people fish now from boats and not from the shore.
23 an Lùnastal, VE 7,749 Cathair dhearg
The Red Hill's harbour
The households of the Red Hill build a landing of laid stone at the river-mouth below the hill, where the harbour of Cathair dhearg is now. It is the Red Hill's first way onto the water, and by the lake and the Abhainn gheal to the sea.
21 an t-Sultain, VE 7,749 Cathair dhearg
Peigi Dhubh of the Red Hill
Peigi Dhubh holds the Red Hill after Lachlann an Altraim. She sends the fostered son of Dùn ìseal home grown, with gifts of salt, and the peace of the ford holds a generation more.
31 am Màrt, VE 7,750 Dùn ìseal
The foster-son returns
The son of Eilidh Ghlas comes home from the Red Hill to Dùn ìseal, bringing the salt-songs of the west. The Stone Kings' list gives him no name and no reign; he is remembered only as the one who went.
2 am Màrt, VE 7,751 Baile ghorm
The first songs kept
The salt-songs of the south and west are sung at the raking of the pans. They are the oldest songs on Rodos whose words are said to survive: a refrain of four lines, which no one can now wholly construe.
14 am Màrt, VE 7,751 Cnoc àrsaidh
Bone pipes at Cnoc àrsaidh
Pipes of hollow bird-bone, bored with four holes, are made in a house at the southern Cnoc àrsaidh near the panther road. They are the oldest instruments of the island.
29 an Giblean, VE 7,751 Imrich nam Pantar
The panthers turn back
The great cats come down the panther road near Imrich nam Pantar and turn back at the foothills without crossing. The hill-folk read it for a hard winter and store double. The winter is hard.
28 an Cèitean, VE 7,751 Muileann bhàn
The cattle lost in the passes
Herders from Muileann bhàn drive cattle into the passes out of season, against the custom of the crossing. The panthers take thirty head in a night, and the herders come down with nothing.
15 am Faoilleach, VE 7,770 Baile dhomhain
The panther season kept at Baile dhomhain
At Baile dhomhain in the south the households cut a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing season and scrape it off at its end. It is the first mark made on the island for a season.
13 an Gearran, VE 7,770 Seann Chwen
The wind-stone at Seann Chwen
One of the eight wind-names is cut in the Ròdach manner on a boulder at the central Seann Chwen, over an older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine. In few places do the marks of the two peoples touch.
14 an Gearran, VE 7,770 Caol bheag
Boats named for the winds
The fishing households of Caol bheag, who fish the north coast from the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm, name their boats for the winds they fish in. A boat named for the wrong wind is held unlucky, and the name of a boat that sinks is never given again.
14 am Màrt, VE 7,770 Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
The Tuam keepers
A family dwelling by Tuam Cnoc dhìreach takes on the clearing of thorn from the old graves. They bury none of their own there. They only keep it.
12 an Giblean, VE 7,770 Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
A grave at Tuam opened
Diggers laying a new row at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach break into a grave older than any they knew, lined with slabs cut in the manner of the Seann-Dhaoine. They close it and move the row, and none opens that grave again.
11 an Cèitean, VE 7,772 Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
Pilgrims at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
People begin to walk to the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and sit a night at the line of the trees without entering. Their small fires, each of a single night, lie all along the edge.
9 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,774 Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
A child lost in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
A child of the settlement at Cnoc bheag goes past the line of stones into Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag and is not found. The searchers stop at the stones, and the telling does not blame them.
8 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,776 Cnoc bheag
The first house at Cnoc bheag
Settlers from the Red Hill build at Cnoc bheag, near the edge of the forest. They take their timber from the far side of the river, and never from the unclaimed wood.
6 an Lùnastal, VE 7,778 Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The spring at Muileann ruadh
Pilgrims come in numbers to the warm springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, and a ring of shelters is built there. Here is set the eldest healing-tale of Rodos: a herder came lame and walked home.
28 an Cèitean, VE 7,780 Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The Hollow Man seen again
Two herders passing the Doire uaine hills after dark see a figure walk the ridge with no breath showing in the cold. They had no fire lit, and so, the telling says, they lived.
26 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,783 Muileann chiar
The covered hearth spreads
The covered hearth, pit-dug and roofed, spreads from the Doire uaine hills to the settlements about Muileann chiar. From this comes the later rule that no open fire is lit on those slopes after dark.
31 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,785 Caol mhòr
Settlers at Caol mhòr
Ròdach households settle at Caol mhòr in the north-west, on the strait where the Seann-Dhaoine once hunted seal. They find the old middens and build on them.
2 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,787 Baile chrom
Settlers at Baile chrom in the north-west
Households from Cnoc ghorm settle again the ground at Baile chrom that the old hunger had emptied. They dig their storage pits deeper than any others on the coast.
3 an t-Samhain, VE 7,789 Muileann àrsaidh
Muileann àrsaidh settled
Houses are built on the stream at Muileann àrsaidh in the north-west. Their flint comes from Cnoc àrsaidh, and their salt from the south, carried the length of the island.
5 an Dàmhair, VE 7,791 Muileann àrsaidh
The salt road to the north-west
A salt road runs from the pans of Baile ghorm by the ford gathering to the north-west. At Muileann àrsaidh the salt costs three times its price at the pans, and is paid for in flint and seal-skins.
26 an Giblean, VE 7,793 Doire ghlas
Doire ghlas settled
Households settle under the oaks at Doire ghlas in the north. The settlement grows in rings, each built outside the last as the wood is cleared back.
28 am Màrt, VE 7,796 Dùn thais
The east settled at Dùn thais
The hill-folk push east and build a banked enclosure at Dùn thais, on a hill above good grazing. It is the first stronghold of the Ròdaich away from Dùn ìseal and the Red Hill.
27 an Gearran, VE 7,798 Achadh chaol
Achadh chaol cleared
Fields are cleared at Achadh chaol in the east by fire and by picking stones. The picked stones are laid in banks round each field, and those banks bound the fields still.
29 am Faoilleach, VE 7,800 Cuan ruadh
Cuan ruadh rebuilt
Cuan ruadh, stripped by the Black Wind, is rebuilt in stone to the height of the eaves. It is the first settlement of the east coast to build its walls against the wind and not only the cold.
13 an Cèitean, VE 7,846 Cathair fhada
Cathair fhada on the south coast
Cathair fhada is founded on the south coast, between the old Seann Dunn and Seann Chwen. It draws its water from a well the Seann-Dhaoine dug, and never speaks of where the well came from.
14 an Giblean, VE 7,893 Caol ruadh
Caol ruadh on the southern strait
Fishing households settle Caol ruadh on the south coast and take the cod of the strait on long lines. Their middens are the first on the south coast to hold more fish than shell.
13 an t-Sultain, VE 7,939 Baile Mòr mhòr
Baile Mòr mhòr in the north
Houses are built at Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern plain, round a spring that never freezes. At its height it has some eighty houses, a great place for the age.
15 an Lùnastal, VE 7,985 Baile gharbh
Baile gharbh in the north-east
Households settle the rough ground at Baile gharbh and live by sheep, not cattle. Their wool goes south along the coast to the ford gathering.
17 an t-Iuchar, VE 8,032 Baile fhiadhaich
Baile fhiadhaich on the west coast
Settlers build at Baile fhiadhaich on the western coast, where boars run in the thickets. They hang boar tusks over their doors, and boar is their chief meat for the rest of the age.
18 an t-Ògmhios, VE 8,078 Cuan shean
Cuan shean settled
Ròdach households take up the harbour at Cuan shean on the west coast, beside an old landing of unknown builders, and use the landing without mending it.
7 am Faoilleach, VE 8,124 Dùn chrom
Dùn chrom raised
A banked hill-fort is raised at Dùn chrom in the midst of the island, between the Red Hill and the hills of the vein. Its bank faces both ways.
9 an Dùbhlachd, VE 8,170 Cathair mhòr
Cathair mhòr below the old outpost
Households settle on the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, where Cathair mhòr now stands. They take no stone from the ruin above them, though it is the nearest quarry.
10 an t-Samhain, VE 8,217 Cnoc naomh
Cnoc naomh
Households come to settle on a hill for its spring, and the hill is already called Cnoc naomh, the holy hill. Why, is not known.
12 an Dàmhair, VE 8,270 Tobar dhearg
Tobar dhearg on the southern cape
The keepers of the beacon at Tobar dhearg build their settlement on the cape itself, round a well whose water runs reddish from the rock. It becomes the greatest place on the south coast.
24 am Faoilleach, VE 8,309 Muileann naomh
Muileann naomh founded
Muileann naomh is founded near the south coast, between the beacon at Tobar dhearg and the old Seann Skell. Its first houses stand on stilts over a marsh, and are afterwards moved to firm ground.
26 an Dùbhlachd, VE 8,351 Ceann mhin
Ceann mhin on the south-eastern shore
The south-eastern Ceann mhin is settled near Làrach an Dùin. Its people are the first to live in sight of the fortress ruin, and they will not go up to it.
23 am Màrt, VE 8,402 Seann Skell
Seann Skell of the south
Ròdach households take up the old harbour at the southern Seann Skell and keep its old name. Within a few generations it is the busiest landing on the south coast.
21 an Giblean, VE 8,448 Achadh shean
Achadh shean resettled
Households return to Achadh shean after the drought and cut new fields on the higher ground. They sink a deep well first and plant after, and the well does not fail again in this age.
20 an Cèitean, VE 8,495 Inis mhin
Inis mhin settled
A few households settle at Inis mhin on the eastern coast. They live by the eggs and birds of the cliffs, and trade feathers inland.
18 an t-Ògmhios, VE 8,541 Muileann chaol
Muileann chaol on its hill
Households settle on the hill at Muileann chaol, above the upper reaches of the rivers. Where the library stands now there is a cattle-fold.
17 an t-Iuchar, VE 8,587 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Cairns on the hill at Muileann chaol
At Muileann chaol a cairn is raised for each head of a household at death, on the slope above the fold. By the end of the age some forty stand there.
15 an Lùnastal, VE 8,634 Baile Mòr ruadh
Baile Mòr ruadh in the east
Baile Mòr ruadh grows up near the eastern Seann Dunn, on land its people call empty. The middens of Seann Dunn lie a morning's walk away, and the settlers do not dig into them.
13 an t-Sultain, VE 8,680 Làrach an Teampaill
The temple ruin avoided
The Ròdaich of the eastern hills pass Làrach an Teampaill without stopping and take no stone from it. A path is worn round it at a distance.
12 an Dàmhair, VE 8,726 Còmhrag Ceann leathan
Ceann leathan's contests
At Ceann leathan the gathering by the wind-stones ends with wrestling and the lifting of stones. The heaviest, a black boulder, lies on the point still, and few have raised it.
3 an Lùnastal, VE 8,773 Fèill Muileann òg
The ford gathering grows
The ford gathering at Muileann òg now draws households from every coast. Its ground is parted by custom: the salt people downstream, the hill people upstream, the flint people on the far bank.
1 an t-Sultain, VE 8,819 Àth àrsaidh
Stone axes from the north
Axes of polished green stone from a quarry near Àth àrsaidh in the north-west are carried all over the island. They are too fine for work; most are laid unused in graves or under house floors.
13 an Giblean, VE 8,870 Àth àrsaidh
The quarry at Àth àrsaidh
The green-stone quarry at Àth àrsaidh is worked by a few households who trade in nothing else, and the chips about it lie knee-deep. Before the age ends the quarry is forsaken, and the axes cease.
19 an t-Sultain, VE 8,911 Doire ghlas
The moor takes the north
The oak falls back, as the pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows. Heather, birch and bog-moss spread over the northern lowlands, and the groves that give the north its many Doire names shrink to the sheltered valleys, where they stand yet. In the north this is remembered as the time the winters lengthened.
15 am Màrt, VE 8,951 Abhainn fhionn
The river crossings of Abhainn fhionn
Stepping-stones are laid across Abhainn fhionn at its shallows, the first made crossing of any river on the island. They are older than the first bridges, and in places lie beneath them.
10 an t-Ògmhios, VE 9,003 Abhainn chaol
A drowning at the fords of Abhainn chaol
A spate on Abhainn chaol takes a party of twelve crossing its fords with salt. Thereafter none crosses there in the wet season.
12 an Cèitean, VE 9,049 Ceann chiar
The Black Wind remembered at Ceann chiar
The people of Ceann chiar, rebuilding after the Black Wind, set a stone in the midst of their settlement and cut on it a mark for every house lost: twenty-two.
7 an Lùnastal, VE 9,094 Muileann bhàn
A dry year on the eastern plain
The rivers of the eastern plain run low for a whole summer, and the households of Dùn ìseal and Muileann bhàn drive their cattle to the warm springs to drink. The shared surplus holds, and no deaths are counted.
9 an t-Iuchar, VE 9,140 Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol
A second wave on the south coast
The sea comes in again over the low ground at Cnoc chaol, less far than before. The new houses stand higher on the slope, and none is lost.
4 an Dàmhair, VE 9,186 Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The ground shakes at Cill ghlas again
The old crack at Cill ghlas moves again, and the spring shifts back uphill. The line of white stones is broken in two places, and is laid again.
5 an t-Sultain, VE 9,231 Cnoc bheag
Cnoc bheag under the Carragh
Households settle on the bank of the Abhainn ìseal at Cnoc bheag, a short walk from Carragh Cnoc bheag. They set their houses so that no door faces the stone.
1 an Dùbhlachd, VE 9,278 Inis bhàn
The seal rocks of Inis bhàn
The households of Inis bhàn on the lower Abhainn ìseal take seals from the skerries off the river mouth by agreement, one household to a rock. A rock taken out of turn is the commonest quarrel in their tellings.
2 an t-Samhain, VE 9,323 Achadh mhòr
Fields at Achadh mhòr
The wide field at Achadh mhòr, near the warm springs, is cleared and banked, the largest single field of the age. Its bank is laid with the stones of an older wall that no one claims.
7 an Cèitean, VE 9,370 Baile ghlas
The harbour at Baile ghlas
The households of the Red Hill draw up their boats at Baile ghlas, along the lake shore from the hill, in sheds of stone and turf. It becomes the fishing harbour of the Red Hill.
5 an t-Ògmhios, VE 9,414 Achadh naomh
Achadh naomh's spring-fields
Settlers at Achadh naomh in the north water their fields from a spring they will not build over, and lead the water round it in channels. The spring is fenced before any house is.
10 am Màrt, VE 9,451 Caol gharbh
Caol gharbh on the rough strait
Households settle at Caol gharbh on the north-east coast and fish the strait in skin boats. They lay paddles beside their dead.
8 an Giblean, VE 9,506 Doire chiar
Doire chiar
A settlement grows up under the dark oaks at Doire chiar in the north. Its people pen pigs in the wood and drive them out to the acorns at the fall of the year.
11 am Faoilleach, VE 9,551 Caol shean
The river landing at Caol shean
Caol shean, on the Abhainn ìseal east of the vein, becomes the river landing of the hill households of the east. Salt, fish and seal-skins come up the river to it from the coast, and go on from it into the keepers' country.
9 an Gearran, VE 9,597 Dùn dhearg
Dùn dhearg raised
A hill-fort with a double bank is raised at Dùn dhearg, east of the vein, by households who owe nothing to Dùn ìseal. The Stone Kings' list does not name its holders; it says only that Dùn dhearg came not to the gatherings.
14 an t-Samhain, VE 9,644 Fèill Muileann òg
Dùn dhearg comes to the ford
In the time of Catrìona Mhòr the households of Dùn dhearg come to the ford gathering for the first time, bringing seal-skins and asking for salt. They are given ground of their own on the far bank.
13 an Dùbhlachd, VE 9,648 Àth fhiadhaich
Settlers at Àth fhiadhaich
Households settle at Àth fhiadhaich in the south-eastern hills, by a ford where wild cattle cross. They take the calves and rear them, and their herds become the best in those hills.
17 an t-Sultain, VE 9,651 Ceann àrsaidh
Ceann àrsaidh
Households from the Red Hill settle the point at Ceann àrsaidh on the Abhainn fhionn. They find an old river landing there and name the place for it: the ancient headland.
19 an t-Sultain, VE 9,651 Cnoc thais
Cnoc thais in the north-west
Households settle on the damp hill at Cnoc thais in the north-west and drain it with ditches. The ditches carry water still.
16 an Dàmhair, VE 9,651 Inis mhòr
Inis mhòr
Households settle Inis mhòr on the Abhainn ghorm in the north-east and live by the fish of its sheltered pools. They build their houses in two rows facing each other, the oldest street on Rodos.
27 an Giblean, VE 9,670 Baile gheal
Baile gheal in the south-west
Baile gheal is founded on the south-western plain round a house with white-limed walls. The lime is burned from the shells of the old middens along the coast.
26 an Cèitean, VE 9,670 Àth bheag
Àth bheag on the eastern coast
Households settle the small ford at Àth bheag on the far eastern coast, the easternmost dwelling of the age on the main island. Their boats go out after the geese on the islands.
26 an Cèitean, VE 9,670 Dùn ìseal
Catrìona Mhòr
Catrìona Mhòr, twelfth of the Stone Kings, holds Dùn ìseal; hers is the last name in the spoken list. It is told that she knew every household of the hills by its line seven names back.
23 an t-Iuchar, VE 9,670 Cathair dhearg
Seumas Òg of the Red Hill
Seumas Òg holds the Red Hill, and with him the spoken list of the Red Hill ends. In the next age what the reciters kept of it is written down.
23 an t-Iuchar, VE 9,670 Fèill Muileann òg
The two lists recited together
At the ford gathering, in the time of Catrìona Mhòr, the list of the Stone Kings and the list of the Red Hill are recited one after the other from the first name to the last. It takes from dusk to dawn. For the first time both are heard whole.
29 am Màrt, VE 9,673 Tobar dhìreach
Lots drawn for the slab
The lot for the keeper of the slab is drawn now among households from every part of the hills, not only those near the crack. The keepers' house at Tobar dhìreach becomes a place of pilgrimage.
28 an Gearran, VE 9,676 Tobar dhìreach
The keepers number nine
The keepers of the slab are made nine, one drawn by lot for each of nine districts of the hills. They meet at the slab when a keeper dies, and at no other time.
9 an Cèitean, VE 9,678
Ore in every hearth by the handful
Every household of the hills burns its handful of ore, measured in a copy of the stone cup, on one night in the dark of the year, the night later kept as Samhain. All burn at once by agreement, so that the colour shows on every hillside on the same night.
10 an Giblean, VE 9,681 Cnoc dhubh
A handful refused at Cnoc dhubh
The household of the Cnoc dhubh trench, where the two diggers were crushed, refuses its handful of ore for as long as any remembers. No household before it is known to have chosen not to burn at all.
4 an Dàmhair, VE 9,684 Dùn ìseal
Counting the households
The people of Catrìona Mhòr count the households of the hills by knots on a cord, a knot to a hearth. The cord of Dùn ìseal is said to have borne some nine hundred knots, the greatest count made on Rodos in this age.
2 an t-Samhain, VE 9,687 Calbh Cnoc ghorm
The saying on the column recut
The words on the column at Cnoc ghorm, worn shallow, are recut in their old grooves by a hand from the hill of the Stone Kings. Some later readers hold that the recutting changed a letter; none can prove which.
1 an Dùbhlachd, VE 9,690 Seann Dunn
The last Seann-Dhaoine midden disturbed
Households at the eastern Seann Dunn cut into the old midden for a house-floor and find the tally stones. They put them back in the order they lay and build elsewhere.
30 an Dùbhlachd, VE 9,693 Eilean ìseal
Eilean ìseal given to the dead
The households of the south-east coast begin to row their dead to Eilean ìseal, after the old manner of the Seann-Dhaoine. Whether they learned it from the Seann Vell graves on Eilean dhearg, or came to it of themselves, is not told.
10 an t-Ògmhios, VE 9,696 Eilean chrom
Gilleasbuig Beag's island
Eilean chrom, where Gilleasbuig Beag was left, stays empty and unfished. His fire is seen on it for three nights, the tellings say, and then no more.
9 an t-Iuchar, VE 9,699 Fèill Muileann òg
The keepers ask to be named
The nine keepers of the slab ask Catrìona Mhòr to declare their charge before the whole ford gathering, so that no king after her may draw the lot at Dùn ìseal. She neither refuses nor agrees, and the matter is left to the next age.
7 an Lùnastal, VE 9,873
The eve of the Binding
So ends the Ancient Age. The handful is kept everywhere in the hills, the keepers are nine, the sharing before the storms is kept on every coast, and the saying is spoken at every gathering. None of it is yet declared, and no god is yet named over the vein. With that naming the next age begins.

Age II · An Aois Naomh the Holy Age · the Flame Era, FE 1 – 2,960

23 an t-Sultain, FE 1
The Binding of the First Flame
Custody is declared over the vein, and the first flame is bound at Dùn ìseal: the undying flame of Brìde, kept over the stone of Crom Cruaich. Its keepers, Òrd Bhrìde, are the first order on Rodos to govern both rite and people, and they are older by centuries than any king.
28 an t-Ògmhios, FE 4 Dùn ìseal
Beathag Bhàn keeps the first flame
At Dùn ìseal under the central mountains the keepers of the slab and the households sworn to the Binding choose Beathag Bhàn to hold the first flame for Brìde and to answer to Crom for what is taken from the vein. The spoken roll of the Keepers begins with her name. Of her life before it nothing is remembered.
27 an t-Iuchar, FE 10 Dùn ìseal
The nine hearths
Nine households about the mountain's foot, one for each district of the old keepers of the slab, take the tending of the flame in turn, each sending a son or daughter to sit with it through a season. The later houses of custody all claim descent from one or another of the nine. Not all the claims can be true.
19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15 Dùn ìseal
Talla na Lasrach raised
A long hall of dry stone and turf is raised over the flame at Dùn ìseal, with one door toward the vein and none toward the sea. It is rebuilt many times on the same footings, and the footings are all of it that anyone can now swear to.
17 am Faoilleach, FE 21
Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach established
At the hearths the eldest of the island's folk-ways takes shape: reverence for the ancestors, for the vein, for the weather that rules the mining season, and for the sìth of the hills and mounds. It keeps no priests, and it has never ceased.
22 an Dàmhair, FE 27 Cnoc ghlas
The weather-cairns of Cnoc ghlas
Watchers build cairns on the ridge above Cnoc ghlas and read the cloud on the high passes from them, to tell the Hall when the galleries may be opened for the season. A wrong reading costs the whole mountain its season, and the watchers are chosen with more care than the Keeper.
20 an t-Samhain, FE 33 Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The ban on fires in sight of Doire uaine
In obedience to the old inscriptions the Keepers forbid any fire, of wood or of ore, to be lit in sight of the Doire uaine hills. Herders who winter on those slopes eat cold for the season. The ban is never lifted, and none is known to have owned to breaking it.
5 am Faoilleach, FE 34 Làrach an Teampaill
Làrach an Teampaill left unentered
Beathag Bhàn walks to Làrach an Teampaill, finds its altar already turned toward the mountain, and declares the place not the Hall's to keep. The Keepers set no foot in it for the rest of the age. Whose it was they did not say, and it seems they did not know.
3 an Gearran, FE 44 Dùn ìseal
Death of Beathag Bhàn
Beathag Bhàn dies at Dùn ìseal and is laid on the slope facing the vein, with her back to the sea. The nine hearths choose Muireach Liath, her sister's son, to keep the flame after her.
15 an Gearran, FE 48 Dùn ìseal
Ore by the basket
Muireach Liath fixes the first common measure for ore carried down from the galleries: a lidded basket of plaited heather, one to a household, filled once a season. Baskets of that weave are made at Dùn ìseal still, for no purpose but the making.
17 am Faoilleach, FE 53 Allt an Àigh
Allt an Àigh named
A stream is held to bring good fortune to any who drink of it in a certain quarter of the moon. Pilgrims come to it, and have never wholly ceased to come.
14 an Giblean, FE 57 Caol shean
The pilgrims' path from Caol shean
A path is worn from the river landing at Caol shean up the valley to Allt an Àigh. It is walked by night, so that pilgrims reach the water in the right quarter of the moon. Fishermen who walk it are said to lose fewer boats; no count was kept either way.
16 am Màrt, FE 59 Allt an Àigh
The Hall declines the stream
Muireach Liath rules that Allt an Àigh belongs to the ancestors and the weather and not to the vein, and that the Hall will not keep it. Here the Keepers' rite and the older folk reverence first plainly part, and each side afterwards cites the ruling as proof that it was right.
22 an Dàmhair, FE 66 Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The sick carried to Muileann ruadh
The sick are carried up in litters to the warm springs below Muileann ruadh and bathed at dawn. The Keepers allow it, for the heat of the water comes from the mountain and no one breaks the stone for it.
23 an t-Sultain, FE 71 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
Muileann chiar founded
A seam of silver is found near the great vein but apart from it. It is the first wealth of the island other than the ore.
20 an t-Samhain, FE 74 Muileann chiar
Fearchar Airgeadach works the silver
Fearchar Airgeadach, a basket-carrier of the nine hearths, is the first known to smelt the silver of Muileann chiar and hammer it into rings. His furnace burns wood and peat. It is the first fire on the island that answers to no one in the Hall.
19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 74 Muileann chiar
Silver is not holy
Asked whether the new seam falls under the flame, Muireach Liath answers that silver does not bleed and so is not the mountain's. Muileann chiar is left free to dig as deep as it likes, and it digs. Every later quarrel over the silver begins from these words.
28 an t-Ògmhios, FE 84 Ros fhionn
Silver for salt at Ros fhionn
Carriers take rings of Muileann chiar down to the river quays at Ros fhionn and trade them for salt fish and sealskin, one ring for a boatload. It is the first trade in anything but food, and the first whose price is remembered.
30 an Cèitean, FE 89 Dùn ìseal
Death of Muireach Liath
Muireach Liath dies at Dùn ìseal, keeping the flame. The nine hearths pass over three of other lines and choose his daughter Gormshuil nic Mhuirich. After her the Keeper's office stays in the house of Muireach for many generations.
11 an t-Sultain, FE 96 Dùn ìseal
Sliochd Mhuirich named
The kin of Gormshuil nic Mhuirich at Dùn ìseal begin to be called Sliochd Mhuirich, the house of Muireach, the first house of custody known by a name and not by a hearth. No account that survives tells of the other eight hearths objecting.
10 an Dàmhair, FE 103
The first school of the druids founded
The first of the Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, the druid schools, gathers about one question: why the vein answers some hands and not others. For the first time within the Old Faith the ore is reasoned about, and not only revered.
8 an t-Samhain, FE 110 Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
Sìleas nic Coinnich in the wood
Sìleas nic Coinnich, a cutter from Muileann chiar in the far east, begins to teach in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. At the galleries she had seen the ore bleed colour freely under some cutters' picks and sullenly under others, and she will not let the question be.
7 an Dùbhlachd, FE 118 Muileann chiar
The stag in the grove
The hearers of Sìleas nic Coinnich at Muileann chiar name themselves the stag's people, for a stag said to have stood in the grove through a whole lesson. The school's later name, the stag's name Camaran, and the telling that it was the white stag of Flidais, lady of the deer, are found first in writings far younger than these days.
18 an Cèitean, FE 125 Dùn ìseal
The Hall shuts the galleries to the stag's people
Gormshuil nic Mhuirich forbids the hearers of Sìleas to cut in the galleries of Dùn ìseal, holding that a question asked of the vein is a demand made of it. The stag's people keep their school in the east and send no cutters to the mountain for a long while after.
16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 132 Cnoc dhubh
The smoke at Cnoc dhubh
In a hard winter a household at Cnoc dhubh burns its ore by the basketful and not by the handful. The smoke settles in the valley, and three of the household and two neighbours die of it. The Keepers are sent for, and the case is argued at Dùn ìseal for the rest of the season.
15 an t-Iuchar, FE 139 Dùn ìseal
Fionnlagh Dall and the stone cup
Fionnlagh Dall, Keeper after Gormshuil, has the old keepers' stone cup cut anew in grey stone to hold just what a cupped pair of hands will hold, and sets it for the measure on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal. He is blind, and fills it by touch before the council, and none can say afterwards that he favoured anyone's hands.
13 an Lùnastal, FE 142
The Small-Burning Law
The custom of the handful is made law: no household may burn more than a measured handful of the ore in a season. It becomes the holy law of the Keepers of Brìde's flame and Crom's stone, and it holds for centuries.
1 an Cèitean, FE 145 Seann Tarr
The first sentence under the Law
A household of Seann Tarr burns twice its measure in a season and loses its right to the ore for the season after, the first sentence given under the Small-Burning Law. Its name is set on the roll with the offence beside it, and for many centuries its descendants petition to have the offence struck out.
30 an Cèitean, FE 148 Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
No ore on the beacons
The Keepers rule that no ore may feed a beacon, since a beacon burns for strangers. The fire on the headland at Tobar dhearg is kept with driftwood and seal fat, and so are all the sea-lights of the island after it.
4 am Màrt, FE 151 Ceann chaol
The carriers' path to Ceann chaol
A carriers' path is cut from the mountain down to the harbour of Ceann chaol, with steps hewn at the steep places. The Hall's baskets go down it to the southern households, and the dried fish of the south comes up.
3 an Gearran, FE 154 Abhainn dhomhain
The carriers drowned on the Abhainn dhomhain
The Abhainn dhomhain rises in the night and takes eleven carriers and their baskets at a ford. The Hall mourns the ore with the carriers, and Fionnlagh Dall asks the council for a way across that the river cannot take.
5 am Faoilleach, FE 157 Drochaid Cathair dhearg
The first bridges
Stone crossings begin to join the mining paths of the interior to the coast. From them in time come Drochaid Cathair dhearg and Drochaid Ros fhionn.
7 an Dùbhlachd, FE 160 Drochaid Ros fhionn
Ailean Clachair's crossing at Ros fhionn
Ailean Clachair and forty masons of the nine hearths bridge the river above Ros fhionn with a single span of fitted stone, from which Drochaid Ros fhionn descends. Ailean sets a hearth-sign in the keystone. Every bridge the masons build after bears one, and a bridge without it is not trusted.
8 an t-Samhain, FE 163 Ros dhomhain
The masons' custom
The bridge-masons form a fellowship bound by an oath sworn on the stone cup at Dùn ìseal: no span to be closed in the dark, and none to be paid for in ore. Their lodge is kept near the western crossing, in the country of Ros dhomhain.
10 an Dàmhair, FE 166 Am Buabhall Fortanach
The tavern roads begin
The first waypoint houses are raised along the mining roads. From them come in time Am Buabhall Fortanach, An Taigh-òsta Grianach and the others of the circuit.
11 an t-Sultain, FE 169 Am Buabhall Fortanach
Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house
Mòr nic Dhùghaill, a widow of Doire shean, keeps the first waypoint house on the site of Am Buabhall Fortanach. She serves the carriers jugged buffalo from her own herd, and the house has served it ever since.
13 an Lùnastal, FE 172 An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The house at the middle of the road
A second waypoint house is built where the carriers' road from the mountain meets the road to the western harbours, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. It is a turf longhouse with a hearth at either end, one for carriers going up and one for carriers coming down.
22 an Dàmhair, FE 175 An Sligeanach Fad' às
The road-peace
The keepers of the waypoint houses agree that no feud may be pursued under an inn roof or within a spear's throw of its door. The custom is first set down at the house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às. It is the oldest law on the island that no Keeper made.
23 an t-Sultain, FE 178 Seann Mhorn
Seann Mhorn resettled
Fishers of the nine hearths settle the harbour at Seann Mhorn and keep the name they find there, which is not of their own tongue; the old name came with the stones, they say. It is the first such name known to be taken over and not replaced.
20 an Dàmhair, FE 181 Seann Warr
Seann Warr resettled
Families walking the new road from the mountain settle the harbour of Seann Warr on the western shore of Loch chrom in like manner. They find house-footings there already, and build on them, as the carriers' song has it, without asking whose.
23 an Lùnastal, FE 184 Dùn ìseal
Death of Fionnlagh Dall
Fionnlagh Dall dies at Dùn ìseal. At his own asking he is not laid on the slope with the Keepers before him, but carried south to the old graves near Cnoc dhìreach, which no living people had yet claimed.
18 an t-Samhain, FE 184 Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
Fionnlagh Dall carried to the old graves
The bearers are eleven days on the road with the body of Fionnlagh Dall, and lay it at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach among graves older than any name. The Keepers after him cannot agree why he asked it; two answers are given, and neither is chosen.
21 an t-Sultain, FE 189
The mausoleum consecrated
Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, already ancient, receives its first burial that is set down by name. The burial-ground that no one claimed is claimed.
26 an t-Ògmhios, FE 194 Cnoc dhìreach
The grave-keepers of Cnoc dhìreach
A few families settle at Cnoc dhìreach to tend Tuam Cnoc dhìreach after the Keeper's burial. The Hall pays them in ore, a handful each a season, the only payment in ore the Law ever allows.
25 an t-Iuchar, FE 381 Dùn ìseal
Eilidh nic Ìomhair keeps the flame
The nine hearths choose a Keeper from outside the house of Muireach for the first time: Eilidh nic Ìomhair, of Dùn dhearg. Sliochd Mhuirich refuses for a season, then yields at Dùn ìseal, on the condition that the stone cup never leaves Talla na Lasrach.
29 an Giblean, FE 385 Dùn ìseal
The Four Houses sworn
Under Eilidh nic Ìomhair the office of Keeper is bound to four houses of custody: Sliochd Mhuirich of Dùn ìseal, Sliochd Ìomhair of Dùn dhearg, Sliochd Thormoid of Seann Dunn and Sliochd Raghnaill of Seann Tarr. The other hearths keep their seats on the council, but lose their claim to the flame. Most of the later nobility of the island descends from one of the four, or says it does.
28 an Cèitean, FE 389 Seann Dunn
The house of Tormod at Seann Dunn
Sliochd Thormoid raises a hall and a shrine at Seann Dunn, facing the mountain across the river. A lamp of ore burns in the shrine at the Law's measure. The other houses complain that the measure of Seann Dunn is always the fullest.
2 am Màrt, FE 393 Seann Tarr
The house of Raghnall at Seann Tarr
Sliochd Raghnaill takes for its seat Seann Tarr on the north-eastern coast, the town whose household was first sentenced under the Law. The house keeps boats and not galleries, and grows rich on the fishing.
31 am Màrt, FE 397 Eilean dhubh
Round Eilean dhubh
Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail round Eilean dhubh and come home, the first voyage made to see a coast and not to fish it. The house's songs name the steersman Tormod Ruadh. He brings back word of rock and birds, and of having gone, and of nothing else.
26 an t-Sultain, FE 401 Spùinneadairean-mara
The outlaws of the north-west waters
Households stripped of their right under the Law for a third offence take to boats, live off the north-western waters, and raid the fishing strands. They are called spùinneadairean, plunderers, and the name stays with those waters after them.
28 an Lùnastal, FE 405 Uilebheist na Mara
The boat lost off the north-west
A fishing boat out of Baile chrom is lost in calm water off the north-western coast. The two men who swim home say that something rose under it. Each year thereafter the boat's village keeps a wake for it. Of the thing they saw no more is told.
23 an t-Samhain, FE 409 Taigh-solais Baile chrom
The fire at Baile chrom relit
After the loss the fishers of Baile chrom light the old beacon on the point again, fed with driftwood as the Law requires. From it comes Taigh-solais Baile chrom.
25 an Dàmhair, FE 413 Seann Bhrenn
Seann Bhrenn resettled
Fishers from the north side of the mountain settle the harbour of Seann Bhrenn on the northern coast and keep its old name, as the western settlers kept Seann Warr's. They find a stone quay under the silt and use it.
20 am Faoilleach, FE 417 Cathair naomh
The ancestor-cairn at Cathair naomh
The people of Cathair naomh in the north raise a cairn for their dead on the hill above the town, and bring it a stone at every burial. It is the greatest ancestor-cairn in the north, and it grows still.
22 an Dùbhlachd, FE 421 Imrich nam Pantar
The panthers let pass
The crossing of the great cats is found to run straight over the carriers' southern road. Eilidh nic Ìomhair rules that no panther may be killed on the road in its season, and the carriers wait in the waypoint houses until the crossing is done. The rule is kept, for it costs the carriers only time.
19 am Màrt, FE 434 Dùn dhearg
The granaries of Dùn dhearg
Sliochd Ìomhair builds stone granaries at Dùn dhearg and fills them from the lowland fields, holding grain against the storm season as the old custom of sharing asks. So the house gains what the Hall never had: people who owe it their bread.
18 an Gearran, FE 448 Baile Mòr dhomhain
Baile Mòr dhomhain at the foot of the pass
Carriers who take the Hall's baskets north over the high pass settle at its southern foot, where Baile Mòr dhomhain now stands, to rest their beasts before the climb. The town lives by the pass, and by little else.
16 an Cèitean, FE 461
The reverent centuries
Generation after generation mines the same small measure and burns the same small measure, and the people neither grow nor dwindle. The rolls call them the reverent centuries.
17 an Giblean, FE 475 Seann Dunn
Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid keeps the flame
Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn becomes the first Keeper of Sliochd Thormoid. He keeps the flame longer than any Keeper before him, and changes nothing while he keeps it.
5 an t-Sultain, FE 488 Achadh chaol
The shepherds of Achadh chaol
Shepherds settle the upland fields at Achadh chaol in the north-east and send their wool down to the harbours. Their headman sits one season on the council at Dùn ìseal, is found to hold no hearth-right, and goes home.
4 an Dàmhair, FE 502 Làrach an Dùin-fhaire
The Keepers' count of the old places
Coinneach Mòr sends walkers to list the ruins of the old people. They bring back Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin, Làrach an Teampaill and the standing stones. The list says who does not own each place, and not who built it; the Keepers rule that it shall not guess.
2 an t-Samhain, FE 515 Carragh Cnoc bheag
The fence round Carragh Cnoc bheag
The people of Cnoc bheag set a ring of stakes round the old standing stone above their town, that the cattle may not rub against it. Every generation after renews the ring. The stone is never moved.
1 an Dùbhlachd, FE 529 Muileann ruadh
The bath-house at Muileann ruadh
A roofed bath-house is built over the warm springs below Muileann ruadh, with sleeping-places for the sick and their bearers. The Hall appoints a keeper of the springs, who tends them in the name of Dian Cècht, the healer. It is the first office the Hall makes that has nothing to do with the ore.
30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 542 Muileann chiar
The silver weights of Muileann chiar
The silversmiths of Muileann chiar cast a set of weights, the least the weight of a barley-corn and the greatest that of a newborn lamb. Every trader on the carriers' roads comes to use them, and for the rest of the age a thing weighed at Muileann chiar is said to be weighed fairly.
10 an Dùbhlachd, FE 556 Dùn ìseal
The market under the Hall
A market is held under the walls of the Hall at Dùn ìseal on the four quarter days, Samhain, Là Fhèill Brìde, Bealltainn and Lùnastal, when the households of the eastern hills come up with their dues. Hides, venison, charcoal, honey and the silver of Muileann chiar change hands there on the new weights. The Keepers allow no ore to be sold on their ground, and none is.
28 am Faoilleach, FE 565 Cnoc bhàn
The stag's people at Cnoc bhàn
A house of the stag's people is founded at Cnoc bhàn, north of the mountain, and after the long exclusion takes cutters again. Its teachers keep the question of Sìleas nic Coinnich as she left it: why does the ore bleed for one hand and not another?
26 an Gearran, FE 574 Dùn ìseal
Seonaid Chiar reopens the galleries to the stag's people
Seonaid Chiar, Keeper of the house of Muireach, lets cutters trained by the stag's people back into the galleries at Dùn ìseal, sworn to ask nothing of the vein aloud. The Hall's roll calls it a reconciling. The school remembers it as a truce.
27 am Màrt, FE 579 Cathair mhòr
Cathair mhòr walled
The people of Cathair mhòr on the southern coast build a wall of fitted stone about their headland town, the first town wall on the island. What they feared no one has told.
16 am Faoilleach, FE 584 Ceann leathan
Ceann leathan's fish-market
Ceann leathan becomes the market of the southern fishing and sends dried fish inland along the carriers' paths. Its harbour-master keeps tallies on notched sticks. Several are kept at Muileann chaol, the oldest counted things in its keeping.
14 an Gearran, FE 589 Inis thais
The shrine at Inis thais
A shrine to the ancestors lost at sea is raised at Inis thais on the western coast. Its keepers burn their season's handful on the shore and not indoors, so that the drowned, gone west over the sea, may see it.
29 an Giblean, FE 594 Cuan shean
Cuan shean's salt-pans
The people of Cuan shean on the western coast dig salt-pans on the flats below the town and boil sea-water over peat. Their salt goes inland along the western road and keeps the fish of half the island.
31 am Màrt, FE 599 Baile fhiadhaich
Salt-carriers on the heath above Baile fhiadhaich
Salt-carriers from Cuan shean settle on the western heath above Baile fhiadhaich, by a stream that runs all summer. The heath about it is not worth the plough, and its people keep goats.
2 am Màrt, FE 604 An Taigh-òsta Grianach
The sunny house
A waypoint house is built on the eastern road where the carriers from Cnoc leathan meet the southern coast path, on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach. It faces south, and from the first is known for its warmth, which is all its name has ever meant.
1 an Gearran, FE 609 Cnoc leathan
Cnoc leathan's market
Cnoc leathan, at the eastern end of the road past the sunny house, becomes the market town of the south-eastern hills. Its carriers' guild holds the right to carry for the Hall on the stretch down to the coast.
23 an Lùnastal, FE 614 Dùn ìseal
The fall in the high gallery
A roof falls in the highest gallery at Dùn ìseal and kills four cutters. The gallery is walled up and left. Seonaid Chiar orders props of oak set in every gallery after, and for the first time the Hall spends timber on the mountain.
25 an t-Iuchar, FE 634 Cathair dhomhain
Cathair dhomhain founded
Carriers settled at the mouth of the western road raise a town on the rise above the harbour and name it Cathair dhomhain. Its shrine keeps the Law's measure strictly, and its people are proud of it.
26 an t-Ògmhios, FE 654 Cathair dhearg
A fishing town at Cathair dhearg
The old settlement of the Red Hill, shrunk to a small fishing town, grows again at the western bridge-foot on the Abhainn dhomhain, a little above its meeting with the Abhainn gheal below Loch chrom. The ground is afterwards called Cathair dhearg, for its red stone. As yet it is a place carriers pass through on the way to somewhere else.
28 an Cèitean, FE 674 Dùn dhearg
Goraidh mac Ìomhair called rìgh
At Dùn dhearg the lowland households who eat from the granaries of Sliochd Ìomhair begin to call its head, Goraidh mac Ìomhair, their rìgh, their king. None before him was ever so called. Goraidh claims nothing over the vein, and is careful to tell the Hall so.
9 an t-Sultain, FE 694 Dùn ìseal
The division of keeping
The council at Dùn ìseal and Goraidh mac Ìomhair agree on a division. The Keeper keeps the flame and the galleries; the rìgh keeps the roads, the granaries and the peace of the lowlands. The rìgh may not enter the galleries, and the Keeper may not raise spears. On this division the island is governed for the rest of the age.
11 an Lùnastal, FE 714 Dùn dhearg
Goraidh Mòr's hall
Goraidh mac Ìomhair, called Goraidh Mòr, builds a timber hall on the hill at Dùn dhearg, with a granary at each corner. Its post-holes could still be seen when the surveyors of the Library walked the hill, and they measured and drew them.
22 an t-Sultain, FE 719 An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The first road-toll
Goraidh Mòr sets a toll on the carriers' roads, one fish in twenty or its worth, to pay the road-guards and keep up the bridges. The keepers of the waypoint houses gather it, and keep a share of it, and the rolls say so.
21 an Dàmhair, FE 754 Dùn dhearg
Mòrag of the Roads
Mòrag nic Ghoraidh takes the hall at Dùn dhearg after her father Goraidh Mòr. She is called Mòrag nan Rathad, Mòrag of the Roads, for in her first years she walks every carriers' road on the island and orders the bad stretches made anew.
26 an t-Iuchar, FE 781 An Taigh-seinnse Òir
The golden house
Mòrag nan Rathad has a waypoint house built on the road north of Seann Dunn, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Òir, to shorten the carriers' stage from the coast to the mountain. It is the first waypoint house raised by a ruler and not by a family.
24 an Lùnastal, FE 794 Drochaid Cathair dhearg
The bridge-foot rebuilt
At the bidding of Mòrag nan Rathad the western crossing of the Abhainn dhomhain is rebuilt in wider stone, so that two laden carriers can pass on it. The hearth-sign of Ailean Clachair is cut again in its keystone. From this time the town at the bridge-foot begins to grow.
16 am Faoilleach, FE 834 Dùn dhearg
Dòmhnall Crùbach
Dòmhnall Crùbach, Dòmhnall the Lame, follows his mother Mòrag at Dùn dhearg. He cannot walk the roads as she did, and rules through the keepers of the waypoint houses, who grow mighty in his reign.
14 an Gearran, FE 863 Ceann mhin
The waypoint-keepers of Ceann mhin
In the reign of Dòmhnall Crùbach the keepers of the waypoint houses about the harbour town of Ceann mhin take the gathering of the road-toll into their own hands and pay the rìgh what they judge fair. Their judgement is generous to themselves, and the rolls keep the sums.
19 an t-Samhain, FE 879 Baile àrsaidh
Baile àrsaidh on the western heath
Settlers from Cathair dhomhain take the wet heath of the west coast and found Baile àrsaidh, where the soil is thin and the yellow scorpions thick. They swear their oaths on a scorpion's sting kept in a box, and their neighbours think it a strange custom.
18 an Dùbhlachd, FE 879 Seann Chwen
The storm at Seann Chwen
A storm drives the sea over the harbour at Seann Chwen and takes the boats and a third of the houses. The Keeper sends the Hall's grain from Dùn ìseal, and Dòmhnall Crùbach sends his from Dùn dhearg. The survivors remember that the Hall's came first.
15 am Màrt, FE 914 Muileann chiar
The stag-letters
At Muileann chiar in the far east the teachers of the stag's people make the cutters' tally-notches into signs for sounds, so that a teaching may be kept without a teacher. These are the first letters the Ròdaich use: the ogham, which the druids call the gift of Ogma. From them come nearly all the later hands of the island.
12 an Cèitean, FE 914 Carragh Cnoc bheag
The letters set against the obelisk
Scholars of the stag carry their new letters to Carragh Cnoc bheag and set them beside the marks on the obelisk. They match nothing. The scholars write that the stone's makers were not their teachers, and that is the first thing the Ròdaich ever write of the old people.
10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 914 Dùn dhearg
Sìleas Dhonn
Sìleas Dhonn, niece of Dòmhnall Crùbach, holds Dùn dhearg after him. In her reign the keepers of the waypoint houses are bidden to render account of the tolls at her hall once a year, and several of them do.
14 an Gearran, FE 991 Caol leathan
The lords of Caol leathan
The harbour town of Caol leathan in the south-west grows rich on the western fishing and the southern end of the carriers' road. Its leading family, under Lachlann Ciar, takes the road-toll for itself and sends none of it to Dùn dhearg.
12 an Cèitean, FE 994 Dùn dhearg
Iain Garbh
Iain Garbh, Iain the Rough, son of Sìleas Dhonn, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and demands the western tolls of Caol leathan. Lachlann Ciar sends back a basket of fish-bones.
13 an Giblean, FE 999 Muileann òg
The War of the Roads begins at Muileann òg
Iain Garbh marches west with the road-guards and the lowland levies, and burns the toll-house at Muileann òg that the men of Lachlann Ciar had taken. It is the first war of Ròdach against Ròdach. The Hall will bless neither side.
19 an t-Samhain, FE 1,000 Dùn ìseal
Uisdean mac Ruairidh's refusal
The Keeper Uisdean mac Ruairidh refuses the messengers of Iain Garbh at Dùn ìseal the Hall's handful for the warband's hearths, saying that the flame does not warm men who go out to kill. The warband winters on peat. Iain Garbh never forgives the Hall, and never enters it.
21 an Dàmhair, FE 1,001 Àth fhiadhaich
The fight at Àth fhiadhaich
The men of Caol leathan meet the levies of Iain Garbh at the ford of Àth fhiadhaich and hold it for a day before they give way. Forty lie dead of both sides. Long afterwards the carriers call it the ford of the forty.
16 am Faoilleach, FE 1,002 Baile ghlas
Baile ghlas burned
The men of Lachlann Ciar, falling back on Caol leathan, burn Baile ghlas, that the levies of Iain Garbh may find no grain. Its people walk to Cathair dhomhain, and many never return.
18 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,003 Baile chiar
Baile chiar holds
Baile chiar, south of the western bridge-foot, shuts its gate on both hosts in the War of the Roads and feeds the burned-out folk of Baile ghlas through the winter. Neither side forgives it, and neither attacks it.
2 an t-Samhain, FE 1,005 Caol leathan
The siege of Caol leathan
Iain Garbh shuts Caol leathan in from the land for a season, but its boats bring in fish from the sea, and the harbour he cannot close. His levies begin to go home for the harvest, and the siege ends without an assault.
4 an Dàmhair, FE 1,006 Am Buabhall Fortanach
The peace at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house
Iain Garbh and Lachlann Ciar meet under the roof of the waypoint house that is afterwards Am Buabhall Fortanach, where by the road-peace neither may draw. Caol leathan keeps half its tolls and sends half to Dùn dhearg, and Lachlann Ciar swears to the Law before the Keeper's witness. So the War of the Roads ends in a house built to feed carriers.
12 am Faoilleach, FE 1,009 Caol leathan
The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan
Men who fought for Caol leathan become its road-guards and swear their watch on a white stone carved as a wolf, kept at the town gate. They call themselves the wolf-sworn. Later ages read more into the stone than they did, and call it Lia Fàil.
14 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,036 Caol fhiadhaich
Caol fhiadhaich rebuilt
Caol fhiadhaich on the south-western shore had sent its boats to feed Caol leathan through the siege. In thanks Lachlann Ciar gives it a share of the western tolls, and with it the town builds a harbour wall.
15 an t-Samhain, FE 1,044 Dùn dhearg
Death of Iain Garbh
Iain Garbh dies at Dùn dhearg. His daughter Catrìona buries him in the floor of the hall and not on the slope at Dùn ìseal, and the Hall does not ask for him.
17 an Dàmhair, FE 1,046 Dùn dhearg
Catrìona Ghlic
Catrìona Ghlic, Catrìona the Wise, rules from Dùn dhearg. She sends her own son to sit a season with the flame, the first child of the royal house to do so since the division of keeping. By the end of her reign the Hall and the hall are on speaking terms again.
8 an Cèitean, FE 1,081 An Leòmhann Buidhe
The house on the northern road
Catrìona Ghlic has a waypoint house built on the northern road above Inis mhòr, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe. It serves the carriers who take the Hall's baskets to the northern households and bring back wool.
9 an Giblean, FE 1,085 An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
The house on the cold road
A stone house is built on the open moor, on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and the northern coast, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, for carriers caught by snow. The Hall pays its keepers in grain and the crown in cloth, and they complain of both.
11 am Màrt, FE 1,089 Inis mhòr
Inis mhòr grows
The river port of Inis mhòr in the north becomes the gathering-place of the northern wool trade and outgrows every other northern town. Its people ask Catrìona Ghlic for a road-guard of their own, and are given one.
22 an t-Samhain, FE 1,122 Baile Mòr dhomhain
The market at the fords of Baile Mòr dhomhain
The lords of the deep river set a market at Baile Mòr dhomhain, where the carriers' road from the south meets the paths down from the hill pastures. Cattle, sheep, horses, hides and the white stone of the hills are sold at the fords on the day after each new moon, and the lords take one fleece in forty from the sellers.
10 an Gearran, FE 1,166 Muileann shean
Muileann shean on the northern road
A mill is built at Muileann shean on the northern road, to grind the grain the carriers bring over the pass, and a town grows round it. The Hall pays the miller in grain, and he pays the rìgh's toll in flour.
1 an t-Sultain, FE 1,211 Dùn dhearg
The unremembered rulers
Eleven rulers hold Dùn dhearg between Catrìona Ghlic and Ealasaid Chiar. The later king-list gives their names and their order, and nothing more. For the same years the Keepers' roll gives five Keepers, and of them too only the names.
3 an Lùnastal, FE 1,255 Muileann chiar
Tormod Scrìobhaiche learns the letters
Tormod mac Iain, a younger son of the house of Tormod, is sent east to Muileann chiar to learn the stag-letters. He is the first of the royal kin to read, and for the rest of his life he is called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the Writer.
22 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,299 Dùn dhearg
Ealasaid Chiar
Ealasaid Chiar takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and brings Tormod Scrìobhaiche there as her clerk. She bids him set down in order the name of every ruler of the hall that the reciters can give him.
20 an Lùnastal, FE 1,299
The first written king-list
Rulers are first set down by name, and no longer only remembered in tales. The rolls of succession in every later age are kept after this pattern.
18 an t-Sultain, FE 1,300 Dùn dhearg
The contents of Tormod's roll
Tormod Scrìobhaiche's roll, kept in the hall at Dùn dhearg, runs from Goraidh Mòr to Ealasaid Chiar. The earlier names he has from the reciters and the later from living memory, and he marks which are which. In three places it differs from the Keepers' spoken roll; Tormod writes down both readings and does not choose.
17 an Dàmhair, FE 1,320 Dùn ìseal
The Keepers' roll written down
Shamed, in the Hall's own words, by the rìgh's clerk, the Keepers have their spoken roll written in stag-letters at Dùn ìseal. It begins with Beathag Bhàn, and it is longer than Tormod's by several centuries.
15 an t-Samhain, FE 1,569 Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The watchers of the dark wood
A small company settles at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the wood never cleared, and keeps watch for a black horned beast that they say walks in it. The people of Cathair dhearg call them the wood-watchers. None of their own accounts is older than Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha, which afterwards claims them and takes the beast for a sign of Dubh Sainglenn, the black horse.
14 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,576 Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
The wood-watchers in the stag's grove
Wood-watchers come east and cut a black-barked tree in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, saying that the beast had shown it to them. The stag's people call it theft from a place of teaching. Both sides send to Dùn dhearg and to Dùn ìseal.
12 am Faoilleach, FE 1,581 Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The stag's people claim the dark wood
In answer the stag's people send teachers west to hold their lessons in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, saying that the first stag came from there. Now each side claims both woods, and in either wood the two companies meet and do not speak.
10 an Gearran, FE 1,589
The holy-wood dispute
Rival rites contend for Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the first such strife that is remembered. It is settled by dividing the keeping of the woods, and no side is judged the victor.
11 am Màrt, FE 1,595 Dùn dhearg
The boundary stones of the woods
The woods are divided at Dùn dhearg before Fearchar Òg, rìgh after Ealasaid Chiar, and the Keeper Calum Liath. The stag's people keep the eastern wood and the wood-watchers the western, and each may walk in the other's wood unarmed and without cutting. Boundary stones are set at the edges of both woods with the terms cut on them in stag-letters. Two of the eastern stones remain.
9 an Giblean, FE 1,602 Dùn ìseal
Calum Liath's surveyors
The Keeper Calum Liath sends cutters with knotted cords and lamps into every gallery at Dùn ìseal, to follow the vein as far as it can be followed and mark where it thickens and thins. The work keeps the cutters from the ore for three seasons, and the households go short to pay for it.
27 an t-Samhain, FE 1,607
The measuring of the vein
For the first time men try to reckon how much ore the mountain holds. Their reckoning proves far too hopeful.
26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,607 Dùn ìseal
The reckoning of the cords
The reckoning of Calum Liath is cut on a slab in the Hall at Dùn ìseal: the mountain can give every household its handful for more generations than there are grains in the granaries of Dùn dhearg. It is read out at the council and heard in silence, and the Hall takes the silence for assent.
22 an Gearran, FE 1,621 Dùn ìseal
The deaths in the lower gallery
Two youths of the nine hearths, sent into the lower gallery at Dùn ìseal without a Keeper's cutter to guide them, break the wrong face and are crushed. They had been less than a season in the galleries. Their families ask the council what the Hall owes them, and the council has no answer.
24 am Faoilleach, FE 1,628
The apprentice-binding custom
Young Ròdaich are first bound for seven years to a master of the vein's custody before they may go near the ore themselves. Every later guild of the mines is shaped on this binding.
21 an Giblean, FE 1,634 Dùn ìseal
Oighrig Bhàn's first bound
Oighrig Bhàn, Keeper after Calum Liath, binds the first twelve apprentices under the new custom at Dùn ìseal, each to a master cutter by name. They swear on the stone cup to serve seven years before they touch the vein. Four of the twelve are afterwards Keepers, which is the best that can be said for the custom.
23 am Màrt, FE 1,641 Cnoc bhàn
The stag's people take apprentices
The house of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn takes the seven years for its own cutters and adds a rule: an apprentice keeps a written account of every stroke, and the account is read. These strike-books are the school's chief record for the rest of the age.
18 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,647 Dùn dhearg
The long reign of Fearchar Òg
Fearchar Òg, who divided the woods, rules long at Dùn dhearg and is remembered chiefly for dying old. He was named Òg, the young, for coming to the hall as a boy, and the name stuck.
20 an Cèitean, FE 1,654 Muileann chiar
The silver tokens
The clerks of Fearchar Òg begin to pay the road-guards in small silver rings of the Muileann chiar weight, stamped with the hall's mark. It is the first payment in metal by any ruler on Rodos. The rings travel further than the guards do.
8 an Cèitean, FE 1,661 Àth ghlas
The toll-house at Àth ghlas
A toll-house is built on the ford at Àth ghlas, where the southern road crosses the river toward Ceann leathan, and the road-guards are paid there in the new silver rings. Its keeper is the first sent from the rìgh's hall, and not chosen in the place.
9 an Giblean, FE 1,665 Còmhrag Ceann leathan
The road-guards' games at Ceann leathan
The road-guards of the south begin to meet each year at Ceann leathan and fight with blunted staves for a silver ring. The meeting outlives its purpose, and on its field Còmhrag Ceann leathan is afterwards fought. The first winner whose name is kept is a woman, Mòrag Dhubh of Cnoc mhòr.
5 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,665 Fèill Muileann òg
The fair at Muileann òg
Muileann òg, burned in the War of the Roads, is rebuilt as a market town. A fair is held there each harvest at Lùnastal for the trade of the western and southern roads, and from it Fèill Muileann òg descends.
3 an Lùnastal, FE 1,665 Cidhe Beag
The landing on the Abhainn uaine
A landing for river-boats is built on the Abhainn uaine at the place since called Cidhe Beag, so that the grain of the lowlands may go upriver by boat and not on carriers' backs. The carriers of the eastern road protest to Fearchar Òg, and lose.
