11 am Màrt, FE 1,685 Abhainn uaine
The river-boats
Flat river-boats of hide over withy begin to carry grain and salt fish up the Abhainn uaine from the landing at Cidhe Beag. The boatmen form a fellowship of their own, sworn on a paddle, and vie with the carriers for the Hall's baskets.
8 an Cèitean, FE 1,685 Muileann chrom
The boatmen of Muileann chrom
Muileann chrom, up the valley from the landing at Cidhe Beag, becomes the home of the river-boatmen and their fellowship. Its yards build the flat hide boats for every river of the island.
6 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,685 Dùn dhearg
Beathag Mhòr
Beathag Mhòr, great-granddaughter of Fearchar Òg, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg. The list calls her banrìgh, queen, the first so called, and not rìgh with a woman's name after it; the change of word is the list's own.
12 am Faoilleach, FE 1,699 Baile Mòr fhionn
The fleece-measure of Baile Mòr fhionn
The lords of the western plain hold a market at Baile Mòr fhionn and make the fleece of a grown ewe its measure. Grain, wine, cattle and the horses of the plain are all priced in fleeces. The silver rings of Muileann chiar are taken there too, but reckoned in wool.
10 an Gearran, FE 1,699 Cathair dhearg
The hall moves to Cathair dhearg
Beathag Mhòr moves her hall from Dùn dhearg to the town at the western bridge-foot, Cathair dhearg, to sit where the roads, the river and the western harbours meet. Dùn dhearg keeps the old granaries and the graves of the house of Ìomhar. From this reign Cathair dhearg is the seat of rule on Rodos, whatever else changes.
22 an Gearran, FE 1,699 Dùn dhearg
Dùn dhearg after the move
Dùn dhearg, left behind, keeps its granaries and its pride. Its people go on calling it the rìgh's hill, and for many generations its reeves will send their accounts to Cathair dhearg in no hand but their own.
23 am Màrt, FE 1,699 Cathair dhearg
The red hall
Beathag Mhòr's hall at Cathair dhearg is built on the rise above the harbour, of the red stone that names the town. Its foundations lie under the later citadel. The masons cut the hearth-sign in its lintel as though it were a bridge.
9 an Giblean, FE 1,699 Cathair dhomhain
Cathair dhomhain against Cathair dhearg
The harbour of Cathair dhomhain, older and larger, grudges the new seat on its doorstep and refuses the queen's toll on its boats. Beathag Mhòr grants it a charter of its own tolls. The two towns, a few miles apart, are rivals for the rest of the age.
22 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,699 Dùn ìseal
Disputed hands
The council at Dùn ìseal is asked to judge more quarrels over the right to the handful than over anything else: new households, divided households, households that claim descent from one of the nine hearths without proof. Dùghall mac Raghnaill, Keeper after Oighrig Bhàn, asks the queen for a counting.
11 am Faoilleach, FE 1,735 Cathair dhearg
Beathag Mhòr orders the count
Beathag Mhòr and Dùghall mac Raghnaill agree that every household on the island claiming the handful shall be counted, its right proved or refused, and its name written. The clerks at Cathair dhearg are to write, and the Keepers to judge.
9 an Gearran, FE 1,735 An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The waypoint houses as counting-houses
The counters make their stations at the waypoint houses, for every household on the island lies within a day of one. The keepers of the houses feed the counters at the queen's cost, and in the houses the count is afterwards remembered as a good year.
22 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,735
The census of hands
The households that hold the old right to burn the ore are counted across the whole island for the first time. So it is shown that the burning of the ore was already rationed by rule.
21 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,735 Cathair dhearg
The count of hands
The rolls of the count, kept at Cathair dhearg, give eleven thousand four hundred households holding the right, and some two thousand whose claims were refused. The refused are written on a roll of their own, and it is that roll later generations search when they would prove an ancestor's standing.
19 an Lùnastal, FE 1,735 Seann Tarr
The refused of Seann Tarr
Most of the refused households of the north-eastern coast are fisher-families about Seann Tarr who had never burned ore at all, and now find they have no right to begin. Sliochd Raghnaill takes up their cause at the council and loses. The fisher-families burn peat and say it is warmer.
17 an t-Sultain, FE 1,735 Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
The light at Baile ìseal
The old beacon on the eastern point at Baile ìseal is rebuilt, kept with driftwood and seal fat as the Law requires, to bring the fishing boats of the eastern coast home in the dark. From it comes Taigh-solais Baile ìseal.
16 an Dàmhair, FE 1,735 Taigh-solais Muileann bheag
The light at Muileann bheag
The old beacon on the northern headland at Muileann bheag is rebuilt; from it comes Taigh-solais Muileann bheag. Its keepers are fisher-families of the north-west, who pay no toll to Cathair dhearg in return for keeping it.
14 an t-Samhain, FE 1,735 Taigh-solais Àth dhearg
The light at Àth dhearg
Sliochd Raghnaill rebuilds the old beacon on the north-eastern cape at Àth dhearg, to mark the way in toward Seann Tarr. From it comes Taigh-solais Àth dhearg.
13 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,735 Dùn dhearg
Death of Beathag Mhòr
Beathag Mhòr dies at Cathair dhearg and by her own command is carried back to Dùn dhearg to lie among the house of Ìomhar. No royal journey before it was so long.
24 an Cèitean, FE 1,736 Cathair dhearg
Ruairidh Liath
Ruairidh Liath, son of Beathag Mhòr, rules from Cathair dhearg. He is grey already when he takes the hall, and his byname is the list's one jest.
19 an Lùnastal, FE 1,745 Muileann chiar
The Silver Feud begins
Ruairidh Liath demands one ring in five of the silver taken at Muileann chiar, saying the tokens that pay his guards should cost him nothing. Sliochd Fhearchair, the silversmiths' house, answers with Muireach Liath's ruling: silver is not holy, and so not the crown's either. They close the workings sooner than pay.
17 an t-Sultain, FE 1,746 Muileann chiar
The closing of the silver
For three seasons no silver leaves Muileann chiar. The road-guards go unpaid, the fair at Muileann òg trades in grain again, and the tolls of the eastern road go ungathered. It is called the Silver Feud, though no one is killed in it.
16 an Dàmhair, FE 1,749 Dùn ìseal
The Keeper's judgment on the silver
At the asking of both sides the Keeper Dùghall mac Raghnaill rules at Dùn ìseal that the words of Muireach Liath stand, and silver is not the mountain's; but also that the crown keeps the roads the silver travels. Ruairidh Liath takes one ring in ten, Sliochd Fhearchair opens the workings again, and each calls it a victory.
14 an t-Samhain, FE 1,750 Muileann chiar
The Muileann chiar weight made law
In the settlement the silver weights of Muileann chiar are declared the only lawful weights on the roads of the island. Copies in bronze are sent to every waypoint house, and the house of Fearchar is paid for each.
25 an Giblean, FE 1,781 Muileann dhearg
The bronze-casters of Muileann dhearg
The bronze copies of the Muileann chiar weights are cast at Muileann dhearg, where a family of casters learned the craft from the silversmiths. They go on to cast bells, pins and lamp-bowls, and their lamp-bowls hold the Law's measure exactly.
24 an Cèitean, FE 1,781 Cathair dhearg
Seonag Chrom
Seonag Chrom, granddaughter of Ruairidh Liath, rules at Cathair dhearg. She gives the clerks a room of their own in the red hall and a wage in silver, and from her reign the king-list is kept year by year and not reign by reign.
22 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,854 Inis bheag
Inis bheag's school of letters
At Inis bheag on the Abhainn bheag in the north a teacher of the stag's people begins to teach letters to fishers' children who will never cut ore. It is the first teaching of letters for their own sake. The Hall's roll notes it, and adds that fish do not need reading.
21 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,926 Cathair dhearg
Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall
Peigi nic Tormoid, of the line of Tormod Scrìobhaiche, is clerk of the hall at Cathair dhearg, the first whose own hand can be told from the others in the copies that survive. Her entries are short, and she never gives a reason where a fact will serve. Much of what is known of the middle of the age is in her hand, or copied from it.
30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,999 Seann Skell
The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell
At Seann Skell on the northern coast the fowler families keep a hawk in every household and feed it before the household eats. They burn their season's handful at dawn with the hawk on the wrist, for the flame, they say, is a hunger and should be fed as a hunger is fed. They call the hawk Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, the grey hawk of time, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, eldest of men, who lived down the ages as a salmon, an eagle and a hawk; between them the two remember all things. From them Òrd an t-Seabhaig counts its beginning.
28 am Faoilleach, FE 2,072 Inis ìseal
The hawk-rite spreads up the Abhainn ìseal
The dawn burning with the hawk spreads from Seann Skell on the northern shore up the Abhainn ìseal to Inis ìseal and Cnoc bheag. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal writes that the rite keeps the measure exactly and is therefore no concern of the Hall. Never again does the Hall say so of any rite.
1 am Faoilleach, FE 2,145 Ros bheag
The sting-oath at Ros bheag
The swearing on a scorpion's sting spreads from Baile àrsaidh up the western coast to Ros bheag, and the harbour court there takes it for every oath of trade. For the rest of the age a merchant who will not swear on the sting is not trusted in the western harbours.
3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,217 Inis thais
The wolf-stone at Inis thais
The wolf-sworn road-guards of Caol leathan set a second wolf-stone at the shrine of Inis thais, and the keepers of the shrine begin to pray before it as well as to the drowned. The stone is white quartz, dragged from the mountain on a sledge at a cost greater than the shrine's.
28 an Gearran, FE 2,290 Cnoc bhàn
The strike-books compared
Donnchadh mac Iain, a teacher of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn, reads through the strike-books of many generations of apprentices. He finds that the ore bleeds brighter for cutters in their later years than in their first, whatever their house, and argues that the vein answers practice. The elders answer that it answers what a cutter was born with, and that practice only shows it.
30 am Faoilleach, FE 2,300 Muileann chaol
Donnchadh mac Iain leaves Cnoc bhàn
Donnchadh mac Iain and twenty-two of his hearers leave the house at Cnoc bhàn and settle at Muileann chaol, taking copies of the strike-books with them. The elders of Cnoc bhàn call it theft of the books. Donnchadh calls it copying, which it is.
7 an t-Sultain, FE 2,317
The founding of the rival druid school
A school of druids breaks away, holding that the vein answers labour and not birth. Centuries later the Long War is fought over the same question in another shape.
9 an Lùnastal, FE 2,330 Muileann chaol
The school at Muileann chaol
The school of Donnchadh mac Iain at Muileann chaol keeps strike-books of its own under a rule the elder school never had: a cutter's parentage is not written in the book at all. The two schools of the stag dispute by letter for the rest of the age, and both keep the letters.
4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,366 Dùn ìseal
The Hall hears the two schools
The Keeper Raonaid Dhubh hears both schools of the stag at Dùn ìseal and gives no ruling, saying that the vein has not asked the Hall to decide. The Hall's roll sets down the hearing and the refusal. No refusal of the Hall is more often cited.
6 an Dàmhair, FE 2,376 Calbh Cnoc ghorm
What the people of Cnoc ghorm say of their stone
Scholars of the stag from Muileann chaol come to Calbh Cnoc ghorm and cannot read it. The people of Cnoc ghorm tell them the stone says: we did not come; we were here. The scholars write that the people say so. No later hand explains either the stone or the saying.
21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,386 Làrach an Dùin
The digging at Làrach an Dùin
Men of Baile ghorm dig under the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin for the riches the ruin was said to hold, and find ash and nothing else. The Keeper has them sentenced as if they had broken the Law, though no law covered it, and the sentence stands as the rule for all the old places after.
23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,391 Baile ghorm
Baile ghorm's penance
The families of the diggers at Baile ghorm do penance by keeping in repair the road from their town to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach. In the southern hills it is called the diggers' road still.
16 am Faoilleach, FE 2,406 Cathair dhearg
Lachlann Bàn
Lachlann Bàn takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. He builds granaries in every province seat that will have one, and makes a law about them, and for these he is remembered.
14 an Gearran, FE 2,411 Cathair dhearg
The shared-meal law written
Lachlann Bàn and the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh make the old unwritten custom law at Cathair dhearg: a household with grain above its winter's need gives the surplus to the common granary of its district before the storm season, and the granary feeds any household of the district that runs short. The successors of Peigi nic Tormoid write it into the rolls in full. It is the first law made by rìgh and Keeper together.
19 an t-Samhain, FE 2,425 Cnoc mhòr
The granary of Cnoc mhòr
Cnoc mhòr builds its common granary under the new law before any other district, and sends word of it to Cathair dhearg. Lachlann Bàn sends back a silver ring for the reeve.
18 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,435 Muileann chiar
The common granaries of the mountain
Common granaries are raised under the new law in the mountain districts round Muileann chiar, where the households live by cutting and carrying and grow little of their own. The lowland districts grumble at filling them.
12 an Cèitean, FE 2,445 Cathair mhòr
The granary at Cathair mhòr
A common granary is built within the old wall at Cathair mhòr, the first behind a town wall. The southern fishing towns, having no grain, send dried fish to it for their share.
10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,455 Spùinneadairean-mara
Raiders in the eastern waters
Outlaws in boats raid the eastern fishing strands from the islets offshore, taking dried fish and nets. Sliochd Raghnaill arms its boats at Seann Tarr and burns two of the raiders' boats. The rest escape.
15 am Màrt, FE 2,461 Cathair dhearg
Oighrig nic Lachlainn
Oighrig nic Lachlainn, daughter of Lachlann Bàn, takes the hall at Cathair dhearg. She has no children, and before her reign is half done the houses begin to count their claims.
13 an Giblean, FE 2,472 Cnoc ghlas
The late snow on the high passes
The weather-watchers on the cairns above Cnoc ghlas see snow lying on the high passes long past the opening of the galleries. The Hall keeps the galleries shut for the cutters' safety, and the mountain households wait.
5 an t-Sultain, FE 2,472 Muileann chiar
The poor season in the mountain
The galleries open late and close early, and the ore carried down is a third of a common season's. The mountain households of Muileann gheal, Doire uaine and Àth dhìreach, who trade their carrying for grain, have nothing to trade, and by the season's end they are eating their seed.
4 an Dàmhair, FE 2,473
The first recorded famine averted
A poor mining season brings three settlements near to starving. The shared-meal law, made a generation before, holds and saves them. It is the first true trial of the custom.
15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,473 Muileann gheal
The granaries opened
Under the shared-meal law the common granaries of the mountain districts are opened at Muileann gheal. When they run low the granaries of Dùn dhearg and the southern coast send grain up the carriers' roads without being asked twice, and the carriers bear it for no fee. None in the three settlements is known to die of hunger that winter.
18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,474 Àth dhìreach
Àth dhìreach after the poor season
At Àth dhìreach, one of the three settlements the granaries fed, the carriers who brought up the grain are given the right to rest in any house of the town without payment for as long as they live. The last of them dies old, and the right with him.
16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,474 Dùn dhearg
The reeves of Dùn dhearg send the grain
The reeves of Dùn dhearg, who had withheld their accounts from Cathair dhearg for generations, open the old granaries of the house of Ìomhar to the mountain without waiting for an order. Oighrig nic Lachlainn writes that she would have given the order had they waited. The successor of Peigi nic Tormoid notes that they did not.
19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,511 Cathair dhearg
Death of Oighrig nic Lachlainn
Oighrig nic Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg with no heir of her body, and with her ends the line of Goraidh Mòr, as the list reckons it. The red hall is shut, and its clerks keep it.
10 an Giblean, FE 2,513 Dùn ìseal
The four houses meet
The Four Houses of custody meet at Dùn ìseal to choose a ruler, for no custom covers a hall without an heir. Sliochd Ìomhair claims it by blood, Sliochd Thormoid by the clerks, Sliochd Raghnaill by its boats. Sliochd Mhuirich, holding the Keeper's office, makes no claim.
12 am Màrt, FE 2,516 Seann Dunn
The election of Gilleasbuig Mòr
The houses choose Gilleasbuig Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn, a grandson of the clerks' line, to hold the red hall. The Keeper sets the stone cup in his hands before the council, and so for the first time a ruler is made at Dùn ìseal. Sliochd Ìomhair consents, on condition that its graves at Dùn dhearg remain the burying-place of the kings.
11 an Gearran, FE 2,517 Cathair dhearg
Gilleasbuig Mòr at Cathair dhearg
Gilleasbuig Mòr takes the red hall. He keeps the clerks' office in the hands of his own house and has the king-list copied again from the beginning, with a line drawn beneath Oighrig nic Lachlainn. The line is in every later copy.
13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,537 Seann Dunn
The shrine at Seann Dunn enlarged
Gilleasbuig Mòr enlarges his house's shrine at Seann Dunn into a temple with a court for pilgrims. The other houses say still that its ore-lamp burns fuller than the measure, and every season a Keeper's cutter is sent to try it.
27 an Giblean, FE 2,541 Dùn dhearg
Death of Gilleasbuig Mòr
Gilleasbuig Mòr dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried among the house of Ìomhar at Dùn dhearg, as was agreed. His son Tormod Òg follows him without a meeting of the houses, and none asks for one.
29 am Màrt, FE 2,558 Cathair dhearg
The gap in the list
Nine rulers of the house of Tormod reign between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh, and the king-list at Cathair dhearg gives their names and years and little else. The successors of Peigi nic Tormoid were diligent and brief; for these reigns the rolls tell mostly of harvests, tolls and the mending of bridges.
24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,571 Drochaid Cathair dhearg
The bridge at Cathair dhearg widened
The bridge at Cathair dhearg is rebuilt a third time, wide enough now for a cart, for carts have come onto the lowland roads. The hearth-sign is cut again in the keystone. The span stands on the piers of Mòrag nan Rathad.
24 an Giblean, FE 2,583 Dùn dhearg
Riders on the lowland roads
The road-guards of Dùn dhearg begin to ride the lowland roads on the small horses of the southern grass country, and a guard can now reach a waypoint house before a quarrel there has cooled. They are the first riders whose names are kept, and for long the only ones.
23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,598 Drochaid Ros fhionn
The crossing at Ros fhionn repaired
A flood takes the eastern approach of Ailean Clachair's span above Ros fhionn, and it is mended. The masons find their founder's hearth-sign still sharp in the keystone, and leave it untouched.
21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,613 Dùn chrom
The bridge at Dùn chrom
The masons' fellowship bridges the river below Dùn chrom, joining the southern road to the western without the long way round by Cathair dhearg. The toll is set at half the road-toll, and Cathair dhearg complains.
19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,628 Ceann àrsaidh
The bridge at Ceann àrsaidh
A bridge is built at the river town of Ceann àrsaidh, the fourth stone crossing of the lowlands. The masons' roll names the forty who built it, all of the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill, who had learned the craft while the boats lay idle.
18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,643 Doire mhin
The bridge at Doire mhin
The masons' fellowship builds a small bridge at Doire mhin to carry the southern road over a stream that floods each spring. Beside the hearth-sign in the keystone is cut the name of Beathag Clachair, who cut it: the first mason's mark known.
16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,658 An Sligeanach Fad' às
The far-off house
The waypoint house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às, the oldest house under the road-peace, is rebuilt in stone. It lies so far from any town that the carriers say one is never nearer to it than halfway, and from the saying it takes its name.
15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,672 An Leòmhann Buidhe
Fire-water on the northern road
The house on the northern road, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe, begins to serve a spirit distilled from barley that the carriers call fire-water. The Keepers rule that it is not a burning and no concern of theirs. The house's trade doubles.
13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,687 Caol mhòr
Caol mhòr in the north-west
The fisher-families of the north-west gather at Caol mhòr under a headman of their own, and send tolls to Cathair dhearg only in the years the road-guard comes to take them. Little is written of the north-west in this age, and most of it is complaint of that.
4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,702 Ceann mhòr
Seal-oil from Ceann mhòr
Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast begins to trade seal-oil down the western coast to Ros bheag for silver rings, and its beacons burn it. For many generations the seal-oil lamps of the western harbours are the brightest light on Rodos.
3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,717 Muileann leathan
The high pastures of Muileann leathan
Herding families take the high pastures above Muileann leathan in the north and keep sheep there for the wool of Inis mhòr. They hold no right to the handful, have never held one, and are not counted in the census of hands.
30 am Faoilleach, FE 2,732 Inis mhin
Inis mhin on the northern shore
Inis mhin, a fishing harbour on the northern shore, comes into the rolls for the first time when its headman goes to the wool-fair of Inis mhòr to complain of the road-guard's toll. The complaint is written down in full, and it is all that is written of the town in this age.
28 an Gearran, FE 2,747 Spùinneadairean-mara
The raid on the western strands
Raiders from the north-western waters take a season's dried fish from the strands of the north-western coast. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag pay for two armed boats to watch the strands, and the raiders move north.
29 am Màrt, FE 2,761 Uilebheist na Mara
The second sighting
Two boats of Baile chrom tell of something vast moving beneath them in the north-western water, the second such sighting remembered. One boat does not come home. The wake that Baile chrom keeps for the first loss is kept now for both.
27 an Giblean, FE 2,776 Seann Tarr
Round the islands
Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail from Seann Tarr round the offshore islands, Eilean ruadh, Eilean dhearg and Eilean fhada among them, and come home in one season. No crew of the age goes further from the coast than the islands, and none is known to have wished to.
26 an Cèitean, FE 2,791 Eilean ruadh
Summer herders on Eilean ruadh
Families from the coast take sheep over to Eilean ruadh for the summer grazing and bring them back before the storms. They build turf shelters there, which later herders use again.
24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,806 Cathair dhearg
Anna Ruadh
Anna Ruadh of the house of Tormod takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. She walks the whole circuit of the roads, the first ruler to do so since Mòrag nan Rathad, and she walks it twice.
23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,809 Am Buabhall Fortanach
Anna Ruadh at Am Buabhall Fortanach
On her first circuit Anna Ruadh stops at the house on the site of Am Buabhall Fortanach, where the War of the Roads was ended, and eats the jugged buffalo like a carrier. The keepers of the house tell of it still.
21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,813 An Taigh-òsta Grianach
Anna Ruadh at the sunny house
On the eastern road Anna Ruadh lodges at the house on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach and grants its keepers a toll of their own for the upkeep of the road to Cnoc leathan, Slighe Cnoc leathan. No other waypoint house on the island holds a royal charter.
12 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,816 Ceann mhin
Anna Ruadh at Ceann mhin
At Ceann mhin on the south-eastern coast Anna Ruadh hears the quarrel of the fishers and the carriers over who may carry dried fish up to the mountain, and rules that both may. The fish going inland is doubled, and its price at Dùn ìseal halved.
11 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,819 Ceann leathan
The contest at Ceann leathan in stone
Anna Ruadh gives the road-guards' contest at Ceann leathan a stone-walled field, and for its prize a silver ring from the red hall. Fighters come to it from all the south, and the losers are fed at the crown's cost.
23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,822 Cathair dhearg
A wood-watcher in the red hall
Anna Ruadh keeps a wood-watcher from Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag in her household at Cathair dhearg to read the omens of the hall. So the rite of the wood-watchers, the rite of Macha, goddess of sovereignty and of horses, first comes to the capital. The Keeper sends a protest from Dùn ìseal, and the rolls give no answer.
24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,826 Cathair dhomhain
Cathair dhomhain and the wood-watchers
The shrine at Cathair dhomhain, proud of its strict keeping of the Law, will take no wood-watcher, and its people say that the capital has given its omens to folk who sit in trees. From this the rivalry of the two towns takes a turn in matters of faith that it never loses.
26 an Cèitean, FE 2,829 Cathair dhearg
Death of Anna Ruadh
Anna Ruadh dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Dùn dhearg among the house of Ìomhar and the kings of her own house. Her son Coinneach Bàn takes the hall.
27 an Giblean, FE 2,832 Cathair dhearg
Coinneach Bàn
Coinneach Bàn rules long and quietly from Cathair dhearg. In his reign the clerks of the hall begin to copy the rolls for the provinces, so that each province seat has its own copy of the laws. Several of those copies survive where the first writings are lost.
16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,835 Dùn ìseal
Seumas Bàn keeps the flame
Seumas Bàn of Sliochd Mhuirich is chosen Keeper. Reading the Hall's roll at Dùn ìseal he finds that more than half the Keepers of the age were of his own house, and has the fact struck from the preface. The unstruck copy survives.
18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,838 Dùn ìseal
The rites counted at Dùn ìseal
Seumas Bàn has the clerks of the Hall list every rite on the island that burns the handful and every one that lays claim to the vein, that the council may know what it keeps. The list holds the Hall's own rite, the ancestor-keeping of the old folk, the dawn-hawk of the north coast, the wood-watchers of the west, the wolf-sworn, the sting-oath, and both schools of the stag. The clerks write that a thousand years before no such list would have been needed.
19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,840 Seann Skell
The hawk-keepers refuse the Hall's cutter
The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell turn away the Hall's cutter who comes to try their measure, saying their measure is the hawk's, and the hawk is not the Keeper's. The cutter goes home with the refusal in writing. No rite had refused the trial of the measure outright before.
21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,843 Caol leathan
The wolf-sworn build a hall
The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan build a hall of their own about the white wolf-stone at the town gate, and swear oaths there that are no longer road-guards' oaths. The stone, they say, watches the whole island as the guard watches the road, and will cry out beneath the rightful king. From this hall comes Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone, and the wolf-sworn begin to be called the Fianna.
3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,846 Seann Skell
The sting-oath at Seann Skell
At Seann Skell in the west the sting-oath of the harbour court becomes a creed. Its keepers hold that one power stings the liar wherever he may be, Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, and that the scorpion is but his sign; theirs is the first teaching on the island to call itself the only true one, and the Hall's roll sets it down as new. Thereafter the oath is sworn over a cup marked with the scorpion, Manannan's Cup of Truth, which is said to break in three at three lies spoken over it and to be made whole by three truths. Òrd Mhanannain dates itself from this court.
4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,849 Seann Vell
Seann Vell swears on the sting
Seann Vell, on the western coast below Cuan shean, takes up the sting-oath of its neighbours. Its shrine keeps a scorpion carved in yellow stone, the first image of the creature made for worship and not for swearing on.
13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,852 Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The dark wood keeps its own rite
The wood-watchers of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag cease to send to the Hall for judgement of their quarrels, and judge them under the trees. They hold that the black beast has two natures, one that keeps and one that devours, and that the vein has the same. The order of Macha afterwards tells of the two horses that drew one chariot, the black Dubh Sainglenn and the grey Liath Macha: two horses, one yoke.
11 an Gearran, FE 2,855
The common root of the orders
The one folk-faith of the island begins plainly to divide into the several ways that later ages name apart: the orders of An Creideamh Sean, the Old Faith, and the hearth-keeping of Na Seann Spioradan, the Old Spirits. From this time the belief of the Ròdaich is no longer one.
16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,858 Dùn ìseal
The council divided by rite
The council at Dùn ìseal, which had sat by hearth and by house, begins to sit in companies by rite. Seumas Bàn complains that he keeps the flame now for eight peoples, each of whom thinks itself its only keeper. The seating holds for the rest of the age.
15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,860 Allt an Àigh
Allt an Àigh keeps its pilgrims
Pilgrims of every rite go on walking to Allt an Àigh in the right quarter of the moon; it is the one custom of the island that the Hall's list sets under no company. In one season the path from Caol shean is paved anew by pilgrims of four rites.
19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,863 Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The springs at Muileann ruadh common to all
The keeper of the springs at Muileann ruadh rules that the sick of every rite shall be bathed without asking which. Her ruling is copied into the rolls of the provinces. It is the last ruling of the age on which every company of the council agrees.
18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,866 Cnoc dhìreach
Cnoc dhìreach's weavers
The town of Cnoc dhìreach in the east, on the carriers' road south of the springs, becomes known for a heavy undyed cloth that the carriers wear on the high passes. It is not the grave-keepers' village by the old tombs, and the rolls tell the two Cnoc dhìreachs apart by that cloth.
23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,869 Muileann bhàn
The dyers of Muileann bhàn
The dyers of Muileann bhàn in the eastern hills learn to fix a pale blue from a hill plant, and the carriers' cloth of all the mountain country is dyed there. The Keepers wear it undyed, and say so.
21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,872 Muileann dhomhain
Muileann dhomhain's mill
A water-mill is built at Muileann dhomhain in the eastern hills to grind the grain of the common granaries of the mountain districts. The miller keeps one measure in sixteen, and the rolls call it fair.
26 an Cèitean, FE 2,875 Àth chiar
The flood at Àth chiar
Rain on the eastern hills brings the river over the ford at Àth chiar, and it carries off the carriers' shelter and six of the townsfolk. The common granary of the district stands on a rise, is untouched, and feeds the town through the winter.
24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,878 Seann Bhral
The oyster-beds of Seann Bhral
The people of Seann Bhral on the south-eastern coast begin to lay oyster-beds in the shallows, a craft that came, they say, with the name of their town. The Library's copy of the provincial roll sets down the claim and marks it doubtful.
20 an Gearran, FE 2,880 Seann Vell
Seann Vell's harbour
Seann Vell on the south-eastern coast grows into a city on the southern fishing and the silver of Muileann chiar brought down the eastern road. Its harbour is the first on the island with a stone quay.
22 am Faoilleach, FE 2,883 Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
The light at Tobar dhearg rebuilt
The old beacon at Tobar dhearg on the southern cape is rebuilt as a stone tower with the fire on its top, the first sea-light raised above the ground. It burns seal-oil of the north-west, carried the whole length of the island.
19 an Giblean, FE 2,886 Muileann naomh
Muileann naomh's mill-shrine
At Muileann naomh on the southern coast a mill and a shrine share one roof, and the miller keeps the shrine's handful beside his millstones. The Keeper's cutter who comes to try it finds the measure kept and the flour good.
21 am Màrt, FE 2,889 Dùn thais
Dùn thais walled
Dùn thais in the eastern hills is walled, and a temple of the stag's people is raised within it, the first of theirs built in stone and not kept in a grove. The elder school at Cnoc bhàn sends it teachers.
16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,892 Inis mhòr
The wool-fair of Inis mhòr
Inis mhòr holds a wool-fair at every shearing, and buyers come to it from all the northern coast and some from Cathair dhearg. Its silver is weighed on the Muileann chiar weights sent to the northern road.
18 an Cèitean, FE 2,895 Baile Mòr mhòr
Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern coast
Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern coast west of Seann Toll, grows great enough on the fishing to send its own member to the council at Dùn ìseal. The Four Houses mislike it, and seat its member at the foot of the hall.
13 an Lùnastal, FE 2,898 Seann Toll
The northern boats at Seann Toll
The harbour at Seann Toll becomes the home of the northern fishing fleet. Its boatbuilders make the longest craft on the island, built for a day's run along the coast and never for open water.
15 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,900 Achadh shean
Drought at Achadh shean
A dry summer burns the pastures round Achadh shean in the east, and by spring the district's common granary is empty. Grain is sent from Baile chaol and Cuan ruadh under the shared-meal law, and the district repays it over the harvests after.
10 an Dàmhair, FE 2,903 Baile chaol
Baile chaol's repayment
The rolls at Baile chaol set down the repayment of the drought grain by Achadh shean, measure by measure, to the last. The clerk adds that no such debt in the rolls was repaid in full before.
11 an t-Sultain, FE 2,906 Imrich nam Pantar
The panthers late
The great cats cross the southern road late, and fewer than the carriers remember. The weather-watchers read it for a hard winter, and are right. The Keepers note it without remark.
13 an Lùnastal, FE 2,909 Baile ruadh
The watch-tower at Baile ruadh
A timber watch-tower is raised at Baile ruadh on the north-eastern coast to look out for raiders from the islands, manned by turns by the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill. It is the only tower of war the age builds.
11 an t-Sultain, FE 2,912 Cuan ruadh
Cuan ruadh's boats
The fishers of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast give boats and men to the watch against the island raiders. In return Sliochd Raghnaill gives the town a place on the council at Dùn ìseal beside its own seat.
10 an Dàmhair, FE 2,915 Inis chrom
The drowned-feast at Inis chrom
At Inis chrom on the western coast the families of the drowned hold a feast on the shore each year and set an empty place for each of the lost. The custom spreads to the harbours northward as far as Seann Warr.
8 an t-Samhain, FE 2,918 Baile ghorm
The potters of Baile ghorm
Potters at Baile ghorm on the south-western coast begin to fire a hard red ware of the local clay, and their jars carry the oil and grain of the western road. Sherds of it lie on every waypoint-house site the Library's surveyors have walked.
19 an Giblean, FE 2,920 Cnoc àrsaidh
Cnoc àrsaidh's kilns
Potters of Baile ghorm set up new kilns at Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west, where the clay is better and the wood nearer. There the red ware of the western road is made for the rest of the age.
18 an Cèitean, FE 2,923 Cathair fhada
Cathair fhada grows
Families leaving the crowded harbours about Cathair dhearg settle at Cathair fhada on the southern coast and raise its long street along the ridge. They bring a wood-watcher with them, and a copy of the laws.
16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,926 Cnoc naomh
Cnoc naomh's ancestor-shrine
The people of Cnoc naomh keep a shrine to the ancestors and to the sìth of the hill in the old folk way, with no hawk, wolf, sting or stag in it. The Hall's list of rites names them among the keepers of the old reverence, which by now is a company of its own.
15 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,929 Cathair dhearg
Mòr nic Coinnich crowned
Mòr nic Coinnich, granddaughter of Coinneach Bàn, takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. The Keeper Catrìona nic Mhuirich sets the stone cup in her hands at Dùn ìseal, as the houses had done for Gilleasbuig Mòr. Hers is the last name written in the king-list of the Holy Age.
2 an Giblean, FE 2,939 Dùn ìseal
The Hall's roll at the close of the age
At the close of the age the Keepers' roll holds one hundred and forty names, from Beathag Bhàn to Catrìona nic Mhuirich, and the king-list more than ninety, from Goraidh Mòr to Mòr nic Coinnich. The Small-Burning Law is unchanged in any word since the stone cup of Fionnlagh Dall, and the cup stands yet on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal.
1 an Cèitean, FE 2,949
The last age of even population
So ends the Holy Age. The chroniclers of after days look back on it with some unease: it is the last time in the history of Rodos that no family's lives ran longer than any other's.

Age III · An Aois Scaraidh the Age of Sundering · the Landfall Era, LE 1 – 1,819

6 am Faoilleach, LE 1
Land is found
Word comes of a land across the open water, where no people like the Ròdaich dwell. Who first found it is not told.
9 an t-Samhain, LE 1 Cathair dhearg
The tidings at Cathair dhearg
Three crews from the western harbours bring word of the far land to the hall of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich, at Cathair dhearg. None claims to have been first. The queen's scribe takes down all three tellings; they agree on the coast and on nothing else.
8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1
The Choosing
A vote, or what the later chroniclers call a vote, settles who will go. Only the willing go; no lots are drawn and none are pressed.
12 an t-Sultain, LE 2 Seann Skell
The roll of the willing
The harbour scribes of Seann Skell open a roll of those who mean to go, written by household and not by name, on boards in the harbour-house. A later hand notes that names were struck out as often as they were added.
11 an Dàmhair, LE 2 Cathair dhearg
The queen neither commands nor forbids
Queen Beathag declares that the crown will send no one across the water and keep no one back. Within the season her younger sister, Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, enters her own household on the roll at Seann Skell.
14 an Lùnastal, LE 3 Muileann dhearg
The custodians count the cost
The vein-house above Muileann dhearg, keeper of Crom's stone and heir to the Keepers' Hall at Dùn ìseal where Brìde's flame was first bound, counts the households of the ore-right that have entered the roll. The custody-book makes it nearly one in five, and says the count was made twice, for the first figure was not believed.
16 an t-Iuchar, LE 5
The ships are built
The shipwrights of the island, used to small coasting craft, build ships to keep the open sea, the first in the memory of Rodos.
14 an Lùnastal, LE 5 Seann Skell
Alasdair Saor lays the first keel
On the river strand below Seann Skell the shipwright Alasdair mac Iain, called Alasdair Saor, lays down the first deep-keeled hull built on Rodos. Until then the island's boats were sewn-plank coasters that never lay a night out of sight of land.
26 an Lùnastal, LE 5 Doire fhionn
The oaks of Doire fhionn
The oak grove that named Doire fhionn is felled for the keels of the fleet and drawn to the coast on ox-sleds. It never grew again, and the village kept a name it had no more cause for.
24 an t-Sultain, LE 5 Seann Skell
The shipwrights' fellowship
Alasdair Saor gathers the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into one fellowship, and binds each apprentice for seven years after the manner of the vein custodians. The custody-book names it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights.
12 an t-Sultain, LE 6 Inis àrsaidh
The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh
The first finished hull is taken down the Abhainn naomh and out past Ros àrsaidh, where the ships of Inis àrsaidh put to sea, for trial in open water. It founders in a following sea and eleven are drowned. Alasdair Saor alters the setting of the keel, and every later hull of the fleet is built to the new pattern.
11 an Dàmhair, LE 8 Cuan shean
The rope-walks of Cuan shean
Cuan shean lays out long rope-walks along its harbour front and gives all its hemp fields to cordage for the fleet. Its rope trade lasts some centuries beyond the Sundering.
9 an t-Samhain, LE 9 Baile àrsaidh
The sail-cloth levy
Every weaving household in Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh owes a set length of close-woven sail-cloth, scored on tally-sticks at the shire seat. The tallies survive; how many paid is not known.
20 an Giblean, LE 13 Cuan ruadh
The star-lore of Cuan ruadh
The old steersmen of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast, the only sailors of the island who had ever held a course by night, teach the pilots of the fleet to steer by the stars. Their lore was written down only in part, and that part is lost.
19 an Cèitean, LE 18 Seann Skell
The willing choose their leaders
The households of the roll meet at Seann Skell and choose Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a custodian of the vein, to lead them. The custody-book records the choice; how it was made is not told.
17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 25 Muileann dhearg
The handful for the new hearth
The vein-house rules that each departing ship may carry one sealed measure of the ore, no more than a single household may burn in a season under the Small-Burning Law. It is the only writing in the custody-book addressed to those who were leaving.
16 an t-Iuchar, LE 30 Seann Skell
The west quay lengthened
Masons from the capital lengthen the west quay at Seann Skell with dressed stone, so that the deep hulls may lie alongside at low water. On these stones the later rite was held.
20 an Gearran, LE 38
The strife over the grain
Strife over how much of the island's stored grain the ships may take all but ends the venture. Within a season it is settled; how is not recorded.
21 am Màrt, LE 38 Àth shean
Àth shean shuts its granaries
In the strife over the fleet's grain Tormod mac Coinnich, reeve of the granaries at Àth shean, bars the store-houses and sets a watch on them until the matter is settled. He holds no office afterward.
3 an Giblean, LE 38 Abhainn dhomhain
Grain down Abhainn dhomhain
The strife settled, grain barges go down Abhainn dhomhain to the capital, on by the coast to Ros àrsaidh, and up the Abhainn naomh to Seann Skell. A tally-keeper at Drochaid Cathair dhearg counts forty-one barges passing.
2 an Cèitean, LE 38 Seann Skell
The fleet assembled
The fleet lies complete at Seann Skell. The custody-book gives nineteen hulls; a later hand in the margin makes it twenty-one. Which is right has never been settled.
18 an Giblean, LE 40 Seann Skell
The night of lamps
On the last night before the sailing every house on the Seann Skell waterfront sets a lamp on its sill and keeps it burning till morning. It is the first custom of the Sundering written down as a custom, and the town kept it long after its cause had become a tale.
19 an Giblean, LE 40
The Setting-Out
The willing sail west. The chronicles of the island fall silent on them as the ships clear the harbour; the Ròdaich tell that the fleet sailed into Manannan's mist, toward the Otherworld.
19 an Giblean, LE 40 Seann Skell
The sunwise turn
Before going down the Abhainn naomh to the open sea the fleet goes once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck, and the watchers on the quay count the hulls as they pass. The harbour scribe's account ends at the foot of the pool.
22 am Faoilleach, LE 44 Muileann dhearg
The years counted from the turn
Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, begins to number the years from the sunwise turn at Seann Skell, and calls them the years of the Diosal. The count is his; the crown's scribes take it up a generation later.
27 an Dàmhair, LE 44 Seann Skell
Tidings reach Seann Skell
Tidings of the fleet reach Seann Skell, by what road or whose mouth is not told. The harbour scribe copies them in a shaking hand; the copy came down to later keepers water-stained and lacking its end.
24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44
Two landfalls
Such broken tidings as come back tell of two coasts reached, not one. In this telling lies the seed of the two peoples that came after.
1 an Lùnastal, LE 46 Cathair dhearg
Mòrag's line struck
Queen Beathag strikes her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the succession, as no longer on Rodos. The act stands without comment between a grain ruling and the mending of a bridge.
3 an t-Iuchar, LE 53
The thinning
Cut off from the vein, the strength the crossing asked of them fades in the children of those who went. By the third generation over the water nothing is left that Rodos would know.
28 an t-Sultain, LE 53 Muileann dhearg
The custodians' second count
The vein-house counts again the households of the ore-right and sets the loss at one hand in five. Beside it Donnchadh mac Thormoid writes that the vein answers no differently for those who stayed.
1 an Lùnastal, LE 54
The Mourning Custom
Rodos sets in order a rite of mourning for the departed, neither wholly grief nor wholly feast. In a far later age it was used again, uneasily, for a very different leaving.
27 an Dàmhair, LE 54 Cathair dhearg
The white sorrow first kept at court
Queen Beathag mourns her sister in undyed wool, with one place left empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast. The court calls it an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and within a generation it is kept in every harbour town of the island.
7 am Faoilleach, LE 55
The custodians fewer
With part of the obsidian-bound folk gone, the Ròdaich order themselves anew about a smaller and closer class of custodians. From this shape every later nobility descends.
4 an t-Iuchar, LE 55 Muileann dhearg
The seven houses of custody
The custodian households that remain are gathered into seven houses, each answerable to the vein-house for its share of the ore and of the measured burning: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. Here for the first time the right to the ore passes by house and not by apprenticeship.
28 an t-Iuchar, LE 55 Cathair dhearg
Death of Queen Beathag
Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, the last ruler of Rodos who saw the fleet. Her son Raghnall mac Uilleim is crowned in the same hall.
25 an t-Samhain, LE 61
The rite of the empty harbour
A rite grows up about the quay the ships sailed from. It is still kept, lessened, on a day that none can now date truly.
24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 64 Seann Skell
The harbour at half trade
The harbour-master of Seann Skell finds his berths at half their old use, for the fishing households that crewed the fleet are gone. The rope-walks of Cuan shean turn off hands for the first time.
8 an Gearran, LE 65
The second silence
There is a rumour of a second, smaller crossing, with fewer ships and no word of where they went. Nothing that survives confirms or denies it.
5 am Màrt, LE 67 Ceann mhòr
The watch at Ceann mhòr
The fishing families of Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast keep a watch from the headland for returning sails, household by household in turn. The watch lapses within a generation. No sail is seen.
13 am Màrt, LE 67
The west quay renamed
The quay the ships sailed from is given a new name, so that common trade might go on under the old one without the memory. It is an early and quiet forgetting, made on purpose.
15 an Lùnastal, LE 67 Seann Skell
Cidhe an Diosail
The departure berth is entered in the harbour rolls of Seann Skell as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn. The name Cidhe an Iar passes to the new fish-wharf at the north end of the strand, and within a few years the fishers use it without a thought.
21 an Lùnastal, LE 67
Roghnaich takes its narrow sense
In the custody-book the verb roghnaich, to choose, begins to stand with no object, meaning to have chosen the crossing. The scribes of the next century use it so without explaining it, the surest sign that it had passed into common speech.
31 an Lùnastal, LE 67
The first generation that never saw the fleet
Children born soon after the Setting-Out grow up never having seen the harbour with those ships in it. To them the leaving is already history.
8 an t-Sultain, LE 67 Seann Skell
Death of Alasdair Saor
Alasdair Saor, who laid the first deep keel, dies at Seann Skell. His last work was a coasting trader of the old sewn-plank kind, built for a fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh.
27 an t-Ògmhios, LE 84
The shipwrights' fellowship ends
No more sea-going ships being wanted, the fellowship that built the fleet of the Sundering quietly breaks up. Its craft is half forgotten by the time anyone needs it again.
29 an Cèitean, LE 85 Seann Skell
The keel-moulds burned
In a hard season the patterns and moulds of the broken fellowship, kept in a shed on the strand at Seann Skell, are burned for firewood. The harbour-master notes the loss of the shed and not of what was in it.
30 an Giblean, LE 109 Muileann dhearg
The mountain divided among the houses
The seven houses draw lots at the vein-house for the galleries each will keep, and the vein-house confirms each its Small-Burning measure. The lot-stones were kept in a bag at Muileann dhearg and shown to visitors for centuries after.
14 an t-Iuchar, LE 109 Doire fhionn
The coppice law of Doire fhionn
The great oaks gone to the fleet, the shire of Doire fhionn forbids the felling of any living oak without the reeve's mark and begins to cut its woods by coppice. The law spreads to every shire with a Doire in its name.
12 an Lùnastal, LE 109 Seann Skell
The lamps kept at Seann Skell
The waterfront of Seann Skell keeps the night of lamps each year on the eve of the rite of the empty harbour. The children are told the lamps are for ships coming home, and the priests do not gainsay it.
9 an Dàmhair, LE 109 Muileann dhearg
Death of Donnchadh mac Thormoid
Donnchadh mac Thormoid, the vein-house scribe who began the count of years, dies at Muileann dhearg. His last entry is the season's burning of ore, household by household, in the same hand as his first.
7 an t-Samhain, LE 125 Cathair dhearg
Raghnall dies; Ìomhar crowned
King Raghnall mac Uilleim dies at Cathair dhearg after a long and quiet reign, and his son Ìomhar mac Raghnaill is crowned. The custody-book gives Raghnall's reign a single line.
6 an Dùbhlachd, LE 149 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silversmiths of Muileann chiar
Silver of the seam at Muileann chiar, mined since the Holy Age, is wrought into neck-rings for the heads of the seven houses. The smiths' fellowship of the seam, heirs of Sliochd Fhearchair, keeps its craft within four families.
4 am Faoilleach, LE 154 Inis mhòr
Inis mhòr's grain fleet
Inis mhòr in the north builds barges to carry grain down the Abhainn ghorm to Caol bheag, and from Ros chiar at the river mouth west along the coast to Cnoc bheag. They are sewn-plank boats of the old kind, and none lies a night out of sight of land.
2 an Gearran, LE 156 Caol fhiadhaich
The coughing sickness at Caol fhiadhaich
A coughing sickness runs through Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast and kills some two hundred before it burns out. The shared meal is kept throughout, and the reeve holds that it saved the rest.
3 am Màrt, LE 164 Am Buabhall Fortanach
Am Buabhall Fortanach rebuilt in stone
The old road-house of Am Buabhall Fortanach burns to its footings, and its keeper, Eilidh nic Chaluim, rebuilds it in stone. It is already known for its jugged buffalo.
7 an Dàmhair, LE 179 Dùn ìseal
The spirit-house at Dùn ìseal
The keepers of the Old Spirits, the faith of the hearths, raise a house for the ancestors at Dùn ìseal, and cut the names of the dead of the eastern shires on wooden posts. The posts are cut anew each generation as the old ones rot.
30 an Giblean, LE 180 Cathair dhearg
Ìomhar dies without an heir
King Ìomhar mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg with no living child, and with him ends the line of Beathag. The heads of the seven houses are summoned to the capital to name a king.
19 an Gearran, LE 182 Cathair dhearg
Fearchar mac Lachlainn chosen
The heads of the houses choose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Baile Mòr dhomhain, of Clann Fhearchair, and he is crowned at Cathair dhearg. He is the first king made by the custodian houses and not by descent.
20 am Màrt, LE 194 Baile Mòr dhomhain
A court at Baile Mòr dhomhain
King Fearchar keeps his court part of each year at Baile Mòr dhomhain, near the mountain, that he may take counsel of the vein-house without a journey. The double court lasts as long as his house.
21 an Gearran, LE 209 Àth fhiadhaich
The fishers of Àth fhiadhaich
After a season of losses the fishing families of Àth fhiadhaich join in one fellowship to share boats and nets. It is the first fishers' fellowship on the east coast.
21 an t-Ògmhios, LE 211 Cathair dhearg
Fearchar Donn crowned
Fearchar mac Lachlainn dies, and his son, called Fearchar Donn, is crowned at Cathair dhearg without dispute.
20 an Giblean, LE 229 Cnoc bheag
Gormshuil of the Hawk
At Cnoc bheag, where the dawn-hawk rite of the Holy Age is still kept, the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair teaches that the hawk of the rite is Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, eldest of men, and remembering all things with him. The vein, she teaches, is the Hungry Hawk, to be fed the measured handful and no more, for a hawk overfed will not hunt and a hawk starved will turn on the hand. Her followers gather the old rite into the first house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the order of the Hawk of Acaill.
22 am Màrt, LE 239 Ros gheal
The hawk-house at Ros gheal
Gormshuil's pupils found a second house of the Hawk at Ros gheal. Its priests take charge of the measured burning for all the country between Ros gheal on the coast and Cnoc bheag up the river.
17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 244 Seann Vell
Flood at Seann Vell
In a wet spring the river at Seann Vell on the south-east coast breaks its banks and carries away the lower mills. The mill-wrights build them again on the higher bank.
5 an t-Ògmhios, LE 251 Cnoc bheag
The sayings of Gormshuil written
After Gormshuil's death her sayings are written at Cnoc bheag as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist, Ùisdean mac Pàdraig, marks every saying he did not hear from her own mouth, and these are the greater part.
23 an t-Samhain, LE 259 Seann Toll
The storm that took Seann Toll's boats
A northern storm, named Am Fuath Mòr in the harbour rolls, breaks the harbour wall of Seann Toll and sinks forty boats at their moorings. Eighteen fishers drown.
16 an t-Iuchar, LE 261 Seann Toll
Seann Toll walls its harbour again
Seann Toll builds its harbour wall again, higher and with a hooked end, to a plan the reeve had from the masons of the capital. The wall stands through every storm of this age.
12 an t-Sultain, LE 261 Dùn dhearg
The walls of Dùn dhearg
Clann Ìomhair, who hold the land about Dùn dhearg in the eastern hills, wall it in stone. These are the first walls on the island raised by a custodian house and not by the crown.
11 an Dàmhair, LE 261 Cathair dhearg
Queen Sìleas's measures
Sìleas nic Fhearchair, crowned after her father Fearchar Donn, fixes one measure for grain across the island, the firlot of Cathair dhearg, so that barter between shires need not begin with a quarrel over the size of a basket. Firlots of oak bound with iron are sent to every shire seat.
22 an t-Sultain, LE 284 Cathair dhearg
Tally-houses in the royal granaries
Queen Sìleas sets a tally-house in each royal granary, where every exchange of grain for cloth, salt or labour is cut on paired sticks, one for each party. It is the first reckoning of trade across the whole island, and it runs without coin.
17 an t-Samhain, LE 287 Cathair fhada
The market charter of Cathair fhada
Queen Sìleas grants Cathair fhada a market on its ridge at every full moon, with a tally-house for the south; it is the first market right cut on paired sticks. The merchants of the long city carry the honey, hemp, wax and pots of the south to the capital, and begin to go as one company to the harvest fair at Muileann òg.
21 an Dàmhair, LE 289 Drochaid Cathair dhearg
Drochaid Cathair dhearg widened
The old stone bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg is widened for two carts to pass. Queen Sìleas's name is cut on the downstream parapet, and may still be read there.
26 an t-Iuchar, LE 304 Imrich nam Pantar
The crossing days of the panthers
In the southern hills near Imrich nam Pantar the herders keep the panther roads clear on the days the great cats cross, and drive their flocks off the paths beforehand. The crossing days are the first thing the southern shires agree on in writing.
24 an Lùnastal, LE 304 An Leòmhann Buidhe
An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north road
An Leòmhann Buidhe, a road-house on the northern mining road, serves the ore-carters oatcakes fried in linseed oil, and fire water. Its keeper is fined for watering the fire water.
29 an Cèitean, LE 314 Dùn thais
The house of disputation at Dùn thais
Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a druid of the schools of Flidais, lady of the deer, founds a house of disputation at Dùn thais, where the old question of the schools, Carson an làmh seo?, why the vein answers some hands and not others, is argued by rule. Pupils come from as far as Caol bheag.
1 an Giblean, LE 324 Dùn thais
Coinneach's question
In open disputation Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn asks whether the hands that went with the fleet were those the vein answered best, and whether it now answers fewer. The seven houses forbid the question at their own tables; it is the first time they forbid a question and not a deed.
30 an Giblean, LE 324 Baile Mòr mhòr
Baile Mòr mhòr grows
After a run of poor seasons Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern plain takes in families from the upland farms and doubles within a generation. Its reeve divides the common grazing anew.
27 an t-Ògmhios, LE 324 Cathair dhearg
Death of Queen Sìleas
Queen Sìleas nic Fhearchair dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than fifty years. Her son Uisdean mac Dhùghaill is crowned.
2 an Gearran, LE 344 Inis àrsaidh
The deep hull that would not float true
A merchant of Inis àrsaidh has a deep-keeled hull built for the long coast run eastward. The wrights no longer remember how Alasdair Saor scarfed his keels; the hull lists so badly at launch that it is broken up for timber.
3 am Màrt, LE 354 Ros fhionn
Salt pans at Ros fhionn
The river town of Ros fhionn in the north-east lays out salt pans at the brine springs on its river flats and sends salt inland over Drochaid Ros fhionn. Within a generation Ros fhionn salt is the common measure of worth in the north-eastern shires.
18 an t-Sultain, LE 361 Baile gharbh
The wool of Baile gharbh
The weavers of Baile gharbh make a heavy undyed cloth that sheds rain, and it becomes the common cloak of the north-east. In this cloth the white sorrow is kept.
20 an Lùnastal, LE 369 Drochaid Ros fhionn
Salt over Drochaid Ros fhionn
So many salt carts cross Drochaid Ros fhionn that the bridge-keeper is granted a handful from each load. His salt-box is said to hold more than some villages' granaries.
27 an Cèitean, LE 379 Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The wells crack at Cill ghlas
An earth tremor in the hills about Cill ghlas cracks three wells and brings down a byre. The custodians of the vein-house note it, and note that the galleries were untouched.
26 an Giblean, LE 394 Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The Hollow Man spoken of again
The shepherds of the Doire uaine hills will light no fires on the high pastures, for the old inscriptions of Marbh-bheò Doire uaine. A reeve sent from Muileann chiar to make them see sense does not stay the night.
25 an Cèitean, LE 394 Cathair dhearg
Aonghas mac Uisdein crowned
Uisdean mac Dhùghaill dies, and his son Aonghas mac Uisdein is crowned at Cathair dhearg. Aonghas is the first king to learn his letters as a child.
23 an t-Ògmhios, LE 394 Àth fhiadhaich
Àth fhiadhaich salt fish
Àth fhiadhaich begins to salt its catch with Ros fhionn salt and send it inland to the mining towns. From this time the mining shires eat salt fish in the lean season.
28 am Màrt, LE 409 Inis thais
Clach first preached at Inis thais
Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, where the wolf-sworn's stone Clach stands, preaches that the stone is Lia Fàil, which cries out under the rightful king, and that its sworn guards are the Fianna, who keep the island as a wolf keeps its range. His hearers are the first congregation of Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone.
16 an Dùbhlachd, LE 419 Inis thais
The wolf-house at Inis thais
The followers of Dòmhnall mac Ailein raise at Inis thais the first temple on the island to Lia Fàil by name. It is roofed with slate brought by sea from the north.
29 am Faoilleach, LE 429 Caol leathan
Hawk and wolf at Caol leathan
The priests of the Hawk and the Fianna of the Stone both claim the harbour shrine at Caol leathan. The king's reeve divides its days between them, as the sacred woods were divided in the Holy Age, and the division holds.
28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 435 Seann Skell
The market inside the new gate
Seann Skell on the Hawk bay is walled, and a market is granted inside the new landward gate, where amber, whale-oil, honey and the sheep of the northern moors are sold. The amber-workers of the bay swear to sell no rough amber outside the walls.
31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 441 Cathair dhearg
Macha at court
King Aonghas takes up the wood-watchers' rite of Macha, which keeps the two horses of one chariot, foaled on one night, Liath Macha the grey and Dubh Sainglenn the black: two horses, one yoke, light and dark two powers in balance, and the vein belonging to both. The court follows him, and Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha, becomes the order of Cathair dhearg and the crown.
28 am Màrt, LE 446 Tobar dhearg
Fire at Tobar dhearg
Fire runs through the thatch of Tobar dhearg and burns most of the village. It is rebuilt with slate from the quarries nearby, and is known thereafter for its slate roofs.
14 am Faoilleach, LE 471 Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
Macha's priests in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The custody of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, shared since the Holy Age, passes by royal grant to the priests of Macha. The other claimants leave the wood without contest. Why is not told.
11 an t-Iuchar, LE 479 Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
The druid schools keep Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
The druids of the schools take the keeping of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, the wood of Flidais's white stag, and walk its bounds each year. The walk becomes the one open rite of the schools.
29 am Faoilleach, LE 484 Àth chiar
The drovers of Àth chiar
Drovers of Àth chiar begin to drive cattle each year over the eastern hills to the mining towns. Theirs are the first roads on the island marked with cairns.
23 an t-Ògmhios, LE 484 Doire chiar
Eilidh Dhubh's tracts
At Doire chiar Eilidh nic Iain, called Eilidh Dhubh, wakes again the teaching of the rival school of the Holy Age, that the vein answers labour and not birth, and sets it out in tracts that her pupils copy. The tracts are read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east.
2 an Dùbhlachd, LE 484 Muileann dhearg
The tracts burned at Muileann dhearg
The vein-house commands every copy of Eilidh Dhubh's tracts brought to Muileann dhearg and burned, and some hundred are given up. Eilidh is not punished. She dies at Doire chiar, still teaching.
31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 484 Cathair dhearg
Death of King Aonghas
King Aonghas mac Uisdein dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried by the rite of Macha, the first king so buried. His son Iain mac Aonghais is crowned.
27 an Gearran, LE 496 Cathair dhearg
Tormod Bàn crowned
Iain mac Aonghais dies after a short reign, and his son Tormod mac Iain, called Tormod Bàn for his white hair, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The houses swear to him without dispute.
8 an Lùnastal, LE 509 An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
Winter at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
An Taigh-seinnse Mòr on the central mining road becomes the house where the ox-teams of the mountain wait out the worst of the snow. Its keeper, Iain mac Mhurchaidh, builds them a second byre and keeps a book of the teams that lodged.
6 an t-Sultain, LE 514 Muileann naomh
The bell-founders of Muileann naomh
A family of Muileann naomh casts the first bronze bell on Rodos to hang in a hawk-house. It cracks in its first frost; the second holds.
5 am Màrt, LE 519 Cuan dhearg
An Gàire Dubh
A storm named in the south-coast rolls An Gàire Dubh, the Black Laugh, drives the sea over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg and spoils the season's salt fish. The town is built again a street further from the shore.
13 an t-Sultain, LE 526 Muileann naomh
The hawk-house at Muileann naomh
Muileann naomh in the south becomes the southernmost house of the Hawk, and rings its bell at each measured burning. There the Hawk's teaching holds when it fades elsewhere in the south.
18 an t-Ògmhios, LE 534 Abhainn fhionn
The king's sons drowned in Abhainn fhionn
Both sons of King Tormod Bàn drown when a ferry overturns on Abhainn fhionn in spate. The king has no other child.
8 an t-Sultain, LE 547 Cathair dhearg
Death of Tormod Bàn
King Tormod Bàn dies at Cathair dhearg without naming an heir, and three claims are laid before the houses at once.
21 an Giblean, LE 552 Cathair dhearg
The three claimants
The crown is claimed by Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais, niece of the late king; by Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain, his half-brother; and by Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house. The seven houses divide among them, and the War of the Three Claimants begins.
20 an Cèitean, LE 553 Seann Warr
Seann Warr shuts its gates
Seann Warr, the port nearest the capital on the west, shuts its gates to all three claimants and declares for none. Twice besieged in the war, it is taken by neither.
22 an Gearran, LE 554 Àth shean
The ford at Àth shean
The host of Dùghall Garbh meets that of Raghnall Ruadh at the ford of Àth shean and breaks it. The custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford.
24 an t-Sultain, LE 555 Doire mhin
The burning of Doire mhin
Raghnall Ruadh's men in retreat burn the village of Doire mhin and its granary, to deny them to Dùghall. The villagers winter at Cathair mhòr on the charity of Macha's priests.
26 an Dùbhlachd, LE 557 Cathair dhomhain
The siege of Cathair dhomhain
Catrìona nic Aonghais besieges Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and takes it after forty days, when its wells are fouled by the dead of the siege lines. She lets the garrison go free on their oath.
24 am Faoilleach, LE 558 Muileann dhearg
The hearths refused
Raghnall Ruadh, holding the vein-house, denies the measured handful of ore to every hearth and temple in the shires that stand against him. Hearths lit with the ore for generations go cold, and this deed turns more against him than any battle.
14 am Faoilleach, LE 560 Muileann chrom
The battle of Muileann chrom
The hosts of Catrìona and Dùghall, joined for the purpose, meet Raghnall Ruadh below Muileann chrom. Raghnall falls on the field, and the next day his own custodians open the vein-house.
16 an Dùbhlachd, LE 561 Baile Mòr dhomhain
Death of Dùghall Garbh
Dùghall Garbh dies at Baile Mòr dhomhain of the wounds he took at Muileann chrom. His followers go over to Catrìona without further fighting.
13 am Màrt, LE 562 Cathair dhearg
Catrìona Bhuadhach crowned
Catrìona nic Aonghais is crowned at Cathair dhearg, and is known thereafter as Catrìona Bhuadhach. So ends the War of the Three Claimants, after some ten years.
12 an Gearran, LE 565 Muileann dhearg
The ruling of the hearth
Catrìona Bhuadhach and the vein-house set down in law that no claimant, house or king may withhold the measured handful from any lawful hearth. It is the first law written to bind the custodians themselves.
10 an Cèitean, LE 584 Am Buabhall Fortanach
Catrìona's road south
Queen Catrìona has the road south from the capital by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach at Doire shean laid with stone, that her own town of Inis thais may be reached in any weather. It is called Rathad na Banrighinn.
11 an Giblean, LE 594 Seann Warr
Seann Warr's gates honoured
In memory of its standing aside in the war, Queen Catrìona grants Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and take its own tolls. The grant is cut over the landward gate.
7 an t-Iuchar, LE 604 Cathair dhearg
Death of Catrìona Bhuadhach
Catrìona Bhuadhach dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Lachlann mac Iain is crowned, and the houses swear to him in a single day, a thing the chroniclers remark on.
8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 624 Cathair dhearg
The Book of the Three Claimants
Seònaid nic Coinnich, a clerk of Queen Catrìona's household, writes the story of the war from the custody-book and from the witness of those who fought. It is the oldest history of Rodos that survives written as one tale and not as entries.
3 an t-Sultain, LE 624 Inis chrom
The sickness at Inis chrom
A spotted fever kills some three hundred at Inis chrom on the south-west coast. The Fianna of the Stone nurse the sick, and many of them die of it; thereafter the town is the Stone's.
5 an Lùnastal, LE 634 Doire shean
The oyster beds of Doire shean
Doire shean, a village on the southern shore, lays out oyster beds in its shallow bay and sends oysters by cart to the capital. The trade makes it rich enough to be a shire seat.
26 an Dàmhair, LE 644 Seann Tarr
The feast-market at Seann Tarr
The crowds that come to the ancestor shrine at Seann Tarr for the great feasts begin to hold a market on the three feast days, chiefly of honey, beeswax for the shrine lights, and the dyes of Baile fhiadhaich. The wax lights of Seann Tarr are soon burned at ancestor shrines all along the north-eastern coast.
1 an t-Sultain, LE 654 Seann Skell
Manannan preached at Seann Skell
At Seann Skell, where the sting-creed of the Holy Age first called itself the only true one, the preacher Mànas mac Ruairidh proclaims its one power to be Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, whose Cup of Truth bears the yellow scorpion. He teaches that Manannan shut the western sea behind the fleet with his mist, which hides Rodos from every ship beyond it, and that the crossing must not be tried again. His hearers are the first congregation of Òrd Mhanannain, the order of Manannan.
30 an t-Sultain, LE 654 Cathair dhearg
Death of Lachlann mac Iain
Lachlann mac Iain, son of Catrìona Bhuadhach, dies at Cathair dhearg, and his daughter Anna is crowned. The chroniclers call his reign quiet, and mean it as praise.
29 an Dàmhair, LE 674 Ros bheag
Manannan's order at Ros bheag and Cuan shean
Fishing families carry the teaching of Manannan's order down the west coast to Ros bheag and Cuan shean. At Cuan shean the rope-makers are among the first to turn to it.
27 an t-Samhain, LE 694 Ros bheag
Within sight of land
The priests of Manannan at Ros bheag lay down that no boat of the faithful may go out of sight of the headlands. The rule is kept on the west coast for centuries, and steering by the stars, already half lost, is lost there wholly.
19 an t-Ògmhios, LE 699 Àth shean
The granaries of Àth shean rebuilt
The royal granaries at Àth shean, standing since before the Sundering, are pulled down and built again in stone on raised floors against the rats. The tally-house is rebuilt with them.
24 am Faoilleach, LE 714 Cuan shean
The rope-walks shortened
Cuan shean takes up half its rope-walks and sows the ground with barley. The rope trade had lived on the fleet and then on the fishing, and the fishing no longer needs rope of such length.
22 an Gearran, LE 724 Cnoc chaol
Wave at Cnoc chaol
A great swell with no storm behind it runs up the beach at Cnoc chaol on the south coast and carries off the drying racks and two children. The village sets its racks higher up the shore.
11 an t-Samhain, LE 731 Baile Mòr dhìreach
The market of the eastern road
Baile Mòr dhìreach, the citadel on the straight eastern road, is granted a market for the east coast. There the fish and sail-cloth of the coast towns meet the furs, hides and dyes of the hills, and the dyers of Baile Mòr ruadh sell their colours nowhere else.
23 am Màrt, LE 739 Muileann dhearg
The two counts reconciled
The vein-house and the crown's scribes find that their counts of years since the Setting-Out differ, and settle the difference by agreement. The same agreement fixes the day of the rite of the empty harbour, which each count had placed otherwise; later scribes cease to pretend it was fixed by proof.
12 am Faoilleach, LE 769 Inis mhòr
The druid school at Inis mhòr
Pupils of Dùn thais found a house of disputation at Inis mhòr, and the question of the vein is argued in the north for the first time. Its first master, Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, is remembered for refusing every answer offered him.
10 an Gearran, LE 769 Cathair dhearg
Queen Eilidh Bhàn crowned
Eilidh Bhàn, fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The annals of her long reign are almost wholly of harvests.
22 an Gearran, LE 769 Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The bath-house at the hot springs
Clann Choinnich rebuilds in dressed stone the old bath-house over the hot springs of Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, and admits the sick of any house one day in seven. Its physicians keep a book of cures, afterwards lost.
24 am Faoilleach, LE 784 Spùinneadairean-mara
The sea-thieves of the north-west
Boats out of the small islands off the north-west coast begin to rob the coasting traders of fish and grain. The sea-thieves are Ròdaich, men of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls name some of them.
26 an Dùbhlachd, LE 789 Baile chrom
Baile chrom half empty
The reeve of Baile chrom on the north-west coast reports half the houses of the town empty, their families gone east before the sea-thieves and the poor harvests. The crown remits the town's grain dues.
27 an t-Samhain, LE 801 Eilean dhubh
The raid on Eilean dhubh
A force sent by Queen Eilidh Bhàn lands on Eilean dhubh and burns the sea-thieves' boats on the strand. Their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, is taken to Cathair dhearg and hanged.
19 an Giblean, LE 819 Gorta Baile chrom
The dearth on the north-west shore
Harvest after harvest fails along the north-west shore, and the dearth is more than the shared meal can bear. Families leave the coast for the inland shires and the east, and the north-west is thinly held from this time to the end of the age.
20 an Cèitean, LE 829 Cathair dhearg
The king-list recopied
The scribes of Queen Eilidh Bhàn copy the king-list of Rodos afresh from its oldest surviving roll, adding the rulers since the Sundering. The new copy begins the present age with the Choosing and not with the fleet.
19 an Gearran, LE 835 Àth fhionn
The strand-market at Àth fhionn
Àth fhionn, the ford town where the coast road crosses the clear river, holds a market on the strand for the north coast, of fish, the flesh and oil of stranded whales, wool and barley. The fishers of the north coast no longer carry their catch to Inis mhòr.
21 an Giblean, LE 841 Cathair dhearg
Eilidh Bhàn dies without an heir
Queen Eilidh Bhàn dies at Cathair dhearg without a child, and the house of Catrìona ends with her. The seven houses meet at the vein-house and not at the capital.
23 am Màrt, LE 846 Cathair dhearg
Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned
The houses name Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill, of the line of the claimant slain at Muileann chrom. He is crowned at Cathair dhearg and keeps the mastery of the vein-house with the crown.
6 an t-Ògmhios, LE 859 Muileann dhearg
The crown and the custody joined
Dòmhnall Ruadh's reeves write into the custody-book that the ruler of Rodos is also master of the vein-house. Thereafter the heads of the seven houses sit as the king's council, and the custodians and the court are one body.
1 an t-Ògmhios, LE 865 Muileann dhearg
The custody's seal on the king's letters
From the joining of the crown and the custody the king's letters bear the vein-house's own seal: a trellis of gold on blue, which the custodians read as the galleries of the mountain, and over it a hollow lozenge for Crom's slab, laid on the first break. The crown adds a white band across the field and nothing more. From this time the seal is the arms of the kingdom.
10 an Dùbhlachd, LE 871 Cathair dhearg
Death of Dòmhnall Ruadh
Dòmhnall Ruadh, the first to hold both the crown and the vein-house, dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Muileann dhearg. His son Raghnall Òg is crowned.
20 an t-Ògmhios, LE 889 Cnoc bheag
The schism of the Hawk
A council of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag divides over whether Mòd's measure may ever be raised. Those who hold it fixed for ever keep the name of the Hungry Hawk and the house at Cnoc bheag; those who hold that a greater flock may be fed a greater handful are called the Fed Hawk.
17 an Lùnastal, LE 899 Seann Chwen
The harbour of Seann Chwen
Seann Chwen builds its harbour mole and becomes the port of the ore-carts coming down from the mountain to the coast towns of the south.
23 an Giblean, LE 909 Seann Skell
The Fed Hawk at Seann Skell
The priests of the Fed Hawk, driven from Cnoc bheag, settle at Seann Skell on the north coast, not the western river port of that name. The custody-book writes their teaching down as an error, and at length.
25 an Lùnastal, LE 919 Seann Skell
The Fed Hawk's petition
From Seann Skell the Fed Hawk asks the king's council to raise the measured handful by a quarter for the hearths of the north coast. The council refuses. It is the first plea on record to alter the Small-Burning Law.
14 an Dàmhair, LE 929 Cill ghlas
The gallery at Cill ghlas
A second tremor in the hills of Cill ghlas brings down a gallery of the vein and kills fourteen labourers of the custodians. The vein-house closes the gallery and sets at its mouth a stone with the fourteen names.
12 an t-Samhain, LE 939 Cathair dhearg
The ore-roads kept by the crown
The king's council takes the roads from the mountain to the coast into the crown's keeping, that no house may stop the carts bearing the measured ore to the temples. The roads are marked with posts bearing the crown's sign: the carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, An Rathad Tuath over the pass by Muileann fhada, Slighe Muileann dhearg south from the hills by Muileann chrom, and Slighe Baile òg down to the southern Seann Skell.
17 an Gearran, LE 944 Cathair dhearg
The crown's riders
Fresh horses are kept for the crown's riders at the waypoint houses on the ore-roads, and a rider changing at every house carries the council's word from Cathair dhearg to the mountain between dawn and dark. The stabling is paid out of the ore-road tolls.
17 an Lùnastal, LE 949 Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The high pastures of Doire uaine forsaken
