The last shepherd families leave the high pastures of the Doire uaine hills for the valley villages. They give the grazing as the reason; every one of them speaks also of the Marbh-bheò.
9 an Lùnastal, LE 959 Ros fhionn
The salt fair at Ros fhionn
Ros fhionn holds its great salt fair, and the reeve counts some four thousand people on the flats in a single day. It is the height of the town, and the chronicle calls it the richest place in the north-east.
31 an Dàmhair, LE 969 Cathair mhòr
Cathair mhòr the largest town
Cathair mhòr, its market drawing the trade of all the south, grows greater than the capital. The capital remains the seat of the crown, and the lesser town.
18 an t-Sultain, LE 979 Toll-dubh
The stair at Toll-dubh
Quarrymen north of the capital break into Toll-dubh, the shaft of the old tales, long lost, and find a stair cut in the rock going down beyond their lamps. The custodians of the vein-house wall up the entrance. The one quarryman who went down never tells what he saw.
11 an Gearran, LE 994 Cathair mhòr
The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr
The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr begin to make cooking pots, which are sold on every road of the island. Each bears its maker's sign, and some are still found in the ground.
31 am Faoilleach, LE 999 Làrach an Teampaill
Ailean measures Làrach an Teampaill
Ailean mac Dhùghaill, a scholar of the druid school at Dùn thais, measures the ruin of Làrach an Teampaill and writes that its altar faces the central mountains and not the sea. Who set it so he will not guess.
20 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,011 Làrach an Dùin-fhaire
Ailean's tables of the old ruins
Ailean mac Dhùghaill finishes his tables of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin and Làrach an Teampaill, with the measure, stone and lie of each. He cannot say whether one people built all three, and because of his tables no scholar after him could say either.
23 am Faoilleach, LE 1,019 Cathair dhearg
Queen Mòrag Ruadh crowned
Mòrag Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg. Hers are the first household accounts of a ruler that survive whole.
18 an Dàmhair, LE 1,034 Carragh Cnoc bheag
The obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag cleaned
The priests of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag clear the moss from the obelisk of Carragh Cnoc bheag and try to read the old letters on it. They cannot, and they write down that they tried.
19 an t-Sultain, LE 1,039 Caol shean
Caol shean's fishing year
Caol shean, whose boats fish the east coast from the mouth of the Abhainn chaol, lands the greatest catch in its rolls, so great that the salt runs short and half is dried in the wind. The dried fish sells poorly, and the town goes back to salting.
15 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039 Seann Skell
The thousandth year
The vein-house marks the thousandth year of its count with a single measured burning of the ore on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell, and Queen Mòrag Ruadh is there. It is told that the flame burned the colour of the vein, and that the crowd went home without a word.
28 an Giblean, LE 1,051 Cnoc bhàn
The market above the mill-race
The hill-lords of Baile ghorm hold a market for the farms of the south-east at Cnoc bhàn, above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada. Its common goods are grain, clay and honey. Its rare good is pearls, which the women of the shore take from the mussel beds in the shallows, and which no other market sells.
16 an t-Samhain, LE 1,064 Baile ghorm
The blue dyers of Baile ghorm
The dyers of Baile ghorm in the south-east make a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own. Cloth of Baile ghorm blue becomes the feast-day dress of the seven houses.
29 an Lùnastal, LE 1,079 Muileann dhomhain
The swallowing cough at Muileann dhomhain
A sickness that closes the throat breaks out at Muileann dhomhain and moves along the coast road. The town loses near a third of its people.
26 an Cèitean, LE 1,081 Seann Bhral
The cough at Seann Bhral
The swallowing cough comes to the port of Seann Bhral. The townsfolk themselves close the harbour, and keep the shared meal by leaving food at the town gate.
7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,082 Cathair dhearg
Queen Beathag Fhionn closes the roads
Beathag Fhionn, crowned after her mother Mòrag, closes the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain and sets reeves at the fords to turn travellers back. The cough goes no further west.
5 an Lùnastal, LE 1,104 Muileann dhomhain
Muileann dhomhain resettled
Families from the hills about Muileann dhomhain settle the town that the swallowing cough emptied, and take the empty houses by lot. The older families of the town say they never again knew half their neighbours.
13 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,119 Drochaid Ros fhionn
Drochaid Ros fhionn repaired
The arches of Drochaid Ros fhionn, worn by seven centuries of salt carts, are built anew at the cost of the salt-masters of Ros fhionn, whose names are cut on the keystones.
2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,129 Cathair dhearg
Death of Queen Beathag Fhionn
Queen Beathag Fhionn, who closed the coast road against the cough, dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Ailean is crowned, first of four kings of that name in the house of Raghnall.
13 am Màrt, LE 1,139 Baile ghorm
The Baile ghorm blue fades
The last dyer who knew the Baile ghorm mordant dies without apprentices, having quarrelled with both of hers. The blue that follows is the common blue of the rest of the island.
11 an Giblean, LE 1,149 Dùn ìseal
The ancestor-posts of Dùn ìseal burned
Lightning fires the ancestor-posts at Dùn ìseal. The keepers cut the names again from memory and from the custody-book, and own in their roll that some are guesses.
29 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,159 Ros fhionn
The silting of Ros fhionn
A shifting bar below Ros fhionn silts up the Abhainn bheag, and the salt barges can no longer reach the quays. The salt-masters take their trade to Caol gharbh on the coast.
8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,169 Caol gharbh
Caol gharbh takes the salt
Caol gharbh, a fishing village, becomes the salt port of the north-east, and its harbour is dug out and walled with the money of the Ros fhionn masters.
25 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,169 Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich
The stone on the neck
Caol gharbh and Caol chrom, the two harbours of the strait, send their headmen to a stone on the neck of land between them, and there settle the dues the salt-boats pay to each. Thereafter they meet at that stone over every quarrel of the strait, and it is called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich, the meeting of the neck.
20 an Cèitean, LE 1,179 Drochaid Ros fhionn
Drochaid Ros fhionn falls quiet
The salt going by sea from Caol gharbh, the carts no longer cross Drochaid Ros fhionn. The office of bridge-keeper is done away with, and from this time the bridge is little used.
16 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,184 Ros fhionn
The market-court stays at Ros fhionn
The salt-masters take their ships to Caol gharbh but leave their market-court on the headland at Ros fhionn, where the weights and tally-sticks are kept. The farms and forges of the north-eastern hills still bring their goods there, and the town keeps its market after it has lost its harbour.
25 am Màrt, LE 1,189 Ros fhionn
Seòlaid Ros fhionn
The salt of Ros fhionn now goes by sea: its boats run down the river past Caol gharbh, round the north-east cape, south along the eastern shore past Seann Tarr and Àth bheag, and west again into the bay below Caol shean, where the salt goes inland. The lane is called Seòlaid Ros fhionn after the town whose salt made it, and the eastern boats keep it long after the salt-pans fail.
15 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,189 Muileann shean
The millers of Muileann shean
The mills of Muileann shean are fitted with a new gearing, cut in oak, that turns two stones from one wheel. Within a lifetime it spreads to the mills of the north.
21 an Giblean, LE 1,199 Uilebheist na Mara
The Sea-Watcher off the north-west
Fishers of the thinned north-west coast see the Sea-Watcher, Uilebheist na Mara, near enough to foul their nets. The few boats still working those waters draw further in.
29 an t-Samhain, LE 1,209 Dùn thais
The table of years at Dùn thais
Raghnall mac Chaluim, a scholar of the druid school at Dùn thais, sets out a table showing that the heads of the custodian houses live some years longer, on the whole, than the tenants of their lands. He asks whether the vein answers the hand that holds it. The finding is set down with unease, and no answer.
29 an Giblean, LE 1,219 Muileann dhearg
The table forbidden
The king's council forbids the copying of Raghnall mac Chaluim's table of years, and the house of disputation at Dùn thais is shut for a generation. Raghnall's own copy is kept in the vein-house and entered in its inventory.
2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,229 Inis mhòr
The great gale at Inis mhòr
Before the autumn grain fleet has sailed, a gale out of the north-east drives the sea up the river at Inis mhòr higher than any then living had seen. Boats are crushed at their moorings, and the grain fleet does not sail until spring.
3 an t-Sultain, LE 1,246 Baile ruadh
Baile ruadh's quarrel with Achadh naomh
Baile ruadh and Achadh naomh in the far north-east go to law over the grazing on the hills between them. The case is heard three times at Cathair dhearg, and settled by dividing the hills along a stream.
10 an t-Samhain, LE 1,259 Allt an Àigh
Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh
The keepers of the Old Spirits renew the pilgrimage to Allt an Àigh, and a guest-house is built beside the stream for those who come to drink at the right phase of the moon. Its book names pilgrims from every shire.
7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,266 Cathair dhearg
Death of King Ailean mac Raghnaill
King Ailean mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, leaving two sons by different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, and each has been told he is the heir.
8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,270 Cnoc naomh
The battle of Cnoc naomh
Alasdair Bàn's men seize Cnoc naomh and Iain Ciar takes it back. The houses divide four to three, and from this battle Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, takes its name.
17 an Lùnastal, LE 1,272 Ceann mhin
The fire at Ceann mhin
Alasdair Bàn's ships burn the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother. The fire takes the rope stores and the granary, and the town begs its bread of Cathair mhòr.
19 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,274 Muileann ghlas
The battle of Muileann ghlas
Iain Ciar defeats Alasdair Bàn below Muileann ghlas. Alasdair is taken alive; his captains are let go home.
12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,276 An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The brothers make peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on neutral ground between their lands. Alasdair Bàn gives up his claim and has the lordship of Seann Chwen for life. Iain Ciar is crowned.
8 an Dàmhair, LE 1,291 Seann Chwen
Death of Alasdair Bàn
Alasdair Bàn dies at Seann Chwen, having kept the peace he made. His lordship returns to the crown.
29 an Dàmhair, LE 1,295 Baile Mòr dhomhain
White stone from Baile Mòr dhomhain
Masons of Ceann leathan buy a veined white stone from the hills above Baile Mòr dhomhain for the new front of their temple. From this time the quarry is worked, and its marble goes south by the carriers' road to every town that can pay for it.
20 an Giblean, LE 1,299 Cathair dhearg
Iain Ciar's grain law
Having seen Ceann mhin beg its bread, King Iain Ciar commands that every shire seat keep a year's grain in store against the next war. The law is kept as long as he lives.
14 an Lùnastal, LE 1,304 Cathair dhearg
The account of the Brothers' War
Pàdraig mac Ruairidh, a clerk of King Iain Ciar, writes the story of the Brothers' War. It praises the king at every turn, and it is the only account that survives, to the vexation of later readers.
28 an Giblean, LE 1,319 An Sligeanach Fad' às
The inns of the mining roads chartered
The crown grants a charter to the seven great road-houses of the mining circuit, An Sligeanach Fad' às among them, and makes their keepers answerable for the roads between them. The keepers meet once a year at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts.
17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,326 Cathair dhearg
Death of Iain Ciar
King Iain Ciar dies at Cathair dhearg. His grain law lapses within a few years, as he had foreseen in a note in his own hand.
22 am Màrt, LE 1,339 An Taigh-seinnse Òir
An Taigh-seinnse Òir's beef
An Taigh-seinnse Òir, at the eastern end of the circuit, is written into the charter-roll as keeping syrupped beef for the custodians' reeves on their rounds. It is the first dish of that house on record; the rest of the entry is a complaint about the price.
20 an Giblean, LE 1,349 An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, the road-house on the bare northern road, is snowed in for a whole season with a party of custodians' reeves within. They live on its pickled spinach and fire milk, and their complaint stands in full in the charter-roll.
11 am Màrt, LE 1,359 Seann Skell
The hull that sank at launch
Seumas mac Iain, a boat-builder of Seann Skell, tries to build a deep-keeled hull again from the scraps of the Sundering fellowship's lore still remembered on the strand. At its launch it fills and sinks, and Manannan's priests preach on it for a year.
31 an Cèitean, LE 1,369 Caol ìseal
The Caol ìseal fishers go east
Their own harbour silted, the fishing families of Caol ìseal on the north coast move east to Caol bheag. Caol ìseal becomes a farming town.
4 an Gearran, LE 1,389 Caol fhiadhaich
The southern lane
The fishers of Caol fhiadhaich, on the wild strait of the west coast, take their boats round into the southern sea, along the whole south coast to the mouth of the Abhainn uaine, and up it to the landing of Cidhe Beag below Baile thais, where they sell dried fish for grain. The older harbours of the south coast, which had never sailed beyond their own capes, begin to follow. The lane is named for its first sailors: Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich.
5 am Màrt, LE 1,389 Cuan shean
The keel-song of Cuan shean
Iseabail nic Lachlainn, a gatherer of songs for the royal household, takes down a work-song of the rope-makers of Cuan shean that names the parts of a deep keel. Half its words mean nothing to those who sing it. It is all that survives, in any form, of the craft of the Sundering fleet.
25 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,389 Inis thais
The Stone's schism at Inis thais
The Stone's congregation at Inis thais divides over whether the dead may be prayed for at Clach. Those who say no keep the temple; the others build a second house at Baile gheal.
3 an Gearran, LE 1,399 Seann Tarr
The grey storm at Seann Tarr
A storm named Gailleann Ghlas comes out of the east and destroys the harbour of Seann Tarr. The village is rebuilt and the harbour is not; its boats go to Cuan ruadh.
8 an Lùnastal, LE 1,399 Baile gheal
The second wolf-house at Baile gheal
The dissenters from Inis thais raise their house at Baile gheal and pray there for the dead by name. The two houses of the Stone are not reconciled in this age.
29 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,409 Cuan ruadh
Cuan ruadh's new harbour
Cuan ruadh builds a second harbour arm for the boats from Seann Tarr, and thrives on the east-coast fishing for the rest of the age.
31 an Cèitean, LE 1,429 Cathair dhearg
Queen Catrìona Bheag crowned
Catrìona Bheag of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg, the first queen in more than three centuries. It is written that she was small, and that no one said so twice.
26 an Lùnastal, LE 1,439 Muileann gheal
The grey glaze of Muileann gheal
The potters of Muileann gheal make a grey-green glaze that no other kiln on the island can match, and the custodian houses buy it for their tables. The secret is kept within one family, Clann Mhic Phàil.
28 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,449 Cathair dhearg
The oath of the seven
Queen Catrìona Bheag has the heads of the seven houses swear to the ruling of the hearth before her, the first renewal of the oath since Catrìona Bhuadhach. Clann Choinnich swears last.
14 am Màrt, LE 1,459 Cathair mhòr
Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr
The priests of Macha raise their great house at Cathair mhòr, the largest roofed building on Rodos in this age. Its floor of black and white was eleven years in the laying.
17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,469 Toll-dubh
The eastern Toll-dubh
Charcoal-burners in the east find again the eastern Toll-dubh of the old tales, with the same cut stair as the one walled up in the west. The custodians wall this one too, and the scribe binds the two entries of the custody-book each to the other.
2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,479 Tiormachd Achadh shean
The dry years at Achadh shean
Three dry seasons one after another empty the wells of the eastern shires about Achadh shean. The shared meal holds, and the crown carts grain in from the south.
2 an t-Samhain, LE 1,489 Achadh shean
The water-rights of Achadh shean
The reeves of Achadh shean share the deep wells among the households by lot and by turn, and write the sharing on a board at the well-head. The board is renewed each generation; the lots are never drawn again.
24 an t-Sultain, LE 1,499 Àth shean
The firlot of Àth shean
The granary of Àth shean finds that its firlot has worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and has been so for generations. The reeve's accounts are put right as far back as anyone can reckon.
30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,509 Muileann gheal
The grey glaze lost
The last of Clann Mhic Phàil dies at Muileann gheal without passing on the glaze. For a generation the potters of the town try to match it, and fail.
18 an Dàmhair, LE 1,519 Baile Mòr ruadh
Baile Mòr ruadh's fair
Baile Mòr ruadh in the east holds a cattle fair that draws drovers from Àth chiar and the eastern hills. It becomes yearly, and the greatest fair in the east.
9 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,529 Cathair dhearg
Queen Sìleas Òg crowned
Sìleas Òg of Clann Raghnaill, named for the queen of the firlot, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. She is the first ruler known to have visited every shire seat.
4 an Dàmhair, LE 1,539 Muileann dhearg
Sìleas Òg's count of hands
Queen Sìleas Òg commands a new count of every household holding the right to the ore. It is smaller than any before, for the right has narrowed into fewer and larger households, and the queen has it entered without comment.
5 an t-Sultain, LE 1,549 Ceann mhin
The fire of Ceann mhin
A second great fire burns Ceann mhin, and this time there is no war to blame. By order of its reeve the town is rebuilt with gable walls of stone between the houses.
31 an Lùnastal, LE 1,559 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silver smelt refused
Clann Choinnich asks leave to burn the ore beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, since the ore burns hotter than charcoal. The council refuses. It is the first asking to burn the ore for work and not for worship.
22 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,569 Dùn dhearg
The lost smithing at Dùn dhearg
The smiths of Dùn dhearg, makers of the ceremonial blades of the custodian houses since the walls were built, lose the last man who knew how their layered steel was folded. After him the blades of Dùn dhearg are ordinary.
2 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,579 Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
The houses bury at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
The custodian houses begin to bury their heads at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, among graves older than any name on them. The tenants of the land about call it unwise, and go on burying their own dead elsewhere.
9 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,589 Cathair dhearg
King Ailean the Fourth crowned
Ailean mac Raghnaill, fourth king of that name, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. He is remembered only for the shortest reign in the king-list.
13 an Giblean, LE 1,590 Seann Skell
The synod of Manannan's order
The priests of Manannan meet at Seann Skell and lay down again the rule of sight-of-land. To it they add a prayer, said at the foot of the river pool, that Manannan keep the sea shut: A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.
12 an Cèitean, LE 1,590 Cathair dhearg
Queen Mòrag nic Ailein crowned
Ailean's sister Mòrag nic Ailein is crowned after him. She reigns forty years, and the king-list has for her its longest run of entries telling of nothing but good harvests and the rite.
16 an t-Samhain, LE 1,619 Cidhe Beag
The ferry at Cidhe Beag
A ferry family settles at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine and carries folk and goods down the river by canoe. They hold the landing for the rest of the age.
1 an Dàmhair, LE 1,626 Àth shean
The dark wine of Àth shean
The growers on the slopes above Àth shean press blaeberry and bramble into a dark wine that keeps a year in the cask. It is sold along the eastern road, and the road-houses serve it as black wine.
2 an t-Samhain, LE 1,634 Inis mhòr
Inis mhòr's grain fleet laid up
The coasting grain barges of Inis mhòr, which had sailed Slighe-uisce fhuar, the cold way along the north coast from Ros chiar to Caol mhin, since the Holy Age, are laid up for good as the roads grow better. The last is kept on the strand as a wonder.
7 an Lùnastal, LE 1,649 Dùn ìseal
Earthquake at Dùn ìseal
An earthquake shakes Dùn ìseal and cracks the spirit-house. No one is killed. The keepers take it for a warning, but cannot agree of what.
21 an Cèitean, LE 1,659 Muileann chaol
Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies
Beathag nic Thòmais, widow of a mill-owner of Muileann chaol, begins to buy old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls from houses that no longer read them. She keeps them in a loft over her mill.
28 am Faoilleach, LE 1,674 Muileann chaol
The paper mill at Muileann chaol
A mill at Muileann chaol begins to make paper from rags, the first on Rodos. In this generation the custody-book is first copied onto paper.
27 an Giblean, LE 1,679 Muileann chaol
Three copies of the landfall tidings
Among her papers Beathag nic Thòmais finds three copies of the tidings of the two landfalls. They differ in the order of the coasts and the number of hulls. She writes out all three side by side and does not choose between them.
3 an Cèitean, LE 1,694 Baile chrom
The north-west coast counted
The crown sends a reeve to list the households of the thinned north-west coast between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr. He counts fewer households than there are harbour berths.
24 an Lùnastal, LE 1,699 Muileann chaol
The loft at Muileann chaol
Beathag nic Thòmais dies, and leaves her loft of papers to the town of Muileann chaol on condition that nothing in it be burned. The town keeps that condition and very little else of her wishes.
6 am Màrt, LE 1,709 Cathair dhearg
King Tormod mac Ruairidh crowned
Tormod mac Ruairidh of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg. His reign is remembered for its roads and its length.
5 an Gearran, LE 1,714 Seann Skell
Manannan's harbour prayer
The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell begin to say their prayer for the shut sea on the day of the rite of the empty harbour, so that both are kept together on Cidhe an Diosail. Neither side is pleased.
6 am Màrt, LE 1,719 Cnoc ìseal
Tormod's bridges
King Tormod builds stone bridges over the fords of the south-central shires, one of them at Cnoc ìseal. Ferry-keepers who lose their living are given land in amends.
9 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,729 Imrich nam Pantar
The panther year
The panthers cross the southern roads in numbers beyond any herder's memory, and for a whole season the crossing days run into one another. Flocks are kept in folds from Cnoc àrsaidh to the coast.
10 an t-Samhain, LE 1,734 Caol gharbh
Caol gharbh loses the salt
The sea rises over the salt pans of Caol gharbh and they fail, and salt comes to the north-east from the south instead. The town that took the trade of Ros fhionn is poorer than Ros fhionn had been.
12 an Dàmhair, LE 1,739 Baile ghorm
Storm at Baile ghorm
A south-westerly storm floods the low town of Baile ghorm and drowns twenty-three. The town raises its sea-wall by the height of a man.
22 an Cèitean, LE 1,749 Seann Skell
The rite kept by few
The rite of the empty harbour on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell is kept by the harbour priests and a few old families. A visiting scribe writes that none there could say on what day the fleet had in truth sailed.
23 an Giblean, LE 1,754 Cuan dhearg
Cuan dhearg flooded again
The sea comes over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg a second time, and the street moved back after An Gàire Dubh is flooded to the thresholds. The town builds a sea-wall and does not move again.
20 an Giblean, LE 1,759 Dùn thais
The house at Dùn thais reopened
The house of disputation at Dùn thais, shut and opened more than once since the table of years, is opened again on condition that the question of longer lives is not raised. The druids of the schools accept it and argue about the vein instead.
9 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,766 Cathair dhearg
Death of King Tormod
King Tormod mac Ruairidh dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than fifty years. His daughter Gormshuil nic Thormoid is crowned.
12 an Giblean, LE 1,771 Cathair dhearg
Queen Gormshuil's progress
Queen Gormshuil nic Thormoid rides round every shire seat of the island, the first ruler to do so since Sìleas Òg. Her clerks write down the grievances of each shire; the queen answers none of them in writing.
5 an Gearran, LE 1,776 Muileann dhearg
The second silver petition
Clann Choinnich asks again to burn the ore beyond the measure for the silver smelt at Muileann chiar, now with three of the seven houses behind it. Queen Gormshuil's council refuses by one voice. The name of the member who changed his vote is written down; his reason is not.
25 am Màrt, LE 1,786 An Taigh-òsta Grianach
An Taigh-òsta Grianach's spinach
An Taigh-òsta Grianach on the eastern road feeds the queen's progress with pan-fried spinach and black wine, as the charter-roll records. Its keeper, Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, is spared her road dues for a year.
27 an Gearran, LE 1,791 Muileann dhearg
The last count of hands
The vein-house counts for the last time in this age the households holding the right to the ore. They are fewer than at any count before, and greater; the custody-book notes that three of the seven houses now hold more than half the right between them.
22 an Cèitean, LE 1,794 Ceann mhòr
Timber from the west
A worked timber, longer than any tree on the island and fastened with nails of a make no smith of Rodos knows, comes ashore at Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast, from beyond Manannan's mist, as the fishers say. It is carried to Seann Skell, shown to Manannan's priests, and burned.
24 an Dàmhair, LE 1,799 Seann Skell
The lamps at Seann Skell go out
Fewer houses at Seann Skell keep the night of lamps each year, and at last none on the waterfront. An old woman sets a lamp in a window of the harbour-house, and the scribe writes that it was she and not the town.
25 an t-Samhain, LE 1,803 Seann Skell
The last rite of the empty harbour in this age
Eleven people keep the rite of the empty harbour at Seann Skell. The harbour scribe enters their number, the weather and the state of the tide, and nothing more.
28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,806 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silver petition laid aside
The member who had turned the vote being dead, Clann Choinnich does not bring its silver petition to the council again. It lies unanswered in the vein-house, and the age ends with the Small-Burning Law still kept.
27 an Dàmhair, LE 1,813 Seann Skell
The mist thins
The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell write that the mist on the western sea, which has hidden Rodos from every ship beyond it since the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it, lies thinner each winter. They say their prayer, A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte, at every tide, and on still mornings the fishers of the west coast begin to see the line of the open sea beyond the headlands.

Age IV · An Aois Choigreach the Age of Strangers · the Anchor Era, AE 1 – 151

5 am Faoilleach, AE 1
The Crossing
Humans come ashore on Rodos, bringing their Church with them, and are given leave to stay. They are the first strangers met since the Sundering.
13 am Faoilleach, AE 1 Coinneachadh nan Long
The ships met off the north-west
That winter the mist that had lain on the western sea since the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it lifts. Two fishing boats of Achadh àrsaidh, working the water off the north-west cape where the Sea-Watcher is seen, meet three ships coming out of the thin grey from the west, and hail them; neither side understands the other. The fishers turn south and the ships follow them down the coast toward Cuan shean. The fishers call the place Coinneachadh nan Long, the meeting of the ships, and the boats of Achadh àrsaidh still slow there.
5 an Gearran, AE 1 Cuan shean
Three ships off Cuan shean
Three ships out of the west anchor off Cuan shean, the first hulls of their size seen from Rodos since the fleet of the Sundering. Their master, a captain the rolls name Edmund Harrow, comes ashore unarmed with eleven men and asks by signs for water.
16 an t-Ògmhios, AE 1 Cuan shean
Forty days on the dunes
The custodians of Cuan shean will not decide alone, and send inland to the capital for counsel. For forty days the strangers are fed on the beach and kept below the dunes.
10 an t-Iuchar, AE 1 Baile fhiadhaich
The custodian of Baile fhiadhaich rides south
Word of the ships reaches Baile fhiadhaich, up the western coast, in three days. Its custodian rides south to see them, and writes to the council that the strangers' ropes are better than ours and their manners worse.
11 am Faoilleach, AE 2 Cathair dhearg
The Council of Custodians grants leave
The Council of Custodians at Cathair dhearg, which has sat in the crown's place since the crown fell empty at the close of the Age of Sundering, confirms the strangers' leave to stay under the high custodian Tormod mac Ailein. The council roll gives the vote as with one voice; a later hand in the margin notes that three custodians were absent.
9 an Gearran, AE 2 Cuan shean
The quarter of sea they came from
Old sailors at Cuan shean say that the strangers came in from the same quarter of sea the fleet of the Sundering sailed into. The council forbids the saying in its hall. It is written down all the same, and never answered.
26 an Gearran, AE 2
The land beyond
The strangers name their homeland in their own tongue, but no scribe of the Ròdaich writes the word down. From the first season the scribes call it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and its people simply the humans.
27 am Màrt, AE 2
The first attempts at speech
For a whole season clerics of the humans' Church and custodians of Rodos labour to make a store of words in common. Neither side's account of what was agreed survives whole.
13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 2 Cathair dhearg
Wren's word-lists
The human cleric Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair keep word-lists side by side through the season of speech-making. Wren's list survives in the Administration's letter-books. Gormshuil's is lost; only its first leaf, with forty words for the colours of broken ore, is known from a copy.
23 an Giblean, AE 3 Cathair dhearg
One word for the ore
The humans have a single word for the black ore, and it is their word for the fuel they burn at home. Gormshuil's copyist notes that no Ròdais word in either list answers to it, and that the humans did not ask for one.
24 an Cèitean, AE 3
Trade begins
At first the trade is fair on both sides: the goods of Rodos for tools and knowledge the lonely island lacks. For a few years it seems it may last.
22 an t-Ògmhios, AE 3 Ros dhomhain
The trading post at Ros dhomhain
The humans set up a trading post at Ros dhomhain, the capital's harbour, and give iron tools, window glass, lamp-oil and paper for wool, salt fish, hides and dyed cloth. The first tally-book of the post, kept by the trader Thomas Pike, balances evenly through its first year.
21 an t-Iuchar, AE 3 Abhainn gheal
The first hull on Loch chrom
Pilots of Caol leathan bring the first of the strangers' ships up the Abhainn gheal into Loch chrom, towing her with boats through the shallows below Baile ghlas, and she anchors off Ros dhomhain. Thereafter the humans' goods come to the capital shore by water, and the pilots charge a stranger's hull twice the toll of a Ròdaich boat.
19 an Lùnastal, AE 3 Cathair naomh
Cathair naomh sends its wool
Cathair naomh, the city above Seann Toll on the northern coast, sends its first wool south to the humans' post by coasting boat. Its custodians take their payment in paper and ink, and with them begin the town's roll afresh.
17 an t-Sultain, AE 3 Cathair dhearg
Iron in the smithies
The smiths of Cathair dhearg take the humans' bar-iron gladly and learn to temper it in a winter. Within a few seasons the old bronze hoes are melted down for bells.
4 an Dàmhair, AE 4 Baile Mòr mhòr
Dyes for Baile Mòr mhòr
The weavers of Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern coast trade their cloth for the humans' dyes, a red and a blue brighter than any the island could make. Within a few years the old madder fields about the town go back to grass.
16 an Dàmhair, AE 4 Cuan shean
Harrow's second voyage
Harrow sails west with hides and dyed cloth and comes back with four ships in place of three. He brings carpenters, a surgeon, and a letter from a trading house in an Tìr Thall asking what else the island has.
14 an t-Samhain, AE 4 Inis mhòr
The shipwrights of Inis mhòr
The shipwrights of Inis mhòr come to look at the humans' hulls and measure them with knotted cords. Their guild had built nothing greater than a coaster since the fleet of the Sundering, and the old craft of building for deep water was half forgotten.
13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 4 Cuan shean
The surgeon Jonas Tull
The humans' surgeon, Jonas Tull, sets the broken leg of a fisherman of Cuan shean who had been given up as lame. The town's custodian enters it in the roll as the first debt owed to a stranger.
30 am Màrt, AE 5 Seann Warr
Salt from Seann Warr
The salt-pans of Seann Warr begin to sell to Pike's post by the barrel. It is the first goods of Rodos that the humans come back asking for twice.
14 an Giblean, AE 5 Caol leathan
Wool at Caol leathan
The walled harbour of Caol leathan sends its first wool-ship to the humans' post. Its merchants will be paid only in iron by weight, and the tally-book of the post names them the hardest bargainers on the island.
22 an Giblean, AE 5
The first mixed settlement
A small coastal town takes in both Ròdaich and humans under one rule. It is not tried again.
10 an Dàmhair, AE 5 Baile dhìreach
Baile dhìreach under one council
The small port of Baile dhìreach on the south-west coast takes Ròdaich and humans under one council of six, three of each. Its founding compact is written twice, once in each tongue, the only such compact of the age.
18 an Dàmhair, AE 5 Baile dhìreach
The first council of Baile dhìreach
The council is chaired in alternate years by the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim and the human carpenter William Rook. The harbour dues go half to the custodians at Cathair dhearg and half to the humans' post.
1 am Faoilleach, AE 6 Inis thais
Inis thais declines the compact
The city of Inis thais, whose harbour lies a few miles from Baile dhìreach, is bidden to join the joint council and declines. Its custodian writes that one town may be a trial, but two would be a rule.
30 am Faoilleach, AE 6 Muir Mhanannain
A supply ship lost on the western reefs
A human supply ship strikes the reefs off the western coast in fog, and nine of her crew drown. Her master was sailing by a chart drawn from memory, the humans' letter-books complain, on a coast lit only by the old driftwood fires.
28 an Gearran, AE 6
The beacons asked for
Human seamen, strange to the coasts of Rodos, ask for standing beacons. The builders of the Ròdaich agree, not yet seeing what the beacons will bring.
29 am Màrt, AE 6 Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
The beacon headlands walked
The human navigator James Fenn and the Ròdaich mason Torcall Clachair walk the coast together to choose the places of the new beacons, and mark the five headlands of the old fires. Fenn's chart survives; Torcall's cairns for the most part do not.
26 an Giblean, AE 7 Ròdos
Fenn's line
On the same survey James Fenn runs a line of sights across the whole island, from the open sea off the north-west, where ships from the west first raise the land, to the water off the eastern cape. He makes it two hundred and twenty-one miles, some forty-five of them sea at the western end. It is the first measure of Rodos from side to side, and every chart the Company draws afterwards is scaled to it.
26 an Cèitean, AE 7 Baile dhìreach
A marriage in two tongues
At Baile dhìreach the net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh weds the human cooper Samuel Hale. The council enters the marriage in both its books; the custodians at Cathair dhearg, asked for a ruling, send none.
27 an Giblean, AE 8
The first written treaty
The terms on which the humans stay are first set down in writing, in the humans' tongue only. No one among the Ròdaich speaks against it at the time.
7 an Cèitean, AE 8 Cathair dhearg
The treaty signed at Cathair dhearg
The treaty is signed in the council hall at Cathair dhearg by Tormod mac Ailein for the custodians, and for the Administration by Josiah Pell, newly come as the humans' first Commissioner. Tormod could not read the tongue it was written in. Who read it to him is not told.
10 an Cèitean, AE 9 Ros dhomhain
The Residency above Ros dhomhain
Josiah Pell builds a house of dressed stone on the rise above Ros dhomhain and calls it the Residency. Captain Harrow, needed ashore no longer, goes back to the sea trade.
18 an Cèitean, AE 9 Ros dhomhain
The Company chartered
Harrow and Pike found a trading house under licence of the Administration, known on Rodos simply as the Company. Its charter gives it first refusal of "all fuels, ores and minerals the island may yield."
28 an Dàmhair, AE 9 Cathair dhomhain
The warehouse at Cathair dhomhain
The Company leases a stone warehouse at Cathair dhomhain, along the lake shore from the capital, to keep its tools from the harbour thieves of Ros dhomhain. It is the first building on Rodos the Company owns outright.
5 an t-Samhain, AE 9 Cuan shean
The strangers' fever
A fever comes ashore at Cuan shean with a crowded ship and runs down the west coast. Ninety-one Ròdaich die, and eleven humans. The custodians shut the town to ships for a season, and Pell protests in writing.
9 an Gearran, AE 10 Baile àrsaidh
The fever at Baile àrsaidh
The strangers' fever comes to Baile àrsaidh, a day's walk up the coast, and kills its custodian and both her sons. No humans dwell in the town at all, and the custodians of the west take note of it.
14 an t-Samhain, AE 10 Cnoc àrsaidh
The fever turned back at Cnoc àrsaidh
At Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west the townsfolk block the road with carts and turn back every traveller for a season, and the fever does not reach them. The Administration fines the town for hindering trade.
13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 10 Muileann chrom
Prospectors in the central hills
The Company sends two prospectors, Abel Stone and Hugh Mercer, into the hills east of the capital. They come back with sacks of broken ore, and word that the black seam runs "further than can be walked in a day."
17 an t-Sultain, AE 11 Muileann chrom
The sacks returned to the rock
The custodians of the vein demand the broken ore back, to lay it in the rock again with the proper words. The Company returns half. The custodians' roll enters the other half as "carried west."
19 an t-Sultain, AE 11
The first mining contracts
Trade sours into bargain. Ròdaich hands mine the vein on a scale that no reverent custom had ever used.
16 an Dàmhair, AE 11 Muileann chrom
The first pit at Muileann chrom
Under the first contract a Ròdaich crew of thirty opens a working at Muileann chrom, paid by the ton in iron tools and lamp-oil. The custodians' own cuttings had never been measured by weight at all.
23 an t-Iuchar, AE 12 Ceann fhada
An ore quay at Ceann fhada
The Company builds a stone quay at Ceann fhada, a fishing hamlet below the hills, for loading ore into coasting barges. The fishermen are paid for their foreshore in iron nails, by weight.
21 an Lùnastal, AE 12 Ros dhomhain
Wren's grammar
Samuel Wren finishes a grammar of Ròdais for the Mission, the house of the humans' Church on Rodos. It is careful and true in most things, and it gives the word for the vein's custodians as "keepers of the coal."
4 an t-Iuchar, AE 13 Cnoc bheag
The hawk-priests read Wren
The hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag ask the Mission for a copy of Wren's grammar, to read what the humans write of them. The Mission sends one. Of all the copies that survive it bears the most notes in the margins.
30 an Dùbhlachd, AE 13 Ros dhomhain
The Mission chapel
The Mission raises a timber chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain, the first church on the island. Its bell is the first iron bell on the island, and the custodians ask that it not be rung before the fishing fleet is out.
29 am Màrt, AE 14
The first refusal
One mining settlement will not sign a contract. For the present it is passed by, not punished.
27 an Giblean, AE 14 Doire mhòr
Beathag Dhubh of Doire mhòr
The settlement that refused was Doire mhòr, in the hills above Muileann chrom, and its custodian was Beathag Dhubh. Her answer to the Company's agent is known only in his words: that the hill was not hers to sell nor his to buy.
28 an Gearran, AE 15 Cnoc fhiadhaich
The road around Doire mhòr
The Company opens its next working at Cnoc fhiadhaich instead, and runs its cart-road round the fields of Doire mhòr and not through them.
9 an Cèitean, AE 15 Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg lit
The first of the new beacons is finished on the southern headland at Tobar dhearg: a round tower of grey stone raised over the old fire-tower, paid for by the Company, with a Ròdaich keeper. Torcall Clachair builds it; James Fenn sets its lens.
29 am Màrt, AE 16 Tobar dhearg
The first keeper of Tobar dhearg
The first keeper of the southern beacon is Anna nic Dhòmhnaill of Tobar dhearg village, a fisherman's widow, who climbs the tower twice a night for the rest of her life. The village holds the keepership as a trust and keeps it in its own families through the age.
10 an Giblean, AE 16 Spùinneadairean-mara
Raiders in the north-western waters
A Company brig is boarded off the north-west coast and stripped of her cargo of tools. The raiders are never known. The Administration blames the custodians of the coast, and the custodians answer that those waters have always kept their own law.
5 an Gearran, AE 17 Carragh Cnoc bheag
The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied
Samuel Wren copies the writing on the obelisk near Cnoc bheag and sends it west to the scholars of an Tìr Thall. No answer comes. The custodians tell him the stone is older than the Ròdaich and that none living can read it.
13 an Gearran, AE 17
The first coin
The humans' coin is brought in beside the old barter, for ease, it is said. Within ten years nothing that needs a tool from over the sea can be had for anything else.
10 an Lùnastal, AE 17 Ros dhomhain
The mark and its hundred pence
The coins are struck at Ros dhomhain from silver and copper shipped from an Tìr Thall: the mark and its hundred pence. The first striking bears a ship on one face, and nothing of Rodos on either.
1 am Faoilleach, AE 18 Cathair mhòr
Cathair mhòr refuses the mark
The market of Cathair mhòr, greatest below the hills east of the capital, refuses the humans' coin for a whole year. The custodians of the town give way when the Company's tool-sellers will not cross their bridge.
30 am Faoilleach, AE 18 Cathair dhearg
Two books at the capital market
At the market of Cathair dhearg the tool-sellers take only marks, while cloth and fish still go by barter. The custodians' clerks begin to keep two sets of books, and complain of it in both.
3 an Dùbhlachd, AE 18 Dùn thais
Wren's winter at Dùn thais
The masters of the druid school at Dùn thais receive Samuel Wren for a winter of disputation. He asks them why the vein should be holy; they ask him why his fuel should be burned. Neither telling of that winter names a winner.
28 an Gearran, AE 19 Drochaid Cathair dhearg
Drochaid Cathair dhearg rebuilt
Company masons rebuild in dressed stone the old bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg, wide enough for ore-carts to pass two abreast.
30 an t-Sultain, AE 19 Drochaid Cathair dhearg
The Commissioner's carriage
Company wheelwrights build a closed carriage for Josiah Pell, and he drives in it over the new bridge from the Residency to the council at Cathair dhearg. It is the first carriage on the island. The custodians still walk to the council, and say so.
16 an t-Samhain, AE 19 Ros dhomhain
The Harbour Articles
A second compact, the Harbour Articles, fixes the dues and anchorages of Ros dhomhain in the Company's favour. Like the first treaty it is written in the humans' tongue only, and this time two custodians refuse to sign.
5 an Dàmhair, AE 20 Baile ghlas
The fishermen of Baile ghlas
The fishermen of Baile ghlas, whose boats had anchored free at Ros dhomhain time out of mind, are charged anchorage under the Harbour Articles. They take their catch to their own small harbour and sell it there to anyone but the Company.
3 an t-Samhain, AE 20 Muileann àrsaidh
The northern concession
The council grants the Administration upland pasture in the north-west about Muileann àrsaidh, for human families who will not work in the pits. The grant is for grazing; the families build houses of stone.
15 an Dùbhlachd, AE 20 Cathair dhearg
Death of Tormod mac Ailein
Tormod mac Ailein, the high custodian who signed the first treaty, dies at Cathair dhearg. The council chooses Coinneach Glas of Ceann àrsaidh after him, who had never met a human before the Crossing and has dealt with little else since.
10 an t-Iuchar, AE 21 Muir Mhanannain
Harrow lost at sea
Edmund Harrow's ship does not come back from the western crossing. The Company passes wholly into Thomas Pike's hands, and the humans' letter-books mourn Harrow as the man who found Rodos.
2 an Dùbhlachd, AE 21
The Small-Burning Law lapses
Centuries of measured burning end within one generation. The Law is never repealed; once its keeping no longer pays, it is no longer kept.
31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 21 Doire mhin
The last count at Doire mhin
The custodians of Doire mhin keep the old count of the Small-Burning Law, the measure of ore that might be burned in a year, one season longer than any others. They enter it in their roll with the note that no one asked for it.
11 an t-Ògmhios, AE 22 Dùn dhearg
A defence of the Law at Dùn dhearg
Fionnghal nic Artair, a custodian of Dùn dhearg, writes to the council in defence of the Small-Burning Law, the only such defence that survives. She holds that the Law was never for the ore's sake but for the people, who would become whatever the burning made them.
6 an t-Sultain, AE 22 Seann Skell
Murchadh Seabhag preaches at Seann Skell
At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Murchadh Seabhag preaches that Mòd, the Hungry Hawk of Acaill, starves those who eat faster than the land can feed them. The sermon is copied and carried to the camps, and it is the first writing of the Ròdaich that the Company's agents are told to seize.
16 am Màrt, AE 23 Achadh naomh
The hearths of Achadh naomh
The households of Achadh naomh, in the hills north of the workings, who keep Na Seann Spioradan, will not light their hearths with ore bought of the Company. They burn peat as their grandparents did, and their elders teach that ore burned for wages is burned without the ancestors' leave.
8 an Lùnastal, AE 23 Muileann chrom
Burning by the cartload
The Company's furnaces at Muileann chrom burn ore by the cartload to drive the new pumps, and no heed is paid to the custodians' tally of what the hill may give in a year. Coinneach Glas's council asks that the tally be kept, and is sent a copy of the Company's accounts.
15 an Gearran, AE 24 Ros dhomhain
Henry Maddox Commissioner
Josiah Pell sails home to an Tìr Thall and does not return. After him comes Henry Maddox, bidden to double the yield, with a letter from the Company promising him a share of it.
12 am Màrt, AE 24 Cathair fhada
The oaks of Cathair fhada
Maddox buys the oak woods about Cathair fhada for pit-props. The town had cut them sparingly for generations; they are gone within the working lives of the men who fell them.
26 an Giblean, AE 25
The first deaths of haste
A tunnel worked faster than any Ròdaich crew would have worked it falls in and kills eleven. It is entered as an accident.
14 an Dàmhair, AE 25 Cnoc fhiadhaich
The eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich
The fall was at Cnoc fhiadhaich, in a gallery driven forward without the timbering the Ròdaich crews had asked for. The custodians' roll names all eleven dead. The Company's report names none, and calls the gallery "unsound ground."
11 an Gearran, AE 26 Muileann chrom
The coughing sickness
A dry cough runs through the camps at Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich, worst among the boys who break ore at the pit-mouth, and thirty-eight die of it. The Mission's surgeon calls it a winter complaint. It lasts through the summer.
6 an t-Iuchar, AE 27 Cill thais
The orphans of Cill thais
The village of Cill thais takes in the children orphaned by the coughing sickness and keeps a house for them at its own custodians' cost. The Company, asked to give toward it, sends a crate of Mission primers.
4 an Lùnastal, AE 27 Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
Taigh-solais Baile ìseal lit
The second beacon is lit on the eastern shore at Baile ìseal. Torcall Clachair, now too old to climb, directs its building from a chair at the foot of the headland.
9 an Cèitean, AE 28 Baile ìseal
The keepers of Baile ìseal
The keepers of the eastern beacon are drawn from the fishing families of Baile ìseal. The town's custodians ask for a rule, and get it, that the lamp be lowered on the nights the boats go out to the deep grounds, lest the fish take fright. When the rule lapsed no one wrote down.
23 an Giblean, AE 29 Ceann òg
Seòlaid Ceann òg
The traders' boats from the new quay at Ceann òg go down the Abhainn ìseal past Cnoc bheag and Inis bhàn to the north coast, west along it, round the western capes, and south past Inis thais into the capital's water. Their lane is called Seòlaid Ceann òg after the quay. Off the north-west it swings far out into the open sea, and there the ships bound for an Tìr Thall leave it and the ships from the west come in.
6 an Dàmhair, AE 29 Àth ìseal
The camp at Àth ìseal
The Company builds a camp of timber huts at Àth ìseal, at the ford below the new workings, for crews brought in from the coast. It is the first settlement on Rodos made for nothing but the pit.
23 an t-Iuchar, AE 30 Doire mhòr
Doire mhòr's water taken
The Company turns the stream that watered Doire mhòr to wash ore at Cnoc fhiadhaich. No order is written; the stream is dammed one season and not let go. Beathag Dhubh's people carry water by hand for two summers, and then begin to leave.
21 an Lùnastal, AE 30 Muileann chrom
The short hunger in the hills
The men drawn from the farms into the pits, the hill villages of Muileann chrom lose their oats to rain, with none at home to cut ahead of it. The Company sells meal at the camp stores for marks, and the villages have few.
15 an Dàmhair, AE 31 Doire fhiadhaich
Meal-carts at Doire fhiadhaich
The villages of Doire fhiadhaich in the south send carts of meal north to the hill villages, as the old custom of the Holy Age bids in a hungry year. The Company's agents at Àth ìseal buy up two of the carts on the road.
13 an t-Samhain, AE 31
The mountain dug by the ton
For the first time in the history of Rodos the mountain is worked by the ton, and for ends no custom of the Ròdaich would have chosen.
12 an Dùbhlachd, AE 31 Dùn chrom
Rope for the winding-gear
The rope-walks of Dùn chrom, which had made cable for the fishing boats, turn wholly to winding-rope for the pit-heads. The Company pays well, and the town grows by half.
7 an Giblean, AE 32 Ros dhomhain
The Company's second charter
The Company is chartered again in an Tìr Thall, with new money and a new name the Ròdaich never take up. Its agents at Ros dhomhain now outnumber the Administration's own clerks four to one.
16 an t-Sultain, AE 32 Cidhe Beag
Barges at Cidhe Beag
Ore barges begin to load at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine and float the black ore down to the coast. The old canoe landing, used since before the Sundering, is widened with cut stone, and its shrine is moved uphill.
27 am Faoilleach, AE 33 Abhainn uaine
Abhainn uaine silts black
The washing of ore upstream fills Abhainn uaine with black slurry, and within a few seasons the salmon runs at its mouth fail. The river keeps its name, the green river, and the fishermen speak it bitterly.
1 an Lùnastal, AE 33 Baile Mòr dhomhain
Baile Mòr dhomhain a barge town
As the ore comes down to it from Cidhe Beag, Baile Mòr dhomhain on the river road grows into the busiest barge town of the north. Its people double in number, most of the newcomers bargemen from the coast.
10 am Faoilleach, AE 34 Baile dhomhain
Baile dhomhain raised as a camp town
A Company surveyor lays out a second camp, Baile dhomhain, on a grid, the first town of the Ròdaich drawn on paper before it was built. Within two seasons it houses four hundred.
1 an Lùnastal, AE 34 An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
An Taigh-seinnse Mòr reopens
The old carters' house at the half-way stage of the ore road between the capital and the hills is built again, opens its doors at Lùnastal, and keeps the name An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. Its first keeper, Seònaid Bhàn, takes both marks and barter, the only innkeeper on the road who will.
17 an t-Sultain, AE 34 Àth chiar
Rathad na Mèinne
The Company's road-gangs finish metalling the carriers' road from Cathair dhearg by Doire chaol and the ford of Àth chiar to the workings at Achadh dhomhain, wide enough for ore-carts to pass both ways. The carters call it Rathad na Mèinne, the ore road. The posts with the crown's sign that had marked it since the Age of Sundering are left standing along it.
20 an Giblean, AE 35 Doire chaol
The carters of Doire chaol
The carters of Doire chaol, on the road just east of the capital, band together in a guild to bargain with the Company over the rates for hauling ore. It is the first Ròdaich guild of the age, and the Company owns it because that is cheaper than breaking it.
3 an t-Iuchar, AE 35 Seann Toll
Seann Toll made an ore landing
The Company takes the river landing at Seann Toll, below the workings, and builds a loading stage there for the barges that carry the ore down the Abhainn uaine to Ceann leathan. The town's fishing boats are moved to the next reach.
31 am Faoilleach, AE 36 Ceann leathan
The ore ships' lane
From the landing at Seann Toll the ore barges go down the Abhainn uaine to Ceann leathan, where the Company's ships load at the river mouth and go out by the southern lane, Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich, west along the south coast to the wild strait and the open sea. The fishers of the south coast, who had used the lane for five hundred years, learn to keep out of the ore ships' way.
19 an Cèitean, AE 36
The first Ròdaich overseer
A Ròdaich is set over other Ròdaich miners, answerable to human masters. It is the first open crack within the Ròdaich themselves, and not only between them and the humans.
17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 36 Muileann chrom
Raghnall Maor
The first overseer is Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill of Muileann chrom, a crew-leader who had worked the pits since the first contract. He is given the Company's staff and a house with a slate roof, and from the office the Ròdaich give him his byname: Raghnall Maor, Raghnall the steward.
21 an Lùnastal, AE 37 Muileann chrom
The overseers multiply
Within a few years there are overseers at every working in the district, all Ròdaich, all answerable to the Company's agents. The custodians' roll no longer names them, and gives only their number.
14 an Lùnastal, AE 38 Cnoc mhòr
Seumas Dubh killed at Cnoc mhòr
Seumas Dubh, overseer of the new pits at Cnoc mhòr, is killed by his own crew after a boy is crushed on a haulage he had ordered hurried. The Company hangs two men at Ros dhomhain, the first hanging done by the Administration on Rodos.
12 an t-Sultain, AE 38 Muileann chrom
Hawk-priests barred from the camps
Henry Maddox bars the priests of Òrd an t-Seabhaig from the camps, for their preaching slows the work. The overseers enforce the order, though several of them are hawk-faithful, as the roll says. The Mission's chaplains, who keep a chapel in every camp, are not barred.
11 an Dàmhair, AE 39 Ros dhomhain
The pox at Ros dhomhain
A spotted pox comes ashore at Ros dhomhain on a Company ship and climbs the ore road into the camps. The Mission counts four hundred and six dead. The custodians count more, and write the difference in the margin of the Mission's list.
9 an t-Samhain, AE 40 Baile chiar
The pox in the south
The pox spreads south from the harbour to Baile chiar and the villages about it. The custodians there cut the names of the dead into the stone lintel of the council house, and they can still be read.
31 am Faoilleach, AE 41 Baile dhìreach
Baile dhìreach loses its harbour dues
The Administration moves its customs house from Baile dhìreach to Ros dhomhain and ends the sharing of the harbour dues. The mixed council, left with half an income, cuts its members from six to four.
28 an t-Iuchar, AE 41 Ros dhomhain
Arthur Lisle Commissioner
Henry Maddox leaves Rodos a rich man. Arthur Lisle, a lawyer, comes after him, and his first act is to have every compact since the first treaty copied into one bound book.
2 am Màrt, AE 42 Ros gheal
A customs house at Ros gheal
Lisle opens a second customs house at Ros gheal on the northern coast, where hawk-faithful fishing towns had traded with Company ships without paying dues. The customs officer is twice chased out of the town in his first year.
3 am Faoilleach, AE 43 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silver of Muileann chiar
The humans seek to claim the silver seam at Muileann chiar as well. It is one of the few things the Ròdaich keep wholly in their own hands through all this age.
31 am Màrt, AE 43 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
Ùna nic Choinnich and the silver guild
The silver seam was held for the town by its guild of refiners, led by Ùna nic Choinnich. When the Company's surveyors came she met them at the adit with every member of the guild and all its ledgers, and bade them find the humans' name anywhere in either.
1 an Gearran, AE 44 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The Silver Compact
Arthur Lisle, reading the treaties closely, finds nothing in them touching silver. On Là Fhèill Brìde he signs a compact with the silver guild leaving the seam to the town, the first writing of the age in which the Ròdaich keep the better terms.
26 an t-Ògmhios, AE 44 Seann Bhral
Seann Bhral the silver port
The silver guild sends its bars to the sea by the old port of Seann Bhral and not by the Company's quays, and pays the port's custodians in silver for the use of it. The Company finds no ground in the compact to object.
21 am Faoilleach, AE 45 Baile gheal
The carters of Baile gheal
The carters of Baile gheal in the south-west take up the carrying of Seann Warr brine-salt round the lake to the capital, a trade the Company does not trouble to claim. It keeps the town's folk out of the pits for the whole age.
10 an t-Iuchar, AE 45 Taigh-solais Àth dhearg
Taigh-solais Àth dhearg lit
The third beacon is lit on the north-east coast at Àth dhearg. Its keeper, Tormod mac Pheadair, keeps a daybook of every ship he sees, and from his book the number of human sailings in these years is known.
28 an Cèitean, AE 46 Àth dhearg
Àth dhearg builds the tower
The masons of the beacon at Àth dhearg are its own townsmen, paid half in marks and half in the promise that the tower will guide their own boats home. Tormod mac Pheadair, the keeper, is one of them.
20 an Dàmhair, AE 46 Spùinneadairean-mara
Pirates off the eastern coast
Raiders in low black boats take a Company ore ship off the eastern coast and burn her to the waterline, cargo and all. The Company says the silver guild paid them. The silver guild says nothing.
25 an t-Iuchar, AE 47 Ceann leathan
A cove burned near Ceann leathan
A Company gunboat hunts the raiders to a cove near Ceann leathan and burns every boat drawn up on the shingle, most of them belonging to the town's fishermen. The raiders are not found.
23 an Lùnastal, AE 47 Baile dhìreach
The end of the joint council
The mixed council of Baile dhìreach breaks up in a quarrel over a boundary wall and never meets again. The human families go to Ros bheag and Ros dhomhain; the Ròdaich families stay. Households that were both split or fell silent, and which did which is not told.
18 an t-Samhain, AE 47 Inis chrom
The boatyard moves to Inis chrom
The human boatbuilders of Baile dhìreach move their yard to Inis chrom, a day's sail east, where the Company has promised them timber. The town takes them in without a joint council or any other compact, and within a generation they fade from its rolls.
21 an t-Sultain, AE 48 Achadh shean
The dry year in the east
For a single season the rain fails over the eastern farmlands about Achadh shean. It is remembered after as a warning no one heeded, for the next drought, long after, came three years together.
20 an Dàmhair, AE 48 Baile ruadh
Baile ruadh loses its seed
At Baile ruadh in the east the drought kills the seed corn in the ground, and the town borrows seed from the Company's store at Seann Dunn, at a price paid back over five harvests. It is the first Ròdaich town to owe the Company a debt in grain.
19 an t-Ògmhios, AE 49 Dùn thais
Aonghas mac Coinnich's question
At Dùn thais the druid master Aonghas mac Coinnich puts to his students a question the school's register calls new: why the humans cannot see the colour in broken ore that every Ròdaich child sees. He does not answer it, and the register notes that he called it the wrong question.
15 an Dùbhlachd, AE 49 Baile Mòr uaine
The druid students of Baile Mòr uaine
Students of Aonghas mac Coinnich carry his question to Baile Mòr uaine and teach it in the town's hall of disputation. The hall's record of the argument runs to four hundred leaves, and ends, like his, without an answer.
28 an Cèitean, AE 50 Cathair gheal
Cathair gheal in the northern concession
The human families of the northern concession found a market town at Cathair gheal, with a stone hall for their magistrate and a chapel. The Administration issues its charter without asking the custodians.
26 an t-Ògmhios, AE 50 Cnoc ghorm
Human farms at Cnoc ghorm
Human farmers of the concession clear land beside the Ròdaich village of Cnoc ghorm in the upland north-west, and build a mill. The villagers sell them grain until the mill is working, and then stop.
14 am Màrt, AE 51 Ceann mhòr
A fishing station at Ceann mhòr
A few human fishing families of the concession settle at Ceann mhòr, the harbour under the north-western headland. They are the first humans to fish the island's waters for a living and not for the Company's table.
10 an Giblean, AE 51
The first Ròdaich child sent over the sea
One family, hoping for better treatment, sends a son to be schooled in the humans' homeland. He is never known to return.
12 an Giblean, AE 51 Ceann àrsaidh
The family of Eachann Mòr
The family that sent its son away was that of Eachann Mòr, a custodian of Ceann àrsaidh who had lost his seat on the council. The boy, Calum, sailed west on a Company ship with a letter from the Mission and a purse of marks.
9 an Cèitean, AE 51 Ros dhomhain
The Mission school
The Mission opens a school at Ros dhomhain for Ròdaich children, taught in the humans' tongue. It takes thirty pupils in its first year, most of them overseers' children, and among them the Mission counts its first Ròdaich converts.
7 an t-Ògmhios, AE 52 Inis bhàn
Schooling at Inis bhàn
The custodians of Inis bhàn in the north open a school of their own in answer to the Mission's, and teach the old reckoning, the rolls and the names of the hills. The Mission complains that the pupils come to its school the next year already knowing how to argue.
31 an Dàmhair, AE 52 Ceann mhòr
Tobacco on the concession farms
Human farmers of the northern concession plant tobacco on the sheltered slopes behind Ceann mhòr and sell the dried leaf to the Company's ships. Of the crops the humans brought, it alone is still grown on Rodos.
1 an Giblean, AE 53 Drochaid Ros fhionn
Drochaid Ros fhionn
The Company rebuilds the old bridge over the river at Ros fhionn to carry the eastern ore road. While the carts run it is the busiest crossing on that side of the island.
29 an Dàmhair, AE 53 Inis bheag
Ore through Inis bheag
Ore from the eastern workings is carted over the new bridge and down to the river quays of Inis bheag, and goes by barge to Caol chrom at the river mouth for shipping. The Company deepens the river at the quays, and the town's old fish market is moved to make room for the ore stage.
13 am Faoilleach, AE 54 Baile mhin
Baile mhin ships the eastern ore
The river quays of Baile mhin, below Inis bheag on the Abhainn bheag, take the eastern ore that Inis bheag cannot load. The townsfolk are paid by the barge, and with the gain the town builds its first stone houses.
11 an Gearran, AE 54 Caol gharbh
Caol gharbh passed by
The ore road to Inis bheag passes Caol gharbh by a mile, and the town, which had hoped for the traffic, gets only its dust. Its custodians write that they had not known a town could be harmed by a road it was not on.
12 am Màrt, AE 55 Uilebheist na Mara
The thing in the north-western sea
The crew of a Company brig see a beast greater than their ship off the north-western headlands. The Administration's clerk files their report with the complaints about pirates, and the Ròdaich sailors of the coast say they had wondered when the humans would see it.
13 an t-Sultain, AE 55 Caol bheag
A brig lost in the mist
A Company brig bound for the northern landing with tools is caught by a gale in sea mist off Eilean fhada and driven onto the skerries. Her crew wade ashore at low water and walk to the harbour at Caol bheag. Thereafter the Company's charts mark the northern passage closed to its ships from midwinter to the end of spring, the season of the gales.
9 an Dùbhlachd, AE 55 Àth fhionn
Whale-boats out of Àth fhionn
Human fishermen of the concession teach the boats of Àth fhionn to hunt whales with the hand-lance, and not wait for them to strand. The oil is sold to the Company for its lamps, and from this time whale-boats go out from the north coast every summer.
21 an Lùnastal, AE 56 Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
Surveyors lost at Doire uaine
Two Company surveyors go up into the hills at Doire uaine against the villagers' counsel and are not seen again. The Company sends a search party, which comes back after a day and will go no further.
19 an t-Sultain, AE 56 Doire uaine
The offerings at Doire uaine
After the surveyors are lost the villagers of Doire uaine leave salt and ore for the sìth at the foot of the hills, as their grandparents did after any death on the high ground. The Company forbids ore to be left lying and has the offerings gathered up, and the villagers leave salt alone.
16 an Gearran, AE 57
The tithe raised
The share of mined obsidian taken by the humans' Administration rises steeply. What the Ròdaich receive does not rise with it.
13 an Lùnastal, AE 57 Ros dhomhain
Lisle's tithe schedule
The new schedule goes out from the Residency under Arthur Lisle's hand and raises the Administration's share from one part in five to one part in three. The custodians receive a copy in the humans' tongue, with a rendering made by a Mission pupil.
4 an Lùnastal, AE 58 Dùn fhiadhaich
Weighing the grain at Dùn fhiadhaich
At Dùn fhiadhaich the tithe-gatherers begin to weigh grain as well as ore, saying the town's farms feed the pits and share in their gain. The custodians' roll calls it the tithe on the tithe.
6 an t-Iuchar, AE 59 Ros dhomhain
The flux at Ros dhomhain
A bloody flux breaks out in the crowded quarters at the Ros dhomhain quays. The Mission's nurse, Anne Colby, makes a sick-house of the chapel, and it is said that she kept the dead below two hundred.
7 an t-Ògmhios, AE 60 Seann Vell
The flux reaches Seann Vell
The ore barges carry the flux to Seann Vell, the river port east of the capital on the Abhainn fhionn. The custodians of the town shut the barge landing for a season, and the Company fines them for it.
3 am Màrt, AE 61 Ros dhomhain
Walter Crane Commissioner
Arthur Lisle dies at the Residency of a fever of the heart. Walter Crane, who had been the Company's chief agent at the pits, is made Commissioner after him, the first to hold both offices one after the other.
6 an t-Sultain, AE 61 Ceann mhin
The pay office at Ceann mhin
Crane moves the Company's pay office for the southern workings to Ceann mhin, and makes the crews walk there to be paid, a day each way, in place of sending the paymaster to them. The crews are not paid for the walk.
12 am Màrt, AE 62 Muileann chrom
Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor
Raghnall Maor dies, and the Company gives his staff to his son Dòmhnall. The overseer's office, which the custodians had hoped would die with the man, becomes a family's inheritance.
11 an Gearran, AE 63 Taigh-solais Muileann bheag
Taigh-solais Muileann bheag lit
The fourth beacon is lit on the northern shore at Muileann bheag, the first to burn ore and not oil. Its keepers say the flame throws a colour on the water that no oil lamp ever did.
13 am Faoilleach, AE 64 Muileann bheag
The fishermen of Muileann bheag
The fishermen of Muileann bheag complain that the colour the ore flame casts on the water drives the herring off. The keepers do not change the lamp. Within a season the herring come back, and the complaint is withdrawn in a letter the Company keeps.
27 an Giblean, AE 64 Làrach an Teampaill
The dig at Làrach an Teampaill
The Mission cleric Edwin Lowe digs for a season at Làrach an Teampaill with Company labourers, seeking proof of an older faith on the island. He finds cut stone, burnt bone and marks he cannot read, and writes that the ruin's builders "were not the present race." The custodians agree, and add nothing.
9 an Lùnastal, AE 65 Colbh Cnoc chiar
The pillar at Cnoc chiar
Edwin Lowe copies the writing on the pillar near Cnoc chiar and sets it beside Wren's copy of the obelisk at Cnoc bheag. He judges that the two scripts are not the same, and that neither is of the Ròdaich. His notes stop there.
28 an Gearran, AE 66 Calbh Cnoc ghorm
The column at Cnoc ghorm
Lowe's last copy is of the column near Cnoc ghorm, and beside it he writes that its marks are like the pillar's, but not near enough to help. He leaves Rodos the next year and takes his notebooks with him.
8 an Lùnastal, AE 66 Baile Mòr dhìreach
The glass-house at Baile Mòr dhìreach
Peter Voss, a glazier left behind when his Company contract ended, builds a glass-house at Baile Mòr dhìreach and melts the white sand of Cuan ruadh with charcoal from the hills. It is the first glass made on Rodos. Within a generation his Ròdaich apprentices carry the craft to the towns of the capital shore.
29 am Màrt, AE 67 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silver guild refuses again
Martha Gale, an agent of the Company, offers the silver guild of Muileann chiar a partnership, on terms the guild's ledger calls generous. Ùna nic Choinnich, now very old, has the offer read aloud twice in the guild hall, and it is refused by show of hands.
1 am Faoilleach, AE 68 Achadh dhomhain
The camp at Achadh dhomhain
A new camp is opened at Achadh dhomhain for the deep galleries under the hill, and within a few seasons it is the most crowded place in the district. Its houses are built of spoil.
30 am Faoilleach, AE 68 Dùn chiar
Cloth for the camps at Dùn chiar
The weavers of Dùn chiar take a Company contract for canvas for the camp tents and sacks for the ore, and the town thrives on it. Its custodians note that never before had the town made anything for a use it did not approve.
7 am Màrt, AE 69
The first of the undying generation
A girl is born in the mining camps who takes more raw ore into her body over her life than any Ròdaich in living memory, and she does not age as the folk about her age. Her name is Aisling.
26 an t-Iuchar, AE 69 Muileann chrom
The coach to the camps
The Company puts a coach on the road between the quay at Ros dhomhain and the camps at Muileann chrom, twice a week each way, changing horses at the old waypoint houses. Clerks and overseers ride in it. The crews walk.
3 an Dùbhlachd, AE 70 Ros dhomhain
The ore weighed at the quay
The Company sets up a great steelyard at the Ros dhomhain quay, and thenceforth the island's yield is known by the ton and the hundredweight. The custodians' old count, kept in seasons of labour, is no longer entered in the roll.
15 an Dùbhlachd, AE 70 Ros dhìreach
Ros dhìreach the second ore port
The Company opens a second ore stage at Ros dhìreach on the southern coast for the workings south of the hills. Its first cargo is lost in a squall off the harbour mouth, and the fishermen moved to make room for the stage will not go out after it.
13 am Faoilleach, AE 71
The nameless change
What is befalling the child born two years before has as yet no name in any tongue spoken on the island. Decades pass before anyone tries to make one.
26 an Cèitean, AE 71 Ros dhomhain
The first steamer
The first ship driven by an engine comes into Ros dhomhain, a Company paddle-steamer out of an Tìr Thall. The fishermen row out to look at a ship going against the wind with no sail set. Within a generation the Company's ore goes out in nothing else.
19 an t-Sultain, AE 72 Cill dhìreach
The shrine at Cill dhìreach
At Cill dhìreach, a village at the edge of the workings, the custodians keep a small shrine where the pit crews leave the first piece of ore from each new gallery. The Company suffers the custom, for it costs a stone a gallery.
18 an Dàmhair, AE 72 Cill ghlas
The keepers of Cill ghlas
The custodians of the shrine at Cill ghlas, in the hills among the workings, keep the old rites at the mouth of the oldest cutting while the Company's pits deepen about them. It is the last shrine in the district that the pit crews still visit on the old feast days.
9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 73
A' Phlàigh Uaine
The Green Death goes through the mining camps. The ore dust is blamed, though no study of it is ever finished. Twenty-six settlements have cases.
5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 73 Achadh dhomhain
The first cases at Achadh dhomhain
The Green Death is first marked at Achadh dhomhain: a greenish pallor, then a cough that brings up dark dust, then weakness. The camp buries forty in the first month, in a field beyond the spoil-heaps still called the green acre.
13 am Faoilleach, AE 74 A' Phlàigh Uaine
Twenty-six settlements
The sickness spreads along the ore roads from the camps at Muileann chrom, Àth ìseal and Cnoc fhiadhaich, and falls hardest on Ros dhìreach, Ceann òg, Inis ìseal, Baile dhomhain, Achadh fhada, Cnoc bheag, Muileann uaine, Cuan àrsaidh and Inis bhàn. The custodians' roll lists the twenty-six settlements that had cases, and leaves a blank line after the last, as though waiting for another.
11 an Gearran, AE 74 Baile chrom
The Green Death at Baile chrom
The Green Death comes to Baile chrom in the hills, not the town of that name in the north-west. The scribes keep the two apart with care, for in later tellings of the island's hungers they are confused.
12 am Màrt, AE 74 Àth ghlas
Àth ghlas burns its huts
At Àth ghlas the custodians order every hut where a death has been burned with its bedding. The Company protests the loss of its property. The custodians note that the sickness stops sooner at Àth ghlas than anywhere else.
10 an Giblean, AE 74 Cnoc naomh
The dead of Cnoc naomh
At Cnoc naomh the dead of the Green Death are laid in the burial ground of the town's old shrine until it is full, and then in a field outside. The field is never ploughed again.
30 am Faoilleach, AE 75 Muileann chrom
Doctor Bright's study
Nathaniel Bright, physician to the Administration, begins to study the sickness at Muileann chrom, weighing the dust in the lungs of the dead. In the second season of the work he falls ill, and his notebooks break off in the middle of a table.
28 an Gearran, AE 75 Ros dhomhain
Walter Crane dies of the Green Death
Commissioner Crane, who had walked the camps in the worst of the sickness, dies of it at the Residency. Martha Gale, the Company's agent at Ros dhomhain, holds his seal for the months until another comes.
13 am Màrt, AE 76 Ros dhomhain
George Tolley Commissioner
George Tolley comes from an Tìr Thall with orders that the yield must not fall for the sickness. He does not visit the camps. His letter-book blames the dust, the Ròdaich custom of sleeping near the fire, and the custodians' shrines, in that order.
11 an Giblean, AE 76 Caol mhin
Quarantine at Caol mhin
Tolley sets a quarantine station at Caol mhin on the northern coast for ships from an Tìr Thall, and holds them offshore until their crews are looked over. It is the first order of his rule the Ròdaich approve, and they say so.
10 an Cèitean, AE 76 Muileann chrom
The camps turn to the hawk
The hawk-priests still barred from the camps, the crews carry their sermons in themselves. The overseers' reports of these years list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a matter for punishment.
17 an Giblean, AE 77 Ros dhomhain
Anne Colby's sick-houses
Anne Colby opens sick-houses at Àth ìseal and Achadh dhomhain and nurses there until the sickness ebbs. She is the only human the camp folk name in their own accounts of the plague, and they name her kindly.
25 an Giblean, AE 77 Cnoc gharbh
The huts of Cnoc gharbh
After the sickness the people of Cnoc gharbh, who had worked the southern galleries, leave their camp huts and go back to the old village on the hill. The next year the Company builds the huts again and brings in crews from the west.
13 an Dàmhair, AE 77
The first strike
A whole mining settlement stops work for eleven days over conditions worsened by the plague two years before. The strike ends when the food, which the humans' Administration holds, runs out.
21 an Dàmhair, AE 77 Baile thais
The strike at Baile thais
The settlement was Baile thais, below Cill ghlas, and the crew-leader Catrìona nic Eachainn called the halt after the Company would not close the galleries where the Green Death had been worst. For eleven days no ore left the town. On the twelfth the Company's store, the only store, was empty.
2 an Dàmhair, AE 78 Baile thais
The Company's granary
After the strike the Company builds a granary of its own at Muileann chrom and forbids the camps to keep grain beyond a week's ration. The overseers enforce the order, and Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor signs it.
31 an Dàmhair, AE 79 Ros gharbh
Fish smuggled from Ros gharbh
The fishermen of Ros gharbh carry salt fish up to the camps by night, past the Company's granary rule. The custodians' roll calls it the only trade of that decade that ran the right way.
29 an t-Samhain, AE 79 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
Catrìona goes to the silver town
Turned out of Baile thais and refused work at every Company pit, Catrìona nic Eachainn goes east to Muileann chiar, and the silver guild takes her on as a refiner. The Company asks that she be sent back. The guild's answer was filed and has not survived.
3 an t-Sultain, AE 80 Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The springs at Muileann ruadh
The Administration builds a new bath-house at the hot springs near Muileann ruadh for its officers mending from fevers. Ròdaich who had bathed there for centuries are let in on certain days, and charged a penny.
11 am Màrt, AE 81 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
Muileann chiar grows
The silver town grows beside the obsidian workings, for the humans want both, and the digging goes faster than the old reverence would ever have allowed.
7 an t-Iuchar, AE 82 Muileann chiar
A second Muileann chiar
