The silver trade crowds the old town, and the guild founds a daughter settlement to the west for its refiners and carters, which takes the same name. The rolls call them the old town and the new, and do not always say which they mean.
8 an t-Ògmhios, AE 83 Muileann chiar
Silver for marks
The silver guild begins to sell bar silver to the Company for marks, at a price the guild sets. It is the only ware on Rodos in this age priced by Ròdaich hands, and the guild's hall fills with human coin.
28 an Dùbhlachd, AE 84 Muileann bhàn
Silversmiths at Muileann bhàn
Silversmiths settle at Muileann bhàn on the road to the silver town and live by working the guild's bar into ornaments for the humans' market. Theirs is the one Ròdaich craft sold in an Tìr Thall under a Ròdaich name.
24 an Gearran, AE 85 Cathair dhearg
Macha's priests bless the coin
At Tolley's asking the priests of Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg, the order of the capital and the crown, bless the Residency's new coin. The priesthood of Macha teaches that the two horses of her rite, Dubh Sainglenn the black and Liath Macha the grey, each have their due; the dissenting priests say the coin is only one of them.
2 an Dàmhair, AE 86
The second change of coin
The barter goods of the Ròdaich are marked down against the humans' coin a second time, on terms the humans' Administration alone sets.
31 an Dàmhair, AE 86 Baile Mòr fhionn
Wool marked down at Baile Mòr fhionn
At Baile Mòr fhionn, where wool had been the measure of every bargain, a fleece is now worth by the Residency's table what a half-fleece was worth before. The town's weavers stop bringing wool to market and send it over the sea on their own account, until the Company refuses them freight.
2 an Gearran, AE 87 Caol fhiadhaich
The boats of Caol fhiadhaich sold
The fishing fleet of Caol fhiadhaich, unable to pay the new harbour dues in marks, sells half its boats to the Company. The men who sailed them go into the pits under the next year's contracts.
25 am Màrt, AE 87 Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The dissenters go to Cnoc bheag
Priests of Macha who refused the blessing leave the capital's temple and settle in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag. There they keep the older reading of Macha's two horses, and take in custodians who have lost their seats.
23 an Giblean, AE 87 Muileann chrom
Iain Maor
Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor dies, and his son Iain takes the overseer's staff. Iain Maor is the first overseer schooled at the Mission; he keeps his reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Ròdais.
4 am Faoilleach, AE 88 Ros dhomhain
The Levy
Tolley issues an ordinance, the Levy, by which every farming village in the west and north must send one in five of its able grown folk to the pits for two years. The villages are paid in marks, at the new rate.
3 am Màrt, AE 88 Caol mhòr
Levy officers at Caol mhòr
The Levy's officers take their first tally at Caol mhòr in the north-west, reading the names of the chosen from a list in the humans' tongue. The custodians of the town write the names again in Ròdais, that they may know whom to look for.
6 an Dùbhlachd, AE 88 Muileann àrsaidh
The Levy in the north-west
The Levy falls hardest on the villages about Baile chrom and the northern concession, which had never sent crews to the pits. The Ròdaich of the concession are taken; its human farmers are spared.
2 an t-Ògmhios, AE 89 Baile ìseal
Baile ìseal sends its people
Baile ìseal sends forty-one of its people to the pits under the Levy, and nineteen come back when their term ends. The custodians' roll names the other twenty-two and the camps they were sent to.
6 an Dùbhlachd, AE 89 Muileann naomh
Muileann naomh buys its way out
The custodians of Muileann naomh pay the Levy's officers in silver to halve the town's tally. The officers take the silver and the whole tally. The complaint is lodged at the Residency and filed.
14 an Dùbhlachd, AE 89 Dùn thais
The druid school's hall shut
George Tolley shuts the hall of the druid school at Dùn thais over a lecture on whether the humans' blindness to the ore's colour is a kind of sickness. The masters go on teaching in their own houses, to smaller rooms each year.
30 an Giblean, AE 90 Doire chiar
The last disputation at Doire chiar
At Doire chiar, a village of the druid schools north of the eastern workings, the masters hold the last open disputation of the school on the eve of Bealltainn, in the open air on the village threshing-floor. Its matter is whether a question may be forbidden. The Administration's clerk who attends writes that it may.
15 an t-Ògmhios, AE 90 Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
Teaching in the sacred forest
Druid masters who may no longer teach in a hall begin to teach under the trees in the sacred forest of Flidais near Muileann chiar, where the Administration has no building to shut.
14 an t-Iuchar, AE 90 Taigh-solais Baile chrom
Building the last beacon at Baile chrom
Work begins on the fifth and last beacon, on the north-western headland at Baile chrom, with masons taken by the Levy from the very villages whose fields they leave untilled.
27 an t-Ògmhios, AE 91 Cnoc thais
The masons of Cnoc thais
The Levy takes the masons of Cnoc thais to build the beacon at Baile chrom. Their foreman, Dùghall Clachair, cuts the names of his crew into the lintel of the lamp-room, the only writing on any of the five towers.
26 an t-Iuchar, AE 91 Taigh-solais Baile chrom
The five beacons complete
The ring of coast beacons is finished: Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag, Àth dhearg and Tobar dhearg. They serve a trade that is by now plunder in all but name.
24 an Lùnastal, AE 91 Cuan ruadh
Cuan ruadh loses its trade
The ring of beacons finished, the Company's steamers round the island without putting in, and within a few years the old coasting trade of Cuan ruadh up and down the eastern shore dies.
22 an t-Sultain, AE 91 Taigh-solais Baile chrom
Taigh-solais Baile chrom lit
The beacon at Baile chrom is lit with an ore flame, and the ring is whole. The Company's ships can now round the island by night, and the keepers' daybooks show the sailings doubled within a few years.
3 am Màrt, AE 94
Gorta Baile chrom
The Great Hunger follows a failed harvest across thirty-four settlements, made worse because the Levy has taken so many to the pits that too few are left to till the land.
1 an Giblean, AE 94 Baile chrom
Baile chrom goes hungry
The hunger is worst at Baile chrom itself, whose people could see the new beacon from their empty fields. The custodians write that more died there than anywhere else, and the Administration, which kept its own count, does not gainsay them.
22 an Cèitean, AE 94 Gorta Baile chrom
The famine country
The custodians' roll draws the bounds of the famine country along the north-west shore and the hills behind it. Within them lie Baile chrom in its own shire; Ceann mhòr, Àth fhionn and Àth dhearg in the shire of Ceann mhòr; Muileann àrsaidh in the shire of Cnoc thais; and Achadh àrsaidh in the shire of Muileann àrsaidh. Thirty-four settlements are counted within the line, and the roll gives the dead of each.
30 an Giblean, AE 95 Doire ghlas
The hunger at Doire ghlas
At Doire ghlas in the north the hunger takes the old and the very young first. The village sends its young folk to the camps for the Company's rations, and by the year's end it is half empty.
29 an Cèitean, AE 95 Inis mhin
Inis mhin eats its seed
In the second winter of the hunger the townsfolk of Inis mhin on the north coast eat their seed corn. The Mission kitchen at the harbour feeds three hundred a day for a season.
7 an t-Samhain, AE 96 Seann Bhrenn
The hunger reaches Seann Bhrenn
The hunger reaches as far east as Seann Bhrenn, where the custodians open the old grain-pits of the Holy Age, unfilled in living memory. They hold only dust.
6 an Dùbhlachd, AE 96 Ros dhomhain
The relief ship
A relief ship with grain from an Tìr Thall lies a month at Ros dhomhain while the Residency and the Company dispute who shall pay for its unloading. Meanwhile the Mission opens kitchens at Cathair gheal and Baile chrom, and Anne Colby, come back to the island, keeps the one at Baile chrom.
20 an Gearran, AE 97 Baile chrom
The Levy set aside
The Levy is set aside in the famine districts, too late for the harvest. It is not repealed. The custodians note that it was never used again, nor needed to be, for the villages had learned what it meant.
17 an Lùnastal, AE 97 Cnoc mhòr
Cnoc mhòr walks south
Rather than starve, the families of Cnoc mhòr in the north walk south to the camps and take work under the Company. Their village stands empty for a generation.
9 an Dàmhair, AE 98 Ros dhomhain
Robert Haskins Commissioner
George Tolley retires with honours. Robert Haskins, who follows him, orders that the custodians' council be consulted on the tithe, and then sets the tithe before the council has met.
7 an t-Samhain, AE 98 Seann Dunn
Customs at Seann Dunn
Haskins opens a customs house at Seann Dunn on the eastern coast, and a Company store with it. The store sells the east its seed and its tools, and within a few years its ledgers hold the debts of half the district.
4 am Faoilleach, AE 99
The first petition
For the first time the custodians of the Ròdaich act together, and not settlement by settlement, and lay a written grievance before the humans' Administration. It is not answered.
3 am Màrt, AE 99 Ceann àrsaidh
The gathering at Ceann àrsaidh
The petition was drawn up at Ceann àrsaidh by custodians of nineteen settlements, meeting for the first time as one body. Peigi Ghlas, custodian of Cill ghlas, carried it to the Residency and handed it to a clerk.
6 an Dùbhlachd, AE 99 Àth fhionn
Àth fhionn signs
Ruairidh mac Thormoid, custodian of Àth fhionn in the south-east, is the eldest of those who signed the petition. He was born before the humans' coin was struck, and says so beside his name.
27 am Faoilleach, AE 101
Grievance first written
From these years come the oldest writings of grievance among the Ròdaich that survive. No hand is yet raised in them; yet in them it is first written that something has gone wrong.
18 an t-Sultain, AE 101 Baile thais
Leabhar Baile thais
The oldest of them is a book of complaints kept at Baile thais, set down by many hands over some years: wages, deaths, the granary, the stream at Doire mhòr. The custodians' copyists call it Leabhar Baile thais.
17 am Faoilleach, AE 102 Muileann dhearg
The songs of Fearchar Bàrd
The poet Fearchar Bàrd, a breaker of ore at Muileann dhearg since boyhood, makes songs of the Levy and the famine, and they are sung in the camps. The overseers forbid them, and because they were forbidden several were written down.
23 an Dùbhlachd, AE 102 An Taigh-òsta Grianach
Songs at An Taigh-òsta Grianach
The songs of Fearchar Bàrd are sung in the roadside houses of the east, and An Taigh-òsta Grianach becomes known for them. The Company's carters sing them too, the keeper writes, not always knowing what they sing.
15 an Gearran, AE 103 Ros dhomhain
The Company's deep-water quay
The Company builds at Ros dhomhain a deep-water quay for the new iron steamships, which burn the island's own ore to carry it away. Fearchar Bàrd makes a song of that, the most quoted of all his songs.
20 an t-Samhain, AE 103 Ceann chaol
The deep quay at Ceann chaol
A second deep-water quay is built at Ceann chaol in the south-east for the eastern ore. Its builders are brought from the coast, and the village of forty houses becomes a town of four hundred.
23 an t-Sultain, AE 104 Baile thais
Baile thais walls its pithead
The Company rings the pithead at Baile thais with a stone wall and a gate, and pays a watchman to count who goes in. It is the first working on Rodos walled against its own crews.
19 an Dùbhlachd, AE 104 Baile thais
Catrìona nic Eachainn dies at the silver town
Catrìona nic Eachainn dies at Muileann chiar, a refiner of the silver guild to the end. The camp folk of Baile thais send men to her burying, and the Company docks each of them a day's pay.
4 an Giblean, AE 105 Ros dhomhain
The quay fire
A fire starts in the Company's ore sheds at Ros dhomhain and burns three days, taking two streets of the harbour quarter with it. The Company's inquiry finds no cause; the harbour quarter's own account has several.
22 an t-Sultain, AE 105 Cathair dhearg
The council without a high custodian
After the death of the last high custodian the Council of Custodians cannot agree on another, and sits for years with the seat empty. Robert Haskins writes to an Tìr Thall that this makes the council easier to deal with.
25 an Lùnastal, AE 106
Tiormachd Achadh shean
The Long Drought lies on the island's dry season three years together, and bears hard on a people already worn thin by the tallies of the pits.
28 an t-Ògmhios, AE 107 Achadh shean
The wells of Achadh shean
At Achadh shean, whose name the drought bears, the wells fail in the second summer, and the cattle are driven west in a column the roll calls a day long. Fewer than half reach water.
27 an t-Iuchar, AE 107 Tiormachd Achadh shean
The dry country
The custodians' roll counts ten districts of the east as drought country, worst at Achadh shean, Àth uaine, Achadh àrsaidh and Muileann chiar, and reaching down to Cuan ruadh and west toward Baile chaol. The Administration keeps no count of its own.
6 an t-Sultain, AE 107 Baile chaol
The cattle of Baile chaol
At Baile chaol the herds are slaughtered in the second summer of the drought, rather than watched as they die. The salt meat is sold to the Company for the camps, at a price the Company names.
5 an Dàmhair, AE 107 Doire fhionn
Doire fhionn walks for water
At Doire fhionn in the east the women walk each day to the spring at Àth ruadh and back for water, half a day's journey. The custodians record it for the three dry years, and then cease.
1 an Cèitean, AE 108 Allt an Àigh
Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh
The spring of Allt an Àigh, said never to have failed, runs on through all three dry years. Pilgrims who keep Na Seann Spioradan come to it from all the east, the first of them at Bealltainn, and the Administration sets a watchman to charge them for the water. He is called back after one season.
30 an Cèitean, AE 108 Inis uaine
The pilgrims' road at Inis uaine
Pilgrims bound for Allt an Àigh gather at Inis uaine, and the townsfolk feed them freely, as the Old Spirits require. The town's own wells are low, and it gives away more water than it keeps.
25 an Giblean, AE 109 Baile Mòr ruadh
Drought-fever at Baile Mòr ruadh
A fever of foul water follows the drought into the towns, worst at Baile Mòr ruadh, where the wells had been deepened into the old middens. Two hundred and sixty die. The Mission's report is the first to name the cause rightly.
3 an Cèitean, AE 109 Cnoc shean
The fever at Cnoc shean
The drought-fever spreads to Cnoc shean, whose one well is found tainted. The custodians close it, and for a year the town drinks from carts.
29 an Dàmhair, AE 109 Achadh shean
The Mission's wells
The Mission sinks deep wells at Achadh shean and Àth chrom with a boring-rig brought from an Tìr Thall, and they hold. The custodians of the east set down the Mission's wells and the Company's tallies on facing pages, without comment.
16 am Màrt, AE 110 Achadh chaol
Achadh chaol goes to the pits
Their fields burned out by the drought, the people of Achadh chaol in the north-east go to the pits for wages, the first villagers of the eastern farm country to do so. Their custodian writes it down as the end of the village, not a flitting.
25 an Lùnastal, AE 110 Baile Mòr dhìreach
The tally not lowered
The ore tally is not lowered in the drought. The custodians of the east, their joint petition unanswered, each write to Haskins alone; to each he answers that the matter is under consideration.
3 an Gearran, AE 111 Àth mhòr
The petition of Àth mhòr
Iseabail nic Leòid, custodian of Àth mhòr, writes the longest of the single petitions, forty pages listing her town's dead beasts. Haskins answers in two lines. Both survive, bound together by a later clerk.
15 an Gearran, AE 111
The first inheritance of mixed blood
A suit over whether a child of one Ròdaich and one human parent may inherit the customary rights of mining is decided, and the Administration makes the ruling wholly to its own gain.
4 am Màrt, AE 111 Ros dhomhain
The case of Thomas Hale
The child was Thomas Hale, grandson of the marriage at Baile dhìreach of Eilidh nic Ruairidh and Samuel Hale, who claimed a share in a customary cutting through his Ròdaich grandmother. Oliver Dunstan, magistrate at Ros dhomhain, ruled that customary rights descend only through the line the Administration owns, and that it owns only its own.
2 an Giblean, AE 112 Ros dhomhain
Dunstan's rule applied
Within a few years Dunstan's ruling is used to pass eleven customary cuttings to the Company, each because some holder in the line had married a human or been born of one. The custodians stop entering such marriages in the roll.
25 an t-Ògmhios, AE 113 Cnoc dhubh
A cutting at Cnoc dhubh taken
Among the cuttings taken under Dunstan's rule is the old customary working at Cnoc dhubh, held by one family since the Holy Age. A great-grandmother of the line had married a human sailor; that is enough.
29 an Dùbhlachd, AE 113 Baile thais
The Lamp-Watch
A fellowship of pit crews calling itself the Lamp-Watch begins to meet at Baile thais and Cnoc chaol under cover of a burial club. Its first known deed is to pay for the burying of an old breaker who had died in the Company's lock-up.
28 an t-Ògmhios, AE 114 Ros dhomhain
Edward Vane Commissioner
Robert Haskins is called home after a quarrel with the Company over the price of steamship berths, and Edward Vane follows him. Vane is the first Commissioner born on Rodos, at the Residency, and he speaks Ròdais, badly, but he speaks it.
27 an t-Iuchar, AE 115 Ros dhìreach
The tram-road to Ros dhìreach
Vane lays an iron tram-road, drawn by mules, from the southern workings down to the ore port at Ros dhìreach. It halves the cost of shipping ore, and ends the carting trade of the villages on the old road.
25 an Lùnastal, AE 116
The night-shift order
For the first time the digging is made to run without ceasing, day and night, and the mountain is given no season of rest at all.
23 an t-Sultain, AE 116 Cnoc chaol
The night crews at Cnoc chaol
The order falls first on Cnoc chaol, where the Company's newest galleries are opened to crews working by ore-lamp in two shifts. The custodians' roll writes that the hill was given no silence at all, and leaves the rest of the page blank.
3 an Lùnastal, AE 117 Cnoc chaol
The night-shift strike
The crews at Cnoc chaol refuse the night shift, and within a week are replaced by crews brought from the coast under the Company's new contracts. The Lamp-Watch keeps the strikers' families for a season, and then its money is gone.
5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 117 Muileann dhomhain
The strikebreakers of Muileann dhomhain
The crews that replace the strikers at Cnoc chaol are brought through Muileann dhomhain, where the townsfolk turn them from every door. They sleep in the Company's barns, and several go home the next season.
17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 118 Ros dhomhain
Matthew Dunne's sermon
Matthew Dunne, the Mission's minister at Ros dhomhain, preaches against the night-shift order from the chapel pulpit, saying the Ròdaich are right that even the ground must rest. The Company complains to the Mission, and Dunne is called back to an Tìr Thall. The Lamp-Watch copies the sermon and reads it in the camps.
14 an Lùnastal, AE 119 Cnoc chaol
The lung-rot at Cnoc chaol
A wasting sickness of the lungs spreads among the night crews at Cnoc chaol and Baile thais. Unlike the Green Death it kills slowly. The Company pays the widows a pension for a year, then stops.
12 an t-Sultain, AE 119 Muileann chrom
Iain Maor and the night shift
Iain Maor, overseer at Muileann chrom, writes to the Company that the night shift is killing his crews faster than it is paying for them. The letter survives because the Company filed it with his dismissal, which was undone a month later for want of anyone else.
22 am Màrt, AE 120 Muileann chrom
The ore line
The Company opens its railway from the pits at Muileann chrom down by Cathair dhearg to the deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain. Its engines burn the island's own ore, as the steamships do, and the tram-road to Ros dhìreach is left to the mules. Within a year the carters' guild of Doire chaol, which had hauled the ore on Rathad na Mèinne for eighty years, loses the long haul. From the first day the Ròdaich call the engine carbad-iarainn, the iron chariot, and the railway the ore line.
18 an Giblean, AE 120 Baile ghorm
Ore-lamps from Baile ghorm
The potteries of Baile ghorm take a contract for clay lamp-bodies for the night crews, thousands in a year. The potters' own book notes that they are the first lamps made on the island for work in the dark by command.
21 an Gearran, AE 121
Fionnan born
A second child is born bound to the ore as Aisling was, half a century after her. So it is known that the thing is no chance of one birth: it comes of the digging, and it will go on.
19 an Cèitean, AE 122 Ros dhomhain
The Administration's count of the people
The Administration counts the people of Rodos by district for the first time. Its figures for the humans are true to the household; for the Ròdaich they are rounded to the hundred, and in the hill districts to the thousand.
20 an Giblean, AE 123 Seann Vell
The district of the outer coasts
The Administration makes the outer coasts one district and rules it from the harbour office at Seann Vell on Eilean ruadh, where its revenue cutters lie: the islands of the west and south, Eilean bhàn with Cuan dhearg and Cnoc chaol, and the southern edge of the windy coast in the far north-west. Its surveyors walk to the edge of the great moss there, which no chain can cross, and go no farther. Beyond it the district map is left blank.
6 an Lùnastal, AE 123 Dùn thais
Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, last of the druid masters
Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, the last master of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean to teach openly in the Age of Strangers, dies at Dùn thais. No one is named after her, and the school's register ends with her death. It is taken up again only long after the humans are gone.
5 am Màrt, AE 124 Muileann chaol
The custodians' rolls at Muileann chaol
The custodians of the east begin to send copies of their rolls for safe keeping to the town of Muileann chaol, which still kept Beathag nic Thòmais's loft of papers, beyond the Residency's reach. The copying is done in the houses of three families, and the copies kept in a cellar.
5 am Faoilleach, AE 125 Muileann chaol
The second Muileann chaol
Some of the copies bound for Muileann chaol go by mistake to the smaller town of that name further north, and are kept there for years before the mistake is found. The custodians note that they were kept just as well.
23 am Faoilleach, AE 126
The word found at last
With two children now known, the custodians agree on a word for what is befalling them: fuil-ghuail, "coal-blood", rendered in the humans' tongue as obsidian-touched. It is meant as a physician's word. It outlives that meaning.
21 an Gearran, AE 126 Cill ghlas
The custodians who named it
The word was agreed at a meeting of custodians at the shrine of Cill ghlas, where the oldest cutting still stood open. They chose a plain word, fit for the physician's book. The roll gives the vote; who first put the word forward it does not say.
26 an t-Samhain, AE 127 Ros dhomhain
The Administration's register
The Residency, hearing of the word, orders that any Ròdaich child showing the change be reported to the Commissioner's office. The custodians obey by reporting none.
7 an Giblean, AE 129
The third change of coin
The old barter of the Ròdaich is struck down as lawful payment altogether. Every bargain on the island now goes by the humans' coin.
17 an t-Sultain, AE 129 Ros dhomhain
The barter houses closed
The barter houses at Ros dhomhain and Cathair dhearg, where cloth and fish had changed hands without coin since before the Crossing, are shut by order. A clerk of the Residency writes that the ledgers are now "complete for the first time."
22 am Màrt, AE 130 Inis mhòr
The fishwives of Inis mhòr
The fishwives of Inis mhòr, who had sold by barter at the river steps since before the Crossing, will take no coin for a week, in protest at the shutting of the barter houses, and give their fish away. The Company's clerks record it as a glut.
17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 130 Cathair dhearg
Marks borrowed at interest
Barter being struck down, the hill villages borrow marks at interest from the Company's stores to buy seed. Within a few years most of the villages of Muileann chrom owe the Company more than a year's crops.
20 an Giblean, AE 131 Muileann òg
The old market at Muileann òg
The old barter market at Muileann òg, where hill and coast had met to trade since the Holy Age, closes after its last season. The ground stands empty until, long after, it is used for a fair.
12 an t-Sultain, AE 131 Muileann chrom
Mòrag nic Iain Maor
Iain Maor dies, and his daughter Mòrag takes the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, the first woman to hold it. The Company approves her in a letter that calls her "a safe pair of hands."
24 an Lùnastal, AE 132 Ros dhomhain
Charles Merriman Commissioner
Edward Vane dies at the Residency. Charles Merriman comes after him with a small company of armed constables, the first standing force the Administration has kept on Rodos.
11 an Dàmhair, AE 132 Muileann shean
The constable post at Muileann shean
Merriman's first constable post is built at Muileann shean on the northern ore road, a stone house with a yard for horses. The townsfolk call it the humans' second Residency, and do not mean it kindly.
25 an Giblean, AE 133 Tobar ghorm
A barracks at Tobar ghorm
A second post is raised at Tobar ghorm, near the northern workings. The village's custodian is paid rent for the ground, and with it buys the village out of its debts to the Company store.
28 an Lùnastal, AE 133 Baile chrom
A grey-night vigil at Baile chrom
The Mission at Cathair gheal reports that human labourers near Baile chrom keep vigil by night in the fields, praying in silence under the sign of a grey goose, which they call the wild goose of the Spirit. The Mission cannot find whence the practice came, and calls it irregular, a superstition learned of the Ròdaich. The Ròdaich of Baile chrom disown it.
21 an Dàmhair, AE 133 Ceann mhòr
Manannan's priests on the grey night
The priests of Òrd Mhanannain at Ceann mhòr answer the Mission's report of the grey-night vigils. The practice owes something to the Ròdaich, they say, but to their own harbours and not to Baile chrom: the human fishing families of Ceann mhòr learned from them the night prayer to keep the sea shut, and the labourers inland keep it as a vigil of their Church, a night of silence under the wild goose of the Spirit in place of a prayer to Manannan. The priests call it Manannan's prayer gone astray, and do not admit its keepers to their house.
1 an Giblean, AE 134 Ros dhomhain
The dockers' strike at Ros dhomhain
The dockers of Ros dhomhain, Ròdaich and human alike, refuse to load ore for nine days over the new berth charges. It is the only strike of the age in which human workers stand with Ròdaich. Merriman's constables break it, and the human dockers are shipped west.
30 an Giblean, AE 134 Seann Vell
Seann Vell's dockers stay out
The dockers of Seann Vell, the harbour next to Ros dhomhain, refuse to load the ore sent to them during the strike. When it ends they are not shipped west, for there are no humans among them; but they are not hired again either.
29 an Cèitean, AE 134
Lorccan born
A third such child is born, in a mining town and not a camp; the thing is no longer bound to any one place.
3 am Màrt, AE 135
Cian born
A fourth is born within a year of the third. Never again do the children of the undying generation come so close together.
4 am Faoilleach, AE 136 Cill ghlas
Blasting-powder at Cill ghlas
The Company begins to drive galleries under the hills about Cill ghlas with blasting-powder shipped from an Tìr Thall. The custodians of the shrine ask that no charge be set within sight of the old cutting. The Company's engineer marks their asking on his plan, and sets the charges below it.
2 an Gearran, AE 136 Caol ìseal
Powder landed at Caol ìseal
The blasting-powder for the new galleries is landed at Caol ìseal on the northern coast, away from the crowded southern harbours, and carted inland under guard. The town's custodians ask what is in the barrels and are told it is lamp-oil.
9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 137
Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The Rending: in the hills east of the capital, about Cill ghlas, the earth tears open along a fault beneath a common working. Dozens are killed, and a whole mining district is shut for a generation.
17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 137
The first open fight
A mining death, which the Ròdaich workers lay at the door of the humans' carelessness, leads to the first bloodshed between the two peoples.
3 an t-Iuchar, AE 137 Cill ghlas
The shrine at Cill ghlas lost
The Rending swallows the old cutting at Cill ghlas, where the custodians had kept the rites through all the age, and its shrine with it. The custodians' roll sets down the loss of the shrine before the loss of the dead; a later copyist has put them in the other order.
13 an t-Samhain, AE 137 Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The district closed
The Company shuts the whole district of the Rending and fences it, leaving Cill ghlas, Àth chaol and their hamlets in the shires of Muileann dhearg and Muileann chiar without work. The villages empty toward Baile thais and Muileann dhearg, and the closed district is left to the thorn.
22 an t-Samhain, AE 137 Coinneachadh an Fhearainn
The meeting on the moor road
The folk turned out of the closed district send their eldest to the custodians of Muileann dhomhain, who meet them at a standing stone on the moor road below the town, lest the Company's clerks see them in the town hall. At the stone the custodians lend them the land at the edge of the fenced ground. The place is called Coinneachadh an Fhearainn, the meeting of the land.
5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 137 Achadh chaol
Achadh chaol raised by the dispossessed
Folk of the closed district build a new village at Achadh chaol, at the edge of the fenced ground, on land lent by the custodians of Muileann dhomhain. It is the only settlement of the age founded by Ròdaich for Ròdaich with no Company surveyor's hand in it.
13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 137 Muileann chrom
The fight at Muileann chrom
The death that began it was a flooded gallery at Muileann chrom, where seven died after the pumps were stopped to save fuel. When the Company's agent came to the pithead the crews stoned him and his constables, and the constables fired. Four Ròdaich and one constable were killed.
4 am Faoilleach, AE 138 Muileann chrom
Mòrag Maor at the inquiry
At the Administration's inquiry into the fight the overseer Mòrag nic Iain Maor bears witness that the pumps were stopped on the agent's order. Her words are struck out. The Lamp-Watch gets a copy of them all the same.
2 an Gearran, AE 138 Baile thais
The grey fever
A fever of the chest comes in on the ships and runs over the whole island, from the capital to the eastern farms. It kills the young and strong more than the old, the Mission notes in alarm. The camps, already hungry, bury more than the towns.
14 an t-Iuchar, AE 138 Cathair mhòr
The grey fever at Cathair mhòr
At Cathair mhòr the grey fever shuts the market for the first time in the town's memory. The custodians' roll gives the dead by street, and the longest list is of the street where the carters lived.
6 an Dùbhlachd, AE 138 Dùn thais
The grey fever at Dùn thais
At Dùn thais the fever takes the physician the Administration sent to treat it, and two of the Mission's nurses. The old houses of the druid masters are opened as sick-rooms.
27 am Faoilleach, AE 139
The second petition
This one carries a threat beneath its words, not a plea. It is the first writing of the Ròdaich the Administration troubles to answer, and it answers with more guards, not with concessions.
12 an Lùnastal, AE 139 Cnoc dhìreach
The signatories of Cnoc dhìreach
Coinneach Ruadh, custodian of Cnoc dhìreach, signs the second petition, and in the same week is turned out of his post as clerk to the Company store. He is one of eleven who sign and lose Company work for it.
29 an Dùbhlachd, AE 139 Baile thais
Eilidh nic Raghnaill
The second petition was drawn up by Eilidh nic Raghnaill, a crew-leader of Baile thais and one of the Lamp-Watch, and signed by custodians and crew-leaders of thirty-one settlements. It ends with a sentence the Residency underlined: that the hill would not be worked by people who were not asked.
25 an Gearran, AE 140 Ros dhomhain
The constables tripled
Merriman answers by tripling the constables and posting companies at Muileann chrom, Baile thais, Ceann fhada and Cnoc chaol, each with a walled store. The constables are paid from the tithe.
26 am Màrt, AE 140 Dùn chrom
Barracks at Dùn chrom
A barracks for the constables is built at Dùn chrom, on the capital side of the hills, with room for two hundred men. For most of its first year it stands empty, for want of constables to fill it.
24 an Giblean, AE 140 Seann Skell
Ìomhar Seabhag
At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Ìomhar Seabhag preaches that Mòd's hunger has turned on those who have eaten the hill. The hawk-shrines of the west begin to serve as meeting-houses for the Lamp-Watch, and the constables do not yet know it.
23 an Cèitean, AE 140 Ros gheal
The hawk-faithful of Ros gheal
At Ros gheal the hawk-faithful fishing families, who had chased out the Company's customs officers a century before, raise a shrine to Mòd on the harbour wall. The constables order it down. It is built again three times in a single season.
21 an t-Ògmhios, AE 140 Inis bhàn
The hawk and the druids at Inis bhàn
At Inis bhàn the priests of the hawk and a few who still keep the questions of the druid school in private meet for a disputation, the first between them in living memory. It is written that it settled nothing, and that both sides afterwards signed the petition.
20 an t-Iuchar, AE 140 Baile chrom
The grey fever in the north-west
The grey fever returns and settles in the north-west, about Baile chrom and the towns of the concession, where it kills humans as readily as Ròdaich. The Mission's hospital at Cathair gheal overflows, and for the first time Ròdaich and human sick lie in the same wards.
6 am Màrt, AE 141 Muileann fhionn
Muileann fhionn shut in
Muileann fhionn, a Ròdaich mill town in the north-west, shuts its roads against the fever and keeps them shut for a season. Human carters of the concession are turned back with their loads at the town's edge.
18 an Giblean, AE 141 Tobar fhiadhaich
The fever at Tobar fhiadhaich
At Tobar fhiadhaich in the north the fever takes one household in three. The custodians of the village burn no huts; they had heard of Àth ghlas in their grandparents' time, but judge it too late.
9 an t-Sultain, AE 141 An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The road-houses make ready
The road-houses along the old mining roads begin to serve as waystations for bands of armed men. The roads make ready for a war not yet declared.
17 an t-Sultain, AE 141 An Taigh-seinnse Òir
An Taigh-seinnse Òir
An Taigh-seinnse Òir, the great house on the eastern road beyond Dùn dhearg, digs a well in its yard and builds a wall round the well. The keeper tells the Company's carters it is against thieves.
14 an Dàmhair, AE 141 An Leòmhann Buidhe
An Leòmhann Buidhe
An Leòmhann Buidhe, the road-house on the northern road through the druid country, takes on six new ostlers in a single season, none of whom know anything of horses.
22 am Faoilleach, AE 142 An Taigh-òsta Grianach
An Taigh-òsta Grianach walled
An Taigh-òsta Grianach, called the singing house since the songs of Fearchar Bàrd, raises a wall round its yard and sets a watch on its gate.
3 an t-Iuchar, AE 142 Am Buabhall Fortanach
Am Buabhall Fortanach barred
Am Buabhall Fortanach, the great road-house on the south-western road, bars its gates at dusk and keeps a watch on the roof. Its keeper, Tormod Buabhall, keeps a list of travellers and sends it up the road each week, to whom is not told.
30 an Lùnastal, AE 142 Doire shean
The harbour of Doire shean
The little harbour of Doire shean, below Am Buabhall Fortanach, becomes the landing for the goods the house cannot take by road. The fishermen of Doire shean are paid in silver from the east.
28 an t-Sultain, AE 142 An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
At An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the northern road the stables are rebuilt with a loft for sleeping men. The Company's carters mark that the loft is never empty, and never holds the same men twice.
27 an Dàmhair, AE 142 An Sligeanach Fad' às
An Sligeanach Fad' às
An Sligeanach Fad' às, on the eastern road near the silver country, becomes the post-house through which the Lamp-Watch sends word from the camps to Muileann chiar. The silver guild pays its keeper's rent.
25 an t-Samhain, AE 142 Àth fhiadhaich
The runners of Àth fhiadhaich
Runners from Àth fhiadhaich carry the Lamp-Watch's letters from An Sligeanach Fad' às to the silver town. They are boys of twelve and thirteen, too young for the constables to stop.
28 am Faoilleach, AE 143 Achadh mhòr
Achadh mhòr keeps the ledgers
The Lamp-Watch's ledgers of the money it has from the silver guild are kept at Achadh mhòr, a village near the house on the eastern road, in the roof of the village shrine.
26 an Gearran, AE 143 An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
Seònaid's house
An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, the carters' house on the ore road that Seònaid Bhàn opened again in the early years of the digging, is kept now by her great-grandson Aonghas. It is the busiest of the walled houses, the one the constables search most often and find least in.
27 am Màrt, AE 143
The first stoppage together
For the first time the mining country stops work on one day in many places at once. Scattered as it is, the resistance of the Ròdaich can act as one when it chooses.
27 am Màrt, AE 143 Muileann bheag
Muileann bheag in the north-east
The workings at Muileann bheag in the north-east, among the druid villages, stop with the rest. The town's custodian writes that it is the first thing the town has done with the hills in a hundred years.
27 am Màrt, AE 143 Àth dhomhain
The northern pits at Àth dhomhain
The pits north of the hills at Àth dhomhain stop with the rest on the day of the stoppage, the word brought by a runner and not by the beacon. Their crew-leaders are among those shipped west.
27 am Màrt, AE 143 Ceann bheag
Ceann bheag stops
The ore stage at Ceann bheag on the northern coast stops loading the same day. Its dockers had not been told; they stop because the ore stops coming.
27 am Màrt, AE 143 Cnoc gheal
The quarrymen of Cnoc gheal
The quarrymen of Cnoc gheal in the north-east, who cut stone for the Company's buildings, lay down their tools on the day of the stoppage unasked. Why, no one says.
27 am Màrt, AE 143 Muileann chrom
The day the pits stopped
On the day of the stoppage every working in the Muileann chrom district halted at once, and with them Baile thais, Cnoc chaol, the silver town and the eastern pits at Ros fhionn. The sign was a beacon fire lit on the hills above Doire mhòr, which the Company took for a heath fire.
27 am Màrt, AE 143 Ros dhomhain
The ore ships wait
The Company's steamships lie six days at Ros dhomhain with empty holds. The agents at the quay write that they have never seen the harbour so quiet, and that it frightened them more than the crowds.
30 an Dùbhlachd, AE 143 Ros dhomhain
The stoppage broken
The stoppage ends when the constables shut the Company stores in every district at once. Forty crew-leaders are taken; thirty-two are let go without charge, and eight are shipped west to an Tìr Thall for trial and never heard of again.
28 am Faoilleach, AE 144 Doire mhòr
Beacon hill at Doire mhòr
Doire mhòr, which refused the first contract and then lost its water, has by now but a few households. The beacon of the stoppage was lit on its hill by the children's children of Beathag Dhubh's people, and the constables burn the heather of the hill to deny it to them.
25 an Giblean, AE 144 Muir Mhanannain
Fewer ships from the west
The keepers' daybooks at the five beacons show fewer ships from an Tìr Thall each year, and the ships that come are older. The Company's letters speak of troubles at home and do not say what they are.
13 an Giblean, AE 145 Caol leathan
Caol leathan's idle harbour
At Caol leathan the wool for the humans' market waits for room in ships that do not come. The merchants of the town begin to sell their wool inland again by barter, against the law.
9 an Dàmhair, AE 145 Caol bheag
Caol bheag's empty quay
The Company's quay at Caol bheag on the northern coast, built for the eastern trade, sees one ship in a season. The Company's agent there writes that he has been forgotten.
24 an Cèitean, AE 146
Leave no longer asked
The humans' Administration begins to give commands without seeking the counsel of the Ròdaich at all. The pretence of leave asked and given is dropped.
2 an t-Samhain, AE 146 Ros dhomhain
Lionel Strake Commissioner
Charles Merriman leaves Rodos in ill health, and Lionel Strake, a soldier, comes after him. His commission, read aloud at the Residency, makes no mention of the Council of Custodians, and he does not call on it.
26 an Gearran, AE 147 Cathair dhearg
The council locked out
Strake has the council hall at Cathair dhearg locked and its keys lodged at the Residency. The custodians meet instead in Macha's temple, whose priests, who had blessed the humans' coin, now shelter those who petitioned against it.
27 am Màrt, AE 147 Ros dhomhain
The iron bird
Strake brings a flying machine from an Tìr Thall in the hold of a Company steamship and has it flown from a field above the Residency over the ore country, to count the workings from the air. The Ròdaich call it eun-iarainn, the iron bird. The custodians enter it in the roll as the first thing seen over Rodos that flew and was not alive.
25 an Giblean, AE 147
The edict of seizure
The humans' Administration claims the right to take any dwelling of the Ròdaich it deems needful for the widening of the workings. Of all the grievances it is the one most often named in every surviving account of what followed.
17 an t-Sultain, AE 147 Doire mhòr
The seizure of Doire mhòr
The first dwellings taken under the edict are those of Doire mhòr, for a new shaft beneath the hill, and constables carry out the last households. The village that refused the first contract is the first emptied by the last.
19 an Dàmhair, AE 147 Baile dhomhain
Evictions at Baile dhomhain
At Baile dhomhain, the first camp laid out on paper, two streets are pulled down for a spoil-tip. The families are offered huts at Àth ìseal and marks for their timber; most go to kin in the hill villages instead.
24 an Cèitean, AE 148 Muileann chrom
Mòrag Maor lays down the staff
Mòrag nic Iain Maor, fourth of her line to hold the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, will not carry out evictions in her district, and breaks the staff at the Company's door. Three other overseers give up their places in the same month, and the Company puts humans in them.
21 an t-Iuchar, AE 148 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silver guild arms
The silver guild of Muileann chiar, still holding its seam under the compact of a century before, begins to buy rifles through the eastern pirates. Its ledger enters them as refining tools.
19 an Lùnastal, AE 148 Spùinneadairean-mara
Rifles by way of the pirates
The silver guild's rifles come ashore from the raiders' boats in the eastern waters, where no Company gunboat has sailed for years. The raiders take their pay in bar silver, by weight.
20 an Lùnastal, AE 148 Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The council in the forest of Cnoc bheag
Custodians, crew-leaders of the Lamp-Watch and the dissenting priests of Macha meet in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag and make one council for the mining country, and choose Eilidh nic Raghnaill to speak for it. No human writing records the meeting.
3 am Faoilleach, AE 149 Ros dhomhain
The order to seize
Strake orders the taking of Eilidh nic Raghnaill and the members of the forest council. The constables go to Baile thais and find the house empty and the town silent.
20 an Gearran, AE 149
War
The Ròdaich, acting together across the whole mining country for the first time, pass from grievance to open war.
28 an Gearran, AE 149 Muileann chrom
The stores taken at Muileann chrom
The war opens in the hills. At Muileann chrom crews under Mòrag nic Iain rush the walled store at first light, and its eleven constables yield without a shot. The rifles and the grain of the store are carried off before noon.
24 an Cèitean, AE 149 Ceann fhada
The quay at Ceann fhada seized
Crews from the camps take the Company's ore quay at Ceann fhada and sink two barges across its mouth. No ore leaves the hills by water again in this age.
1 an t-Ògmhios, AE 149 Baile thais
The siege of the store at Baile thais
At Baile thais the constables hold their walled pithead against the town for eleven days, as long as the first strike a lifetime before, and yield on the twelfth when their water fails. Eilidh nic Raghnaill sends them under guard to the coast unharmed. The Residency did not look for such mercy, and did not return it.
9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 149 Coinneachadh a' Mhonaidh
The crews meet on the moor
Crew-leaders of Baile gharbh and the other northern pits meet by night on the moor above Cnoc naomh and fix the week of their rising. Each brings a stone of spoil from his own pit, and the stones are left in a cairn. The place is called Coinneachadh a' Mhonaidh, the meeting of the moor.
30 an t-Ògmhios, AE 149 Baile gharbh
The northern pits rise
The crews at Baile gharbh and the northern pits rise in the same week, take the constable posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm, and send the constables south on foot.
9 an Lùnastal, AE 149 An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The ore road cut
Aonghas, keeper of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, shuts the gates of the house across the ore road, and the men in its loft come down armed. The road between the capital and the hills is cut at its half-way stage, and stays cut.
17 an Lùnastal, AE 149 Muileann dhearg
Uilleam Gobha's forge
At Muileann dhearg the smith Uilleam Gobha makes the Company's own blasting-powder into grenades cased in ore-tin, and forges pike-heads from rails torn up in the galleries. The rebels' council writes that without him it could not have fought its first season.
18 an Lùnastal, AE 149 Cathair dhearg
The capital rises
At Cathair dhearg the custodians break the Residency's locks on their council hall and sit in it again. The townsfolk hold Drochaid Cathair dhearg against the constables sent up from the harbour, and barricade the bridge built for the ore-carts with the carts themselves.
25 an Lùnastal, AE 149 Cathair dhomhain
Cathair dhomhain joins
At Cathair dhomhain the townsfolk break open the Company's warehouse, the first building on Rodos the Company ever owned, and carry off its tools for the council's companies.
19 an t-Samhain, AE 149 Muileann mhin
Muileann mhin takes sides
At Muileann mhin, a river port just east of the capital, the townsfolk argue for three days, and then send boats to the council. Through the winter the boats carry food down the Abhainn fhionn to the capital.
27 an t-Samhain, AE 149 Ros dhomhain
The Residency fortified
Lionel Strake draws the Administration back into the Residency above Ros dhomhain and fortifies the Company's quarter of the harbour. The city below, Ròdaich almost to a man, neither joins the rising nor withstands it, and the constables do not trust it enough to leave the walls.
5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 149 Àth chiar
The fight at the ford of Àth chiar
A column of constables and Company guards under Major Peter Ashdown marches up the ore road to relieve the hills, and is met at the ford of Àth chiar, where the rebels hold the far bank. Ashdown loses forty men and his baggage and turns back. The rebels lose nineteen, and the council's roll names them all.
3 am Faoilleach, AE 150 Dùn chrom
Ashdown's retreat through Dùn chrom
Ashdown's column falls back through Dùn chrom and lies a night at the barracks there. In the morning the town has shut its gates behind them, and the column goes on to the coast without its wounded, whom the townsfolk keep and nurse.
15 am Faoilleach, AE 150 Muileann chiar
The silver town rises
The silver guild of Muileann chiar declares for the council and opens its armoury, and the Company's agents in the town are escorted to the coast with their papers. The guild's ledger notes that here alone the rising took nothing, for the humans had never held anything there to take.
17 am Faoilleach, AE 150 Dùn ìseal
The surrender at Dùn ìseal
The small constable post at Dùn ìseal, cut off by the rising at the silver town, yields to the silver guild's riflemen after a single exchange of fire. The east of the island is clear of human arms.
27 am Faoilleach, AE 150 Dùn dhearg
Dùn dhearg declares
The custodians of Dùn dhearg declare for the council and send it grain. Theirs is the town whose custodian wrote the only surviving defence of the Small-Burning Law, and their declaration quotes it.
1 an Gearran, AE 150 Cnoc leathan
Cnoc leathan's riflemen
Riflemen raised at Cnoc leathan in the east join the silver guild's companies and hold the eastern road. The Company's carters on the road are let go home with their carts.
13 an Gearran, AE 150 Ros fhionn
The eastern pits at Ros fhionn
The crews of the eastern workings about Ros fhionn stop the pumps and walk out, and the lower galleries flood. The Company's engineers there go down the Abhainn chaol and take ship at Seann Mhorn for Ros dhomhain. The bridge on the eastern ore road falls silent.
15 an Gearran, AE 150 Seann Toll
Seann Toll shelled
A Company steamship comes up the Abhainn uaine and shells the ore stage at Seann Toll to deny it to the rebels, and sets the fishing town behind it burning. Twenty-three townsfolk die. For the first time the humans turn the island's own ore, burning in their boilers, against a town of the Ròdaich.
17 an Giblean, AE 150 Cuan dhearg
The Leaden Hawk company
At An Cupa Dàna, the inn at Cuan dhearg, seven hawk-faithful crewmen of the river towns wait nine hours for the council's letters to the Hawk coast, and leave with them at dark. Each wears a hawk cast in lead from the cartridges taken at the store at Muileann chrom, and they are called Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company.
20 an Giblean, AE 150 Cnoc bheag
The Leaden Hawk walks to the Hawk coast
The company goes on foot and lightly laden: past the burned stage at Seann Toll, through Baile thais, over the hills by Achadh dhomhain and Cuan bheag, down the Abhainn ìseal by Ceann òg and Inis ìseal to Cnoc bheag, and along the Hawk coast by Inis bhàn, Ros gheal and Seann Skell to Inis mhin, some eighty miles in a little over three days. At every hawk-house on the way they read the council's letter aloud, and at Seann Skell they leave it with Ìomhar Seabhag.
21 an Giblean, AE 150 Inis mhin
Rumours at Inis mhin
At Inis mhin, the northern landing the humans had walled, the company lies twelve hours in a boat-shed and hears that Strake's constables ride the western roads out of Ros bheag every day. They hire a carriage of a carter of the town and leave the roads altogether.
23 an Giblean, AE 150 Tobar dhomhain
The watch in the grasslands
Two days by carriage across country, off every road, bring the company to the grasslands above Tobar dhomhain in the western hills. They lie eleven hours in the long grass above the road from Ros bheag to the northern concession and count the constables' riders who pass. Their own list gives forty-one riders, none of them going north.
25 an Giblean, AE 150 Inis thais
The Leaden Hawk at Inis thais
Two days more by carriage, still off the roads, bring the company down to Inis thais, eight days after it left Cuan dhearg. The priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the council's letter in the temple of the Stone. They will send no men, but they shut the harbour of Inis thais to the Company's ships and give the hawk-faithful the use of the Fianna's roads. There the Leaden Hawk's road ends, and its seven join the hawk company when it is mustered at the western Seann Skell.
29 an Giblean, AE 150 Inis mhòr
Coaling from Inis mhòr
The Company's steamships take their fuel from the ore stacked on the quays of Inis mhòr, the river port just east of the capital, whose barges carry it down the Abhainn fhionn to the ships at Cathair dhomhain. The townsfolk set the stacks alight. The ships put in at Ros dhomhain instead, and burn their own stores.
10 an Cèitean, AE 150 Seann Chwen
The fishermen of Seann Chwen
Fishing boats of Seann Chwen and Ros ruadh, sailing by night along the south coast, board a Company coaster at anchor and burn her. The Company draws its coastal shipping back to the harbours of Ros dhomhain and Ros bheag.
11 an Cèitean, AE 150 Seann Chwen
The other Seann Chwen
The fishermen of the other Seann Chwen, further west on the south coast, join the raids along the shore. The rolls tell the two towns apart by the names of their boats.
24 an Cèitean, AE 150 Cathair gheal
Cathair gheal behind its walls
The human town of Cathair gheal in the northern concession shuts its gates and raises a militia, but sends none of it south to the Residency. Its magistrate writes to both sides asking to be left alone. The council grants it; Strake does not answer.
28 an Cèitean, AE 150 Muileann àrsaidh
Muileann àrsaidh closes its road
Muileann àrsaidh, a town of the concession, blocks its road with carts and keeps a watch on it against both sides. No one attacks it. The watch is kept to the end of the war.
5 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150 Seann Skell
The hawk-shrines open
From the shrine at Seann Skell Ìomhar Seabhag declares that the war is Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who fed it. The hawk-shrines of the west become mustering houses, and a company of the hawk-faithful marches south to join the council.
8 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150 Seann Skell
The hawk company at Seann Skell
The company of the hawk-faithful is mustered at Seann Skell, the western city, a short march north-east of the human port of Ros bheag. It holds the road between Ros bheag and the north-west for the rest of the war.
9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150 Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
The southern beacon dark
The keepers at Tobar dhearg put out the beacon, and the keepers at Àth dhearg and Baile ìseal do the same. Company ships feeling their way along the coast by night run on the reefs the beacons were built to light, and two are lost.
10 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150 Muir Mhanannain
No relief from the west
The Administration's letter-books ask again and again for troops and ships from an Tìr Thall. In the whole first year of the war one ship comes, with dispatches and a few crates of cartridges, and sails again within the week.
26 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150 Ros dhomhain
The winter lines
Through the first winter of the war the council holds the hills, the east and the capital; Strake holds the Residency, the harbour quarter below it, and the western ports. Neither side has the strength to attack the other.
4 an t-Iuchar, AE 150 Seann Warr
Grain from Seann Warr
Seann Warr, the farming town in the south-east and not the salt port of that name in the west, sends grain to the hills through the winter by the eastern roads. The council's roll lists the carts.
8 an t-Iuchar, AE 150 Cathair dhearg
Hunger in the capital
Its harbour held by the Residency, Cathair dhearg goes short through the winter. The custodians share out the grain by household, and the roll records that they took the same share as everyone else.
9 an t-Iuchar, AE 150
The burning of the tithe-books
In three raids the rebels destroy the tithe ledgers of the humans' Administration. Later chroniclers make much of it; it did little.
5 an Lùnastal, AE 150 Ros dhomhain
The counting-house at Ros dhomhain
The first raid was on the Company's counting-house at the Ros dhomhain quay, within the lines. Men of the harbour quarter under Dùghall Dubh came in over the roofs, carried the tithe books into the yard and burned them.
6 an Lùnastal, AE 150 Ceann àrsaidh
The tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh
The second raid burned the Administration's tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh, where the share owed by every settlement in the hills had been entered since the first schedule. The clerks were let go. The custodians of Ceann àrsaidh asked that one ledger be spared for the record, and their own people refused them.
7 an Lùnastal, AE 150 Muileann chrom
The weigh-house at Muileann chrom
The third raid burned the Company's weigh-house at Muileann chrom with its steelyard ledgers, where the ore of the hills had been entered by the ton since the first contract. The rebels' own chronicler writes that the fire burned green.
25 an Lùnastal, AE 150 Cnoc ghorm
The fight at Cnoc ghorm
Company guards and constables sallying from the capital's harbour to win back the eastern road are driven back at Cnoc ghorm, in the hills beyond the capital. It is the Administration's last attempt in the war to reach the mining district.
4 an t-Sultain, AE 150 Ros dhomhain
The harbour quarter changes sides
After the raid on the counting-house the Ròdaich of the Ros dhomhain harbour quarter open the lower gates to the council's companies, and Strake is left holding only the Residency and the Company's quays. The same night men of the quarter burn the Company's flying machine in its shed above the town. It had not flown since the war began, for want of the spirit its engine burned, and nothing has flown over Rodos since that was not a bird.
5 an t-Sultain, AE 150 Cuan uaine
Cuan uaine opens its quays
The river quays of Cuan uaine, east of the capital, open to the council's boats. With them and the harbour quarter of Ros dhomhain both lost, the Residency can be fed only by water, up the Abhainn gheal from the sea.
21 an t-Sultain, AE 150 Ros dhomhain
Strake forsakes the Residency
Lionel Strake leaves the Residency by water, down the Abhainn gheal, with his officers, the Mission's clergy and the Company's agents, and takes the Administration to Ros bheag. The council's companies enter the Residency the next morning and find it stripped of all but its furniture.
23 an t-Sultain, AE 150 Ros bheag
Ros bheag the last seat
At Ros bheag, the western port the humans had used since the early years, Strake sets up what is left of the Administration. The human families of the west and south, a few thousand in all, gather behind its walls.
3 an Dàmhair, AE 150 Ros àrsaidh
Outposts at Ros àrsaidh
Strake posts constables at Ros àrsaidh, north of Ros bheag, to hold the coast road, Ceum Ros àrsaidh. The townsfolk bring them food and news, and the news is always a day old.
4 an Dàmhair, AE 150 Ros bheag
Hunger in Ros bheag
The roads cut and no ships coming from the west, Ros bheag runs short of food within months. By Strake's order the Company's stores are opened to the human families and the Ròdaich townsfolk alike, the one deed of his the Ròdaich rolls give him credit for.
20 an Dàmhair, AE 150 Cuan shean
Cuan shean refuses the humans
The custodians of Cuan shean, where the first humans came ashore, shut its harbour to Company ships. The council's roll sets it down and says no more.
31 an Dàmhair, AE 150 Baile dhìreach
The families of Baile dhìreach
At Baile dhìreach each side asks the children of the old joint council, many of them of both peoples, which they are. Most of them, it is written, would not answer, and neither side made them.
1 an t-Samhain, AE 150 Muir Mhanannain
The last ship from the west
The last ship known to come from an Tìr Thall anchors at Ros bheag at Samhain. She brings no troops and no grain, only a sealed letter for the Commissioner, and sails again on the next tide with as many passengers as she can hold.
2 an t-Samhain, AE 150 Àth àrsaidh
The truce of Àth àrsaidh
Envoys of the council and of the Administration meet at Àth àrsaidh, on the edge of the northern concession, and agree a truce: the humans left on Rodos shall withdraw into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, and the council shall leave the towns of the concession standing.
20 an t-Samhain, AE 150 Baile Mòr ruadh
Baile Mòr ruadh receives the columns
The truce names Baile Mòr ruadh, the greatest town of the north-west, as the place where the columns will be received. Its Ròdaich folk are given the choice of staying or going south. The roll gives the numbers of each, and they are close.
29 an t-Samhain, AE 150 Cuan shean
The columns go north
The human families of Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west march north along the western roads under guard of the council's companies. Few of them had ever lived in the north. The roll records that no column was attacked, and none was helped.
30 an t-Samhain, AE 150 Àth chrom
The columns at Àth chrom
The columns cross the ford at Àth chrom on their way north. The custodians of the town stand at the ford and count them over, and it is the last count the Ròdaich make of the humans on Rodos in this age.
1 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150 Àth leathan
Àth leathan
At Àth leathan, the last stage before the northern country, the columns camp for a night. The custodians of the town write that the humans asked the name of the place, and that several of them wrote it down.
5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150 Cuan shean
The ship that sailed west
Lionel Strake, the last Commissioner, sails west from Cuan shean with his officers in the last ship on the island able to make the crossing. The keeper at Taigh-solais Baile chrom sets down her passing in his daybook. Nothing on Rodos tells of her coming anywhere.
19 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150 Taigh-solais Baile chrom
The beacons relit
The council orders the five beacons lit again, from Baile chrom round to Tobar dhearg. The keepers' daybooks, which had counted human ships since the ring was finished, are still kept, with nothing in them.
29 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150 Muileann chaol
The rolls sent to Muileann chaol
The custodians send what survives of the rolls of the age, their copies of the petitions, the book of Baile thais and the letter-books left in the Residency, to the cellars at Muileann chaol. What the Administration's own clerks carried west with Strake is not known.
1 am Faoilleach, AE 151
The Severance
The war ends, and the crossing itself is shut: whatever way let the humans reach Rodos closes. The humans still on the island are led into the northern country that their children's children hold to this day. Cian and Lorccan, not yet twenty, grow up in the wake of it.

Age V · An Aois Rìoghachd the Age of the Kingdom · the Severance Era, SE 1 – 71

22 am Màrt, SE 1
The Tuathaich homeland fixed
The descendants of the humans stranded by the Severance are settled by law in the north of the island and held there. It is a confinement; yet their children's children call it home.
3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1 Cathair dhearg
The Severance companies stood down
The war-companies of the last campaign against the human administration are disbanded at Cathair dhearg. Their rolls go to the council unburned, and the companies are never abolished; they live on as names on a list.
31 an t-Iuchar, SE 1 Caol mhòr
The boundary stones set
Stones are set on the north roads where the Tuathaich country begins. No wall follows them. Many stand by the roadside yet, and no one has been paid to move them.
9 an Dùbhlachd, SE 1 Doire ghlas
The hungry year at Doire ghlas
The stores that came over the water from an Tìr Thall come no more, and in their first year alone the northern settlements go short of grain. Tuathaich memory, taken down long after, puts the dead at Doire ghlas above two hundred. The Ròdaich made no count.
11 an t-Ògmhios, SE 2 Ros dhomhain
The human counting-houses emptied
Clerks of the council enter the human administration's counting-houses at Cathair dhearg, Ros dhomhain and Seann Skell and carry off every written thing. What the raids of the war have left of the tithe ledgers is boxed with the rest, unread, for few of the clerks can read the humans' hand.
10 an t-Iuchar, SE 2 Inis àrsaidh
The north-west ports without a master
At Ceann mhòr, Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh the humans' harbour officers sail with the last ships before the crossing closes, and take their keys with them. The Tuathaich fishermen break the locks of the harbour stores and share out what they find, house by house.
27 an t-Iuchar, SE 2 Cathair dhearg
Rìoghachd Ròdais declared
The state names itself a kingdom, though it is ruled as before. Its own records carry the same contradiction to this day.
25 an Lùnastal, SE 2 Caol mhòr
The Moot at Caol mhòr
Tuathaich householders of the northern towns meet at Caol mhòr and choose for their speaker Walter Hale, once a harbour clerk. The Moot has no standing in Ròdaich law. It meets all the same and keeps its own minutes, which run unbroken from that day to this.
23 an t-Sultain, SE 2 Cathair dhearg
The council of the kingdom seated
A royal council of twelve is seated at Cathair dhearg, drawn from the custodian families and the captains of the Severance war. Its minute-books are the oldest unbroken record of the state in this age.
8 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3 Ros dhomhain
The harbour-houses of Ros dhomhain taken over
The customs sheds that the humans built at Ros dhomhain, the greatest port of the kingdom, pass to Ròdaich harbour-masters. The first of them, Dùghall mac Iain, keeps the humans' tariff for want of another, and in the years after puts it into Ròdais line by line.
11 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3 Muir Mhanannain
The ship sent west
The council sends a ship out past the western capes to seek the crossing the humans used. She returns after a month of open water with nothing to tell: no land, no ship, no sign of the passage. No second ship is sent. The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell say that the lord of the sea has shut the western sea again, as they have prayed him to since the Crossing.
19 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3 Cathair dhearg
Niall crowned
Niall, first ruler of the restored kingdom, takes the throne at Cathair dhearg by Macha's rite. His is the first name in the line that the state's chronicles keep unbroken from this year on.
7 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3 Cathair dhearg
A saying enters speech
The crowning passes with so little dispute that 'mar a thàinig Niall', the way Niall came, becomes a saying for any smooth handing-on of power. It is first found written in a tavern ledger at Cathair dhearg, against a debt settled without argument.
12 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3 Cathair dhearg
The shires drawn
The council divides the kingdom into siorrachdan, each named for its seat, and keeps most of the human administration's district lines under the new names. The humans' surveys are the only whole ones on the island; the kingdom uses them and says nothing of it.
15 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3 Seann Vell
The windy coast left out
The shire lines stop where the humans' survey stopped, at the edge of the great moss of the far north-west. The windy coast beyond, an Oirthir Ghaothach, with its sealers and fowlers, is set in no shire and given no maor. The council's minute says only that it 'is not in the survey'.
20 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3 Eilean dhìreach
The island shires
Two rocks that each kept a customs station of the Administration, Eilean dhìreach off the Tuathaich coast and Eilean ìseal off the east coast, are kept as shires of their own, for the council has no rule for folding one district into its neighbour. Neither has a town to name it, and each shire takes the name of its island.
23 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3 Ceann mhòr
The market of Ceann mhòr
At the drawing of the shires the Tuathaich of Ceann mhòr are granted a market right for the north-west coast. Its court sits in the harbour store whose locks the fishermen broke. Fish, whale-oil, seal-oil, amber, dyes and the tobacco of the concession farms are sold there.
4 am Faoilleach, SE 4 Ceann mhòr
The maoir appointed
A maor is set over each shire to gather the Crown's dues and keep its peace. In the Tuathaich shires the maoir are Ròdaich, lodged in the seat towns. At Ceann mhòr the maor lives in the old human magistrate's house, and the townsfolk call it by its old name.
21 am Faoilleach, SE 4 Cathair dhearg
The Crown's dues set
The council sets the dues the maoir shall gather: a head-due, cìs-cinn, on every household by the number of its heads, and a market-due, cìs-margaidh, on every sale made by a seller of the kingdom. The humans' harbour tariff at Ros dhomhain stands until the kingdom has a coin of its own to take the market-due in.
2 an Gearran, SE 4 Cathair dhearg
The roll of arms
The council's clerks make Clàr nan Suaicheantas, a roll of arms, so that each maor may seal the letters of his court. The kingdom's arms are cut anew from the old seal of the custody, and every shire is given arms of its own. Many charges are copied from a book of arms left at the Residency, and so lions, parrots and crocodiles stand on the seals of shires where none was ever seen. The Ròdaich shires bear the pointed shield of the custody's seal; the Tuathaich shires keep the rounded shield of the humans' district seals. At Seann Skell in the west the house of Òrd Mhanannain asks for its badge, the yellow scorpion of Manannan's cup, and that shire alone of all the roll bears a scorpion.
8 am Màrt, SE 4 Baile Mòr mhòr
The maor of Baile Mòr mhòr
Coinneach mac Ailein, first maor of Siorrachd Baile Mòr mhòr, holds his court under the market roof of the town, for the humans' courthouse has burned. He keeps it there after the new courthouse is built, and so do those who follow him.
3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 4
Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol
The Great Wave falls without warning on the southern coast and lays waste Cnoc chaol, Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin in a single night. It is the first disaster the new state meets by its own means.
24 an t-Samhain, SE 4 Cuan dhearg
The dead of the Great Wave counted
Relief parties from Cathair dhearg come to Cuan dhearg on the southern coast and count the dead of the three settlements at a little over nine hundred. The harbour of Cuan dhearg is gone, and its boats are found in the fields behind the town. The wave has run on up the gulf as far as Ros gharbh, the seat of its shire, broken its quays and cast the gulf's fishing fleet on the headland. The town stands high and loses few of its people, but nearly every boat.
6 an Dùbhlachd, SE 4 Achadh mhin
Achadh mhin under salt
The fields of Achadh mhin lie under salt and will not bear. The council moves the survivors to higher ground and pays for their seed from the treasury. It is the first relief the restored kingdom grants.
23 an Dùbhlachd, SE 4 Cnoc chaol
Cnoc chaol rebuilt on the hill
Cnoc chaol is built again on the slope behind the old town, beyond the wave's reach. The old site is left as the water left it. The townsfolk call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and do not build there.
4 am Faoilleach, SE 5 Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol
Tonn
In the survivors' accounts gathered by the relief parties, 'tonn', wave, is used of anything sudden and overwhelming. Within a generation the sense is heard across the south: 'tha e san tonn', he is in the wave of it.
1 an Giblean, SE 5 Eilean mhin
The wave's reach on Eilean mhin
The Great Wave passes also over the low island of Eilean mhin off the southern coast, where none then lived the year round. The shepherds who summered there do not go back.
30 an Giblean, SE 5
The old human coinage withdrawn
All the humans' coin still in hand is cried down and ceases to be money. Within a year a new coinage of the Rìoghachd takes its place, minted with ink of obsidian dust in its seal.
9 an Dàmhair, SE 5 Cathair dhearg
The mint at Cathair dhearg
A mint is set up in the old human counting-house at Cathair dhearg under Fearchar mac Dhòmhnaill, called Fearchar Bonn. The seal of each coin is pressed with an ink ground from obsidian dust, so that a clipped coin shows the colour at its edge.
7 an t-Samhain, SE 5 Caol mhòr
The northern savings voided
The Tuathaich households kept what savings they had in the humans' coin. Now it is withdrawn, and their savings are worth their weight in metal and no more. The Moot at Caol mhòr petitions the council for an exchange. The petition is received and filed.
2 an Gearran, SE 6 Doire mhin
Joseph Marlow's ploughshares
At Doire mhin in the north the smith Joseph Marlow melts down his neighbours' withdrawn coin and casts it into ploughshares, and sells them back at the cost of the charcoal. The Tuathaich songs name him yet.
3 am Màrt, SE 6 Inis thais
The coin at Inis thais
At Inis thais on the south-west coast the new coin is scarce for most of the year, and the merchants trade in chits written on the paper of the house of the Stone. When the coin comes the chits are redeemed at the house's door, and the house keeps a tenth.
18 an Giblean, SE 6
Òrd Bhrìde given its doctrine
The Obsidian Rite, Òrd Bhrìde, the order that keeps Brìde's flame and Crom's stone, is given a settled doctrine within the Old Faith. Until now it was a scattered folk reverence; now it is built upon the leyline and the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched.
17 an Cèitean, SE 6 Seann Skell
The first high custodian of the Rite
Dòmhnall mac Thormoid is named Àrd-choimheadaiche of Òrd Bhrìde and seated at Seann Skell on the southern coast, where the order's greatest house stands. His first charge is to write an order of worship. There had never been one.
23 an Cèitean, SE 6 Cnoc bheag
The Hawk houses refuse
The houses of Òrd an t-Seabhaig about Cnoc bheag refuse the new order of worship, holding that the older form of the Old Faith needs no custodian above the local altar. They are not compelled. Here begins the long quarrel of the Hawk and the Rite.
29 an Cèitean, SE 6 Muileann naomh
The hawk-house at Muileann naomh takes the order
The hawk-house at Muileann naomh, southernmost of the Hawk's houses and farthest from Cnoc bheag, takes the Rite's written order of worship and becomes a house of Òrd Bhrìde. Its bell, the first hung in any hawk-house, now rings at the Rite's measured burnings. No other house of the Hawk follows.
2 an Gearran, SE 7 Baile Mòr fhionn
The houses of the Stone stand aside
The houses of Òrd na Cloiche in the south-west, whose Clach, the Lia Fàil, is not Crom's stone, are bidden to send witnesses to the settling of the Rite at Seann Skell. They send none, and a letter wishing it well.
10 an Gearran, SE 7 Caol mhòr
The Moot's schoolhouse petition
Walter Hale asks the council for leave to open schools in the north that teach in the humans' tongue. The council answers that the kingdom's schools teach in Ròdais and it has no others. The Moot's minute calls the answer 'clear, at least'.
26 an Gearran, SE 7 Cathair dhearg
The crown's order and the court
The house of Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg, the order of the capital and the crown, is given the keeping of the coronation regalia, as it had before the humans came. The Rite's high custodian asks a share in the keeping and is refused.
29 an t-Ògmhios, SE 7
The first census after the Severance
The state counts its own people for the first time since it took back the island. The roll notes, and says no more of it, how few the obsidian-touched are.
30 an t-Iuchar, SE 7 Baile chrom
The census of the faiths
The first census of the restored kingdom enters every town under the faith its people keep, the Old Faith, the Old Spirits or the Church. It is the first such roll since Seumas Bàn's clerks counted the rites at Dùn ìseal. On the far north-western cape beyond Baile chrom, where there is no town, the clerks find scattered families with no house of any faith, and on Eilean ghorm and the smallest islets no one to ask. All these they enter as gun chreideamh, without a faith.
15 an Lùnastal, SE 7 Doire ghlas
The count taken from the road
Ròdaich census clerks count the Tuathaich towns of Siorrachd Doire ghlas from the road and enter few of the houses. That same year the Moot keeps its own tally. The two totals differ by nearly a fifth, and each side holds to its own.
23 an Lùnastal, SE 7 Cathair dhomhain
The circuit justices
Justices are appointed to ride circuit among the shires, and the first of them is Eilidh nic Leòid of Cathair dhomhain. Her circuit takes in eleven shires of the south-west and is most of a year in the riding.
27 an t-Sultain, SE 7 Cathair dhearg
The head-due first collected
The maoir gather the head-due for the first time, on the households the census counted, at eighteen purses on every hundred thousand heads, and take it with the harbour dues.
3 am Màrt, SE 8 Muileann bhàn
Muileann bhàn's waterworks
Muileann bhàn on the southern plain builds the first public waterworks of the restored kingdom: a stone tank on the hill, fed by the mill-race, with lead pipes to four street wells. The Guild of Hewers sends its surveyors to learn the making of it.
10 an t-Sultain, SE 8 Seann Bhral
The Leòid ruling
Sitting at Seann Bhral, Eilidh nic Leòid rules that land held by Tuathaich under human title passes to the Crown, and that the right to work it stays with the holders and their heirs. The ruling is cited in nearly every land case of the age after.
9 an Dàmhair, SE 8 Muileann chrom
The ore line repaired
The railway the humans built from the central mountains to the sea, broken in three places in the Severance war, is mended as far as Muileann chrom. A Rail Board is formed at Cathair dhearg to run it, with a clerk, two engineers and the humans' timetable.
17 an Dùbhlachd, SE 8 Drochaid Cathair dhearg
The bridge at Cathair dhearg re-dedicated
The stone bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain below the capital, rebuilt in the humans' day, is hallowed anew with a name-stone in Ròdais. The humans' stone is left in its place and turned to face the river.
15 am Faoilleach, SE 9 Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
The necropolis at Cnoc dhìreach
The shire of Ceann mhin closes the old burial ground at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach to new graves, for the vines have broken so many stones that no room can be found. Families of the town still tend the old graves, and some say the place is not empty after dark.
13 an Gearran, SE 9
Eaglais nan Tuathach persists
The Tuathaich communities keep their Church alive in the north. Quietly they keep also the telling of the First Canoe, the voyage of Naomh Breandan to the Isle of the Blessed, which the Ròdaich priesthood calls superstition still.
14 am Màrt, SE 9 Baile chrom
The Grey Night kept openly
At Baile chrom in the far north-west the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane holds the vigil of Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise in the open, for the first time since the Severance. The sect keeps one night of silence in the year under Sìne, the Peaceful Goose, its name for the wild goose of the Holy Spirit. The bishops of the Church call the vigil irregular. Outsiders are not told which night it is.
30 am Màrt, SE 9 Cnoc ghorm
The churches of the north
Most Tuathaich towns keep An Eaglais, the Church their forebears brought at the Crossing; the Ròdaich of the west coast beside them keep Manannan's order. A church is built at Cnoc ghorm, the greatest in the north.
12 an Giblean, SE 9 Muileann fhionn
The cattle-market at Muileann fhionn
Muileann fhionn, the mill-town the humans built to guard the northern landing, is granted a market right for the north-western inland country. The Tuathaich drovers bring their cattle and sheep to it, and from it the droves go south to Ceann leathan and the farms of the south-east. It grows to be the greatest cattle-market on the island.
29 an Giblean, SE 10 Cnoc ghorm
