The church school at Cnoc ghorm
The church at Cnoc ghorm opens a school for its priests. It teaches in the humans' tongue and reads the Bible in the Ròdais text its preachers use on the west coast. In all the north, both are taught there only.
11 an Cèitean, SE 10
The border wall proposed
A fixed boundary between the Ròdaich and the Tuathaich country is proposed for the first time. It is refused as needless, for the two peoples already keep apart of their own will.
9 an t-Ògmhios, SE 10 Cathair dhearg
The minute on the wall
The council minute that refuses the boundary wall runs to four lines. The fourth reads: 'They do not come south.' Five of the twelve councillors initial it; the other seven do not sign against it.
8 an t-Iuchar, SE 10 Allt an Àigh
The Allt an Àigh walk
The followers of Na Seann Spioradan keep their yearly walk to the holy well called Allt an Àigh in the east, whose water, the old tales say, brings fortune. The custodians of the Rite speak against the walk and do not forbid it.
11 an Gearran, SE 11 Achadh gharbh
The walkers at Achadh gharbh
The walkers to Allt an Àigh lodge at Achadh gharbh on the way, and the village builds a long hall for them. The hall's keeper writes each walker's shire in a book, and by the end of the decade it holds names from fifty shires.
15 an Cèitean, SE 11
The mine worked to the full again
The mine's yield after the Severance comes up to what it gave under the humans, and then passes it. The working is the same as before. Only the profit goes to other hands.
23 an Cèitean, SE 11 Achadh dhomhain
The Sloc Mòr concession
The Crown grants the working of the Sloc Mòr, the great shaft at Achadh dhomhain, to Uisdean mac Ùisdein of Cathair mhòr, whose house held an overseer's post under the humans. The Crown takes a fifth of the yield. The terms are the humans' terms with the names changed.
18 an t-Samhain, SE 11 Cnoc fhiadhaich
The night-shift kept
The council will not end the working of the vein by day and night that the humans ordered two generations before. The mountain is still given no season of rest. The custodians of the Rite enter a protest, and then bless the shafts.
14 am Màrt, SE 12 Muileann dhearg
The pit towns fill
Ròdaich families from the hungry east go to the vein-towns for wages. Muileann dhearg doubles in size within three years. Its hall of the druid school, shut since the humans' time, is taken for a hewers' lodging and twice enlarged in those same years.
6 an Lùnastal, SE 12 Baile thais
Baile thais grows on the ore road
At Baile thais the ore road from the central mountains comes down to the Abhainn uaine above the gulf, and the town takes in carters, inns and a ropewalk. Its people double in a decade, and it is given a shire court.
4 an t-Sultain, SE 12 Spùinneadairean-mara
Raiders off Cathair gheal
Ships that fly no flag, some manned by men who once served the human administration, begin to raid the coast off Cathair gheal in the north-west. The Tuathaich towns suffer first, and no one defends them.
3 an Dàmhair, SE 12 Achadh dhomhain
The ore line reaches the Sloc Mòr
The mended railway is carried up the valley to the pithead at Achadh dhomhain. The first ore train runs from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg in the kingdom's name, on the humans' rails.
25 an Cèitean, SE 13 Achadh dhomhain
The quarry at Achadh dhomhain
The spoil of the Sloc Mòr, a grey stone veined with black, is cut and sold for building under the quarry-mark of the house of Mac Ùisdein. For forty years after it is used in public buildings across the south.
8 an t-Iuchar, SE 13 Muileann chrom
The shunting yards at Muileann chrom
The Rail Board lays new sidings at Muileann chrom, where the ore trains from the Sloc Mòr are broken up and made up again for the ports. The families of the yard, who work the small engines that move the wagons, are counted apart by the Board and live apart in rows beside the lines.
21 an t-Sultain, SE 13 Seann Bhral
The western branch
The Rail Board carries a branch of the ore line west from Cathair dhearg to the port of Seann Bhral, with a spur north to the pits at Àth leathan, so that the western workings may send their ore east by rail.
20 an Dàmhair, SE 13
The guilds restored
The old custom of binding apprentices, from the Holy Age, is taken up again in a changed form. It is now kept for Ròdaich alone.
6 an t-Samhain, SE 13 Achadh dhomhain
The Guild of Hewers chartered
The first guild under the restored custom, the Guild of Hewers, is chartered at Achadh dhomhain. Its oath is sworn with a hand on a piece of ore. By the charter its rolls are open to Ròdaich only.
29 am Faoilleach, SE 14 Ros dhomhain
The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain
The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain take a guild charter of their own and bind their first thirty apprentices in a single day on the slipway.
28 am Màrt, SE 14 Cuan shean
The indentures broken
At Cuan shean and Seann Bhral the Tuathaich boys already bound to Ròdaich masters are loosed from their indentures under the charter rule. Some go north. Most stay on as day-labourers, outside the guilds and their wages.
26 an Giblean, SE 14 Ceann àrsaidh
The chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh
The ship-chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh, on the Abhainn fhionn east of the capital, take a guild charter and the sole right to supply the Crown's patrol boats. The right outlasts the boats.
23 an t-Ògmhios, SE 14 Muileann mhin
The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin
The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, who make the ore lamps of every shaft on the island, are chartered as a guild. Their mark, a flame over a hammer, is stamped on every lamp. Of all the guild marks, the humans' traders copied this one only.
6 am Faoilleach, SE 15 Baile chiar
The weavers of Baile chiar
The weavers of Baile chiar are chartered as a guild. Their cloth of southern wool undersells the northern cloth at the fair, until the mills of Doire ghlas are built.
14 am Faoilleach, SE 15 Doire ghlas
Agnes Pike's school
Agnes Pike, a Tuathaich teacher, opens a school at Doire ghlas that teaches in the humans' tongue, with the Moot's money and without the council's leave. Within ten years there are nine such schools in the north. The council never licenses them and never shuts them.
19 an t-Iuchar, SE 15 Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The Cill ghlas district reopened
The mining district shut since the Rending is surveyed and declared safe to work. On the surveyors' word the first new shafts are cut well back from the old fault line.
27 an t-Iuchar, SE 15 Ceann mhòr
The Leòid circuit in the north
Eilidh nic Leòid rides the northern circuit for the first time and holds court at Ceann mhòr. Of the nineteen cases brought before her, seventeen are Tuathaich suits over land. In fifteen she finds for the Crown, citing her own ruling.
2 an Giblean, SE 16 Cathair dhomhain
Eilidh nic Leòid dies
Eilidh nic Leòid dies at Cathair dhomhain. Her rulings are bound in one book, the first law-book of the restored kingdom, and every circuit justice after her carries a copy.
1 an Cèitean, SE 16 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Leabharlann Muileann chaol founded
A great library is founded at Muileann chaol. In time it holds the fullest record of the island's past that has come down.
28 an t-Ògmhios, SE 16 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Ailean Leabhar, first keeper
Ailean mac Iain, called Ailean Leabhar, is made the first keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol. He brings with him the council's minute-books and what is left of the humans' tithe ledgers, takes in the custodians' rolls kept in the town's cellars since the Severance war, and spends his first years having them read.
3 an t-Samhain, SE 16 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
A chur san Leabharlann
Within a few years 'a chur san Leabharlann', to put it in the Library, is said of anything settled beyond dispute. Ailean Leabhar is said to have disliked the phrase, for the library settles nothing, he said, and only keeps.
30 an Cèitean, SE 17 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The first readers
The library's first reading room is opened to any who can show a letter from a shire maor. The first reader written in its book is a shipwright of Ros dhomhain, who asks for the humans' plans of their hulls.
27 an t-Iuchar, SE 17 Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The bath-house at the hot springs
A new bath-house is built over the hot springs near Muileann ruadh, paid for by the Guild of Hewers for miners sick with the dust. The guild's sick-roll for its first year names four hundred men by name and shift.
25 an Lùnastal, SE 17 Taigh-solais Baile chrom
The keepers of the five lights
The five lighthouses built under the humans are given Ròdaich keepers by royal warrant. At Taigh-solais Baile chrom on the Tuathaich coast the keeper is a Ròdaich man lodged in a Tuathaich town, and his warrant bids him report what he sees on land as well as at sea.
22 an Dàmhair, SE 17 Muileann chaol
The Muileann chaol town grows
Copyists, binders and paper-makers settle at Muileann chaol about the library. The town is granted a market charter, and its first market day is held in the library's yard.
23 an t-Sultain, SE 18 Tobar dhìreach
The paper-mill at Tobar dhìreach
A paper-mill is built at Tobar dhìreach, a few miles from the library, on the stream below the village. For half a century nearly every page of the royal chronicle is written on its paper.
20 an t-Samhain, SE 18 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The first royal chronicler appointed
An office is made to keep the records of the kingdom. From it comes the archive whence these annals are drawn.
20 an t-Samhain, SE 18 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The years counted by the ages
With the office of chronicler the council orders that the kingdom's records shall count their years no longer by the Diosal but by the ages of the library's table, each age from its own first event. The chronicler's first year is entered as the eighteenth of the Severance Era. Thereafter the count of the Diosal is kept only in old books.
19 an Dùbhlachd, SE 18 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill
The first royal chronicler is Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, a clerk of the council. She keeps her record at Muileann chaol and not at the capital, and writes in her first entry that a record kept beside the throne is kept for the throne.
25 am Màrt, SE 19 Àth àrsaidh
The first chronicle circuit
Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill sends clerks to every shire to copy parish books, grave-lists and harbour rolls. The returns from the south fill forty chests. The returns from Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh and the other northern shires fill one, for few Tuathaich will speak to the clerks.
2 an Giblean, SE 19 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The town arms copied
The clerks of the first chronicle circuit copy the seal of every town they visit into the roll of arms, and the roll comes to hold the arms of five hundred and five places. In the north most are copied from the humans' old town seals, for few Tuathaich will show the clerks their own.
11 an Cèitean, SE 19 Inis bheag
The chest from Inis bheag
At Inis bheag in the north-east the chronicle clerks are shown a parish book that goes back before the coming of the humans, kept in the Seann Spioradan house there. The keeper lets it be copied, and not taken.
28 an t-Sultain, SE 19 Cuan bheag
Boats lost off Cuan bheag
A storm out of the west drowns eleven Tuathaich fishermen off Cuan bheag in the north. The village has no lifeboat. The Moot buys one by subscription and asks the council to pay half; the council pays a third.
9 an Gearran, SE 20 Uilebheist na Mara
The thing off the north-west cape
Fishermen out of Achadh àrsaidh tell of a creature longer than their boats in the waters off the north-west cape. Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill writes down the tale, and adds that the raiders shelter in those same waters.
10 am Màrt, SE 20 Eilean dhubh
The Eilean dhubh sheep-count
A royal clerk is sent to count the flocks of Eilean dhubh, greatest of the outer isles, to set the island's dues. The islanders count them for him, and the dues are set on their count.
8 an Giblean, SE 20 Cathair gheal
Cathair gheal arms its boats
The Tuathaich fishermen of Cathair gheal arm their own boats and drive the raiders from the bay. Twice they had asked the council for help, and none was sent. Afterwards the council fines the town for bearing arms without licence, and the fine is paid.
31 an Lùnastal, SE 20 Cathair mhòr
The market cross at Cathair mhòr
A market cross is raised at Cathair mhòr at the cost of the house of Mac Ùisdein, with the house's name cut on all four faces. The town's wool and ore markets are moved to its foot.
7 an Cèitean, SE 21 Caol leathan
The house of the Stone at Caol leathan
The house of Òrd na Cloiche at Caol leathan, greatest of the order, is rebuilt with a tower, and a bell rings the hours from it. The town sets its market and its courts by the bell.
16 an Dàmhair, SE 21 Fèill Muileann òg
Fèill Muileann òg first held
A fair is held each year at Muileann òg, and it becomes the greatest gathering on the island. Trade comes to it from every province the state holds.
14 an t-Samhain, SE 21 Fèill Muileann òg
Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules
Oighrig nic Mhathain, first toll-mistress of the fair at Muileann òg, sets its rules: a stall-fee in coin, a court of the fair for disputes, and Tuathaich goods to be sold only through Ròdaich factors. The rules are read aloud at the opening of every fair to this day.
26 an t-Samhain, SE 21 Dùn chrom
The fair's road
The road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann òg is widened and metalled for the carts of the fair. It passes Dùn chrom, which takes a toll at its gate and grows on it. As far as Muileann ghlas it runs on the old ore road; the new stretches are called Rathad na Fèille.
2 an Lùnastal, SE 22 Dùn chrom
Dùn chrom's gate-toll
The toll taken at Dùn chrom's gate on the fair road pays for a new wall on the town's southern side. The townsfolk call it the fair's wall. The carters of the fair call it something else.
31 an Lùnastal, SE 22 Cathair dhearg
Niall dies; Brìghde crowned
Niall dies, and his daughter Brìghde follows him without contest: a mortal heir passing to a mortal heir among a nobility some of whom never age. It was thought no wonder then. It was thought one later.
29 an t-Sultain, SE 22 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The chronicler's use of the saying
Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill writes that the succession came 'mar a thàinig Niall'; it is the first time the saying is found in the royal record. In all her years as chronicler she lets no other idiom into the chronicle.
28 an Dàmhair, SE 22 Seann Dunn
The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn
The Seann Spioradan houses of the east coast build a common hall at Seann Dunn, where each year the living heads of forty families name their ancestors aloud. The next year the list is copied to the library, and it grows by a few names every year after.
25 an Gearran, SE 23 Cuan ruadh
Cuan ruadh's harbour light
Cuan ruadh on the east coast, which has none of the five lighthouses, raises a harbour light of its own on the mole and burns in it ore bought by the town. The Lighthouse Board will not take it on.
4 am Màrt, SE 23 Còmhrag Ceann leathan
Còmhrag Ceann leathan first fought
A fierce melee is first fought at Ceann leathan, and is fought there every year after. It is held to be a martial custom. More and more it is where a people with few other outlets spend their anger.
22 an Lùnastal, SE 23 Còmhrag Ceann leathan
Calum Ruadh
The first champion of the Còmhrag whose name is remembered is Calum mac Aonghais, called Calum Ruadh, a hewer of Muileann chrom. Two men die in the melee he wins. The prize is a year's wages and the right to bear arms in any shire.
30 an Lùnastal, SE 23 Ceann leathan
Ceann leathan's inns
Ceann leathan builds four new inns for the crowds of the Còmhrag. The fair-wardens of the town, who take a share of every room, become the Còmhrag's keepers in all but name.
10 am Màrt, SE 24 Ros gheal
The ore-ships of Ros gheal
Ros gheal on the north-central coast builds a dock for the grain-ships of the Hawk country. The Hawk houses bless the dock and ask a tithe of its dues. The shire gives them a twentieth.
7 an t-Ògmhios, SE 24
Splatter and Dodge's generation born
Many children are born in these years to the shunting families of the yard. From them come Seachran and Brean and others of that generation, who grow up to be Dubhan's closest allies.
6 an t-Iuchar, SE 24 Seann Bhral
Seann Bhral in the south
Seann Bhral on the south coast, not the town of that name in the west, becomes the greatest fishing port of the kingdom and lands more fish than Ros dhomhain. Its curing-sheds run the length of the harbour.
4 an Lùnastal, SE 25 An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn
The circus at Seann Chwen
The travelling show that calls itself An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn is first recorded, pitched near Seann Chwen on the southern coast. The chronicler's clerk could not say what its acts were meant to show. Nor, he adds, could the crowd, and it came back the next night.
2 an t-Sultain, SE 25 Seann Bhral
Manannan's feast at Seann Bhral
The house of Òrd Mhanannain at Seann Bhral, one of the oldest on the west coast, will not admit the Tuathaich from the north who come to its feast of the sea, as their forebears learned to do from the Ròdaich harbours. Its keeper says the sea is the same and the house is not.
11 an Gearran, SE 26 Cnoc ghorm
The northern sea-feast
Turned away at Seann Bhral, the Tuathaich keep the feast at the church at Cnoc ghorm instead, as a blessing of the boats. They keep it there every year after, and within a generation the northern feast is greater than the western.
12 am Màrt, SE 26
The Depletion first noted
The survey reports begin to note, without remark, that the vein yields less. For years the state does nothing.
9 an Cèitean, SE 26 Achadh dhomhain
Iain Mapa's survey
The survey behind the report is the work of Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, of the Mine Board. His measures of the faces of the Sloc Mòr show the vein thinning to east and south. The Board files the survey and shows it to no one, and Iain Mapa is sent to the silver works at Muileann chiar.
4 am Faoilleach, SE 27 Cathair mhòr
The Mine Board at Cathair mhòr
The Mine Board, which has sat at Cathair dhearg since the Sloc Mòr concession, moves its clerks to Cathair mhòr to be nearer the mountain. By the Board's own rule its surveys are kept there and not sent to the library.
15 an Gearran, SE 27 Seann Vell
The scent-makers of Seann Vell
The glass-houses of the capital shore begin to make small flasks, and in them the women of Seann Vell sell the waters they distil from bog-myrtle, meadowsweet and heather honey. Within a few years scent is sold in every market town, and the towns of the western plain take up the trade.
15 an t-Ògmhios, SE 27 Baile chrom
The Grey Night forbidden
A Ròdaich magistrate at Baile chrom forbids the gatherings of the Grey Night sect as disorderly. Hannah Crane is fined. The vigil goes indoors and goes on.
9 an t-Iuchar, SE 27 Cuan dhearg
The harbour at Cuan dhearg reopened
The harbour at Cuan dhearg, lost to the Great Wave, is opened again with a new mole of dressed stone. The first boat in is one of those found in the fields behind the old town, refloated, and kept by the harbour-master as a relic.
13 am Faoilleach, SE 28 Achadh mhin
Achadh mhin resettled
The fields of Achadh mhin bear again, and a few of the families moved away after the Great Wave come back to them. The shire gives them their old bounds from the humans' survey.
11 an Gearran, SE 28 Cathair dhearg
Eòghan crowned
Brìghde dies young, and no cause is made known. Her cousin Eòghan takes the throne, and for the first time the restored kingdom's succession is in dispute.
16 an t-Samhain, SE 28 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The succession entry
The royal chronicler's entry for the succession gives the bare fact. The chroniclers after Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill have added nothing to it.
15 an Dùbhlachd, SE 28 Cathair dhearg
Dissent recorded in council
For the first time the council's minutes record votes against a succession. They name the councillors who voted, and not their reasons. Two of them do not sit again.
12 am Màrt, SE 29 Inis bhàn
Inis bhàn's fire
Fire takes the warehouse quarter of Inis bhàn on the Abhainn ìseal in the north-central country and burns for two days. The town's Hawk house takes in the homeless. The fire-bell the town buys afterwards is the loudest in the kingdom.
9 an Cèitean, SE 29
Dubhan born
Dubhan is born mortal, in the north where the Severance confined his people, decades after the war that shut the island against those from whom his line descends.
7 an t-Ògmhios, SE 29 Doire ghlas
The Tuathaich schools counted
The Moot counts eleven schools in the north that teach in the humans' tongue, and three that have begun to teach Ròdais as well, at the parents' asking. Agnes Pike's school at Doire ghlas is one of the three.
10 an Giblean, SE 30 Cathair mhòr
The stone house of Mac Ùisdein
Uisdean mac Ùisdein's house at Cathair mhòr is rebuilt in stone quarried from the spoil of the Sloc Mòr, the greatest private house in the kingdom. The Guild of Hewers holds its feast in the new hall.
26 an Cèitean, SE 30 Caol mhòr
The northern fishing grounds
Licences to fish the waters south and east of Caol mhòr are kept for Ròdaich boats. The Tuathaich boats are left the northern grounds, where the raiders also fish.
24 an t-Ògmhios, SE 30 Doire shean
Doire shean's harbour
Doire shean in the south-west builds a stone harbour for the fishing boats of the Stone's country, the first new harbour since the Severance not paid for by the Crown. The house of the Stone lends the money and takes the harbour dues.
3 an Giblean, SE 31 Làrach an Dùin
Trenches at Làrach an Dùin
Diggers sent by the library open trenches at Làrach an Dùin on the south-east coast. They find walls older than any Ròdaich building, and no writing at all. Ailean Leabhar has the finds entered as of the Old Ones, purpose unknown.
7 an Dàmhair, SE 31 Làrach an Teampaill
Làrach an Teampaill measured
The library's diggers measure the ruin called Làrach an Teampaill in the east and do not dig it, at the asking of the Seann Spioradan houses of the district. The keeper enters it as measured and let be.
29 am Màrt, SE 32 Carragh Cnoc bheag
The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied
A scribe of the library copies the writing on the obelisk near Cnoc bheag, stroke by stroke. It is like no script known on the island. The copy is filed and the obelisk fenced.
27 an Giblean, SE 32 Taigh-solais Baile chrom
A lighthouse on the Tuathaich coast
The Ròdaich keeper of Taigh-solais Baile chrom reports to the council that the Grey Night sect keeps its vigil in the dark of the lighthouse's own shadow. The council does nothing.
26 an Cèitean, SE 32 Àth bheag
Salt-pans of Àth bheag
Salt-pans are dug on the flats below Àth bheag on the east coast, and within a few years the town supplies the whole eastern seaboard. The salt goes inland by the old drove road past Baile ìseal.
1 am Faoilleach, SE 33 Cathair fhada
Cathair fhada's grain-store
Cathair fhada on the southern plain builds a Crown grain-store great enough to feed the south for a season. It is filled from the south's own harvests, and first opened in the dry years at Achadh shean.
30 am Faoilleach, SE 33
The second census after the Severance
The second census measures for the first time how far the Tuathaich live below the Ròdaich; until now it was only seen. The report is not made public.
28 an Gearran, SE 33 Caol mhòr
Walter Hale dies
Walter Hale, first speaker of the Moot, dies at Caol mhòr. The Moot chooses Mary Coyle, a fisherman's widow, to follow him, the first woman to hold the chair.
30 am Faoilleach, SE 34 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The census clerks' private note
Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire, one of the census clerks, leaves among her papers a note that she asked to see the report on the gap and was refused. The note came to the library with her papers after her death. It is the only mention of the report outside the council.
11 an Gearran, SE 34 Àth àrsaidh
The Tuathaich doctors
The Moot pays for two Tuathaich women to be taught medicine by a Ròdaich physician at Àth àrsaidh, who takes them against the will of his guild. He is struck from its rolls. They practise in the north for forty years.
12 am Màrt, SE 34 Abhainn ìseal
The Abhainn ìseal floods
The Abhainn ìseal, longest river of the island, breaks its banks along its lower reach and carries away three bridges and a stretch of the ore line's embankment. The line is shut most of a year, and the ports live on stored ore.
26 an Cèitean, SE 35 Inis ìseal
The Hawk houses' own custodian
The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag name a custodian of their own, Raonaid nic Iain, and seat her at Inis ìseal. The high custodian at Seann Skell will not own her. The houses carry on as if he had.
23 an t-Samhain, SE 35 Inis ìseal
Raonaid nic Iain at Inis ìseal
Raonaid nic Iain, custodian of the Hawk houses, writes out the Hawk's order of worship, which until now was spoken and never written. The Hawk houses read it aloud once a year and keep the written copy locked away.
29 an t-Samhain, SE 35 Cnoc bheag
A hawk for Siorrachd Cnoc bheag
The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag ask the council to set a hawk on the shire's arms in place of the white billet the roll gave it. The council grants it, and the maor's seal is recut with a white hawk among its twelve crescents. It is the first change made to the roll at the asking of an order.
27 an Giblean, SE 36 Còmhrag Ceann leathan
Six dead at the Còmhrag
Six fighters die at the Còmhrag, the most in any year yet. The custodians of the Rite petition for its ending. The fair-wardens of Ceann leathan, whose town lives off the crowds, refuse.
6 an Dàmhair, SE 36 Ceann leathan
The circus at Ceann leathan
In the year of the six dead An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitches at Ceann leathan and plays to the crowds who stay on after the melee. It is said the fair-wardens paid it to come.
4 an t-Samhain, SE 36 Ceann leathan
The ore line reaches Ceann leathan
The railway is carried through to the port of Ceann leathan, so that ore may be shipped from a second harbour. The quays of Ceann leathan are rebuilt for ore-ships, and the town outgrows its walls.
3 an Dùbhlachd, SE 36 Ros bheag
Ros bheag's shipyard
Ros bheag on the west coast opens a yard for ore-ships, and the western ports need no longer send to Ros dhomhain for hulls. The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain protest to the guild court and lose.
1 am Faoilleach, SE 37 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silver at depth
The silver seam at Muileann chiar, which the Ròdaich kept hidden from the humans, is found richer at depth than any had looked for. The town's old silver guild takes a charter under the restored custom. Iain Mapa, working there since the Board sent him, measures the new faces.
19 an t-Sultain, SE 37 Baile dhìreach
The eastern blank-houses
More silver comes up from Muileann chiar than the mint at Cathair dhearg can refine. The Crown gives the villages of the eastern hills the refining of the guild's bar, with the gold washed from the stream below Baile dhìreach, into blanks for the realm-coin. The mint strikes them. The villages are paid by weight.
3 an Dàmhair, SE 37 Dùn thais
Dùn thais in the west
Dùn thais on the west coast is granted a court of the sea of its own, to judge salvage and wreck along its shore. At its first sitting it awards a raider's hulk to the fishermen who drove it aground.
2 an Gearran, SE 38 Dùn thais
Dùn thais in the east
The other Dùn thais, in the east, seat of its own shire, builds a covered market for the hill farms. For ten years the royal record confuses the courts of the two towns, until Tormod Pinn marks them west and east.
18 an Dàmhair, SE 38 Doire chaol
Siorrachd Doire chaol
Doire chaol, the village laid out south of the capital for the families of the royal household, has grown too great for the maor of Baile chiar to govern from his seat. The council cuts it out as a shire of its own, the only shire made since the drawing.
23 an t-Ògmhios, SE 39 Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The dead and not dead of Doire uaine
Herders near Doire uaine will not graze the hills above the town, where old writings tell of a thing that is dead and does not rest. A shepherd is lost there. The magistrate enters wolves.
1 an t-Iuchar, SE 39 Muileann dhearg
The fall at Muileann dhearg
A gallery of the reopened Cill ghlas district gives way under Muileann dhearg, along a line the surveyors had marked as sound. Thirty-one hewers die. It is small beside the Rending. It is the same fault.
19 an Dùbhlachd, SE 39
The rules of the shafts
After this lesser echo of the old fall of Scàineadh Cill ghlas, new rules for digging are made. They are for Ròdaich workers. In the workings where Tuathaich labour they are kept loosely, and by intent.
27 an Dùbhlachd, SE 39 Àth leathan
The timber at Àth leathan
At the pits about Àth leathan, where Ròdaich overseers work Tuathaich hands, the new rules of timbering are posted and not paid for. The overseers' books, which came later to the library, show the timber ordered and never delivered.
3 an t-Sultain, SE 40 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Mòrag nic Coinnich, keeper
Ailean Leabhar dies at Muileann chaol, and Mòrag nic Coinnich becomes keeper of the library. She begins the custom, kept ever since, of writing beside each item whence it came.
2 an Dàmhair, SE 40 Achadh dhomhain
The pit families of Achadh dhomhain
After the fall at Muileann dhearg forty hewers' families leave Achadh dhomhain for the fishing ports of the south. The Guild of Hewers binds sixty apprentices to fill its rolls. None of them are Tuathaich.
31 an Dàmhair, SE 40 Fèill Muileann òg
Fire at the fair
On the eve of Samhain fire runs through the stalls of the fair at Muileann òg. The next day the fair's court sits in a field, and the fair goes on. Oighrig nic Mhathain, toll-mistress since the first fair, dies of her burns.
29 an t-Samhain, SE 40 Muileann leathan
The Tuathaich wool carts
The Rail Board will not carry goods sent by the Moot, pleading the fair's rule on factors. The wool of the north goes south to Muileann òg by cart, a week on the road, and is sold by factors when it comes.
26 am Faoilleach, SE 41 Àth fhada
The Tuathaich carters' road
The carters of the northern wool go to the fair by Cnoc ghorm, Àth fhada and the old road down to Inis àrsaidh, and the Tuathaich villages on the way open inns for them. In the north the road is called the Carters' Road. In the south it has no name.
2 an t-Iuchar, SE 41
Dubhan's childhood
Dubhan grows up watching a caste that does not age hold every true advantage on an island where his own forebears were pushed to the edge. The obsidian was never his to inherit.
28 an Dùbhlachd, SE 41 Caol mhòr
The Moot's pit register
The Moot at Caol mhòr begins a register of Tuathaich hewers killed or maimed in the western pits, for no Ròdaich book counts them. Mary Coyle's clerks enter the first year's names on the families' own word. The register is kept to this day and has never been sent south.
5 an Cèitean, SE 42 Ros mhòr
Ros mhòr's boatyard
Tuathaich boatbuilders turned out of the guild yards open a boatyard at Ros mhòr in the north. Its boats are built to the humans' old lines and are swifter than anything in the south.
31 an t-Iuchar, SE 42 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Tormod Pinn
Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill lays down the office of royal chronicler. Tormod mac Sheumais follows her, called Tormod Pinn for the speed of his hand. He keeps the record for more than twenty years and writes more of it than any before or since.
25 an Giblean, SE 43 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's last entry
Her last entry as chronicler is a list of what the record lacks: the northern towns' own accounts, the humans' treaties in their own tongue, and the Board's surveys. Tormod Pinn copies the list into the front of his first book and adds nothing to it.
3 an Cèitean, SE 43 Tiormachd Achadh shean
Dry years at Achadh shean
Dry years come again to the country about Achadh shean, where the Long Drought settled in the humans' time. This time the council sends grain up the ore line and pays for it out of the Sloc Mòr's share. No one in the shire dies of hunger, and the chronicler records it.
6 an t-Samhain, SE 43 Achadh shean
The wells of Siorrachd Achadh shean
The maor of Siorrachd Achadh shean has twelve wells dug to the rock along the drove road, each marked with the name of the shire and of the council. Water is drawn from four of them still.
9 am Faoilleach, SE 44 Achadh shean
Grain by the ore line
The grain for Achadh shean comes from the store at Cathair fhada, and for the first time it goes by the ore line. The Rail Board charges the council for the carriage.
7 an Gearran, SE 44 Spùinneadairean-mara
Raiders at Baile ìseal
Raiders land near Baile ìseal on the far east coast and burn the salt-sheds of Àth bheag. The kingdom's patrol boats come two days later and find the sheds cold.
12 an t-Samhain, SE 44 Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
Murchadh mac Coinnich's log
Murchadh mac Coinnich, keeper of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, begins to enter in the lighthouse log every unlit ship he sees, with her heading and the hour. His logs, kept most of his life, are the fullest record of the eastern raiders in the library.
9 am Faoilleach, SE 45 Àth bheag
The pirates' names
The raiders fly no flag, and Murchadh mac Coinnich's log names their ships as the fishermen of Àth bheag name them. From his log the names pass into the royal record.
11 an Dùbhlachd, SE 45 Còmhrag Ceann leathan
The Còmhrag at its height
The Còmhrag draws its greatest crowd yet to Ceann leathan, and the fair-wardens build timber stands along three sides of the field. The champion is Ealasaid nic Coinnich of Àth ghlas, the first woman to win it. She does not fight again.
14 an Dàmhair, SE 46 Cnoc bheag
The Hawk river port of Cnoc bheag
Cnoc bheag, greatest town of the Hawk country, passes Cathair mhòr in its numbers. Its river quays take the grain of the north-central country, and its Hawk house is the richest of any order outside the capital.
12 an t-Samhain, SE 46
Scoiltean nan Draoidhean revived
The druid schools of Flidais, silent since the humans ruled, open again. Their first question, why the vein answers some and not others, presses hard once more, for the vein itself is failing.
11 an Dùbhlachd, SE 46 Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's lectures
The first teacher of the revived school is Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain. She lectures in the sacred wood of Flidais near Muileann chiar in the east, where the druids last met under the humans, and opens with the school's oldest question, plainly put: why the vein answers some hands and not others.
9 an t-Ògmhios, SE 47 Baile gharbh
The druid schools in Siorrachd Baile gharbh
The houses of the druid schools in Siorrachd Baile gharbh in the north-east, silent since the humans' time, open again at Baile gharbh and Àth fhada. Their teachers walk to the sacred wood to hear Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain, and walk back.
5 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47 Caol shean
The school at Caol shean
The druid school takes a house at Caol shean, one of the great druid towns of the east, and teaches there in the wet months, when the wood is too sodden for lectures. Its students copy the census note on the obsidian-touched and dispute it openly.
13 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47 Cnoc bheag
The Hawk given a place
A council of the Rite at Seann Skell offers the Hawk houses of Cnoc bheag a place under the high custodian with their own order of worship. The Hawk houses take the place and keep their order. After this the quarrel is quieter. It does not end.
7 an Gearran, SE 48 Caol chrom
The north-eastern harbours
Caol chrom and Caol gharbh on the north-east coast join their harbour dues to pay for a breakwater across the strait between them. It is eight years in the building and is the longest on the island yet.
23 an Giblean, SE 48 Muileann leathan
Daniel Frayne's copying school
At Muileann leathan in the north Daniel Frayne, a clerk of the Moot, teaches young Tuathaich to copy and bind books, since the guilds of that craft in the south will not take them. The bindings of Muileann leathan are found afterwards in Ròdaich libraries without their makers' names.
22 an Cèitean, SE 48 Cidhe Beag
The Abhainn uaine ferries
The boat-landing at Cidhe Beag on the Abhainn uaine is licensed as a ferry, to carry passengers and small freight down the river toward the coast. The first to hold the licence is an old boatman who had worked the landing without one for forty years.
24 am Faoilleach, SE 49 Loch chrom
Loch chrom
The fishermen of Loch chrom, the only great lake of the island, are licensed to net its trout, which was kept for the Crown's table. Each year the Crown's table is served first.
22 an Gearran, SE 49 Colbh Cnoc chiar
The pillar at Cnoc chiar
Students of the druid schools try to read the pillar near Cnoc chiar by setting it beside the obelisk at Cnoc bheag and the column at Cnoc ghorm. They find signs in common and no meaning. Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes that the Old Ones were here and said so, and that none living can hear it.
23 am Màrt, SE 50 Inis chrom
Flood at Inis chrom
A storm tide floods the lower town of Inis chrom on the south-west coast and drowns the net-lofts and the rope-walk. The town builds both again on piles, and so they stand now.
21 an Giblean, SE 50 Cnoc leathan
Cnoc leathan's schools
Cnoc leathan in the east opens a school in every one of its six parishes, paid from the shire's dues, the first shire to do so. The council asks how it paid for them and is shown the accounts.
20 an Cèitean, SE 50 Cathair mhòr
Alasdair mac Ùisdein's loan
Alasdair mac Ùisdein, grandson of the first holder of the Sloc Mòr concession, borrows against his house's share to pay for a search for a second vein. The Mine Board lends its surveyors. The Crown lends its name.
13 an Giblean, SE 51 Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
The druid school on the search
Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes to the Mine Board that the search asks the wrong question. The school has always asked why the vein answers some hands, she says, and no one has asked why there is one vein. The Board files the letter.
21 an Giblean, SE 51
The search for a second vein
The search for a second seam of obsidian elsewhere on the island is costly, and finds nothing. The Holy Age made the same search and failed in the same way centuries before; it had been forgotten.
17 an Dàmhair, SE 51 Dùn dhearg
Forty-one dry shafts
The borings of the search run from the hills above Dùn dhearg to the moors south of Baile ruadh. Forty-one shafts are sunk, and none strikes the vein. Afterwards Mòrag nic Coinnich finds in a list of the Holy Age at the library the same hills named as searched and barren.
6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 52 Dùn dhearg
Dùn dhearg's claim
The town of Dùn dhearg, whose hills held a dozen of the dry shafts, claims damages from the house of Mac Ùisdein for spoiled grazing. The circuit court awards them. The house pays a third before it sells.
5 an t-Iuchar, SE 52 Cathair mhòr
The house of Mac Ùisdein sells half
To meet its debts the house of Mac Ùisdein sells half its share in the Sloc Mòr back to the Crown. Its stone house at Cathair mhòr is let to the Mine Board, which moves its offices there.
3 an Lùnastal, SE 52 Baile ruadh
The shafts at Baile ruadh left open
The dry shafts of the search are left open on the moors near Baile ruadh. Sheep fall into them, and one child, before the shire fences them at its own cost. The shire's claim on the house of Mac Ùisdein for the fencing is never paid.
9 an Giblean, SE 53 Muileann dhomhain
The Muileann dhomhain mills
The mills of Muileann dhomhain in the south-east ground grain for the vein-towns. When the vein-towns' orders fall they turn to grinding bark for the tanners. The miller-families of the town keep their mark and change their trade.
5 an t-Iuchar, SE 53 Seann Tarr
The rope-makers of Seann Tarr
The rope-makers of Seann Tarr on the north-east coast are chartered as a guild, the last guild the restored custom makes for a trade the humans had not touched. Their hemp comes from the fields about Doire uaine and Achadh naomh.
1 an t-Sultain, SE 53 Seann Tarr
Seann Tarr's chest remembered
By the shire's own rule the rope-makers' charter at Seann Tarr is kept in the shire's chest and not sent to Cathair dhearg. The shire keeper of Seann Tarr keeps a list of what the chest holds and sends the list alone.
30 an t-Sultain, SE 53 An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn
The Circus at Inis àrsaidh
An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn is recorded again, pitched this time on the common near Inis àrsaidh in the west. The magistrate who licenses it enters the acts as 'various' and the fee as paid.
11 am Màrt, SE 54 Ceann mhin
Ceann mhin's fish-market
Ceann mhin, the great port south-east of the capital, opens a covered fish-market over the old strand. Fish from Seann Bhral and the eastern grounds is sold there for the capital.
8 an Cèitean, SE 54 Còmhrag Ceann leathan
Edged tools banned from the Còmhrag
A fighter is killed with a hewer's pick, and the fair-wardens of Ceann leathan ban edged tools from the Còmhrag. Staves and fists are still allowed, and so the deaths go on, fewer.
6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 54 Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
The drowned lighthouse keeper
The keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg on the south coast drowns going out to a boat aground on the reef below the light. The boat's crew are saved by his daughter, Ciorstaidh nic Artair, and she is given the keeper's warrant in his place.
11 am Màrt, SE 55 Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
Ciorstaidh nic Artair's reef mark
Ciorstaidh nic Artair has an iron post set on the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, painted and hung with a bell. While she keeps the light no boat goes aground there.
13 an t-Ògmhios, SE 55 Caol mhòr
Mary Coyle lays down the chair
Mary Coyle lays down the chair of the Moot at Caol mhòr. Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan follows her, the first speaker born after the Severance.
9 an Dùbhlachd, SE 55 Fèill Muileann òg
The Fèill's northern day
The court of the fair at Muileann òg sets aside one day of the fair for goods from the northern shires. They are still sold through Ròdaich factors, but under the northern makers' own marks. It is the first time a Tuathaich name is written on anything sold there.
12 am Faoilleach, SE 56 Baile chiar
The Tuathaich marks at the fair
The first northern mark sold under its own name at the fair is the cloth of the weavers of Doire ghlas, a grey twill with a white thread at the selvedge. The southern weavers of Baile chiar begin to weave a white thread into their own.
11 am Màrt, SE 56
The Depletion laid bare
The quiet note of the survey in SE 26 is now an open trouble. The last unworked stretches of the vein are found, and they are smaller than any wish to own.
14 an Dùbhlachd, SE 56 Achadh dhomhain
Catrìona nic Neacail's map
Catrìona nic Neacail, surveyor-general of the Mine Board, publishes the map of the vein's last unworked stretches. It fits on one sheet. Within the year she gives up her post and goes to teach at the druid school at Caol shean.
9 an Giblean, SE 57 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Iain Mapa's survey found
Among the Board's files Catrìona nic Neacail finds Iain Mapa's survey of thirty years before, which shows the same thinning she has just measured. She sends a copy to the library, with a note of when the Board received it.
8 an Cèitean, SE 57 Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
Iain Mapa dies
Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, dies at Muileann chiar, where the Board sent him. His own copy of his survey is found among his papers with the Board's receipt pinned to it.
6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 57 Muileann dhearg
Muileann dhearg empties
In a few years Muileann dhearg loses a third of its households to the ports. Its druid hall is shut, and its bell sold to the school at Caol shean, where it rings for lectures still.
5 an t-Iuchar, SE 57 Ceann leathan
Ceann leathan's ore quays idle
Ore-ships wait at Ceann leathan for cargoes that come in half-loads. The harbour dues fall by half, and the fair-wardens raise the gate-price of the Còmhrag to make it up.
30 an t-Sultain, SE 58 Baile Mòr dhomhain
Baile Mòr dhomhain's market
As the trade of the ore-towns falls away, Baile Mòr dhomhain in the northern hills becomes the market for the wool and hides of the hill country. For two years together its market day draws more carts than the fair at Muileann òg.
29 an Dàmhair, SE 58 Cathair dhearg
Mairead crowned
Eòghan's reign ends in the decade that the Depletion becomes known to all. Mairead inherits a kingdom whose founding wealth is plainly failing, for the first time since the restoration.
23 an t-Samhain, SE 58 Achadh dhomhain
The Hewers bind no apprentices
For the first time since its charter the Guild of Hewers binds no new apprentices. Its masters vote to keep the rolls open to the sons and daughters of members only.
19 an Giblean, SE 59 Muileann shean
Muileann shean's school of hewers
Muileann shean in the north opens a school for the sons and daughters of hewers who will not be bound, and teaches them to read, reckon and survey. Most of its first pupils go to the ports.
27 an Giblean, SE 59 Doire ghlas
The Doire ghlas mills
Wool mills are built at Doire ghlas with the Moot's money, the first works in the north that owe nothing to the vein. The Rail Board refuses their cloth, until a ruling of the circuit court at Seann Bhral compels it to carry any goods that pay the rate.
31 an Dàmhair, SE 59 Seann Bhral
The Seann Bhral ruling
Ruairidh mac Phàdraig, circuit justice at Seann Bhral, rules that the Rail Board is a carrier of the Crown and must carry for any who pay. It is the first ruling the Moot wins in a Ròdaich court. The Board appeals, and the council lets the appeal lapse.
30 an t-Iuchar, SE 60 Achadh dhomhain
The Crown's share of the Sloc Mòr
The Crown buys the last working shafts of the house of Mac Ùisdein at the Sloc Mòr and leaves the house its share in the spoil and the quarry. Thenceforth the Board works the vein in the Crown's name alone.
28 an Lùnastal, SE 60 Àth fhiadhaich
The copper at Àth fhiadhaich
Copper is found in the hills behind Àth fhiadhaich in the eastern hills. The Board opens a working with men laid off from the Sloc Mòr. It pays wages. It is not the vein, and the town's Seann Spioradan house gives it no blessing.
2 an t-Ògmhios, SE 61 Àth fhiadhaich
Àth fhiadhaich's copper-town
The copper workings at Àth fhiadhaich draw miners from the failing vein-towns. The town builds a new street for them and names it for the Sloc Mòr, and the Seann Spioradan house there speaks against the name.
1 an t-Iuchar, SE 61
Dubhan begins his experiments
Dubhan makes his first attempts to draw a fuel to stand in the ore's place from the waste of the mines. They fail, and little is set down of them.
13 an t-Iuchar, SE 61 Achadh dhomhain
The Sloc Mòr's pumps
The lowest galleries of the Sloc Mòr are let flood, for the pumps cost more to run than the ore beneath is worth. The Board's minute calls it a pause.
17 an Giblean, SE 62 Seann Bhral
The pumps sold
The Board sells the great pumps of the Sloc Mòr to the harbour at Seann Bhral in the south, where they drain the new dry dock. In the next generation they are the only engines of the vein still at work.
16 an Cèitean, SE 62 Imrich nam Pantar
The panthers cross the south-west
A great host of panthers crosses the south-west near Baile dhomhain. For a month the herders lose stock. Tormod Pinn writes it down as a thing named in the lists of the Holy Age and not seen in living memory.
13 an t-Iuchar, SE 62 Baile ghorm
The hides of Baile ghorm
Tanners at Baile ghorm on the south-west coast buy the hides of the panthers the herders kill, and their trade outlasts the crossing by ten years. Saddles of panther-skin from Baile ghorm are sold at the fair at Muileann òg under the town's mark.
11 an Lùnastal, SE 62 Imrich nam Pantar
Imrich nam Pantar in the chronicle
Tormod Pinn's entry on the panthers is the longest in his book for that year. He sets it beside the list of the Holy Age, and notes that the old list names the year after the panthers as a hungry one.
10 an Gearran, SE 63 Muileann mhin
The ore-lamp shortage
The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin halve their making, for want of ore to burn in the lamps they make. Shaft-lamps are lent from pit to pit, and the guild's minute-book records who lent to whom.
18 an Gearran, SE 63 Muileann chrom
Unrest at Muileann chrom
The yard families at Muileann chrom stop the ore trains for three days over cut wages. On the fourth day the Rail Board settles; on the fifth it dismisses eleven men.
7 an Lùnastal, SE 63 Cathair fhada
The hungry year that was not
The harvest after the panthers' crossing is good across the south. Tormod Pinn records it and strikes through his own note of the year before.
8 an Dàmhair, SE 64
The third census after the Severance
For the first time in the Rìoghachd the numbers of the people are published openly. It is a small token of openness, and nothing else is changed.
6 an t-Samhain, SE 64 Caol mhòr
The figures read at the Moot
The published figures are read aloud at the Moot at Caol mhòr. They show the northern towns at about half the Ròdaich measure in every column the clerks chose to take. The Moot's minute says only: 'Now written.'
8 am Faoilleach, SE 65 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The count of the touched
The published census, like the first, has a line for the obsidian-touched. It gives a number and nothing more. Tormod Pinn copies it into the chronicle without comment, as Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill did for the first.
28 an Lùnastal, SE 65 Doire shean
The census in the Stone's shires
In the shires of Òrd na Cloiche in the south-west the houses of the Stone publish for the first time their own count of their people beside the kingdom's. The two agree within a hundred.
26 an t-Sultain, SE 65 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh
Tormod Pinn dies at his desk at Muileann chaol. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh becomes royal chronicler. She is the first to add at the foot of each year a note of what the record could not learn.
10 an Dùbhlachd, SE 65 Ros gheal
The Hawk houses' registers
The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Ros gheal send their birth-rolls to the library for the first time, on condition that they be filed under Òrd an t-Seabhaig and not under Òrd Bhrìde. Mòrag nic Coinnich agrees.
6 an Gearran, SE 66 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first foot-note
Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first note of what the record could not learn concerns the northern shires: the census clerks were told the figures and did not count them, and the figures they were told were the Moot's.
7 am Màrt, SE 66 Seann Tarr
The record-chests called in
Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks go to thirty shire towns to bring their record-chests to Muileann chaol. At Seann Tarr the shire's keeper burns the chest sooner than send it, saying that the shire's record belongs in the shire. He is fined; the chest is lost.
5 an Giblean, SE 66 Cathair naomh
Cathair naomh sends its rolls
The keeper of Cathair naomh in the north sends her shire's rolls to the library in two carts, with the town's own chronicle, kept by one family for four generations. Mòrag nic Coinnich enters it as the best-kept shire record received.
29 am Faoilleach, SE 67 Seann Toll
The Seann Toll chest
Seann Toll in the north sends its chest willingly and asks for a copy of all that is in it. Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks make the copy, and the shire's copy is the pattern for every copy the library has made since.
26 an t-Iuchar, SE 67 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The library enlarged
Leabharlann Muileann chaol doubles its holdings and takes several lesser archives of the provinces into one record. From this time the history of Rodos is kept in one place and not in many.
3 an Lùnastal, SE 67 Caol mhòr
No northern chest
No Tuathaich record is called in. The Moot's minute-books, the schools' registers, the churches' registers and the vigil-books of Baile chrom stay in the north, in private keeping, as they always have.
2 an t-Ògmhios, SE 68 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The library's new wing
The enlarged library is housed in a new wing at Muileann chaol, built of the grey stone of the Sloc Mòr's spoil. The chests of the provinces fill three floors. The fourth is left empty for what was not sent.
30 an t-Iuchar, SE 68 Àth leathan
The branch line to Àth leathan closed
The Rail Board shuts the branch line to Àth leathan, pleading the falling yield of the western pits. The Tuathaich pits go on working, and their coal goes by cart to the western ports and by boat from there.
28 an Lùnastal, SE 68 Àth leathan
The Moot's hewers take the pits
The Board's overseers are withdrawn from Àth leathan, and the Tuathaich hewers there go on working the pits under their own pit captains, paying the Crown's fifth under the Leòid ruling. The Board takes the payments and enters them as arrears.
7 am Màrt, SE 69 Cnoc thais
Cnoc thais in the western hills
At Cnoc thais in the western hills the Tuathaich pits pass to their hewers when the Board's overseers leave, and the father of the pit captain Tom Varley is chosen to keep the accounts. Here the town's own register of the pits begins.
5 an Giblean, SE 69 An Sligeanach Fad' às
The Sligeanach's great year
An Sligeanach Fad' às, the roadside tavern by Ceann bhàn on the southern road, is sold to a family of drovers from Achadh mhòr, who build a second hall for the drove trade. It becomes the greatest house on the old mining roads.
4 an Cèitean, SE 69 Seann Dunn
The eastern fishing grounds fail
For the second year together the herring do not come to the grounds off the mouth of the Abhainn chaol below Seann Dunn. The east-coast boats go north to fish the grounds off Caol mhòr, which the licence law keeps for them, and the Tuathaich boats are pushed farther out.
30 an t-Iuchar, SE 70 Inis mhin
Inis mhin's boats
Pushed from their grounds by the eastern boats, the Tuathaich boats of Inis mhin fish the deep water beyond the northern isles. Two are lost in the first year and none after, and the catch of Inis mhin passes that of Caol mhòr.
28 an Lùnastal, SE 70 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper
Mòrag nic Coinnich lays down the keepership after some thirty years. Raghnall mac Mhuirich, her deputy, becomes keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol.
26 an t-Sultain, SE 70 Fèill Muileann òg
The ore price at the fair
The Board cuts its sales, and the price of ore-fuel at the fair at Muileann òg doubles. The fair's court fixes a ceiling price and cannot hold it.
26 an Cèitean, SE 71 Cnoc fhiadhaich
Ore thieves at Cnoc fhiadhaich
Households of Cnoc fhiadhaich are found picking ore from the spoil-heaps to burn, and the Board posts watchmen there. The watchmen are men of the town, and see nothing.

Age VI · An Aois Dhubhain the Age of Dubhan · the Dubhan Era, DE 1 – 27

19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1
The first working dubhan
Dubhan makes a fuel without the vein, rough but good to burn. It is no trade yet. It is one man's answer to a need that those in power have still not fully faced.
21 an t-Samhain, DE 1 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's note on the fuel
At the foot of the year the royal chronicler writes that a fuel made without the vein is reported from the north, and that she has not seen it. Hers is the first mention of dubhan in the royal record, and she spells the word three ways in two lines.
28 an t-Sultain, DE 2 Caol mhòr
The Board's inquiry
The Mine Board sends two surveyors north to learn whether the new fuel burns as men say. Their report, which came to the library, says that it burns, that it stinks, and that it is not ore.
27 an Dàmhair, DE 2 Cathair dhearg
The lamp-houses of the capital
The street-lamps of Cathair dhearg, which have burned ore since the humans set them up, are left dark in the poorer streets to save fuel. When dubhan comes, the dark streets are the first lit again.
22 am Faoilleach, DE 3 Fèill Muileann òg
The last ore sale at the fair
The court of the fair at Muileann òg records its last sale of ore-fuel by the cartload. After this ore is sold at the fair only by the sack, and at last only by the lump, for altars.
1 an Lùnastal, DE 3 Cathair dhearg
Cathal crowned
Mairead's reign ends while Dubhan's first trials still fail more than they succeed. Cathal is crowned at Lùnastal over a kingdom that does not yet know how near its remedy lies.
30 an Lùnastal, DE 3 Cathair dhearg
The mint's new dies
The mint at Cathair dhearg cuts new dies for the coinage of the reign. They are the first not cut by a pupil of Fearchar Bonn's workshop, and the obsidian ink is still pressed into the seal.
20 an Gearran, DE 4 Seann Skell
The shipmasters' works at Seann Skell
A company of shipmasters sets up a works for the making of dubhan at Seann Skell on the southern coast, the first on the island outside the north. On what terms they had the making of it is not told.
25 an t-Samhain, DE 4 Seann Skell
The high custodian's letter
The Àrd-choimheadaiche at Seann Skell writes to every house of the Rite that the new fuel is not forbidden, since it is not ore, and not blessed, since it is not ore. The letter is read in the houses and argued in the druid schools for years.
24 an Dùbhlachd, DE 4 Seann Skell
The Seann Skell works' first year
The dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast sell their first year's making to the fishing boats of the south coast and the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg. The works' chimney is the tallest thing on the coast.
4 am Màrt, DE 5 Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
Peigi nic Ascaill's trial lamp
Peigi nic Ascaill, engineer to the Lighthouse Board, fits a dubhan burner to a spare lamp in the yard below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and runs it for a hundred nights. Murchadh mac Coinnich, retired from the light, keeps the log of the trial for her.
7 an t-Sultain, DE 5 Caol fhiadhaich
The fishing boats of Caol fhiadhaich
The boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast fit dubhan engines to the first fishing boats. The Shipwrights' Guild calls the work unlawful for its members. The boatwrights leave the guild and keep the work.
23 an Giblean, DE 6 Ros dhomhain
The shipwrights' guild court
The court of the Shipwrights' Guild at Ros dhomhain rules that the fitting of an engine is no shipwright's work and so outside its charter. The boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich are readmitted to the guild. They decline.
22 an Cèitean, DE 6 Taigh-solais Baile chrom
The lights turned to dubhan
The five beacons of the coast, which have burned obsidian-lit flame for more than a century, are the first works of the kingdom turned by order to dubhan.
19 an t-Iuchar, DE 6 Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
The last obsidian flame
The obsidian flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg is borne in a closed lantern to the Rite's house at Seann Skell and let burn out on the altar. Custodians from four shires attend, and Ciorstaidh nic Artair, keeper of the light, carries the lantern.
26 am Faoilleach, DE 7 Taigh-solais Muileann bheag
Taigh-solais Muileann bheag converted
The beacon at Muileann bheag on the Tuathaich north coast is turned to dubhan with the others. Its fuel is carted from the north; of the five lights it alone is not fed by sea from Seann Skell.
25 am Màrt, DE 7 Taigh-solais Àth dhearg
Taigh-solais Àth dhearg converted
At Taigh-solais Àth dhearg on the north-east cape the work takes a month longer than at the others, for the stair is too narrow for the new tank. The tank is lifted to the lamp-room from outside by a crane borrowed from the rope-walk at Seann Tarr.
20 an t-Ògmhios, DE 7 Taigh-solais Baile chrom
Taigh-solais Baile chrom converted
At Taigh-solais Baile chrom on the Tuathaich coast the work is done by Tuathaich fitters from Caol mhòr, for the Lighthouse Board has none of its own to send so far. The keeper's report names none of them.
28 an Dùbhlachd, DE 7 Muileann mhin
The lamp-makers turn
The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin begin to make dubhan lamps and ask leave to set their guild mark on them. After a year's argument the guild court allows it. The flame over the hammer is kept.
9 am Faoilleach, DE 8 Muileann leathan
Daniel Frayne dies
Daniel Frayne, speaker of the Moot, dies at Muileann leathan. The Moot chooses Martha Greaves of Doire ghlas, a mill manager, to follow him.
24 an Gearran, DE 8 Muileann leathan
The binders of Muileann leathan
The Moot sends Daniel Frayne's pupils, the binders of Muileann leathan, to rebind its minute-books from the first meeting. The rebound set is kept at Caol mhòr. A second set is made and hidden, says the Moot's minute, elsewhere.
1 an Cèitean, DE 8 Muileann chrom
The ore line's first dubhan engine
The Rail Board runs its first dubhan engine on the ore line, from the yards at Muileann chrom to Cathair dhearg. It carries no ore. It carries dubhan to the lamp-houses of the capital, and comes back empty.
11 an Dùbhlachd, DE 8 Àth bheag
The eastern salt-road
For the first time salt from Àth bheag goes to the inland towns by dubhan lorry, on the drove road past Baile ìseal. Within a few years the drovers of the east coast sell their oxen.
22 am Màrt, DE 9 Achadh mhòr
Achadh mhòr's drovers
The drovers of Achadh mhòr in the south, with no oxen left to drive, buy lorries. The drove-inn at An Sligeanach Fad' às keeps its trade by selling them dubhan.
30 am Màrt, DE 9 An Taigh-seinnse Òir
The inns take the new lamps
The inns along the old mining roads hang dubhan lamps. In a single decade the oil and the wick, which lit them for centuries, are gone.
15 an Giblean, DE 9 An Leòmhann Buidhe
An Leòmhann Buidhe keeps a wick
At An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north-east road the landlord keeps one wick lamp burning over the door beside the new dubhan lamps. The custom spreads along the roads, and a wick lamp over an inn door is still called a Leòmhann.
25 an t-Ògmhios, DE 9 Seann Skell
The first horseless carriage
Fitters at Seann Skell on the southern coast set a lorry's dubhan engine under a closed carriage for the high custodian of the Rite. It is the first carriage on the island that needs no horse. Within a few years the council and the Mine Board have them too.
25 an t-Sultain, DE 9 Am Buabhall Fortanach
Am Buabhall Fortanach
Am Buabhall Fortanach, the tavern on the south-west road near Doire shean, is the last of the great inns to hang dubhan lamps. Its landlady's account-book gives the cost as a year's takings.
19 an Dàmhair, DE 9 An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The Taigh-seinnse Mòr's hall
An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on the old ore road above Cuan chrom, opens a second hall lit wholly by dubhan. It is let for weddings, wakes and the meetings of the Guild of Hewers, whose own hall at Achadh dhomhain has been sold.
4 am Màrt, DE 10 An Taigh-òsta Grianach
An Taigh-òsta Grianach
An Taigh-òsta Grianach, on the south-east road near Cnoc dhìreach, is rebuilt with dubhan lamps in every room and a dubhan pump at the door. It is the first inn on the island to sell fuel as well as beds.
2 an Giblean, DE 10 Muileann chrom
The ore engines laid up
The Rail Board's ore-fired engines are laid up in a siding at Muileann chrom and never run again. The yard families who drove them are taught the dubhan engines, such of them as will learn.
11 an t-Sultain, DE 10 An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the north road above Muileann fhada is the last of the great inns to keep a wick lamp in every room. Its landlord writes to the Board that the reek of dubhan drives away his guests. It does not, and the next year he puts in the lamps.
10 an Dàmhair, DE 10 Muileann dhearg
Muileann dhearg closed
The last working face under Muileann dhearg is shut. The Board moves the town's remaining families to Seann Toll on the Abhainn uaine, and Muileann dhearg is left with its druid house, its graves and a caretaker.
27 an t-Iuchar, DE 11 Seann Toll
The Muileann dhearg families at Seann Toll
The families from Muileann dhearg are settled in a new row at the edge of Seann Toll, which the town calls the Hewers' Row. Few of them find work on the boats. Most work at the dubhan tanks by the river landing.
25 an Lùnastal, DE 11 Muileann dhearg
Muileann dhearg's druid house
The druid house at Muileann dhearg is given to the town's caretaker to keep, with the graves. Once a year the druid school at Caol shean sends a teacher to give the town's one remaining lecture, and few come.
23 an t-Sultain, DE 11
The word spreads before the fuel does
Men begin to say "dubhan" for the fuel itself, as well as for the man who made it, years before the trade built upon it is whole.
22 an Dàmhair, DE 11 Caol shean
Dubhan-tùsail
The word 'dubhan-tùsail' is first found in a letter of the druid school at Caol shean. It is used of a first attempt that seemed a dead end and proved otherwise, and the letter uses it of the school's own revival.
1 an Cèitean, DE 12 Muileann chrom
The Rail Board's new name
In its own timetables the Rail Board drops 'ore' from the name of its main line and calls it only the line. Everyone else still calls it the ore line.
30 an Cèitean, DE 12 Achadh dhomhain
The Guild of Hewers dissolved
The Guild of Hewers, chartered at Achadh dhomhain in the first years of the restored custom, dissolves itself. Its rolls, its oath-stone of ore and its sick-roll go to the library. Its last master, Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, writes that the guild had outlived the mountain's patience.
28 an t-Ògmhios, DE 12 Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The bath-house given to the Rite
The bath-house at the hot springs near Muileann ruadh, built by the Hewers for their sick, passes with the guild's other goods to the custodians of the Rite. It is opened to any who pay, and for the first time to the Tuathaich.
1 am Màrt, DE 13 Achadh dhomhain
The Achadh dhomhain hall
The Hewers' hall at Achadh dhomhain, sold before the guild was dissolved, becomes a dubhan depot. Its carved lintel, with the guild's oath cut in it, is left in its place above the pumps.
9 am Màrt, DE 13
The trade turns to dubhan
Markets, the supply of the host and the shipping turn wholly to the new fuel. The obsidian caste sees the source of its own power fail, and makes no objection.
5 an t-Iuchar, DE 13 Cathair dhearg
Buses and hired cars
Dubhan buses begin to run between Cathair dhearg, Inis mhòr and Cathair mhòr, and hired cars wait at the bridge in the capital. Ròdais takes the names of both from the humans' tongue as it found them, bus and tacsaidh; for the engine and the train it had made words of its own.
4 an t-Sultain, DE 13 Ros dhomhain
The house of Mac Ùisdein moves
The house of Mac Ùisdein sells what is left of its share in the spoil and quarry of the Sloc Mòr and puts its money into dubhan shipping at Ros dhomhain. Of the families that held the vein it alone moves before the vein fails it.
15 an t-Sultain, DE 13 Ros dhomhain
The fleet's first dubhan hulls
The kingdom's patrol boats at Ros dhomhain are refitted for dubhan, and for the first time they can outrun the raiders. The next two raider hulks taken are brought into Ros dhomhain under tow.
2 an t-Iuchar, DE 14 Ros dhomhain
Raiders taken to Ros dhomhain
The crews of the raider hulks brought into Ros dhomhain are tried at the court of the sea there. Several of them are Tuathaich. The court hangs none; it sends the Ròdaich among them to the quarries at Achadh dhomhain and the Tuathaich home to the north.
29 an Lùnastal, DE 14 Seann Skell
The Fuel-Fitters chartered
The fitters of dubhan engines, who have worked outside every guild, are chartered as the Guild of Fuel-Fitters at Seann Skell on the southern coast. Its rolls, like those of every guild before it, are open to Ròdaich only. The Tuathaich fitters already in the trade are let go.
27 an t-Sultain, DE 14 Caol mhòr
Tuathaich fitters go north
The fitters let go under the charter rule go back to the northern towns and fit engines there without a guild. Within a few years the harbour of Caol mhòr holds more dubhan boats than any port of its size in the south.
24 an t-Samhain, DE 14 Caol mhòr
The Moot on the new fuel
The Moot at Caol mhòr, under Martha Greaves, debates whether the north shall take up the new fuel or keep to its own seams. It votes to take it up. The delegates of the western pit towns walk out.
8 am Màrt, DE 15 Ceann mhòr
The Tuathaich depots
Dubhan depots are opened at Caol mhòr, Doire ghlas and Ceann mhòr, supplied by sea. Martha Greaves writes in the Moot's minute that the north now buys its fire from the south, and does not say whether this is good.
5 an Cèitean, DE 15
The fourth currency reform
For the first time the coin of the Rìoghachd is pegged to the making of dubhan and not to the stores of obsidian. So the kingdom owns, quietly, which of the two now runs it.
5 an Cèitean, DE 15 Cathair dhearg
The Dubhan Era proclaimed
At the same sitting the council proclaims that the Age of the Kingdom ended with the first working dubhan, and that the kingdom's years are counted anew from that day. The year is entered as the fifteenth of the Dubhan Era. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh re-heads fourteen years of her chronicle, and writes at the foot of the page that never before has she had to move a year she was living in.
3 an t-Ògmhios, DE 15 Cathair dhearg
The plain seal
The mint at Cathair dhearg ceases to press obsidian ink into the seal of the coinage. The new seal is plain. Fearchar Bonn's first dies are given to the library and kept in the case beside the oath-stone of the Guild of Hewers.
31 an t-Iuchar, DE 15 Seann Skell
The Rite's protest on the seal
The high custodian at Seann Skell protests to the council that the plain seal is a sign the kingdom no longer holds the vein sacred. The council answers that the kingdom never said it did. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh copies both letters into the chronicle.
27 am Màrt, DE 16 Muileann àrsaidh
The western pit towns meet
Delegates of the western pit towns meet at Muileann àrsaidh, apart from the Moot. They agree to go on working their seams and to sell their coal to any household in the north that will buy it.
6 an Giblean, DE 16 Àth naomh
Àth naomh joins the pit towns
Àth naomh, a Tuathaich town of the western hills with only a few old shafts, joins the pit towns' agreement. Its delegates say the town would sooner be cold with its neighbours than warm alone.
25 an Giblean, DE 16
The northern towns hold out
A number of northern towns will not go over to the new fuel. They work the last good coal seams sooner than trade their freedom for need of one man's fuel.
24 an Cèitean, DE 16 Àth leathan
The holdout towns
The towns that refuse are Àth leathan, Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg in the western hills. Their spokeswoman is Ruth Calder, a pit captain's daughter of Àth leathan. The Moot at Caol mhòr neither joins them nor condemns them.
4 an t-Samhain, DE 16 Cnoc thais
Tom Varley's pits
At Cnoc thais the pit captain Tom Varley opens again two shafts that have lain abandoned since the humans' time. The coal is poor. It is theirs, and it warms the town.
30 am Faoilleach, DE 17 Tobar dhearg
Tobar dhearg of the hills
Tobar dhearg in the western hills, least of the holdout towns, has one pit and forty hewers. It sends its coal to Cathair gheal on the coast and has fish in return.
7 an Gearran, DE 17 Doire ghlas
Ellen Marsh's books
Ellen Marsh, a schoolteacher of Doire ghlas, finishes her gathering of Tuathaich accounts of the Severance and the settlement, taken down over many years from the old folk of the north. It fills eleven books. It is her request that goes to the library.
15 an Gearran, DE 17 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The library's Tuathaich wing proposed
A request is laid before Leabharlann Muileann chaol that the Tuathaich tellings be kept beside the Ròdaich record. It is laid on the table and not refused, and there it lies to this day.
12 an Lùnastal, DE 17 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The keeper's answer
Raghnall mac Mhuirich answers Ellen Marsh that the request awaits the council's view on the standing of spoken witness. The council has given none.
20 an Lùnastal, DE 17 Doire ghlas
Ellen Marsh's reply
Ellen Marsh writes back to the keeper that spoken witness was good enough for the census clerks when they took the Moot's figures. Her letter is filed with the request.
21 an Gearran, DE 18 Doire ghlas
The coal price in the north
The holdout pits sell their coal to Tuathaich households across the north for less than the price of dubhan. The Moot's own wool mills at Doire ghlas buy it. For the first time since the Severance the Board's takings from the north fall.
22 am Màrt, DE 18 Cathair mhòr
The Board's northern revenue
The Mine Board's accounts show its northern takings down by a quarter. Its report to the council names the western pits as the cause and the Leòid ruling as the remedy.
20 an Giblean, DE 18 Seann Bhral
The seams declared Crown property
Under the Leòid ruling the Mine Board declares the western seams the Crown's, holding that the right to work them lapsed when the holders ceased to pay the fifth. The holders say they ceased to pay when the Board ceased to carry the coal. The pits are ordered shut.
16 an Dàmhair, DE 18 Seann Skell
Enforcers posted to the west
A company of the Board's enforcers is posted at Seann Skell in the west to shut the pits. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh notes that it is the first armed company the kingdom has sent toward the north since the Severance.
23 am Faoilleach, DE 19 Seann Skell
The enforcers' depot
The enforcers at Seann Skell in the west build a dubhan depot for their lorries at the edge of the town. The town's house of Manannan will not bless it, and the high custodian of the Rite sends a priest to bless it instead.
31 an Lùnastal, DE 19 Caol mhòr
The Moot's warning
Martha Greaves writes to the council from Caol mhòr that the western towns will not shut their pits for a letter, and asks a year's delay while the Moot treats with them. The letter is received and filed.
29 an t-Sultain, DE 19
First skirmishes
Small fights begin between the state's enforcers and the Tuathaich who hold to their coal. None is written down, and none is great enough to name; together they lead straight into open war.
28 an Dàmhair, DE 19 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The chronicler asks
At the foot of the year Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh writes that fighting is reported in the west, that the Board's reports of it are not given to the chronicler, and that she has asked for them. They were not given.
26 an t-Samhain, DE 19 Muileann àrsaidh
The pit-heads walled
The pit-heads at Muileann àrsaidh are walled with spoil and timber, and the road into the town from the south is dug across. The Board's enforcers at Seann Skell report the town shut against them.
25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 19 Àth leathan
Ruth Calder's letter
Ruth Calder writes to the council for the western towns. She offers to pay the Crown's fifth in coal if the Board will carry it and let the pits work until the seams are spent. The letter came to the library. No answer to it did.
23 am Faoilleach, DE 20 Caol mhòr
The Moot stands apart
The Moot at Caol mhòr resolves that it is no party to the quarrel of the Board and the western towns, and that it will feed any who come hungry to its towns. The resolution is carried by nine votes.
4 an t-Iuchar, DE 20 Doire ghlas
The Moot's granaries
The Moot orders its granaries at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas filled beyond the wont, paying from the takings of the wool mills. The minute gives no reason.
2 an Lùnastal, DE 20 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Sìleas nic Rath
Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh lays down the office, and Sìleas nic Rath, her clerk, becomes royal chronicler. Hers is the record of the war that the library afterwards seals.
28 an Dàmhair, DE 20
The regiments called up
Regiments not called to arms since the Severance itself are formed and armed anew, openly, months before any in power will own that war is coming.
26 an t-Samhain, DE 20 Cathair dhearg
Somhairle mac Lachlainn
Command of the new-formed regiments is given to Somhairle mac Lachlainn, who rose among the Board's enforcers. The rolls of the Severance companies are brought out of the council's chests at Cathair dhearg to name the regiments, and the old names are read aloud before new men.
25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 20 Cathair dhearg
The Moot's last petition
On Christmas Day Martha Greaves carries a petition of the Moot in person to the council at Cathair dhearg. It asks that the western pits be let work out their seams, which the Moot says will be spent in a few years whatever is done. It is received and filed. She is the first speaker of the Moot to enter the council chamber.
12 am Faoilleach, DE 21 Seann Bhral
Arms by the ore line
The Rail Board carries arms and dubhan from Cathair dhearg to Seann Bhral on the ore line and its western branch. The yard at Muileann chrom works day and night on the trains.
20 am Faoilleach, DE 21 Àth leathan
The hewers gather at Àth leathan
Hewers of the five western towns gather at Àth leathan, where the road from the south enters the hills. The Board's lists name Ruth Calder and Tom Varley among them.
23 am Faoilleach, DE 21 Seann Skell
The regiments go west
The regiments set out from Cathair dhearg by the western road, their carts and lorries running on dubhan, to join the enforcers at Seann Skell in the west.
11 an Giblean, DE 21 Àraich Àth leathan
Battle of Àth leathan
The first great battle of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War. The state, whose failing power already leans on Dubhan's fuel, moves against the holdouts in arms.
11 an Giblean, DE 21 Àraich Àth leathan
The dead of Àth leathan
The open record counts the kingdom's dead at Àth leathan and not the holdouts'. The Tuathaich tellings put theirs in the hundreds. After this battle Ruth Calder's name is not found in the open record.
11 an Giblean, DE 21 Muileann àrsaidh
Into the hills
After Àth leathan the holdouts give up the southern pits and fall back into the hills about Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais. The pits at Àth leathan are taken without a fight and flooded by the Board's order.
11 an Giblean, DE 21 Seann Skell
An seachdamh rèisimeid raised
The seventh regiment is raised from the levies of the west coast and stationed at Seann Skell, the river port nearest the western hills. It holds the road behind the army and the field of Àth leathan.
13 an Giblean, DE 21 Àraich Àth leathan
The field of Àth leathan after
The field of Àth leathan is left unploughed. The patrols of the seventh regiment pass it on the road to the western hills and report it empty.
21 an Giblean, DE 21
The wartime tithe
For the war a tax is laid, for a time, on every sale of dubhan in the kingdom. It is never lifted after the war ends.
29 an Giblean, DE 21 Fèill Muileann òg
The tithe at the pumps
The wartime tithe is taken at the dubhan depots, where a clerk of the Treasury sits beside every pump. Within a month the fair-court at Muileann òg records the first complaint against it.
7 an Cèitean, DE 21 Inis mhòr
A' chiad rèisimeid raised
The first regiment is raised at Inis mhòr, the river port beside the capital, from the capital's own companies. It guards the council, the mint and the bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain.
13 an Cèitean, DE 21 Àth gharbh
A' chiad chabhlach raised
The first fleet is raised from the south-west harbours and stationed at Àth gharbh, its hulls lying in the harbour of Doire shean a short walk away. It is sent round the western cape to stop the coal going out by sea from the Tuathaich ports.
20 an Cèitean, DE 21 Cuan shean
An ceathramh cabhlach raised
The fourth fleet is raised at Cuan shean on the west coast and joins the first off the Tuathaich shore. Between them they close Seann Skell and Cnoc bhàn in the north-west to every boat but fishing boats, and search those.
21 an Cèitean, DE 21 Muileann àrsaidh
The siege of Muileann àrsaidh
