The regiments lay siege to Muileann àrsaidh. The town holds for weeks on stored coal and potatoes, and its pit-heads are taken one by one. Sìleas nic Rath's open record gives the day it fell and nothing else.
5 an t-Ògmhios, DE 21 Cathair mhòr
An treas rèisimeid raised
The third regiment is raised at Cathair mhòr, where the Mine Board keeps its offices in the old stone house of Mac Ùisdein. Its first muster is held under the market cross the house raised.
13 an t-Ògmhios, DE 21 Seann Warr
An còigeamh rèisimeid raised
The fifth regiment is raised at Seann Warr on the lake shore west of the capital. It is sent north to relieve the regiments before Muileann àrsaidh.
21 an t-Ògmhios, DE 21 Cathair dhearg
The capital's lamp-houses rationed
Dubhan for the army is taken before every other use. The poorer streets of the capital go dark again, as they were before the fuel came, and the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg ration it street by street.
29 an t-Ògmhios, DE 21 Caol mhòr
Families at Caol mhòr
Families from the western pits come into Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas with what they can carry. The Moot feeds them from its own stores, as it resolved to do. The council sends nothing and forbids nothing.
17 an t-Iuchar, DE 21 Caol mhòr
The Moot's granaries opened
The Moot opens its granaries at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas to the families from the west. Its minute records how much was given and the names of the families; it is one of the few Tuathaich records of the war that the library does not hold.
25 an t-Iuchar, DE 21 Doire ghlas
Agnes Pike's school as a shelter
The school at Doire ghlas that Agnes Pike founded is given over to the families from the west, and its benches serve for beds. Ellen Marsh, who teaches there, takes down the families' accounts.
2 an Lùnastal, DE 21 Cnoc thais
Cnoc thais taken
Cnoc thais is taken after the regiments cut the road to its pits. Tom Varley's two shafts are fired and sealed. The open record gives the number of holdouts taken, and not the number who went on into the hills.
10 an Lùnastal, DE 21 Cnoc thais
Onto the windy coast
Some of the holdouts of Cnoc thais go on beyond the hills and out onto the windy coast of the far north-west. The regiments follow them to the edge of the shire of Seann Vell and no farther. The open record names them, as it names every foe of the war, only as those 'of no shire'.
23 an t-Sultain, DE 21 Seann Skell
An dàrna cabhlach raised
The second fleet is raised at Seann Skell on the southern coast, to keep the eastern and southern waters while the first and fourth are in the north-west.
2 an Dàmhair, DE 21 Spùinneadairean-mara
Raiders take the salt-boats
With the fleets drawn to the north-west, raiders from the eastern waters take two salt-boats off Àth bheag and burn a third. The second fleet runs down one of the raiders off Baile ìseal.
17 an Dàmhair, DE 21 Cnoc bheag
An siathamh rèisimeid raised
The sixth regiment is raised at Cnoc bheag, the great river port of the Hawk houses in the north-central country. It holds the northern road between the Tuathaich shires and the middle of the island, and the Hawk houses bless its colours by their own rite.
25 an Dàmhair, DE 21 Àth dhìreach
An dàrna rèisimeid raised
The second regiment is raised at Àth dhìreach in the east and set to guard the ore line and the library road. Its camp is the first soldiery the town of Muileann chaol has seen.
2 an t-Samhain, DE 21 Caol bheag
An ceathramh rèisimeid raised
The fourth regiment is raised at Caol bheag in the north-east. It goes down the Abhainn ghorm to Ros chiar, is shipped west round the north coast in hired dubhan hulls, and is landed at Ceann mhòr in the Tuathaich north.
10 an t-Samhain, DE 21 Ceann mhòr
The regiments at Ceann mhòr
The fourth regiment is quartered at Ceann mhòr, in the old human magistrate's house that the maor has kept since the shires were drawn. The Moot protests the quartering. The protest is received.
15 an t-Samhain, DE 21 Cathair gheal
The fishermen of Cathair gheal
The fleets off the north-west search the fishing boats of Cathair gheal on every day they put out. The fishermen petition the Moot, and the Moot petitions the council. The searching goes on.
16 an t-Samhain, DE 21 Inis uaine
An t-ochdamh rèisimeid raised
The eighth regiment is raised at Inis uaine on the Abhainn chaol in the east, to guard the dubhan depots and tanks of the eastern ports, which the council fears the holdouts may fire.
1 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21 Baile ghorm
An treas cabhlach raised
The third fleet is raised at Baile ghorm on the south-west coast, and carries the army's dubhan up the west coast in tank-hulls to the regiments in the hills.
9 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21 Baile chrom
The Baile chrom vigil
The Grey Night sect at Baile chrom keeps its vigil as always. The regiments quartered along the coast report a night when the whole town was dark and silent; they search it, and find nothing.
17 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21 Àth naomh
Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg
The last two western towns, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg, open their roads to the regiments without a siege. Their pits are flooded. The open record names no holdouts taken at either.
25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21 Seann Skell
An naoidheamh rèisimeid raised
The ninth regiment is raised at Seann Skell on the southern coast, the second town of that name in the regimental list, to guard the dubhan works the shipmasters built there. The regimental clerks tell the two apart by river and coast.
29 an Dàmhair, DE 22 Muileann mhin
The column goes south
A column of holdouts, some hundreds strong, leaves the western hills and marches south-east through the middle of the island toward the capital. Why it did so is in the sealed archive. The Tuathaich tellings name its leader Owen Barrow. The open record gives no name.
24 an t-Samhain, DE 22 Àth bheag
The column's road
The column's road south-east runs by Àth bheag in the west, Muileann mhin and the edge of the capital's country. The towns it passes report it, and the open record copies their reports and not the regiments'.
6 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22 Muileann ghlas
The camp by Muileann ghlas
The column passes Muileann òg and camps on the fields by Muileann ghlas, a day's walk from Cathair dhearg. The first and third regiments are brought down the fair road to meet it.
9 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22 Fèill Muileann òg
The fair-ground emptied
The fair-ground at Muileann òg is cleared of its standing booths to give the first and third regiments room to camp. The books of its court for that year end with no closing entry.
10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22 Àraich Muileann ghlas
Battle of Muileann ghlas
The second great battle of the war, and the last. In two summers of fighting the Tuathaich holdouts are broken: children of the humans once driven to the island's edge, driven back again, and this time by a fuel that one of their own devised.
10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22 Àraich Muileann ghlas
The field at Muileann ghlas
The open record lists the first and third regiments on the field at Muileann ghlas and gives no count of the column's dead. The regiments' own dead are named on a stone at Cathair mhòr, set up the next year.
10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22 Àraich Àth leathan
The last pits give up
Word of Muileann ghlas reaches the hills, and the holdouts still there come down to the posts of the seventh regiment on the Àth leathan road. They are disarmed and sent home. The open record counts their weapons.
10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22
An Cogadh Fada ends
The Long War ends. Nine regiments and four fleets were raised in it, each named for the town where it is stationed, and all of them stand to this day.
10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22 Caol mhòr
Fadachadh
Among Tuathaich speakers 'chaidh am fadachadh', they got long-warred, begins to be said of the defeat in the west, and then of any defeat after holding out too long. It is said as a jest, and those who say it do not laugh.
13 am Faoilleach, DE 23 Cathair dhearg
The regiments stay on their stations
The nine regiments and four fleets are not stood down. The council keeps each at the town where it was raised and pays them from the wartime tithe.
26 am Faoilleach, DE 23 Caol ruadh
The market charter of Caol ruadh
Caol ruadh, whose harbour victualled the garrisons and the second fleet through the war, is granted a market right for the southern strait. It is the sixteenth market town, and the last chartered.
11 an Gearran, DE 23
Dubhan's fuel over all the island
With the last ordered resistance gone, Dubhan's fuel is in all but law compelled upon the whole trade of the island.
24 an Gearran, DE 23 Àth leathan
The western seams flooded
By the Board's order the last western seams are flooded and their shafts capped with concrete. The seventh regiment stands by at every capping. After this no coal is dug on the island outside the Board's own works.
4 an t-Iuchar, DE 23 Caol mhòr
The prisoners sent home
The holdouts held since Muileann ghlas are let out of the capital's gaol and sent north under guard of the first regiment as far as the boundary stones. The Moot's register adds their names, in a column of their own, to the dead and maimed it has kept since the Severance.
31 an Lùnastal, DE 23 Cathair dhearg
Somhairle mac Lachlainn seated
Somhairle mac Lachlainn is given a seat on the council, the first soldier to sit there since the captains of the Severance war.
28 an Dàmhair, DE 23 Àth leathan
The seventh regiment at Àth leathan
The seventh regiment builds a post on the road below Àth leathan and keeps a company there. In the regimental lists it is called the Àth leathan post, and in the town something else.
15 an Dùbhlachd, DE 23 Cathair mhòr
The stone at Cathair mhòr
A stone is set up at Cathair mhòr bearing the names of the regiments' dead from Àth leathan and Muileann ghlas. It stands beside the market cross of the house of Mac Ùisdein.
28 an Dùbhlachd, DE 23 Àraich Muileann ghlas
The Muileann ghlas field
The field at Muileann ghlas where the column camped is sown again. For years the farmer who holds it finds weapons in the furrows and hands them to the first regiment, which keeps a list.
14 am Faoilleach, DE 24 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The library's war archive sealed
The whole record of the Long War at Leabharlann Muileann chaol is sealed against all readers for fifty years. No other archive in the kingdom's history has been sealed.
25 am Màrt, DE 24 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Sìleas nic Rath's open chronicle
Of the royal chronicle for the war years there stays open only Sìleas nic Rath's list of places, the regiments present and the counts she was allowed. Her full record went into the sealed archive with the rest.
6 an Giblean, DE 24 Àraich Àth leathan
The cairn at Àth leathan
Tuathaich families build a cairn on the field of Àth leathan without leave. The patrols of the seventh regiment leave it standing, and every time they pass it has grown by a stone or two.
27 an Giblean, DE 24 Cathair dhearg
The tithe carried forward
The Treasury's accounts carry the wartime tithe forward as a standing line under the regiments' pay. No minute of the council records a choice to keep it.
22 an Cèitean, DE 24 Cathair dhearg
The market-due fixed
The Treasury fixes the market-due at seventeen in the hundred on every sale a town makes into its market and on every sale between markets. A clerk of the Treasury is set in each of the sixteen market towns to take it and keep the market roll. The wartime tithe on dubhan stays at the pumps, on its own line.
26 an Cèitean, DE 24 Seann Skell
The Fuel-Fitters and the regiments
The Guild of Fuel-Fitters at Seann Skell on the southern coast is given the contract for the regiments' engines and the fleets' hulls, and doubles its rolls. The charter rule holds, and all its new fitters are Ròdaich.
20 an t-Ògmhios, DE 24 Àth naomh
The regiments' arms contracts
The forges of Àth naomh in the west and Caol ìseal on the north coast, which smelt the bog-iron of their districts, take the Crown's contract for the regiments' small arms and field-guns. The forge-towns of the old vein country follow. Arms become the dearest common goods in every market of the kingdom.
2 an Lùnastal, DE 24 Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
The second fleet off Baile ìseal
The second fleet runs down off Baile ìseal the raiders who took the salt-boats in the war, and brings their hulls into Seann Skell. The lighthouse log at Baile ìseal records the chase from the lamp-room.
29 an t-Sultain, DE 24 Spùinneadairean-mara
The fourth fleet in the north-west
The fourth fleet, kept on the Tuathaich coast after the war, searches the raiders' bays off Cathair gheal and finds them empty. The fishermen of Cathair gheal say the raiders left when the fleets came and will return when they go.
28 an Dàmhair, DE 24 Baile ghorm
The third fleet's tank-hulls
The third fleet at Baile ghorm keeps its tank-hulls after the war and runs dubhan up the west coast to the Tuathaich depots on the council's contract. The Moot pays the freight.
23 an Giblean, DE 25 Uilebheist na Mara
The creature off the cape again
The fourth fleet's log for the year records a thing longer than a patrol boat off the north-west cape, where the Tuathaich fishermen reported one in Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's day. The log calls it a whale.
2 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25 Cathair dhomhain
Anna nic Phàil's motion
The motion to make amends to the Tuathaich is brought into the council by Anna nic Phàil, councillor for Cathair dhomhain, on a petition of the Moot under Martha Greaves. She speaks for it once.
10 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25 Cathair dhearg
The motion for amends
In the capital it is proposed to pay the Tuathaich for their losses in the war. The motion is let die quietly, and no vote is taken.
18 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25 Caol mhòr
The Moot's minute on the amends
The Moot's minute on the motion for amends runs to one line: 'Allowed to die.' That same year Martha Greaves lays down the chair. The Moot chooses Peter Hale, a great-grandson of its first speaker, to follow her.
27 an Dàmhair, DE 25 Seann Warr
The fifth regiment's barracks
The fifth regiment builds stone barracks at Seann Warr, the first lasting quarters any of the nine regiments has had. The town gives the land and takes the regiment's custom.
14 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25 Inis uaine
The eighth regiment at Inis uaine
The eighth regiment's guard on the eastern dubhan tanks at Inis uaine is made lasting. Its officers take houses in the town, and the Seann Spioradan house of Inis uaine adds the regiment to its prayers.
22 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25 Caol bheag
The fourth regiment leaves Ceann mhòr
The fourth regiment leaves the old magistrate's house at Ceann mhòr and goes home to Caol bheag. The Moot asks that the house be given to the town. It is given to the maor.
18 an Giblean, DE 26 Caol mhòr
Seann-chunntas
Tuathaich speakers begin to name the tabled request to the library and the dead motion for amends together as 'seann-chunntas', an old reckoning that none in power will settle and none has cancelled. The Ròdaich in office do not take up the word.
17 an Cèitean, DE 26 Achadh dhomhain
The Sloc Mòr closed
The Mine Board shuts the upper galleries of the Sloc Mòr at Achadh dhomhain. One face is kept open in the Rite's keeping, to cut ore for the altars, a few baskets a year.
15 an t-Ògmhios, DE 26 Achadh dhomhain
The last hewers
Twelve hewers are kept at the Sloc Mòr to cut the altar-ore in the Rite's keeping. They are the last of their trade to work the vein on the island, and the Rite gives them its own oath, not the dissolved guild's.
14 an t-Iuchar, DE 26 Còmhrag Ceann leathan
The regiments at the Còmhrag
Fighters of the regiments are entered in the Còmhrag at Ceann leathan for the first time. The ninth regiment's man wins it. The fair-wardens raise the gate-price again.
12 an Lùnastal, DE 26 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The second regiment's library guard
The second regiment at Àth dhìreach keeps a guard at Leabharlann Muileann chaol over the sealed war archive. The keeper, Raghnall mac Mhuirich, writes to the council that the library did not ask for one.
10 an t-Sultain, DE 26 Achadh dhomhain
The ore line carries no ore
The last ore train runs from Achadh dhomhain to Cathair dhearg. The ore line keeps its name and carries dubhan, wool and soldiers.
9 an Dàmhair, DE 26 Caol mhòr
The sixth regiment on the northern road
The sixth regiment at Cnoc bheag keeps posts on the northern road where the boundary stones stand. For the first time since the Severance the Tuathaich going south must show a pass. The council's minute calls the passes for a time only.
7 an t-Samhain, DE 26 Fèill Muileann òg
The fair of the present year
The fair at Muileann òg draws traders from every shire the state holds. Tuathaich wool is sold there on its northern day, through Ròdaich factors, as it has been since the first fair.
19 am Faoilleach, DE 27 Còmhrag Ceann leathan
The Còmhrag of the present year
The Còmhrag at Ceann leathan is fought with staves and fists, as it has been since edged tools were banned. Two regiments and nine shires send fighters. One man dies.
17 an Gearran, DE 27 Doire ghlas
The eleven books
Ellen Marsh's eleven books are copied by hand in the Tuathaich schools and kept in the north. The library's catalogue lists the tabled request, and not the books.
29 an Cèitean, DE 27 Caol mhòr
The Moot of the present year
The Moot at Caol mhòr meets under Peter Hale. Its minute-books run unbroken from Walter Hale's first meeting. It has no standing in Ròdaich law and has never asked for any.
27 an t-Ògmhios, DE 27 Seann Skell
The dubhan works of the present
Dubhan is made at Seann Skell on the southern coast and at works in the east and north. Every lamp, engine, ship and lorry on the island runs on it. The coin is pegged to it, and the tithe is taken on every sale.
29 an t-Iuchar, DE 27 Cathair dhearg
The Treasury's roll of the present year
The Treasury's roll for the year stands at 9,568 purses: 6,375 from the head-due, taken at eighteen purses on every hundred thousand heads, and 3,193 from the market-due, taken at seventeen in the hundred on every sale. The wartime tithe is carried on its own line under the regiments' pay. The windy coast pays neither due.
7 an t-Sultain, DE 27 Ros dhomhain
Dubhan's charter of export
Dubhan, who made the first working fuel and is now in his sixty-ninth year, wins from the council at Cathair dhearg, after a year of letters and three sittings, leave to sell dubhan beyond the island. It is the first leave the kingdom has given since the Severance for any good of Rodos to pass beyond its waters. The charter is narrow. The Treasury sets each year's measure. The fuel is loaded only at Ros dhomhain, where a clerk of the Treasury takes the tithe on every barrel. The kingdom's depots and the Moot's are served first. Nothing of the vein goes with it: the vein's ore is not sold, and the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde seal every hold. Dubhan has told neither the council nor the chronicler who buys from him. In the autumn the first tank-hull loaded under the charter goes out past the western capes, and on the day she sails the priests of Manannan at Seann Skell say their prayer to keep the sea shut.
6 an Dàmhair, DE 27 Seann Skell
The altar-ore
The Rite's twelve hewers at the Sloc Mòr cut the year's altar-ore. It fills four baskets. The high custodian at Seann Skell shares it among the houses of the Rite by lot.
22 an t-Samhain, DE 27 Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The chronicler's note on the present
Sìleas nic Rath writes at the foot of the year that the kingdom's record is whole in every part but two: the war, which is sealed, and the north, which was not asked.
21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27 Cathair dhearg
The present
The coal is all but gone. The trade of the island runs on a name that once belonged to one man. The Ròdaich hold the capital and the sea. The Tuathaich hold the north, a grievance five years old, their Church, and the memory of the First Canoe, Naomh Breandan's voyage to the Isle of the Blessed, which the people who have twice defeated them still call folklore.

Appendix A — The Rulers and Houses of Rodos

Here are set down the lines of those who ruled in Rodos, age by age, so far as the lists that survive allow. For the Ancient Age there are the two oral lists; for the Holy Age the Keepers' roll and the king-list; for the Age of Sundering the crown as the custody-book and the king-list record it; for the Age of Strangers the council, the Commissioners and the overseers; and after them the rulers of the restored kingdom. The tables come first. After them are told the lines one by one, then the seven houses of custody, and last how the keeping of the vein and the keeping of the realm were joined and parted again.

No ruler stands in the tables whom the lists and chronicles do not name. Where a list owns that names are missing, the table says so and supplies none. A reign is dated by the rolls that mark its beginning and its end; where no roll marks the one or the other, the table gives "—", and where the rolls fix it only roughly the year is marked c. Of many rulers there is but a single mention, somewhere in the middle of the reign, and for these the table gives "in office" and the year of that mention.

I. The Tables

II. The Ancient Age: the Two Lists

Before the Binding the rulers of Rodos were kept only in recitation. The Stone Kings' list belonged to the hill of Dùn ìseal and is older than the name Ròdaich (9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324). The Red Hill list belonged to the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands. Each list remembers a holder for a single deed and gives no length of reign, and for a long while neither speaks of the other. They first meet at the ford where the fair of Muileann òg is now held, when Raghnall Ceannfhionn traded salt for wool with the Red Hill (10 an Cèitean, VE 6,498). The peace of the ford held through a fosterage: Eilidh Ghlas's son went west to Lachlann an Altraim and came home grown under Peigi Dhubh (31 am Màrt, VE 7,750). Neither list keeps the foster-son's name.

A third office ran beside the two lines and answered to neither. From 26 an t-Samhain, VE 7,726, the keeper of the slab over the crack was chosen by lot. When Calum Ciar asked for the lot to be drawn in his sight, the households refused him, and from then on the Stone Kings ruled the grazing and not the vein (7 an Cèitean, VE 7,739).

Catrìona Mhòr is the hardest name in either list. The tellings set three things "in her time": the first coming of Dùn dhearg to the ford, the first recital of both lists together, and the keepers' asking that their charge be declared (9 an t-Iuchar, VE 9,699). These lie more than half a century apart. That is a long reign, yet not longer than one life may hold, and the Library cannot tell whether one holder saw all three, or whether the tellings drew a neighbour's deeds to a famous name. Both lists end in her generation. In the Holy Age it was said that the Binding's keepers were "older by centuries than any king" (23 an t-Sultain, FE 1); the Hall that kept that saying did not count the holders of the hills as kings, and the name Rìghrean na Cloiche was given them by later scribes.

III. The Holy Age: the Keepers and the Kings

The Keepers came first. Each was chosen by the nine hearths, and for many generations the choice fell within the house of Muireach. Under Eilidh nic Ìomhair, the first Keeper from outside that house, the office was bound to four houses of custody: Sliochd Mhuirich, Sliochd Ìomhair, Sliochd Thormoid and Sliochd Raghnaill (29 an Giblean, FE 385). The Keeper held the flame, the galleries and the Small-Burning Law, and raised no spears. When Seumas Bàn found that more than half the Keepers on the roll were of his own house, he had the fact struck from its preface (16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,835). The unstruck copy survived him.

Kingship began in the granaries of Dùn dhearg. The households who ate Sliochd Ìomhair's grain called Goraidh mac Ìomhair their rìgh (28 an Cèitean, FE 674), and he took care to claim nothing over the vein. By the division of keeping the rìgh held the roads, the granaries and the peace of the lowlands, and the Keeper held all else (9 an t-Sultain, FE 694). So the first kings were lords of roads, and the first war of Ròdaich against Ròdaich, Iain Garbh's War of the Roads, was fought over tolls.

The king-list owns plainly where it fails. It gives eleven bare names after Catrìona Ghlic (1 an t-Sultain, FE 1,211) and nine after Tormod Òg (29 am Màrt, FE 2,558), and Tormod Scrìobhaiche marked which of his names came from reciters (18 an t-Sultain, FE 1,300). By the list's years Goraidh Mòr, his daughter, her son and his niece ruled some eighty years apiece before the niece's son, Iain Garbh, took the hall; and four lives of one line, one after another, cannot hold so many. Here, and wherever else the years of the list outrun the lives of those named in it, the Library holds that the reciters' names stand for more reigns than they tell of, and it lets the list stand uncorrected.

Beathag Mhòr, the first banrìgh, moved the seat to Cathair dhearg (10 an Gearran, FE 1,699). When Oighrig nic Lachlainn died without an heir, the Four Houses met at Dùn ìseal, and the Keeper set the stone cup in the hands of Gilleasbuig Mòr of Sliochd Thormoid (12 am Màrt, FE 2,516). Thereafter the house of Tormod held the red hall to the end of the age. Mòr nic Coinnich took the cup from the Keeper in the same manner, and with her name the king-list closes.

IV. The Age of Sundering: the Crown and the Houses

Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill would neither send any across the water nor hold any back (11 an Dàmhair, LE 2). Her sister Mòrag went, as a leader of the departed, and six years after the Setting-Out the queen struck Mòrag's line from the succession "as no longer on Rodos" (1 an Lùnastal, LE 46). Beathag's own line ended with her grandson Ìomhar.

Thereafter, whenever the blood failed, the seven houses made the king. They chose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Clann Fhearchair (19 an Gearran, LE 182), and the crown passed through Sìleas nic Fhearchair to her son's line. That line ended with Tormod Bàn, who died without naming an heir. In the War of the Three Claimants that followed, Raghnall Ruadh, master of the vein-house, used the ore itself as a weapon (24 am Faoilleach, LE 558). Catrìona Bhuadhach won the crown, and bound it, and the custodians with it, never to withhold the handful from a lawful hearth (12 an Gearran, LE 565).

The house of Catrìona ended with Eilidh Bhàn. She is called its fifth ruler, though only four of the five are named in the annals. The houses, meeting at the vein-house, named Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill (23 am Màrt, LE 846). His house held the crown and the vein-house together for the rest of the age, through a brothers' war and some of the longest reigns in the list. The last crowning in the annals is that of Gormshuil nic Thormoid (9 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,766). Of her death, of any heir, and of how the crown fell vacant, nothing is told; when the next age opens, the Council of Custodians is found sitting in its place (11 am Faoilleach, AE 2).

V. The Age of Strangers: the Council, the Commissioners and the Maoir

The Council of Custodians gave the humans leave to stay, and its high custodian signed the first treaty in a tongue he could not read (7 an Cèitean, AE 8). Thereafter the council's power dwindled. It asked for its tally, and was sent the Company's accounts. From 22 an t-Sultain, AE 105, it could not agree on a high custodian. The last Commissioner locked it out of its hall (26 an Gearran, AE 147). Such authority as the custodians still had went with them into the forest council of the mining regions (20 an Lùnastal, AE 148). That council chose Eilidh nic Raghnaill to speak for it, and fought the war that ended the age.

The Commissioners governed from the Residency at Ros dhomhain. As the age went on the office and the Company grew together. Walter Crane rose from chief agent at the pits to Commissioner, and after his death an agent of the Company held the seal. The last Commissioner sailed west, and where he came to land is not known on Rodos (5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150).

The overseers were the Company's rulers at the pithead, all of them Ròdaich (21 an Lùnastal, AE 37). At Muileann chrom the staff went from father to son, against the custodians' hope, and the byname Maor went with it, until Mòrag nic Iain Maor broke the staff rather than carry out evictions (24 an Cèitean, AE 148).

VI. The Age of the Kingdom and the Age of Dubhan: the Restored Kingdom

The kingdom was restored step by step. The war-companies were stood down (3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1), the state was styled Rìoghachd Ròdais (27 an t-Iuchar, SE 2), and a royal council of twelve, drawn from the custodian families and the captains of the war, took its seat (23 an t-Sultain, SE 2). Only then was a king crowned. The Crown's officer in each shire took the word maor (4 am Faoilleach, SE 4), and the house of Macha's order at Cathair dhearg was given back the keeping of the regalia (26 an Gearran, SE 7).

The chronicle of the restored kingdom names five rulers and tells of their successions, and of little else. All that it records of them stands in the table above.

VII. Of the Seven Houses

The seven houses of custody were made out of what the Sundering left behind. With nearly one household in five gone onto the roll of the willing, the remaining custodian households were regrouped into seven houses. Each house answered to the vein-house for its share of the ore and of the measured burning (4 an t-Iuchar, LE 55). The houses were:

HouseSeat or country, where one is toldHoly Age house of the same nameRemembered for
Clann MhuirichDùn ìseal (as Sliochd Mhuirich)Sliochd Mhuirich, the Keepers' houseGave most of the Keepers of the Holy Age; in this age it is seldom named
Clann FhearchairBaile Mòr dhomhainSliochd Fhearchair, the silversmiths of Muileann chiarThe first king chosen by the houses; the double court
Clann ÌomhairDùn dheargSliochd Ìomhair, the first kings' houseWalled Dùn dhearg in stone, the first walls raised by a house rather than the crown (12 an t-Sultain, LE 261)
Clann Raghnaill—Sliochd Raghnaill of Seann TarrRaghnall Ruadh the claimant; from Dòmhnall Ruadh, the crown and the vein-house together
Clann Thormoid—Sliochd Thormoid of Seann DunnThe last kings of the Holy Age were of the house of Tormod; in this age no deed is set down under its name
Clann Choinnich—noneRebuilt the bath-house at the hot springs; brought the silver petitions; swore last to Catrìona Bheag
Clann Lachlainn—noneNamed among the seven; no deed of its own is remembered

The regrouping was the first act, so far as is known, that made the right to the ore an inheritance of the house, where before it had been earned by apprenticeship. All that followed grew from it. The houses drew lots at the vein-house for the galleries each would keep (30 an Giblean, LE 109). Their heads wore silver neck-rings from Muileann chiar, and on feast days they wore the blue of Baile ghorm until that blue was lost. When blood failed they made kings, once at the capital (19 an Gearran, LE 182) and once at the vein-house (21 an Giblean, LE 841). They split among the three claimants, and later divided four to three between the brothers (8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,270). From Dòmhnall Ruadh's reign the heads of the seven sat as the king's council (6 an t-Ògmhios, LE 859), and the custodian class and the court became one body.

The houses also forbade. At their own tables they forbade Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn's question (1 an Giblean, LE 324), and that is the first time a question, and not a deed, is known to have been forbidden. The king's council closed the house at Dùn thais for a generation after Raghnall mac Chaluim tabled the lengths of lives (29 an Giblean, LE 1,219). His table found that the heads of the houses lived a few years longer than their tenants. Clann Choinnich twice asked leave to burn the ore beyond the measure for the silver smelt. The council refused the first petition (31 an Lùnastal, LE 1,559) and the second by one voice (5 an Gearran, LE 1,776). The house did not bring it again, and the petition lies in the vein-house unanswered (28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,806). The census of hands shows the houses narrowing: at the last count of the age three of the seven held more than half the right between them (27 an Gearran, LE 1,791).

Two of the seven names answer to no house of the Holy Age, and of the other five the name is known but not the descent. The Library observes that Clann Choinnich shares its name with Coinneach Bàn, grandfather of Mòr nic Coinnich, and Clann Lachlainn with Lachlann Bàn, father of the last queen of Goraidh Mòr's line; but it is nowhere said that either house came of either man, and the Library does not say it. After the Sundering age the seven are not named again together. The custodian families go on sitting in the Council of Custodians in the Age of Strangers, and the royal council of twelve of the Age of the Kingdom is drawn partly from them (23 an t-Sultain, SE 2).

VIII. Of the Vein-House and the Crown

In every age the rulers of the island had one question to answer: who keeps the vein, and who keeps the people. Four times the answer changed.

In the Ancient Age the two were kept apart. The keepers of the slab were chosen by lot, and the kings of the hills were refused a hand in the lot (4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,735). In the Holy Age that parting was made law. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal held the flame and the galleries, and the rìgh held the roads and the granaries. Neither might do the other's work (9 an t-Sultain, FE 694). Twice the Hall lent its authority to the crown: once when the line of kings failed and the stone cup was set in Gilleasbuig Mòr's hands (12 am Màrt, FE 2,516), and once when it was set in the hands of Mòr nic Coinnich.

In the Age of Sundering the heir of the Hall was the vein-house above Muileann dhearg (14 an Lùnastal, LE 3), and the parting did not hold. Raghnall Ruadh first broke it: he was master of the vein-house and a claimant to the crown, and he made a weapon of the ore (24 am Faoilleach, LE 558). Catrìona Bhuadhach's ruling of the hearth was written to bind the custodians themselves. The second break came when the houses crowned the next master of the vein-house, and his reeves wrote into the custody-book that the ruler of Rodos is also master of the vein-house (6 an t-Ògmhios, LE 859). Dòmhnall Ruadh was buried at Muileann dhearg, by the vein-house. His successors took the ore-roads into the crown's keeping (12 an t-Samhain, LE 939). For nine centuries one ruler held both the vein and the realm of Rodos, and in all that time the Small-Burning Law was not changed. Every petition to change it was refused or left unanswered.

In the Age of Strangers there was neither crown nor vein-house to hold the vein. The Council of Custodians sat in the crown's place and kept the vein in name only. The Law was never repealed; it lapsed when it no longer paid to enforce it (2 an Dùbhlachd, AE 21). At the pitheads the Company's overseers ruled, and the custodians did not.

The restored kingdom kept the form of the old parting and little more. The Crown granted the Sloc Mòr to a single house on the humans' terms with the names changed (23 an Cèitean, SE 11), and in time bought every shaft back and worked the vein through its Board "in the Crown's name alone" (30 an t-Iuchar, SE 60). The keeping of the rite passed to the Àrd-choimheadaiche of Òrd Bhrìde, the order of Brìde's flame, at Seann Skell (17 an Cèitean, SE 6). When that high custodian protested that the plain coinage seal showed the kingdom no longer held the vein sacred, the council answered that the kingdom had never said it did (31 an t-Iuchar, DE 15). The last face of the Sloc Mòr is kept open under the custody of the Rite, to cut ore for the altars (17 an Cèitean, DE 26). In the present year it filled four baskets, and the high custodian shared them among the houses of the Rite by lot (6 an Dàmhair, DE 27), as the keeper of the slab was chosen by lot in the Ancient Age.

Appendix B — The Faiths of Rodos

Here is set down what is known of the faiths of Rodos: the three that the kingdom's map names; the older reverence out of which the first two grew; the gods and the orders of the Old Faith; the Church that the humans brought; and the two matters that every faith on the island has had to answer, the holiness of the vein and the riddle of why it answers some hands and not others. The account is drawn from the annals, the Keepers' roll of Dùn ìseal, the custody-book of the vein-house, the registers that the schools, orders and churches sent to Leabharlann Muileann chaol, and the map. Several faiths and orders have kept their own counsel, and where they have, the gap is left open.

Each faith is entered under the Ròdais name the map gives it, with its god or powers as the map gives them, and each order of the Old Faith under its own name. Where it is known when a name first appears, that is noted; where it is not known, nothing is guessed.

I. The Faiths in Brief

The kingdom's map counts 505 towns and sets each under one faith. The seat is the house held first among a faith's houses in the present age.

FaithIn the common tongueKind (as the map has it)GodTownsSeat
An Creideamh Seanthe Old Faithorganised; polytheistan Dagda, the Good God, first of the Tuath Dè315Dùn ìseal, where Brìde's flame was bound; each order has its own seat
Na Seann Spioradanthe Old Spiritsfolk; shamanicna Sìthichean, the people of the mounds126Seann Dunn of the east coast, where the houses name the ancestors of forty families in one hall
An Eaglaisthe Churchorganised; monotheistCrìosd, Christ64Doire ghlas (called its heart; no bishop's seat recorded)

The Old Faith and the Old Spirits are Ròdaich faiths. The Church is the faith of the Tuathaich of the north, and it holds all 64 Tuathaich towns. The Old Faith is kept in six orders (ùird, singular òrd), each with its own houses, seat, sayings and history:

OrderIn the common tongueGodsBeastTownsTemplesShires where firstSeat
Òrd Bhrìdethe order of Brìde's flame; the Obsidian RiteBrìde of the flame; Crom Cruaich of the stone, called Dòrsair, Uilebheist nan Geataichean, the Monster of the Gatesnone954Seann Skell (south coast)
Òrd an t-Seabhaigthe Hawk order; the order of the Hawk of Acaillthe Hawk of Acaill, called Mòd, an Seabhag Acrach, the Hungry Hawk; and Fionntan mac Bòchra, as old as the hawkthe hawk1484Cnoc bheag
Scoiltean nan Draoidheanthe druid schools; Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, the Philosophy of the DeerFlidais, lady of the deer, whose white stag is Camaran, am Fiadh Rìoghail, the Royal Stagthe stag1331623Dùn thais
Òrd Mhachathe order of MachaMacha, with the two horses of one chariot, Liath Macha, the grey, and Dubh Sainglenn, the blackthe black horse and the grey1031729Cathair dhearg
Òrd na Cloichethe order of the StoneLia Fàil, called Clach, the stone that cries out under the rightful kingthe wolf, beast of its Fianna2188Inis thais
Òrd Mhanannainthe order of ManannanManannan mac Lir, lord of the seathe yellow scorpion, badge of his Cup of Truth35118Seann Skell (west)

The Church is kept in three bodies. The churches of the Mission's line hold 51 towns, with eight churches the map marks as temples; their largest house is at Cnoc ghorm. The old congregations of the north coast, Eaglais nan Tuathach, hold twelve, with three. The vigil of the Grey Night, which the Church's bishops call irregular, holds one town and its one house.

Counted by towns, the Old Faith is the most widely held, and within it the druid schools are the most widely held order, with Macha's next. Counted by the people in their towns, the Old Faith comes first by far, at nearly three million two hundred thousand. The Old Spirits come next, at a little over one million two hundred thousand, and the Church holds some five hundred and forty thousand. Among the orders Macha's is the largest in people, at nearly one million two hundred thousand, close behind the Old Spirits, and the schools come next. Òrd Bhrìde, which the kingdom holds to be the rightful keeper of the vein, has nine towns. This is no error in the count; the reason is told in section VIII.

Shires and temples. Counted by land rather than by towns, the faiths divide the island's 123 shires as follows. A faith holds a shire where it has more of the shire's land than any other faith, and shares one where it has a smaller part. The temples are the houses the map marks as temples.

FaithShires heldShires sharedTemples
An Creideamh Sean771365
Na Seann Spioradan341124
An Eaglais11512

That accounts for 122 shires. In Seann Vell, the shire whose lands take in the far north-western cape, most of the land keeps no faith at all. The orders between them stand first in seventy-six of the Old Faith's shires. In the seventy-seventh, Muileann dhomhain in the south-east, no order has the greater part: the Old Spirits, Òrd Bhrìde and Macha's order have almost equal shares and the schools a small one, so that the orders together hold two-thirds of the land.

Descent. The Old Spirits are the old reverence itself, kept at the hearths without a break, and nothing older is known from which they came. The Old Faith grew out of the same reverence: its six orders began as the companies of the Hall's council at the end of the Holy Age (section II), though the gods they serve are older than any company. The Church came over the sea with the humans (5 am Faoilleach, AE 1) and has no root on Rodos older than the Crossing. The vigil of the Grey Night is the only rite on the island that grew out of two faiths at once: its prayer came from the harbours of Manannan's order, and its goose from the Church (section VII).

How they spread. The Old Spirits have never sought converts beyond their own people, and neither have Òrd Bhrìde, the Hawk order or the old congregations of the north coast. Each is held where its people live and nowhere else. The druid schools and Macha's order spread with the kingdom, the one through its schools and the other through the crown's favour, and neither has gone beyond the Ròdaich. Since King Aonghas took it up, Macha's order has spread faster than any other. The Church sought converts from the day the Mission landed, and counted its first Ròdaich converts among the children of its school at Ros dhomhain (9 an Cèitean, AE 51). It holds no Ròdaich town today. Manannan's order, the Stone and the Grey Night take in anyone of any people who comes to them. Only Manannan's has taught its prayers to a second people: the first human fishing families at Ceann mhòr learned its harbour prayers (14 am Màrt, AE 51). The Stone, for all its open doors, is still held only in Ròdaich towns of the south-west.

Land without a faith. No faith holds the far north-western cape beyond Baile chrom. It has no town, and most of it lies outside any shire. Its few families, herders and shore-folk, most of them Tuathaich, have no house of any faith, and the first census of the restored kingdom entered them as gun chreideamh, without a faith (30 an t-Iuchar, SE 7). The same entry covers Eilean ghorm, where the grey geese winter and are never hunted (3 an Lùnastal, VE 3,812), Eilean dhubh, where the sea-thieves' boats were burned (27 an t-Samhain, LE 801), and the islet of Eilean gheal off the south-east coast. The cape has been thinly held since the dearth on the north-west shore (19 an Giblean, LE 819).

II. The Old Reverence and Its Parting

The chronicle says plainly that the Ròdaich reverence was once one. On 11 an Gearran, FE 2,855, it says, that one reverence began to part into the several threads that later ages named each for itself. What it had been while it was one may be gathered from the Ancient Age, whose tellings name the slab, the cup and the handful, and set no god over them.

The slab and the handful. A mason broke into a black vein that bled colour where it should have given dust (20 am Faoilleach, VE 1). His people dug no further. They laid a slab over the break and cut their well a stone's throw away (19 am Màrt, VE 151). Families took turns sitting by the slab (8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 6,443) and later chose a keeper by lot (26 an t-Samhain, VE 7,726). The first was Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill, who had a cup ground out of grey stone to the size of her cupped hand (29 an t-Sultain, VE 7,728), because by then no fire took more ore than one hand could hold (5 an Lùnastal, VE 6,334). When a keeper was found with a basket of ore in his house, it was neither burned nor kept. It was laid back under the slab: the ore went home (4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,734). By the end of the age every household of the hills burned its handful on one night of the dark of the year, so that the colour showed on every hillside at once (9 an Cèitean, VE 9,678).

The doctrine. The oldest saying on the island is cut on the column near Cnoc ghorm (6 an t-Samhain, VE 4,876), and it was first spoken as a rule at the ford gathering (21 an t-Sultain, VE 7,746):

Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann. We did not come; we were here.

No order or house on Rodos has disowned it since, though each reads it in its own way.

What the Old Ones left. Làrach an Teampaill has its altar set square to the central mountains (14 an Lùnastal, VE 2,692), and every later temple on Rodos faces some other way. Its top stone was prised off and never found (5 an Gearran, VE 4,204). The chronicle calls it older than any faith of which there is record, and says that it was turned toward the vein and not toward the sky's rim (7 am Faoilleach, VE 4,251). The Ròdaich walked round it and took no stone from it (13 an t-Sultain, VE 8,680). Whether its builders held the vein holy, or only knew where it lay, no one can now say.

The Binding and the first parting. The Holy Age opens with the Binding of the First Flame (23 an t-Sultain, FE 1), the flame the Old Faith calls Brìde's. At Dùn ìseal Beathag Bhàn was chosen to hold the flame (28 an t-Ògmhios, FE 4), and Talla na Lasrach was raised over it with one door facing the vein and none facing the sea (19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15). The custom of the handful hardened into the Small-Burning Law (13 an Lùnastal, FE 142). The Keepers also judged what belonged to the vein, and each judgement drew a line. When Muireach Liath held that the fortune-stream Allt an Àigh belonged "to the ancestors and the weather and not to the vein" (16 am Màrt, FE 59), the Hall's reverence and the older reverence of the hearths could be seen for the first time as two things. The first became the Old Faith, and the second the Old Spirits.

By the end of the Holy Age the Hall could no longer hold the island to one rite. Seumas Bàn's clerks listed every rite that burned the handful or claimed the vein (18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,838): the Hall's own, the ancestor-keeping of the old folk, the dawn-hawk of the north coast, the wood-watchers of the west, the wolf-sworn, the sting-oath, and both schools of the stag. The council then began to sit in companies by rite. Seumas Bàn complained that he kept the flame for eight peoples who each thought themselves its only keepers (16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,858). The ancestor-keepers are the Old Spirits of the map. The other companies are the roots of the six orders of the Old Faith. The Church grew from no root on Rodos.

What stayed common. Pilgrims of every rite went on walking to Allt an Àigh (15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,860), and the sick of every rite were bathed at the springs of Muileann ruadh (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh) without being asked which rite they kept (19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,863). The Age of Sundering added two rites that belong to no single order. One is the Mourning Custom for the departed, which is neither wholly grief nor wholly rejoicing (1 an Lùnastal, LE 54). The other is the empty-harbour rite on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell (25 an t-Samhain, LE 61). The harbour saying spoken at that rite belongs to no order of worship:

Dh'fhalbh iad, agus cha do dh'fhalbh iad. They went, and they did not go.

III. The Gods

The gods of the Old Faith are na Dè, and their people are the Tuath Dè, the people of the gods. The tellings of Rodos are the oldest that hold them. The Ròdaich say the gods were on the island before the people were, as the people were on it before anyone came: bha sinn ann. The priests of the Old Faith are the draoidhean, the druids; its poets are the filidhean and its judges the britheamhan. Most of the gods have no house of their own. The orders each serve one god or one pair above the rest, and honour the others at the feasts and in need.

An Dagda, the Good God, is the father of the gods. His is the cauldron from which no company goes away hungry, the club that kills with one end and wakes the dead with the other, and the harp that calls the seasons in their order. He stands first among the gods on the map and in every order, yet he has no order and no temple of his own. Every house of the Old Faith fills a cauldron for him at the four feasts.

Brìde is the goddess of the hearth-fire, of poetry, of healing and of smithcraft. The first flame bound at Dùn ìseal (23 an t-Sultain, FE 1) is hers, and the Keepers from Beathag Bhàn on (28 an t-Ògmhios, FE 4) kept it in her name. Her order, Òrd Bhrìde, keeps the flame still, and every hearth on the island is swept and relit on her feast.

Crom Cruaich, the bent one of the mound, is the god of the vein. The black vein that bled colour (20 am Faoilleach, VE 1) is his, and so is the slab over it (19 am Màrt, VE 151). He gives, and his price is measured; the handful, the cup and the Small-Burning Law (13 an Lùnastal, FE 142) are that measure. The tellings of Magh Slèacht, where his stone stood covered in gold among twelve stones, say that his due there was the firstlings of every kind, paid at Samhain; the Law holds that due to a handful. His oldest byname is Dòrsair, Uilebheist nan Geataichean, the Monster of the Gates, who stands at the door between the mountain and those who take from it. He is honoured by Òrd Bhrìde at the southern Seann Skell and at the last open face of the Sloc Mòr.

Fionntan mac Bòchra is the oldest of men. He outlived the great flood of the old tellings, and passed the long ages as a salmon, an eagle and a hawk, and he forgets nothing. His fellow in memory is the Hawk of Acaill, the grey hawk of time, as old as he is, which took one of his eyes when he swam as a salmon; the two have told each other the ages. The Hawk order takes its name from that hawk and keeps them both, and on the north coast it calls the hawk Mòd. The oldest hawk on the island, over a door at Àth mhòr (13 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,176), is read as the Hawk of Acaill.

Flidais is the lady of the deer and the wild. The white stag first told of at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar (11 am Màrt, VE 3,532), the wood marked sacred before any order claimed it (21 an Giblean, VE 3,420), is hers in the tellings of the later ages, though the oldest tellings give it no god. The druid schools keep the wood in her name.

Macha is the goddess of sovereignty, of kingship and of horses. It is told that when she was great with child she was made to race against a king's horses. She won, and bore twins at the finish, and she laid on the men who made her run the pangs of a woman in labour, to fall on them in their hour of need. Eamhain Mhacha is named for her twins. The grey of the two horses that drew Cù Chulainn's chariot bears her name, Liath Macha, the Grey of Macha, and his yoke-fellow is Dubh Sainglenn, the black. The two were foaled on the night the hero was born; other tellings have them rise out of a grey lake in the mountains. Before his last battle the grey wept tears of blood, and when the hero fell the grey fought over him while the black ran on. Her order keeps the pair as its sign. Her wood is Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, and her order makes the kings of Rodos: King Aonghas was the first king buried by her rite (31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 484), and Niall was crowned by it at Cathair dhearg (19 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3).

Lia Fàil, the stone that cries out under the rightful king, which the Tuath Dè brought out of the north of the world and set up at Teamhair, is honoured as a power in its own right by the order of the Stone. The order holds that the Stone is one and its stones are many. Its first stone stood at the gate of Caol leathan (12 am Faoilleach, FE 1,009), and its second was dragged from the mountain to Inis thais (3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,217). Some read the name of the oldest king-list, Rìghrean na Cloiche, the kings of the stone (9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324), as the kings of this stone. The list itself does not say.

Manannan mac Lir is the lord of the sea, and the sea round Rodos is his, Muir Mhanannain. His mist hides the Otherworld, and the Ròdaich tell that the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it (19 an Giblean, LE 40). Until the Crossing the same mist hid Rodos from every ship beyond it. His Cup of Truth breaks in three when three lies are spoken over it, and three truths make it whole again. His order keeps the western coast, and its first seat is the western Seann Skell (1 an t-Sultain, LE 654).

Lugh Làmhfhada, Lugh of the long arm, is the master of every craft. Lùnastal is his feast, which he made in memory of his foster-mother Tailtiu. On it markets open, games are held and oaths are sworn before witnesses, and on the feast itself Cathal was crowned (1 an Lùnastal, DE 3).

Goibhniu is the smith of the gods. The smiths of the old vein country, where the forges of Muileann chrom, Muileann dhearg and Muileann dhomhain now make arms, swear by him. No smith on Rodos could place the nails of the timber that came ashore at Ceann mhòr from beyond Manannan's mist (22 an Cèitean, LE 1,794).

Dian Cècht is the healer of the gods, who made Nuadha's hand of silver. The springs of Muileann ruadh, where the sick of every rite are bathed (19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,863), are his.

The Morrìgan is the goddess of war and the crows. The battlefields are hers, among them the ford of Àth shean, where the custody-book counts three hundred dead (22 an Gearran, LE 554).

Ogma is the god of letters and of eloquence. The first Ròdaich letters, the stag-letters made from the cutters' tally-notches (15 am Màrt, FE 914), are the ogham, which the druids call his gift.

Nuadha is the first king of the gods, who lost his hand in battle and ruled again with the hand of silver that Dian Cècht made him. Ròdais still calls an artificial limb ball-airgid, silver-limb, after him.

Danu is the mother of the gods, and the Tuath Dè are named from her. She has no house; the tellings give her the rivers.

Donn is the lord of the dead. His house, Taigh Dhuinn, is a rock in the sea to the south-west, and the dead go to it. The Old Faith names him at Samhain and at every burial.

IV. The Four Feasts and the Otherworld

The feasts. Four feasts divide the year into quarters (Appendix D). They are older than any order now on the island, and all three faiths keep them in some fashion, each for its own reasons. The Old Faith keeps them as the island kept them before the Crossing, by the moon, each on the first night of its moon; the kingdom and the Church keep them on the first day of the civil month, and the two may fall as much as a fortnight apart.

  • Samhain, the first night of the moon Samhnas and 1 an t-Samhain in the civil calendar, is summer's end, and was the Ròdaich new year before the Crossing, when the Otherworld stands open and the dead are nearest. The Old Faith names Donn and the dead of the year. In the Holy Age the Hall filled the baskets of the Small-Burning Law at Samhain and the galleries closed.
  • Là Fhèill Brìde, or Imbolc, the first night of Gearras and 1 an Gearran, is Brìde's feast. Hearths are swept and relit, and Òrd Bhrìde lights its first lamp of the year from the altar-flame.
  • Bealltainn, the first night of Bealltach and 1 an Cèitean, is summer's beginning, the feast of the bright fire, when the cattle go up to the high pastures between two fires. The first sentence under the Small-Burning Law was given on Bealltainn itself (1 an Cèitean, FE 145).
  • Lùnastal, the first night of Lùghnas and 1 an Lùnastal, is Lugh's feast of first-fruits and gathering.

The Old Spirits keep the same four nights at the hearth and at the mounds, counting to them by nights as the old reckoning did, and the Church keeps the civil days as saints' days and the feasts of the Church's year.

The Otherworld. The Old Faith holds that the Otherworld lies west over the sea, behind Manannan's mist. Its tellings give it two names: Tìr nan Òg, the land of the young, where no one ages, and Magh Meall, the plain of delight. On the way to it, on its rock in the south-western sea, stands Taigh Dhuinn, the house of Donn, where the dead gather. The fleet of the Sundering sailed west into that mist (19 an Giblean, LE 40), and the saying at the empty-harbour rite, they went, and they did not go, is read in the light of it. When the humans came in from the same quarter of sea, old sailors at Cuan shean said so aloud, and the council forbade the remark (9 an Gearran, AE 2).

The sìth. Nearer home the Otherworld opens in the hills. The sìth, the mounds, belong to the sìthichean, the people of the mounds, whom the Old Spirits honour at the hearth and the Old Faith leaves alone.

V. An Creideamh Sean and Its Orders

The Old Faith is the faith of the gods, and it is kept in its orders. Each order has its houses, temples and custodians and its own history, and some have had schisms of their own. All of them honour an Dagda and keep the four feasts. They differ on the vein, on the measure and on which god stands nearest to it, and they have differed since the Holy Age. The druids of every order are trained in the schools or in the order's own houses. No single council speaks for the Old Faith as a whole.

Òrd Bhrìde

Òrd Bhrìde, the order of Brìde's flame, is the Hall of the Holy Age and the Obsidian Rite of the chronicle. It keeps Brìde's flame, bound at Dùn ìseal, and Crom's stone, the vein. In its settled form it is a teaching set in order within the Old Faith, where before there was only the scattered reverence of the hearths, and it is built about the leyline and the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched (18 an Giblean, SE 6). As an ordered body it is the youngest of the orders; as a rite it claims to be the oldest, and the claim is just. Its seat is at the southern Seann Skell, where its largest house stands (17 an Cèitean, SE 6). Its saying is the Law's own:

Làn an dà bhois, agus gun tuilleadh. The fill of the two palms, and no more.

It has nine towns, all in the south-east, and holds four shires: Seann Skell, Tobar dhearg, Muileann naomh and Àth fhionn. It has a third of Muileann dhomhain, and the Old Spirits hold the land on every side. The largest towns are Seann Skell, Tobar dhearg, Muileann naomh, Caol ruadh and Àth fhionn. The map marks five of its houses as temples: Seann Skell, Tobar dhearg, Muileann naomh, Baile gharbh on the coast road and Caol naomh, the pilgrims' landing. Muileann naomh was the southernmost house of the Hawk until it took the order of worship of Òrd Bhrìde (29 an Cèitean, SE 6). The order's history is given in section VIII.

Òrd an t-Seabhaig

What it holds. The Hawk order is the older form of Brìde's rite on the north coast. It teaches that the hawk of the vein is Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, who is as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra and remembers the ages with him, and who must be fed the measured handful and no more, "for a hawk overfed will not hunt and a hawk starved will turn on the hand" (20 an Giblean, LE 229). Too much ruins the hawk, and so does too little; the measure lies between. The Hawk holds, moreover, that the measure is the hawk's to keep, and no custodian's.

Rites and sayings. Each household feeds its hawk before it eats, and the handful is burned at dawn with the hawk on the wrist. The fowlers who began the rite gave its first saying (30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,999):

Is acras an lasair. The flame is a hunger.

Gormshuil's sayings were written down after her death as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist marked every saying he had not heard from her own mouth, and the marked outnumbered the rest (5 an t-Ògmhios, LE 251). The saying most often cut over hawk-house doors is:

Cha shealg seabhag sàthach. A sated hawk will not hunt.

Holy places. The oldest hawk carved on the island is over a door at Àth mhòr (13 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,176), and it is older than any rite. The rite itself began at the Seann Skell of the northern coast (Seann Skell). The first house of the order is at Cnoc bheag.

History. In the Holy Age the dawn-hawk spread along the north coast, and while it spread the Keeper wrote that it was no concern of the Hall's (28 am Faoilleach, FE 2,072). In time it was the first rite to refuse the Hall's measure-check outright (19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,840). The rite was old already when Gormshuil nic Artair gathered it at Cnoc bheag into its first house (20 an Giblean, LE 229), and from that day it was an order. A second house followed at Ros gheal (22 am Màrt, LE 239) and a southern one at Muileann naomh (13 an t-Sultain, LE 526), which is now a house of Òrd Bhrìde. The schism came when a council at Cnoc bheag split over whether Mòd's measure could ever be raised (20 an t-Ògmhios, LE 889). Those who called it fixed kept the name of the Hungry Hawk. The Fed Hawk were turned out to the northern Seann Skell (23 an Giblean, LE 909), and their petition to raise the handful by a quarter was the first recorded request to alter the Small-Burning Law (25 an Lùnastal, LE 919). It was refused, and after that the Fed Hawk are not heard of as a house of their own.

Under the humans the Hawk resisted before there was any ordered resistance for it to join. Murchadh Seabhag preached that Mòd starves those who eat faster than the land can feed them (6 an t-Sultain, AE 22), and his sermon was the first Ròdaich text the Company's agents were told to confiscate. When hawk-priests were barred from the camps (12 an t-Sultain, AE 38), the crews carried the sermons in themselves (10 an Cèitean, AE 76). Ìomhar Seabhag's shrines served as meeting houses for the Lamp-Watch (24 an Giblean, AE 140), and when the war came he called it Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who fed it (5 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150). In the Age of the Kingdom the Hawk houses refused the written order of worship of Òrd Bhrìde (23 an Cèitean, SE 6); only the far southern house at Muileann naomh took it (29 an Cèitean, SE 6). The others named their own custodian at Inis ìseal (26 an Cèitean, SE 35). They then wrote down their order, which until that day had been spoken and never written, and they keep the book locked away (23 an t-Samhain, SE 35). They accepted a place under the high custodian only on condition that they kept that order (13 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47). The quarrel with Òrd Bhrìde has grown quiet, but it is not ended.

Where it is held now. Fourteen towns, all Ròdaich, along the north-central coast and up the Abhainn ìseal. It holds Inis bhàn and Ros gheal. It is the greatest order, though with less than half the land, in Cnoc bheag, where Manannan's order and Macha's hold the rest, and in the northern Seann Skell, which it shares with the Old Spirits and Manannan's order. It also has a quarter of the northern Doire fhionn. Cnoc bheag is the largest, and its Hawk house is the richest house of any order outside the capital (14 an Dàmhair, SE 46). After it come Inis bhàn, Ros gheal, the northern Seann Skell and Ros leathan. The map marks eight of its houses as temples: Cnoc bheag, Inis bhàn, Ros gheal and the northern Seann Skell; Àth shean on the northern march (Àth shean); the Hawk mill of Muileann uaine and its field village Achadh fhada; and Inis ìseal, where the Hawk's own custodian sits.

Scoiltean nan Draoidhean

What it holds. The druid schools are the reasoning order of the Old Faith, and they call themselves by their oldest name, Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, the Philosophy of the Deer. They are schools more than a church. They gathered about one question, why the vein answers some hands and not others (10 an Dàmhair, FE 103), and they were the first within the Old Faith who reasoned about the obsidian as well as revering it. They do not deny that the vein is holy. They ask what its holiness does. Their patron is Flidais, lady of the deer and the wild, whose white stag walks in their sacred wood. In none of the schools' records kept in the Library is the stag, Camaran, worshipped, and his name is first found in writings much younger than the first schools (7 an Dùbhlachd, FE 118). The schools are counted among the orders of the Old Faith, and they have not objected.

Rites and sayings. Their one public observance is the yearly walking of the bounds of Flidais's wood (11 an t-Iuchar, LE 479). All else they do is argument. Their oldest question, as the masters put it to beginners, is:

Carson an làmh seo? Why this hand?

A student who thinks he has solved it is given Aonghas mac Coinnich's answer (19 an t-Ògmhios, AE 49):

Chan e sin a' cheist. That is not the question.

Holy places. Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, which was held sacred long before any order of the Old Faith laid claim to it (21 an Giblean, VE 3,420), and where the white stag was first seen (11 am Màrt, VE 3,532). The wood lies outside the schools' own country, among Old Spirits towns in the shire of Baile chaol, and the people of Cnoc uaine and Àth dhearg on its edge, who keep the ancestors, share its keeping. Dùn thais has the first stone temple of the stag's people (21 am Màrt, FE 2,889). Caol shean is the schools' house in the Age of the Kingdom.

Where it is held now. 133 towns, all Ròdaich, in the north-east and the eastern hills; the east coast itself belongs to the Old Spirits. The schools stand first in twenty-three shires, a block running from Tobar ghorm and Àth mhòr in the north through Caol bheag, Baile gharbh and Dùn thais to Caol shean, Muileann chiar and Muileann dhearg in the hills, and west to Baile Mòr dhomhain in the middle of the island. They share ten more, most of them with the Old Spirits along the line where the two faiths meet, and they have nearly half of Cnoc dhubh, Dùn ìseal and Cnoc gheal. The largest towns are Caol bheag, Baile gharbh, Dùn thais, Caol shean and Caol gharbh. The map marks sixteen of the schools' houses as temples, though the schools call them halls: among them Dùn thais, Caol shean, Caol bheag, Ros fhionn and the church villages whose chapels served the silver-miners and the old bridge. Muileann chaol, the library town, is a school town. The schools' history is given in section IX.

Òrd Mhacha

What it holds. Macha's order keeps "two horses, one yoke, light and dark two powers in balance, and the vein belonging to both" (31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 441). The wood-watchers held that their black beast has two natures, one that keeps and one that devours, and that the vein has the same two (13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,852); the order tells it of the two horses that drew one chariot, the black Dubh Sainglenn and the grey Liath Macha. It is the order of the capital and the court, and the kings of Rodos are made by its rite. Its oldest saying is the wood-watchers':

Tha dà nàdar aig a' bhèist, agus aig an fhèith. The beast has two natures, and so has the vein.

Its own saying is of the pair:

Dà each, aon chuing. Two horses, one yoke.

Rites and holy places. Its priests read omens for rulers and bury the dead by their own rite. King Aonghas mac Uisdein was the first king buried that way (31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 484). Its floors are laid in black and white, and the floor of its great house at Cathair mhòr took eleven years (14 am Màrt, LE 1,459). Its sacred wood is Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, near the lesser Cnoc bheag south of the capital (Cnoc bheag). That town is not the river port of the Hawk that bears the same name.

History. The order began as a watch. A small company settled at the edge of a wood no one had ever cleared and watched for a black horned beast that walked in it (15 an t-Samhain, FE 1,569), the beast the order takes for a sign of Dubh Sainglenn, the black horse. Its quarrel with the stag's people over both sacred woods became the holy-wood dispute, which was settled by dividing the keeping of the woods, and no side was named the winner (10 an Gearran, FE 1,589). Anna Ruadh took a wood-watcher into her household at Cathair dhearg to read the omens (23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,822). Cathair dhomhain refused one, and from that day the rivalry of the two towns has been a matter of faith as well (24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,826). Cathair dhomhain is a town of Macha's order now, with its own temple. The order took its settled form when King Aonghas took up the wood-watchers' rite of Macha (31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 441). By royal grant its priests then had sole keeping of the western wood, and the other claimants withdrew, for reasons that are not told (14 am Faoilleach, LE 471).

Under the humans it split over the Residency's coin. The priests at Cathair dhearg blessed it (24 an Gearran, AE 85). Those who refused went to the sacred forest, where they received custodians who had lost their seats (25 am Màrt, AE 87). Sixty years later the capital's temple sheltered the council that Strake had locked out (26 an Gearran, AE 147). In the forest the dissenters sat with custodians and the Lamp-Watch when the council of the mining regions was formed (20 an Lùnastal, AE 148). In the restored kingdom the house at Cathair dhearg got back the keeping of the regalia and refused Òrd Bhrìde a share of it (26 an Gearran, SE 7).

Where it is held now. 103 towns, all Ròdaich, across the middle and south of the island. It stands first in twenty-nine shires in one block, from the capital's own shire (Cathair dhearg) and its neighbours in the middle of the island south to Ros dhomhain, Cathair fhada and Doire fhiadhaich, and east to Cathair mhòr and Seann Chwen. Manannan's order holds more than a third of Cathair dhomhain, the shire of the capital's old rival, and in Baile ghlas the Stone holds most of the land, though the harbour town is Macha's. The largest towns are Ros dhomhain, Cathair mhòr, Àth shean, Seann Chwen and Baile ghlas. The map marks seventeen of its temples. Five are the great houses of Cathair mhòr, Cathair dhomhain, Cathair dhearg, Ceann leathan and Cuan uaine; the others are the priests' towns, such as Cathair naomh and Cnoc bhàn, where acolytes are trained for the capital's temples, and the chapels along the roads to the capital. Cnoc naomh, whose people once kept the old reverence "with no hawk, wolf, sting or stag in it" (16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,926), is a town of Macha's order on the map.

Òrd na Cloiche

What it holds. The order of the Stone holds that the Stone watches the whole island as a guard watches a road, and will cry out under the rightful king (21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,843). The Stone is Lia Fàil, and its sworn guards are the Fianna, "who keep the island as a wolf keeps its range" (28 am Màrt, LE 409). The Stone's plain name is Clach, the common word for stone. The first stone was a white stone carved as a wolf at the gate of Caol leathan, on which the road-guards swore their watch, and later ages read more into it than the road-guards ever did (12 am Faoilleach, FE 1,009). The tales of Fionn and his Fianna are the order's own. The Stone is not known ever to have claimed the vein. When Òrd Bhrìde was set in order, the houses of the Stone sent no witnesses, only "a letter wishing it well" (2 an Gearran, SE 7).

Rites and sayings. Oaths are taken before the Stone. The houses of the Stone nurse the sick. At Inis chrom the Fianna died of it, and thereafter the town was the Stone's (3 an t-Sultain, LE 624). Its saying comes from the road-guards:

Mar a ghleidheas am freiceadan an rathad, gleidhidh Clach an t-eilean. As the guard keeps the road, Clach keeps the island.

Holy places. Caol leathan, whose house of the Stone is the largest of the order and rings a bell for the hours (7 an Cèitean, SE 21); Inis thais, where a second stone of white quartz was dragged from the mountain (3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,217) and the first temple to Lia Fàil by name was built (16 an Dùbhlachd, LE 419); and Baile gheal.

History. The wolf-sworn were soldiers before they were an order. The order took its form when Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, preached that their stone was Lia Fàil and its guards the Fianna (28 am Màrt, LE 409). Its schism was over the dead. Those who would not pray to the Stone for the dead kept the temple at Inis thais, and those who would built a house at Baile gheal (25 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,389, 8 an Lùnastal, LE 1,399). Of any reconciling of the two houses nothing is told. In the Age of the Kingdom the houses of the Stone have served as banks as well as churches. They issued chits on house paper when coin ran short (3 am Màrt, SE 6) and lent the money for Doire shean's harbour (24 an t-Ògmhios, SE 30). They also published a count of their own people that matched the kingdom's to within a hundred (28 an Lùnastal, SE 65).

Where it is held now. 21 towns, all Ròdaich, in the south-west. It holds six shires outright, Doire shean, Inis chrom, Baile ghorm, Caol fhiadhaich, Cnoc àrsaidh and Baile gheal, and most of Caol leathan and Baile ghlas. In Inis thais, the shire of its chief shrine, Manannan's order holds three-fifths of the land. The Stone also has a share of Seann Dunn, Baile chiar and Seann Warr, where Seann Warr is a town of the Stone in Manannan's country. The largest are Doire shean, Inis thais, Inis chrom, Baile ghorm and Seann Warr. The map marks temples in eight of its towns: Inis thais, still the chief shrine of the order, Caol leathan, Baile gheal, Doire shean, Inis chrom, Caol fhiadhaich, Baile Mòr fhionn and Cnoc àrsaidh, which holds the oldest shrines of the Stone.

Òrd Mhanannain

What it holds. Manannan's order holds that the lord of the sea sees the liar wherever he is, and that his Cup of Truth breaks at the lies spoken over it and is whole again at the truth; the yellow scorpion is the old sign on the Cup, and the order's badge. It was the first teaching on the island that called itself the only true one (3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,846). Its central teaching is about the sea: Manannan shut the western sea behind the fleet of the Sundering with his mist, which hid the island from every ship beyond it, and it must not be tried again (1 an t-Sultain, LE 654). The order keeps the sea shut by prayer. Its priests recorded the mist thinning in the last years of the Age of Sundering (27 an Dàmhair, LE 1,813), and it lifted in the winter the humans' ships came out of it (13 am Faoilleach, AE 1). They held the Crossing to be the price of a prayer grown slack. When no ship came from the west after the Severance, and the council's ship found only open water, they said the lord of the sea had shut the sea again (11 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3).

Rites and sayings. Oaths of trade were first sworn on a scorpion's sting kept in a box (19 an t-Samhain, FE 879). Since the sting-oath became a creed they have been sworn over a cup marked with the scorpion, Manannan's Cup of Truth. No boat of the faithful may go out of sight of the headlands, and on the west coast steering by the stars was lost entirely (27 an t-Samhain, LE 694). At the harbour mouth the priests pray (13 an Giblean, LE 1,590):

A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte. Manannan, keep the sea shut.

Since LE 1,714 that prayer has been said on the day of the empty-harbour rite. So on one quay, on one day, some mourn the departed and some pray that no one follows them. Neither side is pleased.

Holy places. Seann Skell in the west (Seann Skell), where the teaching was declared; Baile àrsaidh, where the sting-oath began; and Seann Vell, which has the first scorpion carved in yellow stone for worship (4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,849).

History. The sting-oath went from Baile àrsaidh up the coast to Ros bheag (1 am Faoilleach, FE 2,145) and became a creed at Seann Skell. The order took its form when Mànas mac Ruairidh named its power Manannan mac Lir (1 an t-Sultain, LE 654). A worked timber longer than any tree on the island, held with nails no smith on Rodos could place, came ashore at Ceann mhòr. It was carried to Seann Skell, shown to Manannan's priests, and burned (22 an Cèitean, LE 1,794). This was twenty-five years before the humans came. The first human fishing families on the north-west coast learned the order's harbour prayers at Ceann mhòr (14 am Màrt, AE 51), and its priests there say the Grey Night grew from them (section VII). In the Age of the Kingdom the house at Seann Bhral turned away the Tuathaich of the north who came for its feast of the sea, and the northerners made a feast of their own at Cnoc ghorm (2 an t-Sultain, SE 25, 11 an Gearran, SE 26); that quarrel is told with the Church. On the eve of the Long War Manannan's house at Seann Skell refused to bless the enforcers' depot (23 am Faoilleach, DE 19). In the present year its priests said the prayer to keep the sea shut on the day the first dubhan was shipped off the island under Dubhan's charter (7 an t-Sultain, DE 27).

Where it is held now. 35 towns, all Ròdaich, on the west coast. Its seat, the western Seann Skell, is the largest town on Rodos. It stands first in eight shires in the west, from Muileann naomh and Baile fhiadhaich south through Seann Skell, Ros bheag and Baile àrsaidh to Cuan shean and the Stone's holy shire of Inis thais, with Seann Warr inland. It also has more than a third of Cnoc bheag and Cathair dhomhain in the middle of the island and a quarter of Caol leathan. The map marks eleven of its houses as temples; besides the holy places above they include Ros bheag and the western Seann Bhral. After Seann Skell its largest towns are Cuan shean and Baile fhiadhaich.

VI. Na Seann Spioradan

What it holds. The Old Spirits keep the reverence of the hearths as it was before the Hall: "reverence for the ancestors, for the vein, for the weather that rules the mining season" (17 am Faoilleach, FE 21). The chronicle calls it the oldest custom on the island that has never been broken. It has no priests, no order of worship and no council. Its powers, as the map gives them, are na Sìthichean, the people of the mounds, and its tellings speak of the ancestors, the sìth of the hills and mounds, and the spirits of weather, wells and streams, not of any one power over them. The gods belong to the Old Faith. When the hearths first gave the powers of the mounds that name, or who first gave it, is not known.

Rites and sayings. The living heads of families name their ancestors aloud. The names of the dead are cut on wooden posts, which are recut each generation as the old ones rot (7 an Dàmhair, LE 179). The faith keeps the walk to Allt an Àigh as its own, and after the Keepers declined the stream it took Muireach Liath's ruling for its saying:

Buinidh an t-allt do na sinnsearan agus don t-sìde. The stream belongs to the ancestors and to the weather.

The old night-count is kept at its hearths: a journey, a mourning or a guest's stay is reckoned in nights, and the dead are waked for three nights (Appendix D). It blesses what comes from the vein, and nothing else. When copper was found behind Àth fhiadhaich, the town's Seann Spioradan house held no blessing for it (28 an Lùnastal, SE 60).

Holy places.
