Dùn ìseal and its spirit-house; Seann Dunn, where the east-coast houses built a common hall for naming the ancestors of forty families (28 an Dàmhair, SE 22); Allt an Àigh, which lies in the schools' country behind Caol shean, with the walkers' hall at Achadh gharbh, a school village (11 an Gearran, SE 11); and Làrach an Teampaill, which at the houses' request was entered by the library as "measured and let be" (7 an Dàmhair, SE 31).

History. By the end of the Holy Age the Hall's list counted the old folk as "a company of its own" (16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,926). In the Age of Sundering they built a guest-house at the stream, and its book records pilgrims from every shire (10 an t-Samhain, LE 1,259). Under the humans this was the first faith to refuse the Company's ore on grounds of belief. The households of Achadh naomh burned peat, and their elders taught "that ore burned for wages is burned without the ancestors' leave" (16 am Màrt, AE 23). In the Long Drought the Administration's watchman at Allt an Àigh, posted to charge pilgrims for the water, was recalled after one season (1 an Cèitean, AE 108). In the Age of the Kingdom the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde discouraged the walk and did not forbid it (8 an t-Iuchar, SE 10).

Where it is held now. 126 towns, all Ròdaich, and more land than any single order of the Old Faith. It holds thirty-four shires: the whole south-east, from Seann Bhral and Achadh mhòr to Baile ghorm and Ceann mhin; the east coast from Ceann leathan north through Seann Tarr and Achadh shean to Baile ruadh; the hills round Dùn ìseal, where the schools hold nearly as much (Dùn ìseal, Cnoc dhubh, Cnoc dhìreach); and a band of the north coast between the Hawk and the schools, from Baile Mòr mhòr and Seann Bhrenn to Seann Toll and Caol ìseal. It has a share of eleven more, among them Muileann bheag, which it divides almost evenly with the schools. The largest are Seann Bhral, Achadh mhòr, Baile Mòr mhòr, Muileann bhàn, Achadh naomh and Dùn dhearg. The map marks temples in twenty-four of its towns, more than for any single order. The chief are Dùn ìseal, Seann Dunn, Seann Tarr, whose shrine draws the whole north-east at the great feasts, and Cathair naomh, whose elders the shrine-keepers of the north answer to. The rest are the shrines of wells, springs, fords and holy woods, and the houses of the largest towns.

VII. An Eaglais

What it holds. The Church is the faith the humans brought over the sea at the Crossing (5 am Faoilleach, AE 1). It holds that there is one God, Dia, and that Crìosd, Christ, is his son. Its book is am Bìoball, the Bible. Its clergy are sagairt and ministearan, priests and ministers, under easbaigean, bishops; it has had manaich, monks, and it keeps the days of its naoimh, its saints. On Rodos it is the faith of the human labourers and the Residency in the Age of Strangers, and of the Tuathaich, their descendants, since. It brought the week with it, and keeps it: its day of rest is Didòmhnaich, the Lord's day, and its fasts from meat are on Diciadain and Dihaoine, which take their names from them. Its feasts fall on their days in the civil calendar, and it has never kept the moon (Appendix D).

The Mission. The Church came to the Ròdaich as the Mission. It raised a timber chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain, the first church on the island (30 an Dùbhlachd, AE 13), and ran a school there that taught Ròdach children in the humans' tongue (9 an Cèitean, AE 51). Samuel Wren made his grammar of Ròdais for its use (21 an Lùnastal, AE 12), and the hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag asked it for a copy (4 an t-Iuchar, AE 13). The Mission kept lists of the dead in the camps, and the custodians wrote their own count in its margins (11 an Dàmhair, AE 39). Samuel Wren asked the masters of the schools why the vein should be holy, and they asked him why his fuel should be burned (3 an Dùbhlachd, AE 18). The Mission's house in the north was at Cathair gheal.

The churches of the north. Most Tuathaich towns keep the Church their forebears brought at the Crossing, in the line the Mission left, while the Ròdaich of the west coast beside them keep Manannan's order (30 am Màrt, SE 9). How the churches of the Mission's line came to outnumber the older congregations of the north coast is not told. Their largest house is at Cnoc ghorm. It opened a school for its priests that taught in the humans' tongue and read the Bible in the Ròdais text its preachers use on the west coast; it is the only place in the north where both are taught (29 an Giblean, SE 10). In the early Age of the Kingdom the northerners came south to the feast of the sea at Seann Bhral, as their forebears had learned to from the Ròdaich harbours. The house of Manannan's order there turned them away, and its keeper said "the sea is the same and the house is not" (2 an t-Sultain, SE 25). They kept the feast at the church at Cnoc ghorm instead, as a blessing of the boats, and within a generation it was the larger of the two (11 an Gearran, SE 26).

These churches hold 51 towns. They hold seven shires in the north-west, Cnoc ghorm, Ceann mhòr, Cnoc thais, Muileann àrsaidh and Baile ìseal, and on the north coast Caol mhòr and Àth àrsaidh. The map marks eight of their houses as temples, among them Cnoc ghorm and Cathair gheal. Their largest towns are Caol mhòr, the Moot's town, Ceann mhòr and Cnoc ghorm.

Eaglais nan Tuathach and the voyage of Naomh Breandan. The old congregations of the north coast keep the Church in their own way (13 an Gearran, SE 9), and among their ways, quietly kept, is the telling of the First Canoe, the voyage of Naomh Breandan to the Isle of the Blessed, which the Ròdaich priests still call superstition. Beyond this almost nothing is known of them, and what is known comes from outside. Few Tuathaich would speak to the chronicle clerks (25 am Màrt, SE 19); the north's books stayed in private keeping (3 an Lùnastal, SE 67); and the request that Tuathaich memory be kept in the Library was laid on the table, neither granted nor refused, and it lies there still (15 an Gearran, DE 17). Their rites and their sayings are not known here, nor how far they differ from the churches of the Mission's line. Of their holy places three are known, the houses the map marks as temples: Doire ghlas, called the heart of the Church in the north, whose keepers are said to hold the First Canoe fragment and have not let the library copy it; Muileann leathan; and Cill chaol, a Ròdaich chapel village whose chapel the Tuathaich made a church, leaving the old carvings on its doorposts beside their own.

The only one of their tellings known outside the north is the fragment its tellers set in the Ancient Age: "a steersman with a name, and a first crossing" (9 an t-Samhain, VE 2,851). The steersman is Naomh Breandan, Saint Brendan the Navigator of the humans' Church, who sailed west from an Tìr Thall in a boat of hides to the Isle of the Blessed, and the north's tellers say that isle was Rodos. His name is in no Ròdaich record. In his voyage there is a mist on the sea and an island of the blessed in the west, as there is in the Ròdaich tellings of Manannan's sea; the Library notes the likeness and draws nothing from it. How families whose forebears came over the water in AE 1 came to keep the telling of a crossing set so long before the Sundering, no one has explained. It is left here where its tellers set it; the north keeps it still in the present day (21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27).

The old congregations hold twelve towns, all Tuathaich, along the north. They hold three shires, Doire ghlas, Muileann leathan and the island shire of Eilean dhìreach off the coast to the west of them, and have a share of six more, among them the land west of Baile chrom on the north-western cape, a quarter of Àth àrsaidh and a sixth of Inis mhin and Caol mhòr. The largest are Doire ghlas, Muileann leathan, Inis mhin and Baile ghlas in Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh (Baile ghlas).

Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise. Of the Mystery of the Grey Night four things are known: its name, its goose, one custom and one town. The goose is Sìne, an Gèadh Sìtheil, the Peaceful Goose, the keepers' name for an Gèadh Fiadhaich, the wild goose of the Holy Spirit. The custom is "one night of silence in the year", a vigil, and outsiders are not told which night it is (14 am Màrt, SE 9). No saying is known.

The vigil first appears in a Mission report that human labourers near Baile chrom were keeping a vigil at night in the fields, praying in silence under the sign of a grey goose, which they called the wild goose of the Spirit (28 an Lùnastal, AE 133). The Mission called it irregular, a superstition learned from the Ròdaich, and the Ròdaich of Baile chrom disowned it. Manannan's priests at Ceann mhòr said the Mission was half right. The first human fishing families on that coast had settled at Ceann mhòr (14 am Màrt, AE 51) and learned Manannan's night prayer to keep the sea shut there, and the labourers inland kept it as a Christian vigil, a night of silence under the wild goose of the Spirit instead of a prayer to Manannan. The priests called it Manannan's prayer gone astray and would not have its keepers in their house (21 an Dàmhair, AE 133). The Church's bishops call the vigil irregular and have not put it down. From the Ancient Age there is a telling of the grey geese that winter on Eilean ghorm and are never hunted there (3 an Lùnastal, VE 3,812); no one has shown that the two are joined, and it is not claimed here. After the Severance the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane held the vigil openly (14 am Màrt, SE 9). A magistrate fined her, and the vigil moved indoors (15 an t-Ògmhios, SE 27). The keeper of Taigh-solais Baile chrom reported that the vigil was kept in the lighthouse's shadow (27 an Giblean, SE 32). In the Long War soldiers searched the town on a night when it lay wholly dark and silent, and found nothing (9 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21).

The vigil holds one town, Baile chrom in the far north-west (Baile chrom), and with it the whole of its shire (Baile chrom) and a tenth of Ceann mhòr next door. It is not the Baile chrom in the hills (Baile chrom), and the rolls take care to keep the two apart (11 an Gearran, AE 74).

Where the Church is held now. 64 towns, every Tuathaich town on the map, and eleven shires, all in the north and north-west. It has a share of five more: a quarter of Seann Skell and of Seann Vell, a sixth of Inis mhin, and smaller parts of Baile fhiadhaich and Muileann naomh. The map marks twelve of its churches as temples.

VIII. Of the Obsidian Rite

The Rite is older than any name it has borne. Its root is the slab over the crack and the handful in the cup. What the chronicle calls the Obsidian Rite, and the Old Faith calls Òrd Bhrìde, is the part of the old reverence that holds the vein itself to be sacred. The vein is Crom's, and Brìde's flame is lit from what it gives; yet the Rite does not hold it to be the token of a god or the dwelling of a spirit. It is itself the holy thing.

The vein as sacred. The Rite holds that the vein bleeds because it is alive, in some fashion the Ròdaich are not asked to understand. What is broken from it must be burned in measure or returned. The vein answers a line of people, and that answering is itself holy. The doctrine of SE 6 is "built upon the leyline and the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched" (18 an Giblean, SE 6): the vein under the ground and the blood of those it has answered. Fionnghal nic Artair's defence of the Small-Burning Law, the only one that survives, argued that "the Law was never for the ore's sake but for the people, who would become whatever the burning made them" (11 an t-Ògmhios, AE 22). She wrote it two generations before Aisling was born, and it has been read as prophecy since; she made no such claim herself.

Under the Keepers. In the Holy Age the Rite belonged to the Hall. The Keepers held the cup, took the census of hands (22 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,735) and sentenced households that burned beyond the measure (1 an Cèitean, FE 145). Their roll holds one hundred and forty names (2 an Giblean, FE 2,939).

Under the vein-house. Each ship of the Sundering carried one sealed measure of ore and no more (17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 25). The vein-house above Muileann dhearg kept the custody-book, and in LE 859 the crown and the custody were joined. The Rite's worst hour in that age came in war. Raghnall Ruadh, holding the vein-house, refused the handful to every hearth in the shires that stood against him, "and this deed turns more against him than any battle" (24 am Faoilleach, LE 558). The council refused the Fed Hawk's petition, and refused Clann Choinnich leave to smelt silver with the ore (31 an Lùnastal, LE 1,559), which was the first time any asked to burn the ore for work and not for worship.

Under the humans. The Small-Burning Law was never repealed; it lapsed when it no longer paid anyone to enforce it (2 an Dùbhlachd, AE 21). The Rite lived on in shrines at the pit mouths. At Cill dhìreach the crews left the first piece of ore from each new gallery, and the Company allowed it, "for it costs a stone a gallery" (19 an t-Sultain, AE 72). At Cill ghlas the custodians kept the rites at the mouth of the oldest cutting (18 an Dàmhair, AE 72). They agreed the word fuil-ghuail there (21 an Gearran, AE 126), and the Rending swallowed that shrine (3 an t-Iuchar, AE 137).

The Rite set in order. The Rite was given its settled form on 18 an Giblean, SE 6. Dòmhnall mac Thormoid was seated at the southern Seann Skell as Àrd-choimheadaiche, and his first charge was a written order of worship: "there had never been one" (17 an Cèitean, SE 6). The Hawk refused the order and the Stone stood aside. When the council kept the night shift, the custodians "enter a protest, and then bless the shafts" (18 an t-Samhain, SE 11). So the Rite has done ever since: it protests at the kingdom's use of the vein, and then it blesses it.

The Depletion. The high custodian ruled that dubhan was "not forbidden, since it is not ore, and not blessed, since it is not ore" (25 an t-Samhain, DE 4). When the beacons were converted (22 an Cèitean, DE 6), the obsidian flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg was carried to Seann Skell and left to burn out on the altar (19 an t-Iuchar, DE 6). When the coinage seal lost its obsidian ink, the high custodian protested. The council replied that the kingdom had never said it held the vein sacred (31 an t-Iuchar, DE 15).

The Rite now. One face of the Sloc Mòr is kept open under the Rite's custody (17 an Cèitean, DE 26). Twelve hewers work it, the last of their trade (15 an t-Ògmhios, DE 26). On 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27, they cut the year's altar-ore. It filled four baskets, and the high custodian divided it among the houses by lot.

That is why Òrd Bhrìde holds only nine towns. Most Ròdaich who hold the vein sacred keep it at the hearth, as the Old Spirits do, or at the local altar, as the Hawk does. In name the Rite is the right faith of them all; in only nine towns is it the whole of their practice. It was set in order after the vein had begun to fail. In less than a century it went from an order of worship for the whole island to four baskets of ore.

IX. Of the Schools' Question

Carson an làmh seo?

The druid schools began with one question, asked at Muileann chiar in the Holy Age: why does the vein answer some hands and not others (10 an Dàmhair, FE 103)? Some have made much of the nearness of fèidh, deer, to fèith, vein. The schools' own writings make nothing of it.

Forbidden and allowed. The Hall shut the galleries to the stag's people, "holding that a question asked of the vein is a demand made of it" (18 an Cèitean, FE 125). They were later let back in on an oath "to ask nothing of the vein aloud" (26 an Gearran, FE 574). The Hall called it a reconciliation, and the schools a truce. Long after, the stag's people made the first Ròdaich letters out of the cutters' tally-notches (15 am Màrt, FE 914), the letters the schools call ogham, and nearly every later hand on the island descends from them.

Birth or effort. Apprentices kept strike-books, written accounts of every blow (23 am Màrt, FE 1,641). Reading them, Donnchadh mac Iain found that the ore bled brighter for older cutters, whatever house they came from (28 an Gearran, FE 2,290). There followed a parting of the schools. A school broke away holding that the vein answers to effort and not to birth (7 an t-Sultain, FE 2,317); and over that same question, in another shape and many centuries later, the Long War was fought. The breakaway school at Muileann chaol did not write a cutter's parentage in the book at all (9 an Lùnastal, FE 2,330). The Keeper Raonaid Dhubh heard both schools and gave no ruling, "saying that the vein has not asked the Hall to decide" (4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,366).

The years of disputation. At Dùn thais the question was argued by rule (29 an Cèitean, LE 314). Eilidh Dhubh's tracts for the effort-school were read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east (23 an t-Ògmhios, LE 484). Then Raghnall mac Chaluim showed that the heads of the custodian houses lived a few years longer than their tenants, and asked whether the vein answers the hand that holds it (29 an t-Samhain, LE 1,209). The house was later reopened only on condition that the question of longer lives was not raised (20 an Giblean, LE 1,759). His table was made nearly seven hundred years before the first of the immortal generation was born.

Under the humans. Samuel Wren asked the masters why the vein should be holy, and they asked him why his fuel should be burned (3 an Dùbhlachd, AE 18). Aonghas mac Coinnich asked why the humans cannot see the colour in broken ore, and said it was the wrong question (19 an t-Ògmhios, AE 49). Tolley closed the hall at Dùn thais (14 an Dùbhlachd, AE 89). The last public disputation asked whether a question may be forbidden, and the Administration's clerk recorded that it may (30 an Giblean, AE 90). After that the masters taught under the trees (15 an t-Ògmhios, AE 90), until the last of them died in AE 123.

The revival. The schools reopened in SE 46, when the vein itself began to run short and their question was all at once pressing again. Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain lectured in the sacred wood (11 an Dùbhlachd, SE 46), and the schools took a house at Caol shean, where students debated the census note on the obsidian-touched openly (5 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47). When the Mine Board searched for a second vein, she wrote that "no one has asked why there is one vein" (13 an Giblean, SE 51). The Board filed her letter, and the search found nothing (21 an Giblean, SE 51). The schools' own word for their revival is dubhan-tùsail (22 an Dàmhair, DE 11).

What the question has come to. In the Holy Age it asked whether the ore bled for birth or for practice. In the Age of Sundering it asked whether the vein lengthened lives. Under the humans it asked why the humans could not see the colour. Since AE 126, when the custodians agreed a plain word for what the vein had begun to do to a few children, the answer has had a name but no reason. The masters do not say that their question brought on the Long War, and no one has laid it to their charge. They say only that it was asked in the Holy Age, and has not been answered.

Appendix C — Hosts, Wars and Calamities

Here are gathered out of the annals every war and armed struggle of which they tell, the hosts that stand on the map today, and the calamities that have fallen on the island, whether they came from the sea, the ground, the weather or the vein. Nothing is added that the annals do not hold. Where the annals disagree, the entries are given as they stand; where the record is sealed, or was never made, that is said, and no more.

Much is missing, and the reader should know how much. The Ancient Age cut its dead on tally stones and did not say what killed them. The Age of Sundering left two histories of its wars, and one was written to praise a king. For the Age of Strangers the custodians' rolls, the Mission's lists and the Residency's letter-books seldom agree in their numbers. The complete record of the Long War is sealed at Leabharlann Muileann chaol until the fifty years run out (14 am Faoilleach, DE 24).

Part I. The Wars

Before the wars

The oldest deed of force that is remembered was no war, and who did it is not known. On 29 an Dàmhair, VE 3,980, the single gate of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire was blocked with rubble from the inside, by people who left by another way or did not leave. More than a century later the cistern of Làrach an Dùin, which had served four hundred people, was found choked with the bones of whole cattle (4 an Giblean, VE 4,092). Both were works of the Seann-Dhaoine. What was fought over there, and by whom, no chronicler has ventured to guess.

The first war in either of the oral king-lists is the salt-flats raid. On 9 am Faoilleach, VE 5,995, Mòrag Chruaidh, fifth of the Stone Kings, led the hill-folk down to the salt-pans at Baile ghorm and carried the salt away. Seven of the hill side died, and the telling keeps the number. Her successor Iain Dubh went down to repeat the raid and was killed on the shingle (8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 6,050). The list says only that he was brought home. After him no war is remembered in the Ancient Age.

The War of the Roads

Cause. In the Holy Age the carriers' road ran from the mountain to the sea, and its tolls went to the rìgh of Dùn dhearg. Lachlann Ciar, head of the leading family of the harbour town of Caol leathan, began to keep the southern tolls for himself and send none of them to Dùn dhearg (14 an Gearran, FE 991). Iain Garbh, son of Sìleas Dhonn, took the hall at Dùn dhearg and demanded the western tolls, and Lachlann Ciar sent him back a basket of fish-bones (12 an Cèitean, FE 994).

Sides. On the one side stood Iain Garbh of Dùn dhearg, with the road-guards and the lowland levies; on the other Lachlann Ciar and the men of Caol leathan. The Hall at Dùn ìseal refused to bless either side.

Course. On 13 an Giblean, FE 999, Iain Garbh marched west and burned the toll-house at Muileann òg, which Lachlann Ciar's people had taken. The annals call this the first war between Ròdaich and Ròdaich. At the ford of Àth fhiadhaich the men of Caol leathan held Iain Garbh's levies for a day before they gave way (21 an Dàmhair, FE 1,001). Forty lay dead of the two sides together, and long afterward the carriers called it the ford of the forty. Falling back, Lachlann Ciar's men burned Baile ghlas so that the levies would find no grain there (16 am Faoilleach, FE 1,002). Its people walked to Cathair dhomhain, and many never came home. Baile chiar shut its gate against both armies and fed the burned-out people of Baile ghlas through the winter (18 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,003). Neither side forgave it, and neither attacked it. Iain Garbh then closed Caol leathan from the landward side for a season, but its boats brought in fish and he could not close the harbour. His levies drifted home for the harvest, and the siege ended without an assault (2 an t-Samhain, FE 1,005).

End. The two leaders met under the roof of the waypoint house that would later be called Am Buabhall Fortanach, where by the road-peace neither of them could draw (4 an Dàmhair, FE 1,006). Caol leathan kept half its tolls and sent the other half to Dùn dhearg, and Lachlann Ciar swore to the Law with the Keeper as witness. So the war ended in a house built to feed carriers. Muileann òg was rebuilt as a market town, and from its fair came Fèill Muileann òg (5 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,665).

Lesser strife of the Holy Age

The Silver Feud (17 an t-Sultain, FE 1,746) was a closing of the roads, and no war. For three seasons no silver left Muileann chiar. The road-guards went unpaid and the eastern tolls went uncollected. It has always been called a feud, though no one was killed in it. At sea, outlaw boats from the eastern islets began raiding the fishing strands. Sliochd Raghnaill armed its boats at Seann Tarr and burned two of them (10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,455), and the rest were never caught. Late in the age raiders from the north-western waters took a season's dried fish from the north-western strands. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag paid for two armed boats to watch the shore, and the raiders moved north (28 an Gearran, FE 2,747).

The War of the Three Claimants

Cause. King Tormod Bàn's two sons were drowned together when a ferry overturned on Abhainn fhionn (18 an t-Ògmhios, LE 534). The king died at Cathair dhearg without naming an heir (8 an t-Sultain, LE 547), and three claims were laid before the houses at once.

Sides. The claimants were Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais, the late king's niece; Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain, his half-brother; and Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house above Muileann dhearg (21 an Giblean, LE 552). The seven houses divided among the three. Seann Warr, the western port nearest the capital, shut its gates to all three and declared for none (20 an Cèitean, LE 553). It was twice besieged in the war, and taken by neither claimant.

Course. Dùghall's host broke Raghnall's at the ford of Àth shean on 22 an Gearran, LE 554. The custody-book counts some three hundred dead, the most of them drowned in the ford. Raghnall's men burned Doire mhin and its granary as they fell back (24 an t-Sultain, LE 555), and the villagers spent the winter at Cathair mhòr on the charity of Macha's priests. Catrìona besieged Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and took it after forty days, when the dead of the siege lines had poisoned its wells (26 an Dùbhlachd, LE 557). She let the garrison go free on their oath. Raghnall, who held the vein-house, then refused the measured handful of ore to every hearth and temple in the shires that stood against him (24 am Faoilleach, LE 558). Hearths that had burned ore for generations went cold. By the judgement of the annals this deed turned more against him than any battle did. Catrìona and Dùghall joined their hosts against him and met Raghnall below Muileann chrom on 14 am Faoilleach, LE 560. Raghnall was killed on the field, and his own custodians opened the vein-house the next day.

End. Catrìona was crowned at Cathair dhearg on 13 am Màrt, LE 562 and was known afterward as Catrìona Bhuadhach. The war had lasted some ten years. Her first great law bound the custodians themselves: no claimant, house or king could withhold the handful from a lawful hearth (12 an Gearran, LE 565). Seann Warr's neutral gates were later honoured by the crown (11 an Giblean, LE 594). Seònaid nic Coinnich's Book of the Three Claimants (8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 624) is the oldest history on Rodos told as a single tale, and not as a list of entries.

The sea-thieves of the north-west

Boats working out of the small islands off the north-west coast began to take fish and grain from coasting traders (24 am Faoilleach, LE 784). The thieves were Ròdaich, men of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls give some of their names. A force sent by Queen Eilidh Bhàn landed on Eilean dhubh and burned their boats on the strand (27 an t-Samhain, LE 801). Their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, was taken to Cathair dhearg and hanged.

The Brothers' War, Cogadh nam Bràithrean

Cause. King Ailean mac Raghnaill died at Cathair dhearg leaving two sons by different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, and each of them had been told that he was the heir (7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,266).

Sides. The seven houses divided four to three between the brothers.

Course. Alasdair Bàn's men seized Cnoc naomh, and Iain Ciar took it back on 8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,270. The war is named from that battle. Alasdair's ships burned the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother, taking the rope stores and the granary, and the town had to beg its bread from Cathair mhòr (17 an Lùnastal, LE 1,272). Iain Ciar defeated Alasdair below Muileann ghlas on 19 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,274. Alasdair was taken alive, and his captains were allowed to go home.

End. The brothers made peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on neutral ground between their lands (12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,276). Alasdair gave up his claim and was given the lordship of Seann Chwen for life. Iain Ciar was crowned. Alasdair kept the peace until his death (8 an Dàmhair, LE 1,291), and his lordship went back to the crown. Iain Ciar, having seen Ceann mhin beg for bread, ordered every shire seat to keep a year's grain in store against the next war (20 an Giblean, LE 1,299). The only surviving account of the war was written by his clerk Pàdraig mac Ruairidh (14 an Lùnastal, LE 1,304). It praises the king at every turn, and later readers have found it a trial.

The humans' campaigns and the forerunners of war

For the most part of the Age of Strangers the humans made war only at sea. Raiders stripped a Company brig off the north-west coast (10 an Giblean, AE 16) and burned an ore ship off the east (20 an Dàmhair, AE 46). The Company's first armed reply was a gunboat that burned every boat on the shingle of a cove near Ceann leathan (25 an t-Iuchar, AE 47). Most of them belonged to the town's own fishermen, and the raiders were not found.

On land the Administration kept no standing force until Charles Merriman brought a company of armed constables (24 an Lùnastal, AE 132). They broke the dockers' strike at Ros dhomhain (1 an Giblean, AE 134). After the Rending the roll tells of the first bloodshed between the two peoples (17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 137), which its fuller entry sets at Muileann chrom (13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 137): a gallery drowned seven when the pumps were stopped to save fuel, the crews stoned the Company's agent, and the constables fired. Four Ròdaich and one constable died. Merriman answered the second petition by tripling the constabulary and fortifying the stores of four mining towns (25 an Gearran, AE 140). The roadside houses became waypoints for a militia with no name (9 an t-Sultain, AE 141). The first stoppage held in concert across the pits was broken by the closing of the Company stores (30 an Dùbhlachd, AE 143). After the confiscation edict (25 an Giblean, AE 147) the silver guild began buying rifles from the eastern pirates (21 an t-Iuchar, AE 148), a council for the mining regions met in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag (20 an Lùnastal, AE 148), and Strake ordered its arrest (3 am Faoilleach, AE 149).

The War of the Hills

Here it is called the War of the Hills, after the country where it began. Later rolls call it the Severance war, after the manner of its ending.

Cause. On 20 an Gearran, AE 149, the Ròdaich of several mining regions rose together for the first time, and grievance became open war. The grievances are those told above, and the one most often named is the confiscation edict.

Sides. With the Ròdaich stood the council of custodians and crew-leaders under Eilidh nic Raghnaill, with the crews of the camps, the Lamp-Watch, the silver guild of Muileann chiar and its riflemen, the riflemen of Cnoc leathan (1 an Gearran, AE 150), the company of the Hawk order's faithful mustered at Seann Skell (8 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150), and the towns that declared for the council one after another. With the Administration stood Commissioner Strake, the constabulary, the Company's guards, and the Company's steamships and coasters. Some towns held aloof. The human town of Cathair gheal shut its gates and raised a militia that it sent to neither side (24 an Cèitean, AE 150). The concession town of Muileann àrsaidh closed its road against both sides for the rest of the war (28 an Cèitean, AE 150). Ros dhomhain, the Ròdaich city below the Residency, neither joined the rising nor stood against it until late in the war.

Course. The war opened in the hills. Crews under Mòrag nic Iain rushed the store at Muileann chrom at first light, and its eleven constables surrendered without a shot (28 an Gearran, AE 149). Crews sank two barges across the mouth of the ore quay at Ceann fhada (24 an Cèitean, AE 149). At Baile thais the constables held their walled pithead for eleven days and surrendered on the twelfth, when their water ran out, and Eilidh nic Raghnaill sent them to the coast unharmed (1 an t-Ògmhios, AE 149). The northern pits rose (30 an t-Ògmhios, AE 149), and An Taigh-seinnse Mòr shut its gates across the ore road, which stayed cut (9 an Lùnastal, AE 149). The capital rose next and barricaded Drochaid Cathair dhearg with ore-carts (18 an Lùnastal, AE 149), and Strake drew the Administration into the Residency above Ros dhomhain (27 an t-Samhain, AE 149).

The first relief column, under Major Peter Ashdown, was met at the ford of Àth chiar on 5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 149. Ashdown lost forty men and his baggage. The rebels lost nineteen, and the council's roll names every one. Dùn chrom shut its gates behind the retreating column and nursed the wounded it left (3 am Faoilleach, AE 150). In the east the silver town rose (15 am Faoilleach, AE 150), and the post at Dùn ìseal surrendered after one exchange of fire (17 am Faoilleach, AE 150).

The humans struck back from the sea. A Company steamship came up the Abhainn uaine and shelled the ore stage at Seann Toll and burned the town behind it, killing twenty-three (15 an Gearran, AE 150). On 10 an Cèitean, AE 150, fishing boats from Seann Chwen and Ros ruadh burned a Company coaster at anchor. The keepers of the southern beacons put out their fires, and two Company ships were lost on the reefs (9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150).

Through the first winter neither side could come at the other (26 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150), and the capital went hungry (8 an t-Iuchar, AE 150). While the war stood still the rebels burned the tithe ledgers in three raids, at Ros dhomhain, Ceann àrsaidh and Muileann chrom (9 an t-Iuchar, AE 150). The Administration's last sally toward the mining country was driven back at Cnoc ghorm on 25 an Lùnastal, AE 150. The Ros dhomhain harbour quarter opened its gates to the council (4 an t-Sultain, AE 150), Strake left the Residency by water (21 an t-Sultain, AE 150), and Ros bheag became the last seat of the Administration (23 an t-Sultain, AE 150), where the human families went hungry within weeks (4 an Dàmhair, AE 150).

End. The last ship recorded from an Tìr Thall came to Ros bheag with a sealed letter and left on the next tide (1 an t-Samhain, AE 150). Envoys met at Àth àrsaidh and agreed a truce (2 an t-Samhain, AE 150). The humans still on Rodos would go into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, and the council would leave the concession towns standing. The columns went north (29 an t-Samhain, AE 150) and camped a night at Àth leathan (1 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150), where several of the humans wrote down the name of the place. Strake sailed west in the last ship able to make the crossing (5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150). On 1 am Faoilleach, AE 151, the war ended, and the crossing itself was closed. That is the Severance. The war-companies were stood down, but they were never disbanded by any act (3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1).

Raiders in the Age of the Kingdom

After the Severance, ships flying no flag, some crewed by men who had served the Administration, raided the coast off Cathair gheal (4 an t-Sultain, SE 12). The council sent no help. In the end the fishermen armed their own boats and drove the raiders off, and were fined for bearing arms without licence (8 an Giblean, SE 20). Not until the patrol boats were refitted for dubhan could they outrun the raiders (15 an t-Sultain, DE 13).

An Cogadh Fada, the Long War

Cause. Some of the northern towns would not take the place made for them in the new trade (25 an Giblean, DE 16), and went on working the last coal seams sooner than hang on one man's fuel. When the Mine Board's northern revenue fell by a quarter (22 am Màrt, DE 18), it declared the western seams Crown property and ordered the pits closed. Enforcers were posted at Seann Skell (16 an Dàmhair, DE 18), the first armed company sent north since the Severance, and there followed skirmishes too small to name (29 an t-Sultain, DE 19). Ruth Calder's offer to pay the Crown's fifth in coal went unanswered (25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 19). The order to muster raised the regiments again (28 an Dàmhair, DE 20) under Somhairle mac Lachlainn (26 an t-Samhain, DE 20), and the Moot's last petition was filed (25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 20).

Sides. For the kingdom, in the reign of Cathal, were the Board's enforcers, the regiments raised again, and later the fleets, all running on dubhan. Against them were the holdouts of five western towns, Àth leathan, Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg, with Ruth Calder and Tom Varley named among them. The Moot stood apart and fed the hungry.

Course. Arms went west by the ore line (12 am Faoilleach, DE 21). The hewers gathered at Àth leathan (20 am Faoilleach, DE 21), and the regiments marched west (23 am Faoilleach, DE 21). The Battle of Àth leathan, fought on 11 an Giblean, DE 21, at Àraich Àth leathan, was the first great battle of the war. The open record counts only the kingdom's dead. The Tuathaich tell of the holdouts' dead in the hundreds, and Ruth Calder's name is not found in the open record again (11 an Giblean, DE 21). The holdouts fell back into the hills (11 an Giblean, DE 21). The regiments besieged Muileann àrsaidh, which held for weeks on stored coal and potatoes (21 an Cèitean, DE 21). Cnoc thais was taken after its road was cut (2 an Lùnastal, DE 21), and Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg opened their roads without a siege (17 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21). In the autumn of the next year a column of several hundred holdouts came down out of the hills and went south-east toward the capital (29 an Dàmhair, DE 22). Why it went is written only in the sealed archive. The Tuathaich name its leader Owen Barrow; the open record names no one. It made camp by Muileann ghlas, a day's walk from the capital (6 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22), and the first and third regiments were brought down the fair road to meet it. The Battle of Muileann ghlas, fought on 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, at Àraich Muileann ghlas, was the second and last great battle of the war. The open record gives no count of the column's dead (10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22). It was the second battle fought below Muileann ghlas of which the annals tell; the first was fought there in the Brothers' War.

End. When word of the battle reached the hills, the last holdouts came down to the seventh regiment's posts and were disarmed and sent home (10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22). An Cogadh Fada ended on 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, and nine regiments and four fleets remained on their stations. By the Board's order the western seams were flooded and capped (24 an Gearran, DE 23). The wartime tithe (21 an Giblean, DE 21) was carried on in the Treasury's accounts, though no minute of the council shows that anyone decided to keep it (27 an Giblean, DE 24). Tuathaich families built a cairn on the field of Àth leathan (6 an Giblean, DE 24). The kingdom raised a stone with the regiments' dead at Cathair mhòr (15 an Dùbhlachd, DE 23).

Part II. The Hosts

The older hosts

Until the Long War the island kept no standing host. In the Holy Age the rìgh of Dùn dhearg fought with road-guards and with levies raised from the lowland farms, and those levies went home at harvest whether the war was done or not (2 an t-Samhain, FE 1,005). The claimants and the brothers of the Age of Sundering fought with the followings of the seven houses. The queen who burned the sea-thieves' boats sent a force raised for that errand alone (27 an t-Samhain, LE 801). In the Age of Strangers the only standing force on the island belonged to the humans: Merriman's constables and the Company's guards and gunboats. The Ròdaich fought the War of the Hills with companies raised by the council, the silver guild and the hawk-houses. Those companies were stood down in SE 1 and kept only as names on a roll. For ninety years the kingdom's regiments stood on paper alone, and its coast was guarded by patrol boats. The first armed company it sent north after the Severance was a company of Board enforcers (16 an Dàmhair, DE 18).

The regiments and fleets

The thirteen hosts on the map were all raised in DE 21, the first year of An Cogadh Fada, and none has been stood down (13 am Faoilleach, DE 23). Each takes its name from the town where it is stationed. The numbers do not follow the order of raising: the seventh regiment was raised first and the ninth last, and the fleets in the order first, fourth, second and third. Why they were so numbered is not told. The rolls of the Severance companies were read out when the regiments were raised again (26 an t-Samhain, DE 20), and the numbers may have come from those rolls; but the open record is silent. Two of the towns named Seann Skell have hosts. The seventh regiment stands at the western one. The ninth regiment and the second fleet stand at the one on the southern coast. The regimental clerks tell them apart by river and coast (25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21).

The regimental rolls of the present year count 5,577 foot, 3,022 riflemen and 2,322 horse in the nine regiments, with seventy-nine guns. The first regiment is the largest, at 1,818 men, and the eighth and ninth are the smallest, at about 850 each. The horse are kept for the hill roads of the west and the north, where lorries cannot go and the dubhan depots are far apart. The four fleets are small. The first and second have two hulls each and the third and fourth one each, with about a hundred men to a hull.

Part III. The Calamities

The five stricken districts

The map shades five districts, each for the calamity that gave it a name. All five fell in the Age of Strangers or after, and in each of them the annals show that the same ground had been struck before.

A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death. Struck: Ros dhìreach, Ceann òg, Inis ìseal, Baile dhomhain, Achadh fhada, Cnoc bheag, Muileann uaine, Cuan àrsaidh, Inis bhàn, all but the last two in the shire of Cnoc bheag. From 9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 73, the Green Death went through the mining camps. The ore dust was blamed, but no inquiry into it was ever brought to an end. At Achadh dhomhain, where it was first noticed, forty were buried in the first month in a field still called the green acre (5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 73). It spread along the ore roads to these nine towns and to twenty-six settlements in all, and the custodians' roll leaves a blank line after the last (13 am Faoilleach, AE 74). Àth ghlas burned the huts of its dead and was free of it soonest (12 am Màrt, AE 74). No reckoning of all the dead survives. After it came the first strike, at Baile thais, over the galleries where the sickness had been worst (21 an Dàmhair, AE 77).

Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger. Struck: Baile chrom, Àth fhionn, Ceann mhòr, Àth dhearg, Muileann àrsaidh, Achadh àrsaidh, all Tuathaich towns today, in the shires of Ceann mhòr, Muileann àrsaidh, Baile chrom and Cnoc thais (22 an Cèitean, AE 94). The oldest hunger on Rodos with a place to it was here, in pots of boiled bark and doubled grave-rows (7 an Cèitean, VE 7,289), and a dearth emptied the same shore in the Age of Sundering (19 an Giblean, LE 819). The Great Hunger began on 3 am Màrt, AE 94, when the harvest failed in thirty-four settlements; and it was the worse because the levy had taken so many that too few were left to work the land. It was worst at Baile chrom, whose people could see the new beacon from their empty fields (1 an Giblean, AE 94); the Administration did not dispute the count. At Seann Bhrenn the grain-pits of the Holy Age were opened and held only dust (7 an t-Samhain, AE 96). The Levy was suspended too late for the harvest and never repealed (20 an Gearran, AE 97).

Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought. Struck: Achadh shean, Àth uaine, Achadh àrsaidh, Muileann chiar, in the shires of Achadh shean and Doire fhionn. The springs of Achadh shean failed in the Ancient Age (8 an Giblean, VE 7,329), and dry years came again in the Holy Age (15 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,900) and in the Age of Sundering (2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,479); each time the shared grain brought the district through. The Long Drought began on 25 an Lùnastal, AE 106 and held three years. Fewer than half of Achadh shean's cattle reached water (28 an t-Ògmhios, AE 107), and the custodians counted ten districts as drought country while the Administration kept no count (27 an t-Iuchar, AE 107). The fever of bad water that followed killed two hundred and sixty at Baile Mòr ruadh (25 an Giblean, AE 109). When dry years returned in the Age of the Kingdom the council sent grain up the ore line, and none died of hunger (3 an Cèitean, SE 43).

Scàineadh Cill ghlas, the Rending. Struck: Cill ghlas, Àth chaol, Achadh chaol, in the shires of Muileann dhearg, Muileann chiar and Muileann dhomhain. The ground here has moved in every age: a crack across the valley (5 an Lùnastal, VE 6,150), cracked wells (27 an Cèitean, LE 379), a fallen gallery with fourteen names on a stone at its mouth (14 an Dàmhair, LE 929). The Rending came on 9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 137, while a common working was being driven with blasting-powder. It killed dozens, swallowed the old cutting and its shrine (3 an t-Iuchar, AE 137), and closed the district for a generation behind the Company's fence (13 an t-Samhain, AE 137). The displaced built Achadh chaol on the edge of the fenced ground (5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 137). The district was reopened (19 an t-Iuchar, SE 15), and on 1 an t-Iuchar, SE 39, a gallery under Muileann dhearg gave way along a line the surveyors had called sound, and thirty-one hewers died. It was, the annals note, the same fault.

Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol, the Great Wave. Struck: Cnoc chaol, Cuan dhearg, Achadh mhin, Ros gharbh, on the coasts of the shires of Seann Vell, Cnoc naomh and Ros gharbh. Sea sand a hand thick lies over an Ancient Age village at Cnoc chaol (7 an t-Iuchar, VE 6,100), a swell took two children there in the Age of Sundering (22 an Gearran, LE 724), and Cuan dhearg was twice flooded before it built its sea-wall (23 an Giblean, LE 1,754). The Great Wave struck without warning on 3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 4 and wrecked the three towns in one night. It was the first calamity the new kingdom met by its own means. The relief parties counted a little over nine hundred dead (24 an t-Samhain, SE 4). The wave ran on up the gulf to Ros gharbh and broke its quays, though the town on its headland lost few (24 an t-Samhain, SE 4). Cuan dhearg's harbour was gone and its boats lay in the fields. The shepherds of Eilean mhin did not go back (1 an Giblean, SE 5).

Other calamities of the annals

Plagues. A coughing sickness killed some two hundred at Caol fhiadhaich (2 an Gearran, LE 156); a spotted fever some three hundred at Inis chrom, where the Fianna of the Stone nursed the sick and died of it (3 an t-Sultain, LE 624); the swallowing cough near a third of Muileann dhomhain (29 an Lùnastal, LE 1,079). The strangers' fever came ashore with a crowded ship and killed ninety-one Ròdaich and eleven humans (5 an t-Samhain, AE 9). The spotted pox at Ros dhomhain killed four hundred and six by the Mission's count, and more by the custodians' (11 an Dàmhair, AE 39). The grey fever (2 an Gearran, AE 138) killed the young and strong before the old, and in the north-west put Ròdaich and humans in the same wards for the first time (20 an t-Iuchar, AE 140).

Famines. The first famine known to have been turned aside (4 an Dàmhair, FE 2,473) was the first trial of the shared-meal custom, and the custom held. Beyond the Great Hunger the annals record hunger in the capital and in Ros bheag during the War of the Hills (8 an t-Iuchar, AE 150, 4 an Dàmhair, AE 150), and the north's first year alone, when Tuathaich memory puts the dead at Doire ghlas above two hundred and no Ròdaich count was made (9 an Dùbhlachd, SE 1).

Storms, floods and fires. The first storm given a name is remembered only for the naming (30 am Faoilleach, VE 5,470); the oldest whose name survives is A' Ghaoth Dhubh (1 an Gearran, VE 7,740). Am Fuath Mòr drowned eighteen at Seann Toll (23 an t-Samhain, LE 259), a storm drowned twenty-three at Baile ghorm (12 an Dàmhair, LE 1,739), and another eleven Tuathaich off Cuan bheag (28 an t-Sultain, SE 19). The Abhainn ìseal cut the ore line for most of a year (12 am Màrt, SE 34). Fire burned Ceann mhin twice (5 an t-Sultain, LE 1,549) and the fair at Muileann òg once (31 an Dàmhair, SE 40).

The vein's own dead. The mountain has killed those who worked it in every age: from the basket burning at Achadh dhìreach (7 an t-Iuchar, VE 6,389) to the first deaths laid to the humans' pace of work, eleven of them, entered as an accident (26 an Giblean, AE 25).

Appendix D — The Reckoning of Years

Here it is told how the years of Rodos are now counted, by the six eras, and how that reckoning grew out of the older counts. After that comes the island's own reckoning of the moon, which the Ròdaich kept before the humans came and the Old Faith keeps yet; then the humans' calendar, and how it became the civil calendar of the island, and how its months and the days of its week got their Ròdais names; then the feasts. Last it is told how the Library at Muileann chaol turned every old date into the civil calendar, and that is why the annals give a civil day and month to every age alike.

I. The Six Eras

The island counts its years by eras, linntean, one to each of the six ages of Clàr nan Aoisean, the table of the ages, as the Library received and extended it. Each era is counted from the first thing remembered in its age. That first year is year 1, and there is no year nought. A date is written with the day, the month and the year of its era, 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1, and a year alone as DE 27; in Ròdais it is read air an naoidheamh latha deug den Ògmhios, sa chiad bhliadhna de Linn an Dubhain. In running prose the chroniclers are content to write "in the year 214 of the Flame".

AgeRòdais nameIn the common tongueEraSpanFirst eventLast event

IIAn Aois Naomhthe Holy AgeLinn an Teine, the Flame Era (FE)FE 1 – 2,960The Binding of the First Flame, 23 an t-Sultain, FE 1The last age of even population, 1 an Cèitean, FE 2,949

The names are plain. Linn na Fèithe is the era of the vein, counted from the crack in the stone where the vein first showed, which is the oldest thing the island remembers; nothing before it is dated. Linn an Teine is the era of the fire, from the Binding of Brìde's flame at Dùn ìseal. Linn na Tìre is the era of the land, from the word that came back of a land across open water. Linn an Acair is the era of the anchor, from the day the humans' ships came to anchor at the Crossing. Linn an Dealachaidh is the era of the parting, from the Severance and the settling of the north. Linn an Dubhain is the era of Dubhan, from the first fuel that burned without the vein. It is the only era of the six named for a living man, and the north is apt to observe that he was one of theirs.

Three things in the table need a word.

An era's last year is also the first year of the next. The year in which an age opens is counted in the old era until the day of its first event, and in the new era from that day.

The Age of Sundering is usually said to open with the Choosing, but the Choosing (8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1) is not the first thing in it. The age opens with the finding of the land (6 am Faoilleach, LE 1), without which there would have been nothing to choose.

The Severance closes the Age of Strangers on the first day of AE 151, and the first events of the Age of the Kingdom follow it within that same year, which is therefore also SE 1. The copyists of the cellar entered the Severance as the last act of the age it ended, and the Library has left it there.

II. How the Ages Counted Their Years

The Ancient Age. The Ancient Age kept no count of years that anyone has found. Its people counted other things. The Seann-Dhaoine cut strokes on stones at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household, and the first strokes were cut on 31 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,631. The tally wall at Seann Warr grew to some three thousand strokes, and in one stretch the tallies of three coasts thicken together (6 an Giblean, VE 5,793). These are counts of the dead. None of them has been read as a count of years.

The first tide-count (28 am Faoilleach, VE 6,994), a rock on which someone marked the high-water line, comes nearer. Its marks fall at intervals regular enough that later scholars have suspected a reckoning of the moon in them. The custom was carried to Ros dhomhain with the interval unchanged. What the interval was for no one knows, and the Library has declined to guess. The hill-folk also knew the crossing season of the great cats and kept off the passes while the panthers went over (20 am Faoilleach, VE 5,212). That season they kept year by year, but the years they did not number.

The oldest oral king-list, Rìghrean na Cloiche, begins with Ailean Mòr (9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324) and "gives no lengths of reign." The Red Hill list is the same. When both lists were recited together at the ford gathering (23 an t-Iuchar, VE 9,670), the recital lasted from dusk to dawn; yet it measured nothing but a line of names. Here and there the tellings of the age bind a few deeds fast to one another, and where they do, those deeds are remembered as falling in one year or within a few. Between such points the tellings keep the order of things and little of the distance between them, and the years of the age are known only so well as the tellings know them.

The Holy Age. The Holy Age counted in two ways, and neither of them ran from a fixed beginning.

The first was by reigns. From the Binding of the First Flame (23 an t-Sultain, FE 1) the Keepers of the flame were remembered in a recited roll that begins with Beathag Bhàn. After Goraidh mac Ìomhair was first called rìgh at Dùn dhearg (28 an Cèitean, FE 674), the rulers of the lowlands had a list of their own. A year was named by whoever held it: "the ninth year of Iain Garbh," "the third winter of the Keeper Seumas Bàn." That served well enough for a debt within living memory; for the distance between two reigns it was of no use, since the recited lists gave no lengths. The first written king-list, Tormod Scrìobhaiche's roll (20 an Lùnastal, FE 1,299), marks which names came from reciters and which from living memory. The Keepers had their own roll set down in answer (17 an Dàmhair, FE 1,320), and it proved several centuries longer than Tormod's. From the reign of Seonag Chrom the clerks of the red hall kept the king-list year by year. Between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh the list gives nine rulers of the house of Tormod, "their names and years and little else" (29 am Màrt, FE 2,558). Those years were counted within each reign and did not run on from one reign to the next.

The second was by burnings. From the Small-Burning Law (13 an Lùnastal, FE 142), a household might burn no more than its measured handful of ore in a season, and the Hall at Dùn ìseal kept the record of those seasons. It counted them from the Law: the first burning, the second, and on through the centuries. A Small-Burning year ran from one filling of the baskets to the next, and the Hall filled them at Samhain, when the galleries closed and the hearths began to need the ore. The first sentence under the Law (1 an Cèitean, FE 145) took from a household its right "for the season after," and it was entered by the burning in which it fell. Of all the island's counts the count of burnings came nearest to an era, because it ran from a single act and was meant never to stop. It long outlived the age. The Law was never repealed; it lapsed (2 an Dùbhlachd, AE 21), and the custodians of Doire mhin kept the old count one season longer than anyone else (31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 21), with the note that nobody had asked for it.

By the close of the age the Keepers' roll held one hundred and forty names and the king-list more than ninety (2 an Giblean, FE 2,939). The two did not agree in every place, and the Hall's count of burnings did not always agree with either.

The Age of Sundering. In this age the island first numbered its years from a single day, and the count it made was the count of the Diosal.

III. The Count of the Diosal, and How It Was Given Up

Diosal is the island's word for the sunwise turn: the way a hand moves, a boat rounds a point, or a procession goes about a cairn, with the right shoulder toward the centre and the course following the sun. Before going down the Abhainn naomh to open water the fleet of the Sundering went once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise, for luck, and the watchers on the quay counted the hulls as they passed. The harbour scribe's entry for the turn is the last thing any roll says of the departed.

The count was not made at the time. On 22 am Faoilleach, LE 44, Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house above Muileann dhearg, began to number the years from the sunwise turn and called them bliadhnaichean an Diosail, the years of the Diosal. By his own reckoning only a few of them had yet passed. There was no year nought, and the years before the turn were counted backwards, ron Diosal, "before the Diosal". The count was his alone at first. The crown's scribes at Cathair dhearg took it up about a generation later.

The harbour scribe sets the Setting-Out and the sunwise turn on one day, the sailing on 19 an Giblean, LE 40 and the turn on 19 an Giblean, LE 40, the same morning. The custody-book, however, enters the turn under a later day than the sailing, after the next Samhain. No one has accounted for that gap of half a year, and the keepers have left both entries as they stand. Donnchadh counted from the turn as the custody-book entered it. The crown's scribes, taking up the count when the court remembered the departure as a single thing, counted from the year the ships sailed. Both began each year at Samhain, by the moon, as the Hall had done; so by the old year the sailing and the turn lay in different years, and the two counts stood a year apart. So, the Library believes, the counts came to differ. The rolls do not prove it, and it leaves unexplained why the turn is entered so long after the sailing.

The difference stood for more than six hundred years, until 23 am Màrt, LE 739, when the vein-house and the crown's scribes found that their counts disagreed and settled the matter by agreement. The same agreement fixed the day of the empty-harbour rite, which the two counts had placed differently. A later hand in the custody-book adds that the scribes afterwards "cease to pretend it was fixed by proof." From that day there was one Diosal count on Rodos, and it followed the harbour scribe, setting the sailing and the turn both in its first year. The vein-house marked its thousandth year (15 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039) with a single measured burning on Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn.

For the rest of the Age of Sundering, through the Age of Strangers and into the first years of the kingdom, the island dated its writings by the Diosal. The custodians set its year beneath the humans' year at the head of their pages (section VI). The keeper's proclamation at the founding of the Library (1 an Cèitean, SE 16) is dated "the year one thousand nine hundred and forty-five of the Diosal", and it is among the last public writings so dated.

The count had served the scribes of the rolls well enough. It served the Library ill. Everything older than the sunwise turn had to be counted backwards in years that ran into the thousands: the Binding fell nearly three thousand years before the Diosal, and the crack in the stone nearly thirteen thousand, a number no keeper could write with a steady hand, since no roll and no telling measured it. The count ran, moreover, from an absence; and the Library's first keeper said that a people ought not to have to name every year of its life after the day its kin went away.

The copyists of the cellar had already cut the past into ages (section XII), and Ailean Leabhar, when he came to the Library (28 an t-Ògmhios, SE 16), took their table as the frame of his work. He counted each age from its own first event, and he wrote the dates of the ledgers he was having read in the years of their age and not of the Diosal. The council followed him. With the creation of the office of royal chronicler (20 an t-Samhain, SE 18) it ordered that the kingdom's records should count their years by the ages of the Library's table (20 an t-Samhain, SE 18). Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill entered her first year as the eighteenth of the Severance Era. The Diosal count was kept thereafter only in old books. Its name lives on in the day of the empty-harbour rite, Là an Diosail, and in the quay at Seann Skell, and nobody has proposed to change either.

No one foresaw the sixth era. The first working dubhan was made on 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1, and for years it was one man's fuel and no more; Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, then chronicler, noted it at the foot of that year and spelled it three ways. When the council pegged the coinage to the making of dubhan in place of the obsidian reserves, it proclaimed at the same sitting that the Age of the Kingdom had ended with the first working dubhan, and that the kingdom's years were counted anew from that day (5 an Cèitean, DE 15). The Severance Era closed with its seventy-first year, and the year of the proclamation became the fifteenth of the Dubhan Era. Beathag re-headed fourteen years of her own chronicle, and wrote at the foot of the page that she had never before had to move a year she was living in.

The Tuathaich were not asked about either change. The northern parish books, so far as the Library has seen them, give the civil day and month and the kingdom's era in their dealings with the kingdom. What count they keep among themselves the Library cannot say, for few of those books come to it.

IV. The Reckoning of the Moon

Before the humans came the Ròdaich had no calendar fixed to the sun. They reckoned by the moon, and they counted time by nights and not by days. The night went before its day, as the dark half of the year went before the bright: a feast began at dusk on its eve, Oidhche Shamhna was the first night of Samhain and not the night before it, and a debt of "ten nights" fell due at the tenth dusk. The custody-book calls this reckoning cunntas nan oidhcheannan, the count of the nights, and the Library's word for it, cunntas-oidhche, the night-count, is shortened from the custody-book's.

The year began at Samhain, with the dark half of the year. It held twelve moon-months, mìosan-gealaich, of thirty nights and twenty-nine nights in turn. Each moon-month was halved. It began on the night of the full moon and waned through its dark half, an leth dubh; at the dark of the moon it turned, and its bright half, an leth geal, waxed to the next full. Below the month the Ròdaich had the half-moon, cola-deug, "fourteen nights", though the halves were of fourteen or fifteen nights as the moon ran. They had no week. In the rolls of the Holy Age and of the Sundering a debt, a sentence or a turn in the galleries is set by the half-moon, and the markets met at the full; Queen Sìleas's charter to Cathair fhada (17 an t-Samhain, LE 287) grants a market at every full moon. The night of the full and the night of the dark were rest-nights, oidhcheannan-tàmh, on which the Hall let no ore be cut and the fishing households set no nets.

Twelve moons make three hundred and fifty-four nights, some eleven fewer than the sun's year, so that without help the feasts would have walked backwards through the seasons. About every thirty moons, two and a half years, the keepers of the reckoning put in a thirteenth moon of thirty nights at the end of the year, after Damhrach and before Samhnas, so that Samhain should not come before the summer had ended. They called it Eadrach, the between-moon. In the Holy Age the Hall at Dùn ìseal declared it; after the Hall's day the vein-house did, and since the vein-house's day the druid schools declare it, and the orders of the Old Faith follow them. The Hall's roll of the years in which Eadrach was put in is the thread on which every older date of the island hangs (section XII), and the thread is broken in places.

The four fire-feasts were fixed by the moon, each on the first night of its moon: Samhain at the opening of Samhnas, Là Fhèill Brìde of Gearras, Bealltainn of Bealltach, Lùnastal of Lùghnas. Against the sun they wander by as much as half a month from year to year, and the between-moon brings them back.

The names of the thirteen moons are old, and some of them were in dispute already when the Hall first wrote them down. The meanings given below are those the Library holds most likely.

V. The Humans' Calendar

The humans who came at the Crossing (5 am Faoilleach, AE 1) brought a calendar of another kind. It was fixed to the sun and paid no heed to the moon. Its year began in the dead of winter and had twelve months of set lengths, thirty or thirty-one days and one of twenty-eight, with a twenty-ninth day put into that short month every fourth year. They counted by days from midnight, not by nights from dusk, and they divided the month into weeks of seven days, one of which was kept for rest and worship. Their years they numbered from an epoch in their own land, which they named and did not explain, and their numbers were far larger than the island's. No Ròdaich scribe set down the name of that land (26 an Gearran, AE 2), and the letter-books do not explain the epoch either.

In the season of translation Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair kept their word-lists side by side (13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 2). Wren's list, which survives in the Administration's letter-books, sets each of the humans' months against the moon it most nearly matched, and it is the first writing on Rodos in which the two reckonings meet. From that pairing the Ròdaich named the humans' months (section VII).

VI. How the Civil Calendar Came In

The humans' calendar was never proclaimed on Rodos. It came in by paper. The first written treaty (27 an Giblean, AE 8) was drawn up in the humans' tongue only and dated by the humans' day, month and year. The custodians entered it in their roll under its Diosal year and the moon in which it was signed, and left the day to the Administration. The Harbour Articles (16 an t-Samhain, AE 19), the Company's charter and every contract for extraction (19 an t-Sultain, AE 11) were dated the same way, and the contracts paid their crews by the week and let them rest on the humans' day of rest. So the Ròdaich who worked for the Company learned the week before any of them was christened. The same clerks who kept two sets of books for coin and barter (30 am Faoilleach, AE 18) came to keep two dates at the head of every page, the humans' year and day above and the Diosal year and the night of the moon beneath, and they complained about both.

A contract that fell due on the humans' day could not be settled by the moon, and the clerks who had to settle it went over to the humans' months first and to the humans' new year after. By the third currency reform (7 an Giblean, AE 129) every contract on the island ran from am Faoilleach, and the Ròdaich civil year had moved to the humans' beginning without any decree. The moon-year survived in the shrines, in the Hall's count of burnings until it lapsed, and among the custodians of Inis bhàn, who taught "the old reckoning" in their school (7 an t-Ògmhios, AE 52). The Administration's census (19 an Cèitean, AE 122) and its register (26 an t-Samhain, AE 127) were dated by the humans' reckoning alone.

After the Severance the kingdom kept the civil calendar, since a century of contracts, ledgers and letters already stood on it, and no one on the council wished to return the kingdom's debts to the moon. The kingdom has kept it since. Its months have the names the Ròdaich gave them, and its years are counted by the eras (section III).

VII. The Civil Months

The civil months are the humans' months under Ròdais names. For ten of them the clerks took the name of the moon that Wren's list set beside the month, in the form it had in the speech of their day; two names they took from the humans themselves. Beside each month is set the island's work in it, as the rolls of every age describe that work, reckoned into the civil months.

An Gearran takes a twenty-ninth day in every fourth year, as the humans' calendar has it. The reckoning of the moon had no such day and needed none, for the between-moon did its work.

VIII. The Week

The week, seachdain, came to Rodos with the Mission. The humans' Church kept seven days, the first of them for rest and worship and two others for fasting, and when the Mission raised its chapel at Ros dhomhain (30 an Dùbhlachd, AE 13) and opened its school (9 an Cèitean, AE 51) it taught the week with its prayers. The Company's contracts had already taught it to the crews (section VI).

The names came with it. Each begins with Di-, the Mission's church-tongue word for a day, written solid with the rest of the name. Four are the church-tongue's own names put into Ròdais mouths. Three the first converts made for themselves, from the Mission's fasts. The names below are given in the forms the royal chronicler uses.

DayRòdaisThe name
1Didòmhnaichthe Lord's day, from the church-tongue; the Mission's day of rest and worship. The Company's contracts let no ore be cut on it
2Diluainthe moon's day, from the church-tongue
3Dimàirtthe day of the war-god of the humans' forebears, from the church-tongue; the same name as the month am Màrt
4Diciadainthe day of the first fast
5Diardaointhe day between the fasts

The two fasts are the Mission's own: on the fourth day and the sixth the Church abstained from meat, and in the north it abstains still. Nobody else on Rodos keeps them. An older opinion of the Library, that they were fasts from fire kept by Holy Age households under the Small-Burning Law, did not survive the reading of the Mission's letter-books; and the unlit hearth found under the peat (2 an Dàmhair, VE 6,225), which was once cited for it, proves nothing about weeks.

The Ròdaich had rested by the moon, on the nights of the full and the dark, and the Mission made a great deal of the difference. The custodians made little of it. It was the Mission's own minister Matthew Dunne who told the Company, against the night-shift order, that the Ròdaich were right that even the ground must rest (17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 118), and the Mission recalled him for it.

IX. The Three Faiths and the Two Reckonings

The kingdom lives by the civil calendar; but the moon was never put away, and it runs on beside the civil months as the reckoning of the Old Faith.

An Creideamh Sean, the Old Faith, keeps its feasts by the moon. Its four fire-feasts fall on the first nights of Samhnas, Gearras, Bealltach and Lùghnas, and its orders reckon the moons as the druid schools declare them, between-moon and all. Òrd Bhrìde lights its first lamp of the year on the first night of Gearras and not on the civil day, and in a year when the moon runs late its lamp is lit nearly a fortnight after the Church's candles.

Na Seann Spioradan, the Old Spirits, keep the night-count at the hearth. They count a journey, a mourning or a guest's stay in nights, and their dead are waked for three nights and not three days. They keep the feasts with the Old Faith, by the moon, at the hearth and at the mounds.

An Eaglais, the Church, keeps the civil calendar and the week it brought, with its day of rest, its two fasts and its own feasts on their civil days. The kingdom keeps the quarter-days on the first day of their civil months (section X), and the council, the courts and the markets follow the kingdom.

So a feast of the Old Faith and the same feast in the kingdom's calendar may fall a fortnight apart, and no one on Rodos thinks it strange.

X. The Quarter-Days

Four feasts divide the year into quarters. They are the great feasts of the Old Faith and older than any order now on the island, and all three faiths keep them in some fashion, though each for its own reasons (Appendix B). The kingdom keeps them on the first day of their civil months. The Old Faith keeps them on the first night of their moons (section IV).

Là Fhèill Brìde, 1 an Gearran, also called Imbolc, is the feast of Brìde, whose flame was bound at Dùn ìseal. Every hearth is swept and relit and the year's first work in the fields begins. The followers of Na Seann Spioradan set a sheaf by the door. Òrd Bhrìde and the Hawk order, the two forms of her rite, light their first lamp of the year from the altar-flame. The Church keeps the day as the feast of a saint of the same name.

Bealltainn, 1 an Cèitean, takes its name from a bright fire, and it is the feast of summer's beginning, when the Otherworld stands near. Cattle go up to the high pastures between two fires. In the Holy Age this was the day the Hall asked the cairn-watchers of Cnoc ghlas whether the galleries might open. The first sentence under the Small-Burning Law is dated 1 an Cèitean, FE 145, on Bealltainn itself. Whether the day was chosen for the sentence the roll does not say.

Lùnastal, 1 an Lùnastal, is Lugh's feast of first-fruits and gathering, which he made in memory of his foster-mother Tailtiu, and the month is named for it. Markets open, contests are held, and oaths are taken before witnesses. Cathal was crowned on the feast itself, 1 an Lùnastal, DE 3.

Samhain, 1 an t-Samhain, marks summer's end, when the Otherworld stands open, the sìth of the mounds are abroad, and the Old Faith names Donn and the dead of the year. Before the humans came it was also the beginning of the Ròdaich year. The Hall filled the baskets of the Small-Burning Law at Samhain, the galleries closed, and the dead were thought nearest. The Tuathaich, whose calendar came to them from an Tìr Thall, keep the day with the rest of the island, in the Church's way, as the feast of all the saints and the day of the dead. They have never counted the year from it.

XI. Feasts and Days Particular to Rodos

Beside the quarter-days Rodos keeps days that spring from its own history. Those that the chronicles bear witness to are given below, on their civil days; under "since" stands the day on which the custom is first found.

DayWhereWhat is keptSince
