The days of the older customs are given as the Library turned them (section XII). The night of lamps and the empty-harbour rite were fixed by the moon, and since the civil calendar came in the harbour towns have kept them on the civil days that the Library's tables give.

The day of the Setting-Out has never been kept as a feast. The chronicles say nothing more of the departed once the ships clear the harbour, and the island has kept its remembrance of them there, at the harbour where the rolls fall silent, on the day the custody-book gives for the turn and not on the day they sailed. Since 23 am Màrt, LE 739, the empty-harbour rite has fallen on that day, though the harbour scribe, whose count the island followed, sets the turn on the day of the sailing. The Library does not forget that the custody-book may have taken its day from the rite, and not the rite from the book. By the last entry of the Age of Sundering the rite was kept by eleven people (25 an t-Samhain, LE 1,803). How many keep it now the chronicles of the later ages do not say.

The Severance, 1 am Faoilleach, AE 151, is kept at Cathair dhearg by the council as the day on which the latter history of the kingdom begins, and the era named for it bore its memory in every date for seventy-one years. The Mourning Custom of the Sundering, first made for a parting that was chosen, was used again, uneasily, for this parting that was not, and the council's keeping of this day is the use most often meant. In the north the day is not kept. It is worked through like any other, and the Tuathaich say that this is their way of keeping it.

The Long War left two days. The Battle of Àth leathan, 11 an Giblean, DE 21, opened An Cogadh Fada. Tuathaich families have raised a cairn without leave on the field at Àraich Àth leathan, and it grows by a stone or two whenever the patrols pass; whether they come on the day of the battle nobody has written down. The Battle of Muileann ghlas, 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, ended the war, and the regiments raised in the campaign keep that day at their stations. So the two days are kept by two peoples; and the Library, whose record of the war is sealed (14 am Faoilleach, DE 24), holds what it can of both.

XII. How the Library Turned the Old Dates

Every date in these annals is given in the civil calendar, with a day of the civil month and a year of the era, though for most of the island's history nobody who lived it counted so. The Library made it so, and the labour took three generations.

It began with Beathag nic Thòmais, the mill-owner's widow who bought up old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls and kept them in a loft over her mill at Muileann chaol (21 an Cèitean, LE 1,659). She did not reckon years. But she set copies that disagreed side by side and declined to choose between them (27 an Giblean, LE 1,679), and that became the way of all who worked in Muileann chaol after her. She left her loft to the town on condition that nothing in it be burned (24 an Lùnastal, LE 1,699).

The joining of the counts was done in the cellar. From 5 am Màrt, AE 124, the custodians of the east sent copies of their rolls to Muileann chaol for safekeeping, away from the Residency's reach, and three families did the copying. While they copied, they laid the counts against each other. Where the king-list gave a ruler's years and the Hall's roll gave the burnings of the same reign, the two could be made to meet, and each meeting fixed a stretch of the older count against the newer. The copyists called the result Clàr nan Aoisean, the table of the ages. It is the first writing that runs one numbered line of years from the Binding to the copyists' own day, in the years of the Diosal. It is also the first to divide the island's past into ages, and to set before the Holy Age an older age whose length, the table owns, it cannot measure. When the custodians sent what survived of the Age of Strangers to the same cellars (29 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150), the table was carried through to the Severance, and in that form it gave the ages down to the Severance the bounds that historians of Rodos still use.

Leabharlann Muileann chaol, founded 1 an Cèitean, SE 16, took the table as one of its first possessions. The council's clerks had emptied the humans' counting-houses (11 an t-Ògmhios, SE 2) and boxed the ledgers unread, because few of them could read the humans' hand. Ailean Leabhar, the Library's first keeper, spent his first years having them read (28 an t-Ògmhios, SE 16), and he had every date in them, and in the custodians' rolls, turned into the civil calendar. For the Age of Strangers the double-dated pages of the custodians' clerks were his guide, since they set the humans' day above the night of the moon. For the ages before the Crossing he had only the moons, and he turned them by the Hall's roll of the between-moons, reckoning moon by moon back from the first double-dated page to the Binding. Each date so turned he set in the era of its age, as the council afterwards ordered for all the kingdom's records (section III). When the Library absorbed the provincial archives (26 an t-Iuchar, SE 67), the table was checked against them and corrected where the archives knew better. When the sixth era was proclaimed, the Library re-headed the years since the first working dubhan as the chronicler had done.

So a reader of these annals who finds a Holy Age deed set on 3 an t-Samhain should remember that those who did it knew no such day. They knew a night of the moon Samhnas, and they began their year at Samhain and counted it by nights. The Library's day is the civil day on which that night would have fallen, as near as the roll of the between-moons allows. Where the roll has gaps, the day may be a half-moon out, and the Library says so. Ailean Leabhar disliked the saying a chur san Leabharlann, "to put it in the Library," on the ground that the Library settles nothing and only keeps it (3 an t-Samhain, SE 16). The turned dates should be read in the same spirit.

Where the dates come from. For the Age of Dubhan, the Age of the Kingdom and the Age of Strangers the days are remembered: they come from rolls, ledgers, letter-books and the chroniclers' own entries, and from the Crossing on they were written in the civil calendar or beside it. For the Age of Sundering they are remembered more thinly, from the custody-book, the harbour rolls and the crown's king-list, all dated by the moon, and a good many were settled by agreement, as the day of the empty-harbour rite was. For the Holy Age the years come from the Keepers' roll, the king-lists and the Hall's count of burnings, which do not always agree, and the days mostly from the feasts and moons the rolls name. For the Ancient Age all rests on the tellings, the king-lists without lengths of reign, the tally walls and the tide-count. The tellings keep the order of things well and the distance between them poorly. Where they agree, the date is as sure as they are; where they disagree or fall silent it is not, and such a date should be trusted for the order it keeps rather than for its year.

Appendix E — Words Born from History

Here are gathered the words, names and sayings of Ròdais that the island's history made, or bent to a new sense. They are set out in the manner of a historical dictionary. Each entry gives the headword and its part of speech, what it says word for word, what it has come to mean, the event that gave it that meaning, and a line from the annals or the six books.

At the heart of it stands the chronicle's own list of Words Born from History, and every word on that list is entered here with the meaning the chronicle gives it. The rest are taken from the annals and the books: titles and offices, laws and customs, the names of storms, places and quarrels, and the sayings that the annals quote. A few are the words that Ròdais made for the strangers' things. Ròdais took few words from the humans, and most of those late (Appendix F). Where the humans said train, engine or strike, the island made a name out of old roots, and some of those names are entered here under the years in which the annals first had need of them.

How to Read an Entry

The headword is given in full. An article (an, am, a') is written with it but not counted in the order, which is the island's order of eighteen letters, a b c d e f g h i l m n o p r s t u, the grave accent being ignored. Dates are given in the era of each age (Appendix D). Where no annal marks the first use of a word, the entry says so and gives only the event from which the word comes. Citations are given as the sources give them: the annals as this history renders their prose, the verses in Ròdais (Appendix F, Of Translation).

n. noun · m., f. masculine, feminine · pl. plural · v. verb · v.n. verbal noun · adj. adjective · phr. phrase or saying · lit. literally

The Glossary

A

a chur san Leabharlann phr. · lit. "to put it in the Library" To make a thing official and past dispute. From the founding of Leabharlann Muileann chaol (1 an Cèitean, SE 16); within a few years it was said of anything settled (3 an t-Samhain, SE 16).

"Ailean Leabhar is said to have disliked the phrase, for the library settles nothing, he said, and only keeps." — annals, SE 16

Aisling-aois n. f. · lit. "Aisling-age" An unnaturally long youth in anyone; said half in jest of ordinary people who look young for their years. From the first of the immortal generation, born in the mining camps (7 am Màrt, AE 69). No annal marks its first use. Of all the words on the chronicle's list, in this one alone the jest and the legend are the same.

"…and she does not age as the folk about her age. Her name is Aisling." — annals, AE 69

Àrd-choimheadaiche n. m. · lit. "high watcher" The high custodian of Òrd Bhrìde, the order of Brìde's flame, seated at Seann Skell. The office came when the Rite was set in order (18 an Giblean, SE 6), and Dòmhnall mac Thormoid was the first to hold it (17 an Cèitean, SE 6). It is not the "high custodian" of the Age of Strangers, who headed the Council of Custodians; the two share a name in translation, and nothing more.

"The Àrd-choimheadaiche at Seann Skell writes to every house of the Rite that the new fuel is not forbidden, since it is not ore, and not blessed, since it is not ore." — annals, DE 4

B

bonn-rìoghachd n. m. · lit. "realm-coin" Currency. Under the humans the coin was the mark, and barter was driven out in three reforms (13 an Gearran, AE 17, 2 an Dàmhair, AE 86, 7 an Giblean, AE 129). The Ròdais word belongs to the coinage struck when the humans' coin was withdrawn (30 an Giblean, SE 5). Its first mint-master was called Fearchar Bonn from his work (9 an Dàmhair, SE 5). After the re-pegging to dubhan (5 an Cèitean, DE 15) the realm-coin no longer rested on the vein.

"Within a year a new coinage of the Rìoghachd takes its place, minted with ink of obsidian dust in its seal." — annals, SE 5

C

carbad-iarainn n. m. · lit. "iron-chariot" A train; the first of the iarainn words Ròdais made for machines. The kingdom mended the humans' ore line (9 an Dàmhair, SE 8) and ran its own first train on 3 an Dàmhair, SE 12.

"The first ore train runs from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg in the kingdom's name, on the humans' rails." — annals, SE 12

Cha do chaill sinn blàr, ach chaill sinn an teine phr. · lit. "we did not lose a battle, but we lost the fire" A defeat without fighting. An unsigned verse of the cold shires, from the day Raghnall Ruadh refused the measured handful to every hearth that stood against him (24 am Faoilleach, LE 558).

"…this deed turns more against him than any battle." — annals, LE 558

Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann phr. · lit. "we did not come; we were here" The doctrine of the Ancient Age, complete on Calbh Cnoc ghorm (6 an t-Samhain, VE 4,876). Who cut it is not known.

"Here, it may be, the belief was first spoken." — annals, VE 4,876

Cha loisc clach na beinne do choigrich phr. · lit. "the mountain's stone will not burn for strangers" The Keepers' ruling that no ore might feed a beacon (30 an Cèitean, FE 148). It held until the humans' towers were lit with an ore flame (22 an t-Sultain, AE 91).

"The Keepers rule that no ore may feed a beacon, since a beacon burns for strangers." — annals, FE 148

Cha tàinig long phr. · lit. "no ship came" The entry in the beacon-keepers' daybooks from the Severance on, after the council had the five beacons relit (19 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150).

"The keepers' daybooks, which had counted human ships since the ring was finished, are still kept, with nothing in them." — annals, AE 150

Chaidh a' mhèinn dhachaigh phr. · lit. "the ore went home" The tellings' words for the ore taken by Gilleasbuig Beag (2 an Lùnastal, VE 7,732), which was neither burned nor kept but laid back under the slab (4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,734).

"The tellings make much of it: the ore went home." — annals, VE 7,734

Cidhe an Diosail n. m. · lit. "the quay of the sunwise turn" The berth at Seann Skell from which the fleet of the Sundering sailed. Its old name, Cidhe an Iar, passed to a new fish-wharf so that trade could go on without the memory (13 am Màrt, LE 67, 15 an Lùnastal, LE 67).

"The departure berth is entered in the harbour rolls of Seann Skell as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn." — annals, LE 67

Cogadh nam Bràithrean n. m. · lit. "the war of the brothers" The war between Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, named from its first battle (8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,270).

"The houses divide four to three, and from this battle Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, takes its name." — annals, LE 1,270

Comann nan Saor-luinge n. m. · lit. "the fellowship of the ship-wrights" The guild that built the fleet of the Sundering (24 an t-Sultain, LE 5). It melted away when no more ocean-going hulls were wanted (27 an t-Ògmhios, LE 84).

"The custody-book names it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights." — annals, LE 5

Còmhrag n. f. · lit. "combat" With the article, the yearly melee at Ceann leathan (4 am Màrt, SE 23), fought on the field of the Holy Age road-guards' games (9 an Giblean, FE 1,665).

"Two men die in the melee he wins." — annals, of the first champion, SE 23

cridhe-iarainn n. m. · lit. "iron-heart" An engine. The annals first have need of it for the shunting engines at Muileann chrom (8 an t-Iuchar, SE 13), and again when the Shipwrights' Guild court ruled that fitting one to a boat was not shipwrighting (23 an Giblean, DE 6).

"The families of the yard, who work the small engines that move the wagons, are counted apart by the Board and live apart in rows beside the lines." — annals, SE 13

cuimhne-coinneimh n. f. · lit. "meeting-memory" Minutes. Above all, those of the Moot at Caol mhòr, which has no standing in Ròdach law and has kept its minutes since its first sitting (25 an Lùnastal, SE 2). See Tha e scrìobhte a-nis.

"It meets all the same and keeps its own minutes, which run unbroken from that day to this." — annals, SE 2

D

diosal adv., n. m. · lit. "sunwise" The sunwise turn. The fleet went once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise (19 an Giblean, LE 40), and the years were counted from that turn (22 am Faoilleach, LE 44).

"Before going down the Abhainn naomh to open water the fleet went once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck." — the Third Book

dòrlach n. m. · lit. "a handful" The sealed measure of ore. The vein-house allowed one to each departing ship (17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 25). See Làn na glaice.

Dòrlach airson an teallaich ùir, / is an seann teallach fhathast blàth. "A handful for the new hearth, and the old hearth still warm." — the Third Book

Dubh an gual, 's dubh an dubhan phr. · lit. "black the coal, and black the dubhan" A rhyme of the north, heard in both tongues, from the years when the coinage was pegged to the new fuel (5 an Cèitean, DE 15).

Dubh an gual, 's dubh an dubhan, / ach cò leis an teine? "Black the coal, and black the dubhan; but whose is the fire?" — the Sixth Book

dubhan n. m. · lit. "the black one" (dubh + -an) The made fuel, written with a small letter. From the name of Dubhan, born SE 29, whose first working fuel came on 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1. So a man's name wore down into a common noun.

"…for the fuel itself, as well as for the man who made it, years before the trade built upon it is whole." — annals, DE 11

dubhan-tùsail n. m. · lit. "dubhan of the beginning" A rough first attempt that looked like a dead end and later mattered; used in any field. From Dubhan's failed experiments (1 an t-Iuchar, SE 61). First recorded in a letter of the druid school at Caol shean, of the school's own revival (22 an Dàmhair, DE 11).

"It is used of a first attempt that seemed a dead end and proved otherwise…" — annals, DE 11

F

fadachadh v.n. m. · lit. "lengthening", from fadaich, fada To be crushed after holding out too long; am fadachadh, a total and final defeat. Narrowed by An Cogadh Fada, from Àth leathan (11 an Giblean, DE 21) to Muileann ghlas (10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22), and first heard among Tuathaich speakers of their own defeat (10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22).

"…'chaidh am fadachadh', they got long-warred… It is said as a jest, and those who say it do not laugh." — annals, DE 22

faire-obrach n. f. · lit. "work-watch" A shift. The annals first have need of it for the humans' night-shift order (25 an Lùnastal, AE 116), which the kingdom kept (18 an t-Samhain, SE 11).

Cha d' fhuair a' bheinn fois a-riamh, / is cha d' fhuair sinne. "The mountain never got its rest, and neither did we." — the hewers' saying, the Fifth Book

Fèill n. f. · lit. "feast-day, fair" With a town's name, a fair; above all Fèill Muileann òg (16 an Dàmhair, SE 21), heir to the harvest fair held there after the War of the Roads (5 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,665).

"A fair is held each year at Muileann òg, and it becomes the greatest gathering on the island." — annals, SE 21

Fo mhullach an taighe, chan eil nàmh ann phr. · lit. "under the roof of the house there is no enemy" The road-peace, the oldest law on the island that no Keeper made (22 an Dàmhair, FE 175). The War of the Roads ended under such a roof (4 an Dàmhair, FE 1,006).

"…no feud may be pursued under an inn roof or within a spear's throw of its door." — annals, FE 175

fuil-ghuail n. f. · lit. "coal-blood" The condition of those who bond with the vein and do not age as others do, and the people who have it. For half a century it had no name (13 am Faoilleach, AE 71), until the custodians made this one (23 am Faoilleach, AE 126). The humans rendered it obsidian-touched.

"It is meant as a physician's word. It outlives that meaning." — annals, AE 126

G

Gaoth Dhubh, A' n. f. · lit. "the black wind" The oldest storm whose name is kept (1 an Gearran, VE 7,740); the first named storm lost its name (30 am Faoilleach, VE 5,470). The harbour rolls went on naming storms: Am Fuath Mòr, "the great hate" (23 an t-Samhain, LE 259), and An Gàire Dubh, "the black laugh" (5 am Màrt, LE 519).

"Of all storms it is the eldest whose name is kept." — annals, VE 7,740

gun chreideamh adj. phr. · lit. "without a faith" Of land or people that keep none of the three faiths. The first census of the restored kingdom so entered the far north-western cape beyond Baile chrom, Eilean ghorm and the smallest islets (30 an t-Iuchar, SE 7); the phrase has stood on the map for that land since.

"All these they enter as gun chreideamh, without a faith." — annals, SE 7

I

Ithidh Mòd an neach a dh'itheas an cnoc phr. · lit. "Mòd will eat whoever eats the hill" The saying of the feathered doors, from the years when the hawk-priests were barred and the crews carried the Hawk order's sermons themselves (10 an Cèitean, AE 76). Mòd is the Hawk of Acaill, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, and the hill is the vein.

"The overseers' reports of these years list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a matter for punishment." — annals, AE 76

L

Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig n. m. · lit. "the law of the small burning" The Small-Burning Law: no household might burn more than a measured handful of ore in a season (13 an Lùnastal, FE 142). The ruling of the hearth bound the custodians never to withhold that handful (12 an Gearran, LE 565). The Law was never repealed; it lapsed (2 an Dùbhlachd, AE 21).

"The Law is never repealed; once its keeping no longer pays, it is no longer kept." — annals, AE 21

Làn na glaice, 's gun tuilleadh phr. · lit. "the fill of the hollow hand, and no more" The measure of the Ancient Age (5 an Lùnastal, VE 6,334). When Fionnlagh Dall re-cut the stone cup to hold two palms (15 an t-Iuchar, FE 139), the saying became Làn an dà bhois, agus gun tuilleadh.

"It is nowhere written and everywhere kept." — annals, VE 6,334

Loisc iad an leabhar, ach cha do loisc iad an cnoc phr. · lit. "they burned the book, but they did not burn the hill" Said of the raids on the tithe ledgers (9 an t-Iuchar, AE 150).

"Later chroniclers make much of it; it did little." — annals, AE 150

M

maor n. m., pl. maoir · lit. "steward" Under the humans, an overseer: a Ròdach set over Ròdaich for the Company. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill took his byname from the office (19 an Cèitean, AE 36, 17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 36). The kingdom gave the word to the Crown's officer in each shire (4 am Faoilleach, SE 4). The kenning maor-obrach, "work-steward", is a manager.

"…from the office the Ròdaich give him his byname: Raghnall Maor, Raghnall the steward." — annals, AE 36

mar a thàinig Niall phr. · lit. "the way Niall came" Any passing of power that goes uncommonly smoothly. From Niall's crowning (19 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3), which passed without dispute (7 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3).

"It is first found written in a tavern ledger at Cathair dhearg, against a debt settled without argument." — annals, SE 3

Marbh-bheò n. m. · lit. "dead-alive" The Hollow Man of the Doire uaine hills, which attacked anyone who lit a fire in its sight (9 an Giblean, VE 3,251). The rule against open fires after dark came from it (26 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,783), and shepherds still named it when they left the high pastures (17 an Lùnastal, LE 949).

Na las teine far am faic e thu. "Light no fire where it can see you." — the First Book

O

ogham n. m. · lit. "Ogma's letters" The letters of Rodos. The teachers of the stag's people made them from the cutters' tally-notches (15 am Màrt, FE 914), and the druids name them for Ogma, god of letters. Nearly every later hand on the island descends from them (Appendix F).

"These are the first letters the Ròdaich use: the ogham, which the druids call the gift of Ogma." — annals, FE 914

R

rìgh n. m. · lit. "king" A ruler of the lowlands, as against the Keeper of the flame. Goraidh mac Ìomhair was the first so called (28 an Cèitean, FE 674); under the division of keeping the rìgh had the roads and the granaries, the Keeper the flame (9 an t-Sultain, FE 694).

"None before him was ever so called." — annals, FE 674

Rìghrean na Cloiche n. pl. · lit. "the kings of the stone" The oldest oral king-list, opening with Ailean Mòr (9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324). The name was given to it later.

"…it gives no lengths of reign, and it is older than the name Ròdaich." — annals, VE 5,324

roghnaich v. · lit. "choose" With no object: to have chosen the crossing, to choose exile for good. From the Choosing (8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1); the narrow sense is in the custody-book from 21 an Lùnastal, LE 67. The plain sense was never lost.

Roghnaich iadsan, agus dh'fhuirich sinne. "They chose, and we stayed." — the Third Book

S

scàinte adj. · lit. "rent, split" Reeling, shaken, of a person as well as a building. From Scàineadh Cill ghlas, the Rending (9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 137). No annal marks its first use.

"Dozens are killed, and a whole mining district is shut for a generation." — annals, AE 137

Scaradh, a' n. m. · lit. "the parting" The Sundering (19 an Giblean, LE 40); loosely, any lasting parting, chosen, between people who belonged together. Later it was used also of the Severance (1 am Faoilleach, AE 151), which was not chosen, and the one word now serves for both.

"The chronicles of the island fall silent on them as the ships clear the harbour…" — annals, LE 40

seann-chunntas n. m. · lit. "old account" A grievance nobody in power acts on and nobody cancels. Tuathaich speakers coined it (18 an Giblean, DE 26) for the tabled archive request (15 an Gearran, DE 17) and the reparations motion left to die (10 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25).

"The Ròdaich in office do not take up the word." — annals, DE 26

Seann-Dhaoine n. pl. · lit. "old people" The Old Ones, the people before the Ròdaich. The name is a plain Ròdais description, and no annal dates it. Their first sure trace is the midden at Seann Dunn (28 an Lùnastal, VE 771).

"The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin…" — annals, VE 5,671

siorrachd n. f., pl. siorrachdan · lit. "shire" Named in the annals from the Age of Sundering (9 an t-Samhain, LE 9). The kingdom redrew the shires on the humans' district lines (12 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3), and has had a hundred and twenty-three since SE 38 (Appendix H).

"…the kingdom uses them and says nothing of it." — annals, SE 3

sliochd n. m. · lit. "seed, offspring" A house of custody known by a founder's name, not a hearth. Sliochd Mhuirich was the first (11 an t-Sultain, FE 96); four were bound to the Keepers' office (29 an Giblean, FE 385).

"…the first house of custody known by a name and not by a hearth." — annals, FE 96

stad-oibre n. m. · lit. "work-halt" A strike. The first lasted eleven days (13 an Dàmhair, AE 77); the first held in several regions on one day came in AE 143.

"The strike ends when the food, which the humans' Administration holds, runs out." — annals, AE 77

T

Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic phr. · lit. "the ship is eating the hill" Fearchar Bàrd's most quoted song, made when the Company's steamships began to burn the island's ore to carry it away (15 an Gearran, AE 103).

Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic / gus an cnoc a ghiùlan air falbh. "The ship is eating the hill to carry the hill away." — the Fourth Book

Tha e scrìobhte a-nis phr. · lit. "it is written now" The Moot's whole minute on the day the census figures were read at Caol mhòr (6 an t-Samhain, SE 64). The Fifth Book takes it for its epigraph.

"The Moot's minute says only: 'Now written.'" — annals, SE 64

Tìr Thall, an n. f. · lit. "the land beyond" The humans' homeland, whose own name no Ròdach scribe set down (26 an Gearran, AE 2).

"From the first season the scribes call it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and its people simply the humans." — annals, AE 2

tonn n. m. · lit. "wave" A sudden, overwhelming change: tha e san tonn, "he is in the wave of it". From Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol (3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 4), by way of the survivors' accounts (4 am Faoilleach, SE 5).

"Within a generation the sense is heard across the south." — annals, SE 5

Tràigh Bhàthte, an n. f. · lit. "the drowned strand" The old site of Cnoc chaol, left as the Great Wave left it (23 an Dùbhlachd, SE 4).

"The townsfolk call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and do not build there." — annals, SE 4

Tùrsa Geal, an n. m. · lit. "the white sorrow" The mourning for the departed, neither wholly grief nor wholly rejoicing (1 an Lùnastal, LE 54), first kept at court by Queen Beathag for her sister (27 an Dàmhair, LE 54). In a much later age it was used again, uneasily, for a departure of a very different kind.

"…with one place left empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast." — annals, LE 54

U

uaine adj. · lit. "green" Beside its plain sense, sickly, plague-marked. From A' Phlàigh Uaine (9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 73), first seen as a greenish pallor at Achadh dhomhain (5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 73).

"…in a field beyond the spoil-heaps still called the green acre." — annals, AE 73

Of What Is Not Known

Fewer first uses can be proved than a reader might wish. Scàinte, Aisling-aois and the loose sense of a' Scaradh stand on the chronicle's list, but no annal marks the day any of them was first said. The rope-makers of Cuan shean sing a keel-song whose words have lost their sense (5 am Màrt, LE 1,389). The Tuathaich's own memory of the Long War is filed as folklore, and the northern towns' own accounts are among the things the royal record says it does not hold (25 an Giblean, SE 43). Where the history of a word is lost, the gap is left as it is.

Appendix F — The Tongues and Peoples of Rodos

Here is gathered what the rolls and chronicles hold of the peoples who have lived on Rodos and of the speech they used. It is drawn from the royal chronicles, from the rolls and custody-books copied into Leabharlann Muileann chaol, from the map of the kingdom, and from the word-lists that survive from the Age of Strangers. Where the sources are silent, that is said, and the silence is left as it was found.

I. The Peoples

Five peoples, or kinds of people, stand in the island's history. Two of them are gone. One, the fuil-ghuail, is hardly a people in the common sense of the word; yet the chronicles have come to speak of it as one, and so it is set down here with the rest.

PeopleRòdais nameIn the chroniclesOn the map today
The Old Onesna Seann-DhaoineAge I; their works end before the Holy Ageno town; thirty towns and thirteen shires bear their names
The people of Rodosna Ròdaich (sg. Ròdach)every age441 of 505 towns; the capital and the sea
The humansthe chronicles' plain name for themAge IVnone by that name; their descendants are the Tuathaich
The northernersna Tuathaich (sg. Tuathach)Age V64 towns in the north and north-west
The coal-bloodedan fhuil-ghuail; in the humans' tongue, obsidian-touchedfrom Age IVnot counted on the map; counted, briefly, in the censuses

The Seann-Dhaoine

The Ròdaich call the people before them na Seann-Dhaoine, the Old Ones. The name is a Ròdais one, given from outside. What the Old Ones called themselves is not known, and cannot now be known.

What survives of them is stone, shell and names. The oldest sure trace is the midden at Seann Dunn (28 an Lùnastal, VE 771): limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many lifetimes, with no tool in it shaped the way any later Ròdach shaped tools. After it come the notched net-weights of Seann Chwen, every stone cut with the same three strokes (26 an t-Sultain, VE 851); the unmortared mole at Seann Skell on which every later quay wall there stands (1 an t-Iuchar, VE 930); the two hundred and twelve steps of Seann Bhral (30 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,010); the stone boxes on Eilean dhearg to which the dead of Seann Vell were rowed (4 an Cèitean, VE 1,090); the fish-channel of Seann Toll (2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,170); the shell causeway of Seann Warr, the first made road on the island that can still be walked (7 am Màrt, VE 1,249); the fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn (17 an Giblean, VE 1,408); and the slipways of Seann Bhrenn, wide enough for hulls bigger than any hide boat; the hulls are gone, and so is any telling of where they went (16 an Cèitean, VE 1,488).

At their widest reach (8 an Cèitean, VE 3,870) they held every coast of the island: the ten places whose names begin with Seann, and the islands off them. Their largest landing was at the place now called Seann Skell, on the Abhainn naomh.

The ruins inland are theirs by the oldest tellings. The telling of the counting of the dead (29 an Lùnastal, VE 5,671) names the Seann-Dhaoine as "the people who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin". Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, the walled outpost on the spur above the ground where Cathair mhòr now stands, has a single gate, and it faces inland, away from the sea (19 an Cèitean, VE 2,524); Làrach an Dùin, near Ceann mhin, had three rings of wall and room inside for some four hundred people with their beasts (17 an t-Ògmhios, VE 2,580); and Làrach an Teampaill, in the eastern hills, has its altar set square to the central mountains (14 an Lùnastal, VE 2,692), toward the vein and away from the sea. All three were already ruined when the first reliable chronicles begin (27 an t-Samhain, VE 4,036, 6 am Màrt, VE 4,148, 7 am Faoilleach, VE 4,251). Whether the builders of the outpost built the fortress too has never been settled. After the high places were left, every new work of the Seann-Dhaoine lies within sight of salt water (9 an Dùbhlachd, VE 4,316).

The standing stones are harder. Carragh Cnoc bheag, Colbh Cnoc chiar and Calbh Cnoc ghorm were raised in the Ancient Age (17 an t-Iuchar, VE 4,651, 9 an t-Sultain, VE 4,770, 6 an t-Samhain, VE 4,876), and no telling says by whom. The upper face of Carragh Cnoc bheag bears a line of the unread script; the four Ròdais words, Bha teine sa chloich, "there was fire in the stone", lie lower down, cut with a narrower tool by another hand, and "when that second hand came is not known" (11 an Lùnastal, VE 4,708). On these stones, and nowhere else, the marks of two peoples lie on the same face. The wind-stone at the central Seann Chwen is another: a Ròdais wind-name cut over an older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine (13 an Gearran, VE 7,770).

Their counting. Late in their time the Seann-Dhaoine began cutting single strokes on flat stones at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household (31 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,631). At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones were built into a wall of some three thousand strokes (3 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,712); at Seann Tarr in the north-east they were cut in fives and set in the floor of a house (2 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,751). At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone was left half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and abandoned (5 an Cèitean, VE 5,833).

Their end. After the half-cut stone no new work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their script is not cut again (7 an Gearran, VE 5,874). How they ended no telling knows, and no guess is offered here. The chronicles do not say that they were driven out, or that they died, or that their blood ran on in some later people; nor do they say otherwise.

The hill-folk. Alongside, or after, the Seann-Dhaoine the tellings set a second people: the hill-folk of the high valleys around the crack (10 an t-Samhain, VE 4,428), who buried their dead in the ground rather than on islands, and cut no script. They burned the ore, though sparingly: one sliver, one fire, at Àth gharbh (12 an Dàmhair, VE 4,484). Whether they shared the island with the Old Ones or came after them no telling knows. Their own answer, given later, is that they were always there, and it is the answer the Ròdaich give of themselves in the doctrine carried on Calbh Cnoc ghorm: Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann, "we did not come; we were here." When stag-scholars came to Calbh Cnoc ghorm in the Holy Age and could not read it, the people of Cnoc ghorm told them what it said, and "the scholars write that the people say so" (6 an Dàmhair, FE 2,376).

The Ròdaich

The Ròdaich are the people of Rodos: the majority in every age of the island's history, the holders of the capital, Cathair dhearg, and of the sea. Their name is the island's name with the people-ending -aich; a single person is a Ròdach. Writers of the humans' tongue called them Rodian, and that word is kept in this history for the adjective.

Custodians. The Ròdaich enter history as custodians. In the Ancient Age a custom set in across the hill settlements that no fire should take more of the ore than one cupped hand could hold. The Binding of the First Flame (23 an t-Sultain, FE 1) made the custodianship of the vein a formal order, "older by centuries than any king", and the Small-Burning Law (13 an Lùnastal, FE 142) made the custom into rule. The first man in any roll to be called rìgh was Goraidh mac Ìomhair at Dùn dhearg (28 an Cèitean, FE 674), and he claimed nothing over the vein. For the whole of the Holy Age the kings ruled the roads and the granaries, and the Keepers at Dùn ìseal ruled the mountain. The Holy Age closes on the last age of even population (1 an Cèitean, FE 2,949). After it, the chroniclers note with some unease, there was never again a time on Rodos when no family held more years of life than any other.

The kingdom. After the Severance the state restyled itself Rìoghachd Ròdais, the Kingdom of Rodos (27 an t-Iuchar, SE 2), and Niall was crowned at Cathair dhearg (19 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3). The rulers since are set down in Appendix A. Here it is enough to say that the kingdom is a Ròdach kingdom: its schools teach in Ròdais "and it has no others" (10 an Gearran, SE 7), and the old apprentice-binding custom, when it was revived, was reserved for Ròdaich applicants only (20 an Dàmhair, SE 13).

The sea. The Ròdaich have always been a people of the coast as much as of the mountain. The largest towns on the map today stand on the sea or on the rivers that run down to it, and the two largest bear a name older than Ròdais:

TownShireFaith (order)Population

⟦burg:431Seann Skell⟧Seann SkellAn Creideamh Sean (Òrd Bhrìde)57,907
⟦burg:27Ros dhomhain⟧Ros dhomhainAn Creideamh Sean (Òrd Mhacha)51,589
⟦burg:110Seann Bhral⟧Seann BhralNa Seann Spioradan49,681

⟦burg:23Cathair mhòr⟧Cathair mhòrAn Creideamh Sean (Òrd Mhacha)49,298

The capital itself is not among them. Cathair dhearg is counted at 10,274; its harbour, Ros dhomhain, is five times its size.

The departed. Part of the Ròdaich people is not on Rodos. Land was found across the water (6 am Faoilleach, LE 1); volunteers chose to go, by "a vote, or what the later chroniclers call a vote" (8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1); the fleet set out, turning sunwise round the river pool at Seann Skell, in the year from which the old count of the Diosal ran (19 an Giblean, LE 40). A broken report told of two landfalls (24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44), and of the thinning: cut off from the vein, "by the third generation over the water nothing is left that Rodos would know" (3 an t-Iuchar, LE 53). The departed stand in the chronicles only as a gap. The island kept them in rites (the empty-harbour rite, 25 an t-Samhain, LE 61; the white sorrow, an Tùrsa Geal, 27 an Dàmhair, LE 54) and in words, of which more below. When the humans came, old sailors at Cuan shean remarked that the strangers had come in from the same quarter of sea the Sundering fleet once sailed into. The council forbade the remark in its hall; it was written down all the same, and never answered (9 an Gearran, AE 2). Whether the humans descend from the departed, no one on Rodos knows.

The humans of an Tìr Thall

The Crossing. Humans made landfall on Rodos and were granted leave to stay (5 am Faoilleach, AE 1): the first contact since the Sundering. Three ships out of the west anchored off Cuan shean, and their master, whom the chronicles call Edmund Harrow, came ashore unarmed and asked by signs for water (5 an Gearran, AE 1). So the first dealing between the two peoples was made without words.

Their homeland. The strangers named their homeland in their own tongue, but no Ròdach scribe set the word down. From the first season the chronicles call it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and its people simply the humans (26 an Gearran, AE 2). Their own name for their country is written on Rodos in no hand, and it cannot now be recovered.

What they called things. The humans' names for the island's things were few, plain and, to Ròdach ears, careless. They had a single word for the black ore, and it was the word for the fuel they burned at home; Gormshuil nic Fhearchair's copyist noted that no Ròdais word answered to it, and that the humans did not ask for one (23 an Giblean, AE 3). So the vein became, in their tongue, coal, and the custodians of the vein became, in Samuel Wren's otherwise careful grammar, "keepers of the coal" (21 an Lùnastal, AE 12). Their offices and bodies came with names in the humans' tongue and kept them (they are given here in English): the Company, the Administration, the Mission, the Residency above Ros dhomhain (10 an Cèitean, AE 9), the Commissioner, the Levy, the constable posts. Their faith was the Church, which the Ròdaich call an Eaglais, and the Mission was its house on Rodos. Their coin was the mark. The townsfolk of Muileann shean called the constable post there "the humans' second Residency", and did not mean it kindly (11 an Dàmhair, AE 132).

The camps. What the humans built for themselves on Rodos they built for the pit. The camp of timber huts at Àth ìseal was the first settlement on the island raised for the pit and for nothing else (6 an Dàmhair, AE 29); Baile dhomhain was laid out on a grid by a Company surveyor, the first Ròdach town drawn on paper before it was built (10 am Faoilleach, AE 34); the camp at Achadh dhomhain was built of spoil (1 am Faoilleach, AE 68). Ròdach hands worked the camps and human officers ruled them, and the record of them is kept in two tongues that seldom agree: the Mission counts four hundred and six dead of the spotted pox, and the custodians count more, and write the difference in the margin of the Mission's list (11 an Dàmhair, AE 39). Human families lived on Rodos as well as human officers: upland pasture in the north-west, around Muileann àrsaidh, was granted for human families who would not work in the pits (3 an t-Samhain, AE 20). This was the first human settlement in the north; and to the north, in the end, their descendants were sent.

Mixing. The first mixed settlement (22 an Giblean, AE 5) was Baile dhìreach on the south-west coast, under a council of three Ròdaich and three humans, whose founding compact was written twice, once in each tongue, the only such compact on record in the age (10 an Dàmhair, AE 5). There the net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh married the human cooper Samuel Hale, and the council entered the marriage in both its books (26 an Cèitean, AE 7). It was not tried again, and the first inheritance case of mixed blood (15 an Gearran, AE 111) the Administration decided wholly in its own favour.

The going north. War was declared in AE 149. Before the end, the human families of Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west marched north along the western roads under guard of the council's companies; few of them had ever lived in the north; no column was attacked, and none was helped (29 an t-Samhain, AE 150). The war ended with the crossing itself closed (1 am Faoilleach, AE 151). Whatever way had let the humans reach Rodos was shut, and those still on the island were herded to the northern country their descendants hold today.

The Tuathaich

From the Severance the chronicles stop calling them humans. The descendants of those left on Rodos are na Tuathaich, the northerners, from tuath, north, with the same -aich that makes Ròdaich; on the page the two names stand like brothers, though the two peoples' fortunes have been far apart. Their homeland in the north was fixed formally (22 am Màrt, SE 1): "It is a confinement; yet their children's children call it home." A formal wall between the two peoples was proposed and rejected as unnecessary, because the two were already keeping apart on their own (11 an Cèitean, SE 10).

What the Tuathaich call themselves in their own speech the chronicles do not say. The name used here is the kingdom's name for them.

Their towns. The kingdom's map counts sixty-four Tuathaich towns, all in the north and north-west, with some 543,000 people in them. The Ròdaich hold the other 441. The Tuathaich country is some fifteen parts in a hundred of the island's land, the windy coast of the far north-west among it, and the Ròdaich country the other eighty-five (Appendix H). The largest Tuathaich towns are these:

TownShireFaithPopulation
⟦burg:95Caol mhòr⟧Caol mhòrAn Eaglais42,002
⟦burg:209Doire ghlas⟧Doire ghlasAn Eaglais (Eaglais nan Tuathach)40,740
⟦burg:143Ceann mhòr⟧Ceann mhòrAn Eaglais32,420
⟦burg:305Baile chrom⟧Baile chromAn Eaglais (the vigil of the Grey Night)27,319
⟦burg:142Cnoc ghorm⟧Cnoc ghormAn Eaglais25,112

Every Tuathaich town but one bears a Ròdais name, and most of them were Ròdach towns before the Severance; the north-west had been thinly held since the dearth on that shore in the Age of Sundering (19 an Giblean, LE 819). One of them, Seann Skell in the shire of Muileann àrsaidh, bears an Old One's name. The Tuathaich have added no names of their own to the map.

Their assembly. Tuathaich householders from the northern towns met at Caol mhòr and chose a speaker, Walter Hale, a former harbour clerk (25 an Lùnastal, SE 2). The Moot has no standing in Ròdach law; it meets anyway, and its minutes run unbroken from that meeting to the present.

Their faith. All sixty-four Tuathaich towns keep An Eaglais, the Church, which their forebears brought over the sea at the Crossing; no Ròdach town keeps it. Fifty-one keep it in the line the Mission left, and their largest church is at Cnoc ghorm. Twelve are the old congregations of the north coast, Eaglais nan Tuathach, whose towns lie together in the shires of Doire ghlas, Muileann leathan, Inis mhin and Àth àrsaidh. One, Baile chrom, keeps the vigil of the Grey Night, Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise, which the Church's bishops call irregular. The old congregations keep, quietly, the First Canoe fragment (13 an Gearran, SE 9): among coastal Tuathaich families, "a named steersman, a first crossing", which their church tells as the voyage of Naomh Breandan to the Isle of the Blessed, and which the druids of the Old Faith dismiss as superstition (9 an t-Samhain, VE 2,851). The fragment is set at the head of the Ancient Age, for there its tellers place it. The Library has neither upheld it nor struck it out. It is one of the two suppressed histories that stand at either end of the island's story, and it is left here as it was found.

The fuil-ghuail

This section holds to what the rolls and chronicles say.

A child born into the mining camps was exposed to more raw ore across her lifetime than any Rodian in living memory, and did not age the way the people around her did. Her name is Aisling (7 am Màrt, AE 69). What was happening to her had no word, in any language spoken on the island (13 am Faoilleach, AE 71). A second, Fionnan, was born half a century later (21 an Gearran, AE 121), and it became plain that this was no single mischance: it came of the working of the pits, and would come again while they were worked. With two sure cases before them, the Ròdach custodians settled on a word (23 am Faoilleach, AE 126): fuil-ghuail, "coal-blood", rendered in the humans' tongue as obsidian-touched. It was meant as a physician's word. It was agreed at a meeting of custodians at the shrine of Cill ghlas, and the roll records the vote but not who proposed it (21 an Gearran, AE 126). The Residency ordered every Ròdach child showing the condition to be reported; the custodians complied by reporting none (26 an t-Samhain, AE 127). A third case, Lorccan, was born in a mining town (29 an Cèitean, AE 134), and a fourth, Cian, within a year of him (3 am Màrt, AE 135).

After the Severance the Obsidian Rite, Òrd Bhrìde, was set in order within the Old Faith, built around the leyline and "the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched" (18 an Giblean, SE 6). The first census of the kingdom noted, without further comment, exactly how few such people exist (29 an t-Ògmhios, SE 7), and the published census of a later generation gave a number and nothing else (8 am Faoilleach, SE 65). The number is printed nowhere else, and it is not printed here.

Whether the fuil-ghuail are a people is a question of words. They are born to Ròdach families; in Ròdach speech the word names the gift that sets the Ròdaich apart from the Tuathaich; and the druid schools have asked since the Holy Age why the vein answers some hands and not others. The chronicles do not settle it.

II. The Tongues

Ròdais

Ròdais is the tongue of Rodos, spoken by the Ròdaich in every age. Three things mark it at once on the page:

FeatureRòdaisExample
Long vowelsgrave accent only: à è ì ò ùmòr, sìth, Ròdais
The cluster /sk/written sc, never sguisce, scoil, sceul, Scàineadh
"City"cathairCathair dhearg

Its greeting of thanks is gu robh math agad. Its verbs come first in the sentence (Chunnaic Cian an long, "Cian saw the ship"); it has no word for "a", no words for yes and no, and two initial mutations.

Lenition. After many words an initial consonant softens, and the change is written with h: b > bh, c > ch, d > dh, f > fh, g > gh, m > mh, p > ph, s > sh, t > th. The possessives, the past tense, a feminine noun after the article, an adjective after a feminine noun, most simple prepositions and the second element of a name all cause it. It does not touch vowels, nor l, n, r in writing, nor the clusters sc, sp, st, sm; and after a word ending in n it spares d, t and s, which is why the map has Seann Dunn and Seann Toll but Seann Bhral.

Broad and slender. Vowels are broad (a o u à ò ù) or slender (e i è ì), and within one word a consonant takes vowels of the same class on both sides: caol le caol, leathan le leathan, slender with slender, broad with broad. That is why so many endings come in pairs, and why the small rivers are Ciaras but Àrsaidheas.

Sounds. For the reader who would say these names aloud:

writtensaidexample
bh, mhvSeann Bhral
chas in lochSeann Chwen
dh, gha voiced ch before broad vowels; y before slenderCathair dhearg
fhsilentÀth fhada
sh, thhDùn thais
scskScàineadh

The stress falls on the first syllable.

How Ròdais names new things. Ròdais was long spoken on an island that few new things reached, and it was slow to borrow. The humans brought many new things, and the kingdom after them more. In the first generations after the Crossing the Ròdaich named nearly all of them from old roots, calling the thing by what it does or what it is like: head first, the describer after, hyphenated, two elements and seldom three. Many of these kennings are still the common words. The loans Ròdais did take came mostly later: bus, the bus; tacsaidh, the taxi; rèidio, the radio; and many words of the sciences, such as ogsaidean, oxygen, and the names of the elements. Some of the kennings, with their literal sense:

EnglishRòdaisliterally

enginecridhe-iarainniron-heart
computerinntinn-iarainniron-mind
aeroplaneeun-iarainniron-bird

cameracìste-scàileshadow-chest
filmsceul-scàileshadow-tale
novelleabhar-sceòiltale-book
documentarysceul-fìrinnetruth-tale
plasticcèir-chruaidhhard-wax

internetlìon-fiosatidings-net

tyrebròg-cuibhlewheel-shoe

The kennings fall into families: machines are iarainn, of iron; screens and pictures are scàil and scàthan, shadow and mirror; electricity is dealan, spark, and dealanach, lightning. A crossing for feet is a ford, àth, the same word the map uses for a town at a river.

Words born of the island's history. Old words have also taken new senses from what the island lived through. The royal chroniclers keep a list of these, and the rolls date the first use of most.

WordPlain senseSense given by historyFirst recorded

Of the Sundering the language also keeps one strange relic. A work-song of the rope-makers of Cuan shean names the parts of a deep keel, and half its words have no meaning to anyone who sings it (5 am Màrt, LE 1,389). Nothing else of the fleet's craft survives in any form. Whether the lost words are old Ròdais, or the cant of the wrights, or something else, no one has shown.

The tongue of the Seann-Dhaoine

Of the Old Ones' speech nothing survives but names. Ten roots are known, each standing after the Ròdais word seann, "old", which lenites it where Ròdais lenites:

RootAs written on the mapTowns bearing itShires named from it
DunnSeann Dunn3yes
CwenSeann Chwen3yes
SkellSeann Skell4yes (three)
BralSeann Bhral3yes
TarrSeann Tarr3yes
VellSeann Vell5yes (three)
MornSeann Mhorn2—
BrennSeann Bhrenn2yes
TollSeann Toll3yes
WarrSeann Warr2yes

Thirty towns on the map bear these names, and thirteen shires are named from them.

The Ròdaich did not translate these names; they took them over. The fishers who resettled Seann Mhorn in the Holy Age kept "the name they find there, which is not of their own tongue", and said the old name came with the stones (23 an t-Sultain, FE 178). It is the first such taking-over on record. So the harbour-names of an older people outlived them inside a newer tongue, kept whole and hard like shells in a stone, and never put into Ròdais.

What can be said. The roots are single syllables. Seven of the ten end in a doubled consonant (-nn, -ll, -rr). Three of them hold letters that Ròdais writes nowhere else: k in Skell, v in Vell, w in Cwen and Warr. Everywhere else Ròdais writes the sound sk as sc, yet no scribe has ever written Seann Scell; they kept the foreign k as they found it, and the grammarians count sk- among the clusters that do not lenite.

What cannot be known. What any root meant. Whether seann was ever the Old Ones' own element, or only the Ròdaich's word for places they found already named (the second is the common reading, and the likelier; but it is no more than a reading). Whether the roots come from one tongue or several. Two of them look like Ròdais words, toll, a hole, and dunn beside dùn, a fort. The likeness has tempted scholars in every age and proves nothing, and the Library takes no side.

The script. The Seann-Dhaoine also cut signs. Rows of them stand on the cliff above Seann Tarr (5 an Giblean, VE 1,329), in the script that is found again on the standing stones. It is not Ròdais. It has never been read, and not one sign of it has an agreed meaning. The stag-scholars of the Holy Age set their own new letters against the obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag and found that they matched nothing, and wrote down that the stone's writers were not their teachers (12 an Cèitean, FE 914). Samuel Wren copied the obelisk and sent it west to the scholars of an Tìr Thall; no reply is recorded (5 an Gearran, AE 17). Edwin Lowe copied the pillar near Cnoc chiar, compared it with Wren's copy, and decided that the two were not the same script and that neither was Ròdach; his notes stop there (9 an Lùnastal, AE 65). The strokes on the midden stones are a count, and have nothing to do with this script. Whether the script records the Old Ones' tongue, or some other, or no tongue at all, is not known.

The humans' tongue

The humans spoke a plain tongue, and this history renders it in English (see Of Translation below). The names they carried were names of that tongue: Edmund Harrow, Thomas Pike, Samuel Wren, Josiah Pell, Henry Maddox, Arthur Lisle, Samuel Hale, Edwin Lowe.

The season of translation. Human clerics and Ròdach custodians spent a full season trying to build a shared vocabulary, and neither side's account of what was agreed survives intact (27 am Màrt, AE 2). Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair kept parallel word-lists. Wren's survives in the Administration's letter-books; Gormshuil's was lost, and only its first leaf is known from a copy: forty words for the colours of broken ore (13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 2). Against those forty the humans had one word, and it was coal.

The tongue of rule. The humans wrote their agreements in their own tongue only. The first written treaty (27 an Giblean, AE 8) was signed at Cathair dhearg by Tormod mac Ailein, who could not read the tongue it was written in; who read it to him, no roll says (7 an Cèitean, AE 8). The Harbour Articles were written the same way, and that time two custodians refused to sign (16 an t-Samhain, AE 19). The Mission's school at Ros dhomhain taught Ròdach children in the humans' tongue (9 an Cèitean, AE 51); a generation later Iain Maor, the first overseer schooled there, kept his reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Ròdais (23 an Giblean, AE 87). The Levy's officers read the names of the chosen at Caol mhòr from a list in the humans' tongue, and the custodians took the names down again in Ròdais, "that they may know whom to look for" (3 am Màrt, AE 88).

Loanwords. Few crossed, and most of those late. In the first generations Ròdais took the humans' goods and named them in its own way, as told above, and kept few of the humans' words for them. The humans for their part, so far as the rolls show, used the Ròdais names of places as they found them; fuil-ghuail they did not borrow but turned into their own tongue, obsidian-touched, and that word, rather than the Ròdais, is the one the kingdom's own later entries use of the Rite's "unbroken line". What passed the other way, into the humans' speech, is best seen after the Severance, in the north.

The Ròdais word for the humans' country, an Tìr Thall, is the only name the island has for it.

Tuathaich speech

The speech of the north is a mixed speech, and the chronicles speak of it only in passing. This much they say.

The Tuathaich kept the humans' tongue. Walter Hale asked the council for leave to open schools in the north teaching in it, and was refused (10 an Gearran, SE 7); Agnes Pike opened one at Doire ghlas anyway, with Moot money and without the council's leave, and within a decade there were nine (14 am Faoilleach, SE 15). The Moot later counted eleven such schools, and three that had begun to teach Ròdais as well, at the parents' asking (7 an t-Ògmhios, SE 29). The church at Cnoc ghorm taught its priests in the humans' tongue while reading the Bible in the Ròdais text its preachers use on the west coast: the only place in the north where both are taught (29 an Giblean, SE 10).

The Tuathaich live among Ròdais names and use Ròdais words. The words the north has added to the island's speech in the present age are Ròdais in form: fadachadh, from fada, long, the name of the war they lost (10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22), and seann-chunntas, an old reckoning, which official Ròdach usage pointedly does not take up (18 an Giblean, DE 26). The word dubhan for the fuel came out of the north, from the name of Dubhan, a Tuathach, and it spread before the fuel did (23 an t-Sultain, DE 11); the royal chronicler who first set it down spelled it three ways in two lines (21 an t-Samhain, DE 1).

Beyond this the chronicles do not go. The northern towns' own accounts are among the things the royal chroniclers say they do not hold (25 an Giblean, SE 43). How far the humans' tongue has drifted in the north since the crossing closed, how much Ròdais is spoken at a Tuathach hearth, and in which tongue the First Canoe is told, the Library cannot say.

Names and naming

Personal names. Ròdach names are the old given names of the island: Ailean, Beathag, Catrìona, Dòmhnall, Eilidh, Fearchar, Gormshuil, Iain, Mòrag, Raghnall, Sìleas, Tormod. A person is further named from the father, with mac, son, or nic, daughter, and the father's name in the genitive, lenited where Ròdais lenites: Tormod mac Iain; Eilidh nic Iain; Gormshuil nic Fhearchair; Donnchadh mac Thormoid; Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill; Oighrig nic Lachlainn.

Bynames are as common as patronymics and often outlast them. They name a colour, a trade, a size or a deed. After a woman's name the byname is lenited, after a man's it is not: Seònaid Mhòr, Eilidh Dhubh, Beathag Bhàn, but Ailean Mòr, Calum Liath, Dùghall Garbh. Trade-names are nouns and stand as they are: Alasdair Saor, the wright; Iain Maor, the overseer. Some bynames are earned: Tormod mac Iain, the first of the royal kin to read, was called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the Writer, for the rest of his life (3 an Lùnastal, FE 1,255).

Kindreds take Sliochd, the seed or line, or Clann, the children, with a founder's name in the genitive: Sliochd Ìomhair, Sliochd Mhuirich, Clann Choinnich.

Human and Tuathaich names are of the humans' tongue and are kept in their own spelling: Walter Hale, Agnes Pike. The humans' names for the island's things were lost at the Severance; their names for themselves lived through it.

Place names. Ròdach places are named by a generic noun and a describing word after it. On the map the describer is always lenited, whatever the gender of the generic (Baile ghorm, Cnoc bheag, Dùn thais). In speech it would not be lenited after a masculine noun; the names keep an old fixed usage, as old compounds are kept. The generics are these:

GenericSenseUsed for
Cathairstone fort; citycapital, city
Dùnfortified hillcapital, city
Baile Mòrgreat settlementcity
Bailesettlement, towntown
Àthfordtown
Cnochilltown
Muileannmilltown
Cillholy cell, shrinevillage, hamlet
Tobarwellvillage, hamlet
Achadhfieldvillage
Doireoak grovevillage
Carraigrockhamlet
Rosheadlandport
Ceannhead, pointport
Cuanharbourport
Caolstraitport

The describers are colour, size and character words: mòr, beag, dubh, geal, bàn, dearg, ruadh, uaine, glas, fada, domhain, ìseal, fiadhaich, naomh, fionn, ciar, gorm, sean, òg, garbh, min, caol, leathan, crom, dìreach, àrsaidh. The great rivers are Abhainn with a describer; the small ones take a root and the ending -as or -eas by broad and slender. A shire, siorrachd, takes the name of its seat, or, where it has no town, of its island (Appendix H). Names repeat freely: there are four Baile chrom and four Seann Skell, and the rolls tell them apart by where they lie.

Beside these stand the Old Ones' names, which follow none of the rules above except that the Ròdaich put seann before them.

Writing

Before letters. The first marks on Rodos made on purpose are the Seann-Dhaoine's: the notched net-weights of Seann Chwen, their unread script, and their tally strokes. The Ròdaich's forebears kept counts too, but not in letters. Someone began marking the high-water line against a fixed rock in the Ancient Age (28 am Faoilleach, VE 6,994), and at Ros dhomhain Seònaid Mhòr cut her marks in pairs, one for the high water and one for the low (25 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,747). The king-lists of that age were oral, and the Small-Burning custom was "nowhere written and everywhere kept".

The Ròdais words on the stones. Bha teine sa chloich on Carragh Cnoc bheag, Cuimhnich an teine on Colbh Cnoc chiar, Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann on Calbh Cnoc ghorm: these are the oldest Ròdais words in stone. When they were cut no roll tells. The stones were raised in the Ancient Age; the Ròdais on Carragh Cnoc bheag was cut later, by another hand. The words on Calbh Cnoc ghorm were recut along their old grooves by a hand from the Stone Kings' hill, and some later readers say the recutting changed a letter (2 an t-Samhain, VE 9,687). This does not prove that there were letters to change in that day; the Library keeps the claim and passes no judgment on it.

The stag-letters. The first letters in use by the Ròdaich were made at Muileann chiar in the far east, where the teachers of the stag's people, the first of the druid schools, later called Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, turned the cutters' tally-notches into signs for sounds, "so that a teaching can be kept without a teacher" (15 am Màrt, FE 914). The druids call them the ogham, the gift of Ogma, god of letters. From them nearly every later hand on the island descends. From them too came the first written king-list (20 an Lùnastal, FE 1,299), kept by Tormod Scrìobhaiche at Dùn dhearg; the Keepers' own roll, written down at Dùn ìseal in answer to it (17 an Dàmhair, FE 1,320); boundary stones cut with treaty terms (11 am Màrt, FE 1,595); and the first teaching of letters for their own sake, to fishers' children at Inis bheag, which the Hall recorded with the remark that fish do not need reading (22 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,854).

Books and paper. The Age of Sundering is the age of the custody-book, kept by the vein-house, and of the first books: Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the sayings of Gormshuil (5 an t-Ògmhios, LE 251), and Seònaid nic Coinnich's Book of the Three Claimants, the oldest surviving history on Rodos written as one narrative (8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 624). Aonghas mac Uisdein was the first king to learn his letters as a child (25 an Cèitean, LE 394). A mill at Muileann chaol began making paper from rags, the first on Rodos, and the custody-book was copied onto paper in that generation (28 am Faoilleach, LE 1,674).

Two tongues of record. The humans brought paper in quantity, and the custodians of Cathair naomh asked for their first payment in paper and ink (19 an Lùnastal, AE 3). They brought, too, a written tongue the Ròdaich could not read, and for a century the island kept its records in two. Whether the humans' letters and the stag-letters share any shapes, no roll says. The earliest Ròdach grievance text to survive, Leabhar Baile thais, was set down in Ròdais by many hands (18 an t-Sultain, AE 101).

The kingdom's record. After the Severance the kingdom founded Leabharlann Muileann chaol (1 an Cèitean, SE 16) and the office of royal chronicler (20 an t-Samhain, SE 18), and in time drew the provincial archives into one place (26 an t-Iuchar, SE 67). This account is written in that Library.

Of Translation

This history is written in English for readers who have no Ròdais, and some account is owed of what that has done to the tongues it tells of.

The humans' speech is rendered in English. The humans did not speak English. They spoke the tongue of an Tìr Thall, whose name for itself, like the name of their country, is not recorded on Rodos. It was a plain tongue, as English is plain beside Ròdais. Its speakers were strangers to the island and its things, and it has become, in the north, the everyday speech of the Tuathaich. For those reasons it is given here as English, and its names are given as English names, as the letter- books would have them. When this history says the humans called the ore coal, it means that they used their ordinary word for their ordinary fuel, and that coal is the nearest English word for what they meant. When it gives a custodian's title as "keepers of the coal", it is rendering Wren's rendering. Obsidian-touched is likewise an English stand-in for the humans' word, chosen because it keeps the plainness of the original and the error in it. The ore is not obsidian, and it is not coal.

Ròdais is kept as it is. The Ròdaich are the people of this history and Ròdais is its first tongue, and it is not translated into something else here. Names of places, persons, faiths, laws and offices are left in Ròdais spelling, with the grave accent and the sc, and with their lenitions: Cathair dhearg, not "Red City"; fuil-ghuail, not "coal-blood", except where a gloss is wanted. Where a Ròdais phrase is translated, the translation follows it in quotation marks, as a help to the reader; the Ròdais stands first. The six ages have Ròdais names and are also given English ones for convenience; the English names are this archive's, not the chroniclers'. The adjective Rodian is English, and is used as such.

The island's own name. Written in Ròdais it is Ròdos, with the accent. In the English text of this history it is written Rodos, the form the humans used, and the one most readers will have met. It is the same word.

The Seann tongue is left untranslated, for it cannot be translated. Its ten roots are given as the Ròdaich wrote them, with the foreign letters the Ròdaich kept. No meaning is offered for any of them.

What has been lost in the rendering. Some things do not cross. The forty colour-words on Gormshuil's leaf are one; the Tuathaich jokes about being long-warred are another, since fadachadh is funny, and not funny, only in a tongue where fada is also the name of the war. Where there was a choice between a rendering that reads easily and one that keeps what the words did, the second has been taken.

Appendix G — The Goods and Markets of Rodos

Here is set down what the island grows, digs, catches and makes; the sixteen market towns through which nearly all of it is bought and sold; the chief roads of trade between them; and the dues the Treasury takes on that trade. The account of the present day is drawn from the Treasury's market roll for the last full year, which the clerks of the market-due keep in each of the sixteen market towns and send to Cathair dhearg, and from the books of the fair-court at Muileann òg. The older history comes from the annals, and where a trade has a first date in them the date is given.

The roll counts goods in the measures the markets use: grain, fish, clay and sand by the wain; timber by the pile; stone by the pallet; ore by the wagon; silver and gold by the bar; cattle, sheep, horses and oxen by the head; oil, dubhan, wine, honey and tar by the barrel; salt and dyes by the bag; cloth by the bolt; books by the volume. Prices are given in the realm-coin.

I. The Countries of the Island and What They Grow

Rodos is a wet and windy island, mild for so northerly a place, and most of it is forest and moor. Its husbandry follows the lie of five countries.

The high bare north. Along the northern coast from Ceann mhòr to Seann Tarr, and inland over the moors behind the Hawk bay, the ground is bare and windswept, with snow on the high moor in winter. Yet it grows more than its look promises. Barley and oats are sown in every sheltered hollow, hemp grows in the valley bottoms, and the heather feeds bees and sheep. The shore is the richer half. The northern and north-western waters hold the island's herring grounds and its whales, and amber is gathered from the wrack on the strands of the Hawk bay and the north-west. The market towns of this country are Ceann mhòr, Seann Skell, Àth fhionn, Muileann fhionn and Seann Tarr.

The birch and pine hills. The largest single country on the island is the belt of birch, pine and hill pasture that runs from the western plain across the middle of Rodos into the eastern hills. It is cattle and sheep country before all else, and it gives besides timber, venison, honey and a dark wine pressed from blaeberry and bramble. Almost all of the island's ore-bearing ground lies in these hills: the silver of Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid and of the hills of Cuan ghlas, the copper and tin of Ceann àrsaidh, Cnoc bhàn and Doire fhionn, the gemstones of the Muileann dhearg hills, the marble of Baile Mòr dhomhain, the old spoil-heaps where dubhan is made for the forges, and the charcoal woods that fed the forges before it. Copper was little worked before the Age of the Kingdom. The humans shipped theirs in for the first coinage (10 an Lùnastal, AE 17), and the first great working is the copper-town of Àth fhiadhaich (2 an t-Ògmhios, SE 61). The market towns of the hills are Baile Mòr dhomhain, Ros fhionn, Dùn ìseal, Baile Mòr dhìreach and Ros bheag.

The wet western and southern woods. South and west of the capital the forest is oak, alder and hazel, dripping for half the year. Timber, game, clay, white sand, hemp and honey are its chief goods, with barley on the cleared ground. The potteries and glass-houses stand in this country because its clay and sand are the best on Rodos, and the dyers of the south take their colours from its plants. Its market towns are Baile Mòr fhionn, Cathair fhada, Cnoc bhàn and Caol ruadh.

The oak country of the capital and the east. Around the capital and along the eastern road the woods are broad-leaved and the soil is deeper. This is the island's best mixed farming: cattle and sheep, grain, wine, hemp, and the horses of the Doire chaol country. Its farms sell through Cathair dhomhain, Ceann leathan and Dùn ìseal.

The eastern plain and the mosses. The open grassland east of Dùn ìseal, where the herders of the Ancient Age drove their cattle to the warm springs (7 an Lùnastal, VE 9,094), is thin pasture and bees. The wet mosses of the west coast and the western plain give peat, reeds and wildfowl, and at Baile ghorm the salt-pans the Stone Kings fought over (12 an Gearran, VE 6,006).

Some goods grow in only one or two places. Flax grows only in the lake-shore fields of Seann Warr, and its seed is pressed there for linseed oil, in which the road-houses were frying their oatcakes as early as LE 304. Tobacco grows only on the old concession farms behind Ceann mhòr, where the humans first planted it (31 an Dàmhair, AE 52). Gold is washed only from the streams below Baile dhìreach and Cnoc dhìreach, and the pearl-mussels lie only in the shallows of the south-eastern coast off Cnoc bhàn and Caol ruadh.

Rodos grows no spices, tea, sugar, silk or dates, and has no camels or elephants. Before the Severance the ships of an Tìr Thall brought small amounts of spice, tea and sugar to the Company's stores. No ship has come from the west since the last one sailed from Ros bheag (1 an t-Samhain, AE 150), and those goods are not sold on the island now.

The vein itself no longer appears in the roll. Ore-fuel from the Sloc Mòr was sold at the fair by the cartload until 22 am Faoilleach, DE 3, and the western coal seams sold their coal to the north until the Board closed them. The western seams were flooded and capped in DE 23, the upper galleries of the Sloc Mòr were closed in DE 26, and the few baskets of altar-ore cut each year under the Rite's custody are not sold in any market. Dubhan, the fuel that took the ore's place (19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1), is a wrought good, and the only one the roll counts among the raw goods. It is made from the spoil of the old workings (1 an t-Iuchar, SE 61) at the works of Seann Skell on the southern coast and in the east and north (27 an t-Ògmhios, DE 27). The works sell it by the barrel into the markets for the forges, kilns and glass-houses, which burned charcoal from the hill woods before it, as the charcoal-burners of the eastern woods had burned it since the Age of Sundering (17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,469). Lamps, engines and lorries buy it at the works' own depots and pumps and at the inns that keep a pump (4 am Màrt, DE 10), and the wartime tithe on it is taken at the pump by a clerk of the Treasury (29 an Giblean, DE 21).

Dubhan is also the one good of Rodos sold off the island. In the present year Dubhan, who made the first working fuel, won from the council the right to export it (7 an t-Sultain, DE 27), the first leave for any good to go beyond the kingdom's waters since the Severance. The export is held to a measure the Treasury sets each year and is loaded only at the quay of Ros dhomhain, where a clerk of the Treasury takes the tithe on every barrel and the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde seal every hold, so that nothing of the vein goes with it. The kingdom's own depots and the Moot's are served first. In this year dubhan goes abroad under that charter and under no other.

II. The Wrought Goods

The greater part of the worth that passes through the markets lies in goods made in the towns. In the order of their worth in the last roll they are these.

Salted and smoked food. Salt fish, salt meat and smoked meat are made in almost every town and are the largest trade on the island by value. Salting is as old as the fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn (17 an Giblean, VE 1,408) and the salt road of the Ancient Age (5 an Dàmhair, VE 7,791); the mining shires have eaten salt fish in the lean season since LE 394. The biggest salting towns are Cathair mhòr, Dùn ìseal, Seann Dunn and the harbours of the gulf.

Arms and field-guns. The forges of the old vein country, of Àth naomh in the west and of Caol ìseal on the north coast smelt bog-iron and bronze into arms, and a few of them cast field-guns. Every market in the kingdom sells arms back to its towns, where the regiments and fleets raised in An Cogadh Fada are stationed. The trade is young. It grew from the Crown's contracts for the regiments (20 an t-Ògmhios, DE 24), and arms are now the dearest common goods in every market. The forge-town of Muileann dhearg, where Uilleam Gobha made the rebels' grenades (17 an Lùnastal, AE 149), stands in the same hills.

Books, paper and ink. Rodos is a country of copyists. Paper has been made from rags and hemp at Muileann chaol since LE 1,674 and at Tobar dhìreach since SE 18, and books are bound and sold in more than eighty towns. The largest trade in books is at Dùn ìseal, Cathair dhomhain, Baile Mòr ruadh, Inis àrsaidh and Dùn chrom.

Soap and candles. Soap is boiled from tallow and seal-oil, and candles are dipped from beeswax and tallow, in most towns of the north and the gulf. The wax lights of the ancestor shrines were the first of this trade (26 an Dàmhair, LE 644).

Ships, sails and rope. Seagoing ships are built at nine yards: the two Seann Dunns on the east coast, Inis thais, Seann Skell of the Hawk bay, Ros fhionn, Inis ìseal, Ceann leathan, the royal quays of Cathair dhearg and Inis mhòr. Their sails are cut from hemp cloth in the same towns, and their rope comes from the rope-walks of Baile ghlas and Seann Tarr. The first deep keels since the Sundering were measured from the humans' hulls at Inis mhòr (14 an t-Samhain, AE 4).

Glass and pottery. Glass is blown from the white sand of Cuan ruadh, Ceann mhòr and the southern Seann Skell in some seventy towns, most of all at Cathair mhòr on the north road, Baile Mòr dhìreach and Seann Vell. The first glass-house on Rodos was built at Baile Mòr dhìreach in AE 66. Pottery is older. The red ware of the western road was fired at Baile ghorm and Cnoc àrsaidh in the Holy Age (8 an t-Samhain, FE 2,918, 19 an Giblean, FE 2,920). Today the largest potteries are at Dùn fhiadhaich, Ros dhìreach and Àth bheag, and Cathair fhada sells their ware to the north.

Cloth, garments and leather. Wool is spun and woven in every sheep country. The chartered weavers are those of Baile chiar (6 am Faoilleach, SE 15) and the mills of Doire ghlas (27 an Giblean, SE 59). Hides are tanned at Baile ghorm (13 an t-Iuchar, SE 62) and Muileann dhomhain (9 an Giblean, SE 53), and boots and harness are made in most of the market towns.

Scent. Scent waters are distilled from bog-myrtle, meadowsweet and heather honey and sold in small glass flasks. This trade belongs to the capital shore and the western plain: Seann Vell, Caol fhiadhaich, Cnoc àrsaidh, Baile ghlas and Doire shean. It began at Seann Vell in the first years of the restored kingdom (15 an Gearran, SE 27).

Drink and cheese. Barley spirit, the fire-water of the northern road (15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,672), is distilled in some forty towns. Ale is brewed for sale only at Ceann chaol, Muileann fhada and Seann Bhral in the south-east. Cheese is made in the cattle towns, most of all at Ceann leathan and Cathair fhada.

Coin. The realm-coin is struck only at the mint at Cathair dhearg (9 an Dàmhair, SE 5). The blanks it is struck from are refined in the villages of the eastern hills from the silver of Muileann chiar and the gold of Baile dhìreach (19 an t-Sultain, SE 37), and the Treasury counts those blanks among the goods of the Dùn ìseal market.

III. The Sixteen Market Towns

Every town on Rodos belongs to one of sixteen markets. A town sells its surplus into its market and buys what it lacks there. The market town holds the market-court, weighs goods on the Crown's weights and keeps the clerk of the market-due. Each of the sixteen has a market square, and so do some hundred and seventy lesser towns that hold a weekly market of their own. Only the market towns keep a tithe-clerk.
